##### Introduction

###### Welcome to _Protocols_ .

This book is a guide for improving your health and performance. If you’re struggling with one or more areas of your health, it can help you. If you’re generally feeling good and you want to level up one or more of those areas, it can also help you.

What is a protocol? A protocol is an established formula to help you overcome common obstacles, achieve a speci�c health or performance goal, or generally improve your day-to-day physical or mental state. Each is simple to implement. Each is designed to take the minimum amount of time to produce the greatest possible results. Each can work the �rst time, and every time.

As you learn these protocols, you’ll discover the science behind why they work and, in doing so, you’ll also discover a lot about how your brain and body work. Because each is based on known aspects of our physiology. They work because they are based in how we work. The science is important for at least two reasons that go beyond just substantiation. First, by understanding how a given protocol can, say, improve your sleep or your ability to focus and learn new things, you place yourself in the position to customize it to suit your needs, while still allowing it to produce the e�ect you want. Second, you’ll start to see similar biological themes turning up in what otherwise would seem like disparate systems. Our brains and bodies repurpose a lot of the same mechanisms to allow these systems to work in concert. Knowing some of the science behind each protocol a�ords you insights not just into how that protocol works, but how di�erent protocols synergize. Practically speaking, that gives you a level of control over your health that simply learning “do protocol A to get e�ect B” just can’t provide. You can determine what works for your needs and your goals in the context of your life, without having to make the pursuit of health a singular focus.

Because let’s face it: The real reason to do any of these protocols is to feel and perform better, mentally and physically, and to have more energy so you can go about the rest of your life.

I should say, too, what this book is not. This book is not about “optimization,” at least not in the typical sense. That word calls to mind the idea of spending a lot of time perfecting your daily routine. True optimization is about rescuing time—not just by increasing the number of years of your life, but by increasing the number of e�ective hours of your days (and the number of hours of great sleep at night). Many protocols in this book take only a few minutes to do and can be done whenever you’d like. Others take a bit more time or need to be done within a certain time frame each day or week.

You’ll also notice from just these few short paragraphs that I eschew the whole notion of “biohacking.” A hack is a shortcut that involves leveraging something toward a typically unrelated goal, like jury-rigging a paperclip and tape to �x broken eyeglasses. Hacks are never long-term solutions. The protocols in this book are the opposite of hacks. They are science-supported tools, grounded in robust physiological mechanisms—neural circuits, hormones, and neurotransmitters that have been hardwired into your brain and body starting from even before you were born. You just need to learn how to access them.

You’ll notice that I mostly emphasize the behaviors that can make the greatest di�erence in your immediate and long-term health. However, because I often get asked which prescription drugs, supplements, and devices are useful to help achieve a given health or performance goal, I discuss those tools too.

Indeed, “What should I take?” is one of the most common questions I get from both men and women. Many people have a perception that the secret to health and performance resides in exogenous molecules—meaning something that comes from outside our body. Make no mistake: Certain pills, powders, or injectables can make a positive di�erence in health and performance. But because certain behaviors can so potently activate multiple physiological mechanisms, including the release of endogenous molecules—meaning, you guessed it, something that comes from inside our bodies—there is simply no replacement for them. That is why no pill can (or ever will) replace exercise, or sleep, or proper stress control. Even drugs that allow for neuroplasticity, or your

brain’s capacity to rewire and learn, won’t produce learning on their own. Plasticity must be directed toward a particular endpoint. That requires certain behaviors. We must do the right things in the right sequence. Or, as a colleague of mine aptly put it, “better living through chemistry still requires better living.”

Which means you don’t have to buy anything to achieve your health or performance goals. Some people have disposable income to devote to tools for health and performance. Others do not. I wrote this book for everyone and can assure you that it is (and I believe always will be) a core fact that behavioral tools really move the needle in the right direction. And the right ones can work for everyone. Whether you are young or old, currently �t or out of shape, the protocols in this book can make you feel, look, and think far better, and thereby show up better at work or school or on the �eld or in the gym, and in your relationships… even in your relationship to yourself. I know that statement to be true because literally millions of people have implemented these protocols to great success and continue to do so every day. I also know because I personally use them.

In fact, I discovered many of the protocols in this book because I needed them, in some cases urgently. I, like so many others, have struggled with sleep and stress, �nding the “right” diet, knowing the best way to exercise to meet speci�c goals, and on and on.

But if I have one innate quality, it’s curiosity. I love to learn. I also love to share what I learn with others. And what drives my curiosity—at least in the realm of health and performance—is the same thing that likely brought you to this book: I wanted to know the best solutions to those challenges.

There are no tools included in this book that I have not personally tried. Some I have used for brief periods because they are for overcoming a sticking point, and then best set aside. Others are mainstays in my daily life and will remain so until I die because they are so central to my physical and mental health, and my ability to focus and learn e�ectively as they continue to help me reach my performance goals. I stand by every tool and every concept.

These protocols cover what I know works. Whereas on the _Huberman Lab_ , my podcast, I explore and share both topics of which I am certain as well as topics that I’m still exploring—such as peptides or psychedelics—this book

focuses mostly on the former. Its chapters on sleep; exercise; stress control; nutrition; light; focus, motivation, and learning; and personal growth are the result of years of research, both in the lab and in life, from experts in every topic, and from my own work. Some protocols are basic; others are more advanced. You’ll be able to decide which are best for your needs and goals.

For those of you who are new to my work, I’ll share a bit about my background for context and how we—yes, me and you—got here. If you’re going to read this book and use these tools, my hope is that you’ll come to see that we are collaborators on this journey. Again, I discovered many of the protocols in this book because I need them. If you do too, know that you are not alone.

As of writing this introduction, I’m �fty years old. Sleep is the subject of the �rst chapter of this book because sleep profoundly impacts every aspect of our physiology and psychology. Put simply, sleep is the foundation of our mental health, our physical health, and our performance.1 We win by sleeping.

I came to that realization pretty early but only because I struggled with sleep. As a kid I slept like a log—always a solid eight to nine hours, rarely waking up in the middle of the night even once. As a teen I would stay out late and sleep in on the weekends, as most of us did. I never thought about my sleep.

When I reached my junior year in high school, however, everything changed. I would lie down, fall asleep right away, but then wake up three to four hours later, wide awake. Then I would toss and turn. Eventually I would fall back asleep but then needed to sleep really late into the morning to feel rested. School started at 8:00 a.m., so that wasn’t an option most days. That had me falling asleep in class, feeling wide awake in the evening, and then the whole cycle would repeat.

Toward the end of high school when I started getting into �tness, I learned that we recover from exercise during sleep. That was the early 1990s and the public was not yet aware of the importance of sleep. There was some science on it—in fact some of the best work on the role of sleep for health and cognition was coming from the Stanford Sleep Lab just a few miles up the road from where I lived. But it was from a prominent trainer in the world of �tness that I �rst learned to take sleep seriously. He gave me one mostly good suggestion for sleep, and one terrible one. The mostly good suggestion was to read the work of Allan Hobson—a sleep researcher from Harvard—and I eventually did, although I discovered Allan’s focus was mainly on the importance of dreams, which felt like a bit of a tease for someone with sleep issues. The terrible advice he gave me? He told me if I woke up in the middle of the night and couldn’t fall back asleep that I should drink a half mug of white wine. I was seventeen! I tried it anyway, and it didn’t work for me. Thankfully. We now know alcohol greatly

reduces the quality and restorative properties of sleep, even if it does help some people fall asleep.

Eventually I �gured out how to master the art of getting a great night’s sleep, but it took time. Years, in fact. The science progressed too, of course, and we now know a lot about both the importance of sleep and ways to remedy pretty much any sleep issue. I wish I had the information you are about to read back in high school, and college, and graduate school, and my postdoc. The reality is, the busier we are, the more important sleep is to our health and performance. But no matter how busy or calm our life is, a great night’s sleep is crucial to our mind and body.

If you are like the majority of people, and you struggle to get a great night’s sleep, you want to remedy that as soon as possible ~~.~~ 2 But even if you are one of those rare individuals who sleeps deeply every night and wakes up feeling fully refreshed every day, there are still ways to improve your sleep and thus, your quality of life. Regardless of which category you fall into, this chapter will help.

I’d like to mention here that this chapter is a long one. We go deep into the science of sleep, but I promise you it’s all made accessible. I know that understanding this science will help you get a great night’s sleep. I wrote this chapter so you can browse by topic or tool. Start with the parts that interest you most, or the protocols that you think will help you right now.

I prefer to focus on the bene�ts of doing things correctly, but when it comes to sleep, it’s worth thinking a bit about the downsides of getting things wrong too, and learning to avoid those. Sleep deprivation—a term that means getting too little sleep or waking up too many times during the night—has been linked to signi�cantly elevated risk of heart disease, stroke, and numerous hormonal imbalances involving—just to name a handful: cortisol, estrogen, testosterone, and insulin, the latter of which can cause type 2 diabetes.3 Obesity, mental health issues, physical injuries, cancer, car accidents, depression, hypertension, and age-related dementia have all also been linked to poor sleep.4 Sleep deprivation doesn’t necessarily _directly_ create these problems; rather it impairs cellular mechanisms that cascade to produce multiple issues within and between di�erent organs and systems.

To be clear, everyone has a bad night’s sleep now and again. But here’s a good goal for you: Aim to sleep well 90 to 95 percent of the nights of your life, and allow the remaining 5 to 10 percent of those nights to be bad due to uncontrollable negative circumstances, like a work con�ict, or joyful experiences, like a great party. Do your best to make sleep a top priority so that the rest of your life can be that much better.

Compulsive overuse of phones and other screen-based technologies at night is a major factor for the poor sleep of adolescents and teens, but also for the poor sleep habits of adults.12 A central feature of life in the twenty-�rst century is to always be connected online and by text. ###### **SLEEP PROTOCOL**

1

### View Sunlight as Soon as Possible After Waking

###### WHAT TO DO:

- Get morning sunlight in your eyes as soon as possible after waking. Go outside and look in the direction of the sun for at least �ve to ten minutes each morning. Your goal should be to get sunlight in your eyes within the �rst thirty to sixty minutes of waking up.

- A few things to keep in mind. If you wake up before the sun rises, you’ll obviously have to wait. If you can view the sun as it comes up across the horizon, great, but that’s not vital for this protocol to work.

Morning sunlight, as we will review, di�ers in quality from sunlight at other times of the day. It is best viewed by facing the sun without any physical barriers, like awnings or buildings, obscuring your view. Don’t wear a brimmed hat, as it blocks some of the light that would otherwise reach your eyes from overhead. Wearing eyeglasses or contacts is �ne but, alas, this protocol won’t work nearly as well through a window or windshield, as that will �lter out many of the relevant wavelengths of light. Skip the sunglasses while doing this protocol. What about clouds? No matter how overcast, there is always some sunlight coming through once the sun is up. In fact, the more accurate way to state this protocol would be “get as-early-in-your-dayas-possible _daylight_ in your eyes,” but that is a mouthful. The point is that the sun provides daylight even on overcast days. Just compare how bright it is

at 8:00 a.m. on an overcast day to midnight the night before. So forget the “there is no sun out in winter where I live” argument. There is daylight, and you want to view it. Indeed, this protocol is especially important on cloudy days.

Caution: Do not stare at the sun. Never force your eyes to stay open. Allow your natural squint and blink re�exes to protect your eyes. If the sun still feels too bright, look a few degrees to the side of the sun.

###### HOW IT WORKS:

The power of this protocol arises from its impact on three synergistic elements: your circadian clock, your eyes (or more speci�cally, the nerve cells in your eyes that detect sunlight and communicate its presence to your circadian clock), and speci�c qualities of light that come from the sun, especially when it is low, relative to the horizon. Together, these three elements make up a robust network that drives many of the biological processes in your brain and body.

###### Your Circadian Clock

Located a few centimeters above the roof of your mouth is a small cluster of neurons called the _suprachiasmatic nucleus_ , or SCN ~~.~~ 17 The SCN is your master circadian clock. Its job is to coordinate the activities of all the cells and organs in your body into a coherent twenty-four-hour rhythm so that certain cells and organs in your body are more active, and other cells and organs are less active, depending on the phase of that twenty-four-hour rhythm. The SCN keeps your body and brain on schedule.

The �rst documented discovery of a circadian clock came not from studies of humans or even of rodents, but of plants. In 1729, a French astronomer named Jean-Jacques d’Ortous de Mairan noticed that a mimosa plant kept in a totally dark room continued to rhythmically fold and unfold its leaves every twentyfour hours, just as if the sun was shining through the window.18 It was a mystery: If the plant was not unfurling to absorb sun or other light, then what was guiding its movements? About two hundred years later, German biologist Erwin Bünning tracked the movements of bean plant leaves and reported that they followed a cycle lasting 24.4 hours. Observations such as these con�rmed that plants had internal, or what scientists call “endogenous,” clocks that followed what later became known as… a circadian rhythm, named for the Latin _circa diem_ , or “around a day.” And as decades of research would eventually con�rm, the vast majority of organisms on Earth—not just plants but also

insects, rodents, reptiles, and all mammals, including humans—have an endogenous timekeeper that keeps a twenty-four-hour circadian rhythm, even in the absence of any external cues about the status of the outside world.19

Our core body temperature, the release of certain hormones, and most notably our sleep-wake cycle, all follow a twenty-four-hour circadian rhythm.20 Even when scientists extracted individual cells from the body, the cells continued to follow this rhythm.21 And which genes they expressed and when, the proteins downstream of those genes, the cells’ enzymatic activities—indeed not just _some_ things but nearly everything about cellular function—appeared to vary, not randomly, but rather systematically every twenty-four hours. That was remarkable.

But what is equally remarkable is that all cells in our body can coordinate their individual rhythms in a manner that is timed perfectly with one another— like a well-practiced symphony, except this symphony involves not a few hundred or even a thousand participants, but trillions. And just like a symphony, it is not as if every cell simply needs to start and end its activity at the same time. Some cells need to be active at the same time, or _in-phase_ with one another; some need to be active at opposite times, or in _anti-phase_ , and still others repeat their cycles of activity faster, then slower, then faster, again with a unique signature and yet, still repeating once every twenty-four hours. And the start and end time of each cell’s twenty-four-hour rhythm must be tightly bound to all the other cells of the body, just like the start and end of a symphony. Without this coordination, you end up with noise rather than music, illness rather than wellness. The only di�erence is the symphony that is your physiology never ceases; it repeats every twenty-four hours, from the day you’re born until the day you die.

The basis of that persistent and extraordinarily precise biological coordination remained a mystery until somewhat recently. Clues came from multiple sources. First, studies in which people were placed into constant dark environments—such as caves or windowless bunkers—con�rmed the existence of a circadian rhythm in humans. Back in 1938, two physiologists spent a month in Mammoth Cave, Kentucky (perhaps �guring this experiment was best done on themselves before asking anyone else to try it).22 There, they con�rmed that

human body temperature has a circadian rhythm whereby it increases upon waking, decreases approximately ten to twelve hours later, drops to its nadir during sleep, then rises once again—all once every twenty-four hours, even though the subjects/researchers had no access to sunlight or other cues about time of day. And other studies con�rmed that, in the absence of an alternating pattern of ambient light and darkness, the human body still maintains a circadian rhythm for numerous aspects of our physiology.23

In 1966, a German physician named Jürgen Ascho� initiated what became known as the bunker experiment, in which subjects (not researchers this time!) spent several weeks in a sealed bunker, living life as usual but without any windows or other ways to determine the passage of time ~~.~~ 24 They found that subjects generally spent about one-third of each twenty-four-hour period sleeping and two-thirds of it awake, just as most humans living aboveground do. However, the wake-up and to-sleep times of the people in the bunker drifted— they woke up slightly later and went to sleep slightly later each day. Thus, the bunker experiment con�rmed the existence of a circadian rhythm, but one that requires some external cue to anchor it. What remained mysterious was the biological basis of the circadian clock—was it a bloodborne factor? In the liver? In the brain? In the pineal gland? Theories abounded but none of them held up to experimentation. And another major question remained: In the environment outside the bunker, which external cues were responsible for setting that clock to a speci�c start and �nish time each day?

Subsequent discoveries, �rst in rodents and later in humans, revealed the existence of a small cluster—or what is called a “nucleus”—of neurons located a few centimeters above our mouths that had a key part to play. It was later named the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) for “above the chiasm”—the chiasm being the location at the base of the brain where the nerve �bers from both eyes partially cross. As I mentioned earlier, the SCN is the master circadian clock: the structure that coordinates the activities of all our cells and organs. In other words, the SCN is the orchestra conductor that makes sure each cell’s twentyfour-hour rhythm starts on time ~~.~~ 25 In 1972, Irving Zucker’s lab at UC Berkeley and Robert Moore’s lab at the University of Chicago independently discovered

that lesions to the SCN render organisms’ circadian pattern arrhythmic and disorganized.26 Naturally occurring SCN lesions caused by tumors eventually showed the SCN is necessary for sleep-wake, hunger, and other bodily rhythms to obey circadian cycles in humans as well ~~.~~ 27 Moreover, animal studies showed that transplanting even just a small number of healthy SCN neurons into an arrhythmic brain restored a coherent twenty-four-hour rhythm, proving the SCN is both necessary and su�cient for endogenous circadian rhythms ~~.~~ 28

If ever there was a brain structure whose function is beautifully organized to help ensure our survival as a species, it is the SCN. Even the SCN’s seeming imperfection turns out to be perfect after all.

Stay with me here. For example, the SCN generates a period—meaning a cycle length—that is close to but not quite twenty-four hours. The SCN’s period tends to be a bit longer than that, up to 24.5 hours.29 By virtue of this, it can shift the start of the circadian rhythm forward or backward according to seasonal changes in day length or other survival-based needs, without making a mess and setting our cells on di�erent schedules.30 In other words, allowing a little room in its period duration a�ords us more �exibility and overall precision, not less, which is great because as we all know life is rarely the same from one day to the next. What’s more, it is also what allows for _phase shifting_ ~~,~~ 31 or the ability to change the start time of the daily cycle. If you’re wondering why this doesn’t have us waking up later and going to sleep later each day, it’s because viewing morning light and evening light nudges your clock back and forth perfectly, to keep it regular. Later I’ll explain how you can leverage that to overcome jet lag or any new schedule fast, but for now, all you need to know is that the not-exactlytwenty-four-hour rhythm is a feature, not a �aw.

As you probably already realize from the call to action that is Sleep Protocol 1, our SCN cares about whether it is light or dark out. And of course light-dark cycles are set by the spin of the earth. But how is it that our SCN—a tiny cluster of neurons embedded deep in the darkness of our brains—“knows” about the spin of the earth? Let’s consider how to answer that question with insights from planetary science and cosmology.

We’re all on this big sphere in space, spinning around at about one thousand miles per hour, causing us to face the sun, then away from the sun, then back toward the sun every twenty-four hours. Because the earth is round, the exact duration of sunlight we can experience each day depends, of course, on where we happen to be on earth. The variability is large, ranging from rather equal light-dark splits at the equator to nearly full days and/or nights of darkness or sunlight exposure at the poles. But no matter where we are on earth, inside each of our brains, our SCN steadily churns out that slightly longer than twentyfour-hour rhythm of coordinated cellular activity across our whole body.

Ultimately it is our SCN that tells us when to sleep and when to wake. We are a diurnal, not a nocturnal, species. We can stay up late and sleep all day if we choose, but even for night owls, all our bodily systems of hormones and neurotransmitters, our immune system, our levels of focus and quality of that focus, all of it, function much better when we live diurnally and wake just before or during the early daylight hours and go to sleep some hours after sundown.32 (Yes, night owls would be wise to do this too—that is, if mental and physical health are your priority.)

Keep in mind these are independent phenomena; the earth’s spin and travel around the sun is not what causes our SCN to have a twenty-four-hour rhythm, nor does it tell us when to sleep and when to wake, but they do need to be linked. So how do we link—or what is called _entrain_ —our SCN’s rhythm with the light-dark cycle generated by the earth’s spin and travel around the sun? Remember, our SCN resides deep in our brain. It lives in the darkness of our skulls. To synchronize our circadian clock with the day-night cycle cast on us by our location on earth, we need a way for the presence or absence of sunlight to be conveyed to the SCN. And the best way to do that is to call upon the one part of our brain that has direct access to sunlight: our eyes.

###### Your Eyes

Wait, did I say that your eyes are part of your brain? Yes, that is correct. Lining the inside-back part of each of your eyeballs is a thin sheet of brain tissue called the neural retina. Your neural retinas were squeezed out and away from the rest of your brain during the �rst trimester of your life, while you were still in your

mother’s womb, and then grew wirelike extensions into the brain proper, forming two optic nerves. Your optic nerves convey electrical signals about the presence or absence of sunlight, objects, faces, moving vehicles, and on and on to di�erent brain areas, including—you guessed it—the SCN.33

The connections between your eyes and your brain are truly a spectacular product of biological engineering. First, they solve the problem of how to inform image-forming regions of your brain about “what is out there” in the world, so you can see faces, moving objects, and colors. They also solve the problem of letting your SCN know “ _when_ it is out there” in the world, by the presence of sunlight. The neurons that convey the presence of sunlight to the SCN are not of the image-forming kind; they don’t respond to the shape of the sun, but instead to its brightness and to the speci�c wavelengths of sunlight that reach your eyes when the sun is low in the sky. We refer to these speci�c wavelengths as low solar angle sunlight.34

Have you ever noticed that low solar angle sunlight appears more yellow than midday sun? Or even orange? Check out a sunrise or sunset and compare the color of sunlight to the color of sunlight at noon. Of course, sunlight doesn’t change according to where it is in the sky, but what portions of sunlight are visible to us does.

Sunlight is always full spectrum: It contains all wavelengths of light, redorange-yellow-green-blue-indigo-violet, or ROYGBIV, just as they taught us in elementary school. The R(ed), O(range), and Y(ellow) are longer wavelengths of light, the G(reen) is medium wavelength, and the B(lue), I(ndigo), and V(iolet) are shorter wavelengths. And of course, the sun emits UV and far-red, or infrared wavelengths, too, but we can’t see those (although many other animals and insects can). When the sun is high in the sky, it appears white, because all the wavelengths of light arrive at our eyes at roughly the same intensities. When the sun is low in the sky, we see the sun as more yellow, orange, or red, because molecules in the atmosphere preferentially redirect the shorter blue, indigo, and violet wavelengths of light—a process called Rayleigh scattering. (We’ll discuss the properties of light in depth in chapter 5.)

All mammals, us humans included, have evolved a special system of light detection that responds speci�cally to the presence and contrast of short and

long wavelengths of bright light, which is exactly what reaches your eyes if you view sunlight early or late in the day, while the sun is fairly low in the sky. In other words, we all have a sunrise and sunset detecting system in our eyes that communicates the time of day to our SCN.35

As I mentioned earlier, this timekeeping eye-to-brain circuit is also a fairly recent discovery. And by recent, I mean _recent_ : In the late 1990s, there still wasn’t general agreement among circadian biologists whether light—and not some other cue like social interactions—was the dominant force entraining our SCN. Then, in 1998, neuroscientist Ignacio “Iggy” Provencio made a key discovery. Iggy found a molecule in the skin of an African frog species that caused its skin to darken when exposed to sunlight was also present in the eyes of mice ~~.~~ 36 The molecule was an opsin, which is a kind of protein that absorbs light, and when it does, it changes its conformation to set o� a signaling cascade.37 Since the same opsin was known to cause darkening of dermal melanophores in frog skin, Provencio called the mouse retinal opsin _melanopsin_ . Other labs con�rmed melanopsin-containing cells are abundant in the human retina, too, mostly in the lower portion that views the upper visual �eld, which, you might have guessed, corresponds to the sky.38

So we have a frog-skin-like set of cells in our eyes? Not quite. To explain what makes melanopsin-containing retinal cells so special, �rst a bit about photoreceptors. Photoreceptors are neurons that convert light into electrical signals the rest of the retina and brain can interpret. But the retinal cells that contain melanopsin are not like other photoreceptors. The melanopsincontaining retinal neurons Iggy discovered turned out to be both photoreceptive and retinal ganglion cells—the neurons that connect the eyes to the brain and the very cells whose wirelike extensions, or axons, make up the optic nerves. Soon after, a group of neuroscientists, David Berson and Felice Dunn at Brown University and Samer Hattar and King Wai-Yau at Johns Hopkins University, along with several of their students and postdocs, con�rmed that melanopsin RGCs send their axons to the SCN _and_ that they �re electric signals, thereby releasing neurotransmitters, when light is shone on them.39 Remarkably, they did this when they were isolated from all other retinal cells. As long as the light

shone was very bright and long lasting, they �red electrical signals. These cells were therefore named intrinsically photosensitive RGCs (ipRGCs) to di�erentiate them from the other 99 percent of RGCs that can’t respond directly to light on their own. Some years later, work from the Neitz Color Vision Lab at the University of Washington in Seattle and by others showed that the optimal stimulus for ipRGCs isn’t just bright light.40 They discovered that the best way to activate the ipRGCs that connect to the SCN is with sustained very bright light, similar to what we see as blue or green light, contrasted with medium wavelengths of light, or what we typically see as yellow or orange—in other words, features prominent in low solar angle sunlight. The color contrasts in sunrises and sunsets tell your brain about what time it is in the twenty-fourhour cycle. That collection of work, from the discovery of melanopsin to ipRGCs, and how they work, was revelatory. It meant that there was a speci�c neural circuit extending from the eye to the brain dedicated to entraining the SCN and our circadian rhythms. That circuit is tuned to—neuroscience lingo for “responds to”—the presence of low solar angle sunlight. The SCN then handles the job of body- and brain-wide synchronization of circadian rhythmicity. This sunlight-driven circadian entrainment circuit requires no learning or practice to activate. It is present from birth and functions the �rst time and every time to control, among other things, your sleep-wake cycle.

###### The Sun

Which brings us to the �nal piece of the puzzle—the part that is not hard-wired but that you control with your behavior—and that is the call to action of this protocol: exposing your eyes to morning sunlight (or in its absence, to the next best alternative, which I describe below). Doing so activates the ipRGC-to-SCN circadian entrainment circuit and initiates dozens of bene�cial processes that get and keep your brain and body going throughout the day. And toward the evening, it puts you in the best possible position to get a great night’s sleep.

In fact, we have copious evidence that this is foundational to both our daytime well-being and nighttime sleep. As one small example, a group of architects and neurologists came together in 2014 to investigate how windowless o�ces a�ected the people who worked in them.41 They asked twenty-seven

o�ce workers who had either no windows, or work areas situated far from windows, and twenty-two people working in o�ces with windows, about their well-being and sleep quality. The questionnaire scores were decidedly poorer among the windowless workers. They reported more sleep disturbances and an overall unsatisfactory quality of sleep.

In the early 2000s, a group of chronobiologists (scientists who study biological timing) at the Institute for Medical Psychology, in Munich, Germany, surveyed �ve hundred people about their sleep times, light exposure, and chronotype—as in, morning person, night owl, et cetera (you’ll �nd out how to determine yours in Sleep Protocol 4) ~~.~~ 42 They found that the amount of light exposure during the day correlated with what time people went to bed: More exposure during the day meant earlier bedtimes. This link can be partly explained by external factors, like employment: People whose livelihoods depend on being outdoors are more likely to be early-to-bed types, especially if their work requires them to rise early or is physically demanding. But that doesn’t explain the connection entirely. It turns out that it’s also due, in part, to the fact that exposure to daylight has a regulating e�ect on our physiology—causing elevated levels of alertness by a host of di�erent pathways, including hormonal and neural pathways. As one review put it, “In sum, research seems to agree that daylight (at high intensities) is bene�cial for sleep.”43

There are also numerous studies showing that bright-light exposure early in the day—at the intensities that one would get from being outdoors in the morning—is bene�cial for everything from mood to hormone health, daytime energy levels, and on and on ~~.~~ 44 But before you say, “Okay, got it!,” there’s just a bit more to understand about the underlying mechanisms in this protocol, and that’s the relationship between sleep and wakefulness. And it will help you get the most out of this protocol, regardless of where you live and the time of year.

Our daytime levels of alertness re�ect the quality and duration of our nighttime sleep. That’s a giant “duh.” We all know that if we sleep poorly, we drag both mentally and physically the next day. We also all know that if we sleep great, we’re focused and motivated to do all kinds of things that require energy… and that we have the energy to do them.

But what most people do not know is that the relationship between sleep and wakefulness works in the other direction too. When we are alert during the morning and daytime, we are more likely to expend mental and physical energy that in turn helps us sleep at night. Even those of us who sleep well typically �nd that increasing our daytime physical activity—especially in the hours between sunrise and 2:00 p.m.—leads to signi�cantly better sleep,45 which in turn leads to more energy the next day, which improves sleep, and so on. Again, you’re probably thinking, “This is common knowledge. Do we really need science to explain this?”

Here is the lesser-known fact: Morning sunlight viewing is the best way to increase our morning and daytime energy levels ~~.~~ 46 Not food (although �ne to eat early in the day), not ca�eine (also �ne). It’s morning sunlight.

Morning sunlight increases your energy levels through at least three di�erent mechanisms. First, it suppresses any residual melatonin you may have circulating in your brain (Sleep Protocol 3 includes an extensive look at melatonin, a hormone that helps promote sleepiness) ~~.~~ 47 As discussed above, when the ipRGCs are activated by sunlight viewing, they send electrical signals to the SCN. The SCN, in turn, stimulates a collection of neurons in the nearby paraventricular nucleus, or PVN. The PVN then sets o� a cascade of signals that go through the spinal cord and back up to the pineal gland in the brain, shutting o� melatonin production ~~.~~ 48 Voila! You’ve suppressed the primary hormone that promotes sleepiness by viewing morning sunlight.

Second, bright light reaching your eyes helps suppress the action of adenosine, a chemical that also leads to feelings of sleepiness ~~.~~ 49 Sunlight does this indirectly via its e�ects on other systems in the brain and body, but nonetheless, it has a potent adenosine-reducing e�ect. (We’ll take a deep dive into adenosine in Sleep Protocol 7). After a full night’s sleep, adenosine levels tend to be low, but if you happen to not get enough sleep (as so many of us do), morning light helps reduce any residual adenosine. That both increases your alertness and prevents the residual adenosine from delaying your circadian clock, which would otherwise bias you toward waking up later the next day, then going to sleep later, then waking up even later the following day, and so on (what

chronobiologists call a _phase delay_ ).50 Such circadian “drift” brought on by mild sleep deprivation is very common. It is best remedied by viewing morning sunlight to reset your circadian rhythm.51

Third, we need to talk about cortisol. Because it’s often discussed in the context of chronic stress, which is bad, most people think cortisol is “bad” too. But it’s not bad. Cortisol is essential to health and your levels of energy—you just don’t want your cortisol levels to be elevated at the wrong times.52

Your SCN is located in your hypothalamus (H), which is part of a biological circuit that also includes your pituitary gland (P), a small, stalk-like protrusion at the base of your brain that releases hormones into your bloodstream. The circuit also includes your adrenal glands (A), which reside atop your kidneys. This circuit is known as the HPA axis ~~.~~ 53 The HPA axis is one of the main systems that responds to stress (which is why you’ll hear more about it in chapter 3). Here’s how it works: It starts with signals from the hypothalamus, which then stimulate the release of speci�c hormones from the pituitary, which in turn stimulate adrenaline and cortisol release from your adrenals.

The HPA axis is also involved in the sleep-wake cycle. When your ipRGCs are activated by low solar angle morning sunlight and your SCN receives the ensuing signal, it alerts your adrenal glands to release adrenaline and cortisol via the HPA axis.54 Cortisol and adrenaline dramatically increase levels of alertness, the latter likely by activating receptors on your vagus nerve,55 a large portion of which extends from the organs in your body up into your brain and stimulates areas there such as the locus coeruleus to make norepinephrine, which has the net e�ect of “waking” you up.56 Cortisol does a lot of things. It also decreases in�ammation and regulates our immune systems to protect against viral and bacterial infections.57 And it helps regulate our energy levels. Think about cortisol as a wakefulness-promoting hormone, not a stress hormone, if you want to understand what the cortisol in your body is doing most of the time. It’s also useful to consider how cortisol ebbs and �ows across time due to signals from your circadian clock. By measuring cortisol levels every twenty minutes in human subjects, researchers found cortisol reaches its apex at about sixty minutes or so after you wake up and that it is lowest about four to �ve hours

after you fall asleep.58 Then it begins to rise sharply across the �nal two to three hours of your sleep until—boom! You wake up due in large part to what is called the cortisol awakening response (CAR). Yes, reaching a threshold level of cortisol is a major factor in what ultimately rouses you from sleep. As mentioned above, your cortisol continues to rise and peaks about sixty minutes after waking, then slowly drops down as you head into the early and late afternoon. Cortisol levels generally stay low and continue to drop in the evening and at nighttime (assuming it doesn’t spike from stress or intense exercise—more on that below), and then it falls to its nadir in those �rst four to �ve hours of sleep before starting to rise again toward morning. We return to this _circadian cortisol curve_ in chapter 3, and the role it plays in promoting health in women and men of all ages. For now, the key thing to know is that for cortisol to support our health, it needs to peak in the �rst hour or so after waking; it then needs to drop precipitously in the evening and night and continue falling to reach its nadir in those initial four to �ve hours of sleep.59

Viewing morning sunlight doesn’t directly cause the morning peak in cortisol, but it can dramatically amplify its rise by as much as 50 percent ~~.~~ 60 This also helps ensure that this peak comes early in the day and isn’t shifted to the afternoon. Late-day elevations in cortisol have negative consequences over time such as sleeplessness, anxiety, and metabolic disease.61

A quick note: A morning workout, morning ca�eine, and breakfast (provided it isn’t a huge and/or carbohydrate-laden one) will all promote wakefulness, too, and thereby contribute to a well-aligned circadian rhythm. But morning sunlight is the most potent lever for increasing morning cortisol and thus energy during your day, and for improving your sleep at night. Don’t underestimate its power.

Keep your circadian rhythm attuned to the sun, and all of these mechanisms will work as they should.

###### COMMON QUESTIONS:

If you wake up before sunrise, and you want to start your day, I suggest turning on as many bright indoor lights in your home—or hotel room, or wherever you may be—as possible. Sunlight cannot be replaced by standard indoor lighting, but turning on indoor lighting �rst thing won’t hurt. Then get outside to view morning sunlight once the sun is up.

If you wake before sunrise every day, or if you live in a part of the world where it is very dark in winter, you may want to invest in a 10,000 lux light to help ensure you get enough light in the morning (lux is a measure of brightness). Most cost about $100, and some are portable for travel. I often wake up before sunrise, and because the ipRGCs can be activated by very bright arti�cial lights if those bright lights include su�cient short wavelengths, I keep a 10,000 lux lamp in my kitchen and bathroom ~~.~~ 62 It lacks long wavelength light, so I also have a red incandescent light next to it and I turn that on too. I use the red incandescent light from SaunaSpace (no a�liation). I turn them both on �rst thing in the morning and then I get outside to view morning sunlight once the sun is up. I am well aware these lights are not a replacement for sunlight, but they help bridge the gap until the sun is up. Once the sun is up, you can be sure I go outside to view it!

And I will sometimes keep the 10,000 lux lamp and a red incandescent light on and facing me for an hour or so once I’m back working at my desk or getting ready for the day. Chapter 5 further explains the logic and bene�ts of this extended morning light exposure. There I also mention options that can be of real help for sleep as well as other aspects of health too, such as metabolic health.

But remember, morning sunlight is the best stimulus for your ipRGCs, SCN, and circadian rhythm, and it costs nothing! Figure out how to view it each morning. Again, you don’t need to see it cross the horizon as it rises. If you do, great, but if you wake up after sunrise, that’s �ne. Do your best to view sunlight within the �rst thirty to sixty minutes after waking up. Bring your co�ee or tea outside with you. Bring your spouse or kids if they’re awake. Bring your dog if you have one. Remember, dogs, cats, cows, and other animals have ipRGCs and an SCN, too, and they bene�t from morning sunlight in many of the same ways and via the same mechanisms as we do ~~.~~ 63

To activate your ipRGCs fastest, go outside and face east toward the sun on a nice, clear morning with no clouds in the sky. Obviously, this isn’t possible for everyone every day.

Again, fortunately, sparse clouds do not interfere with the interaction between sunlight and our circadian clock. However, if the sky is densely overcast and gray, a 10,000 lux light can be a real help, but still aim for getting more sunlight in your eyes to compensate for the lower intensity of sunlight and reduced yellow-blue contrast exposure you’re likely to get on very overcast days. In fact, it’s _especially_ important that you get sunlight in your eyes on overcast days. This is for three reasons: (1) dense clouds reduce the number of photons reaching your eyes in a given amount of time; (2) they �lter out much of the longer (yellow, orange, and red) wavelengths of light, and (3) you are likely to be indoors more on cloudy days, which can cause the SCN to fall out of sync with the solar cycle, which leads to later nights, more arti�cial light exposure at night, more circadian disruption, and so on.

Aim to extend the sunny, clear day recommendation of a minimum of �ve to ten minutes, to at least �fteen minutes on cloudy days, and thirty minutes (minimum) on densely overcast days. That may seem like a long time, but remember, you don’t need to stand in one place gazing at the sky. Take a walk. Make a call. Listen to a book or podcast or talk to a friend, partner, or other family member. And even if you can’t be outside for the full time recommended above, some sunlight hitting your eyes in the morning is better than none. If you miss a day completely due to travel or sickness or other reasons, don’t despair— your energy levels that day may be lower because you didn’t get the cortisol spike bright morning light causes, but your circadian rhythm is the re�ection of your previous three to four days of sunlight viewing activity.

Excessive UV light exposure can cause cataracts and, as we have all heard, skin damage, accelerated skin aging, and some forms of skin cancer, topics I cover in more detail later in the book. But viewing morning sunlight is much safer than viewing overhead midday sunlight—because that Rayleigh scattering of short

wavelength light when the sun is low in the sky includes UV and thus reduces your UV exposure signi�cantly. It is when the sun is overhead that the UV index is high. UV light isn’t bad, per se, but you don’t want too much of it reaching your eyes or skin. Chapter 5 goes into the bene�ts and drawbacks of UV.

NEVER, EVER force yourself to stare at the sun—or any light source for that matter, at any time of day. Your natural blink and “look away” re�ex is a built-in circuit (yes, there is a dedicated circuit for this) to protect your eyes. People with macular degeneration or other eye conditions ought to be especially careful about viewing midday sunlight, and if very sensitive to sunlight, they may want to consult with their ophthalmologist before doing any deliberate sunlight viewing.

Eyeglasses and contact lenses are both perfectly �ne to wear while viewing morning sunlight. Neither one blocks light from reaching your eyes, even if your eyeglasses or contacts have UV �lters.

Sunglasses and transition lenses, however, should be avoided while viewing morning sunlight because they block out a lot of the relevant wavelengths that trigger the valuable mechanisms covered in this protocol. Moreover, they reduce the number of photons reaching your eyes. Of course it’s �ne to wear sunglasses as needed for comfort and safety at other times of day.

People relentlessly ask me this and my response is equally persistent: No, it’s not the same. It’s far less e�ective, though better than nothing. But if there is any way to get outside, do. Windows and windshields, especially nowadays, �lter the intensities and wavelengths you want for this protocol to work. “How come viewing morning sunlight through eyeglasses or contacts is �ne but not windows or windshields?” you may wonder. Because windows do something called spectral �ltering: They reduce the amount of light—especially short wavelength light—that would otherwise reach your eyes. Corrective lenses don’t; they let far more light through. That’s their job. Well, that and to correct any optical errors in the structure of your eyeballs so you can see things clearly. Windows and windshields do neither.

### View Sunlight in the Late Afternoon

###### WHAT TO DO:

- Get sunlight in your eyes in the late afternoon or early evening. Ideally, go outside and spend at least ten to �fteen minutes there before the sun sets. If at all possible, face or walk west toward the sun. You do not need to see the sun drop below the horizon. That’s a wonderful thing if you can—who doesn’t love a sunset? Alas, most of us don’t live or work in the right place to do so. Luckily, just going outside and getting some ambient light in your eyes in the late afternoon or early evening is bene�cial. Seeing the sunset is a bonus.

- A few things to keep in mind. As with the previous protocol, it is best to face the sun directly, not through a window or windshield, and without wearing sunglasses or a brimmed hat. Perhaps you can get an unobscured view by going up to a rooftop or by walking a few blocks from where you work or live. From a health perspective, that is well worth it. Again it’s especially important to do this protocol on overcast days.

###### HOW IT WORKS:

We’ve already unpacked the basic physiological processes linking your circadian clock, your eyes, and speci�c qualities of light that drive the sleep-wake cycle. Afternoon sunlight exposure taps into some of the same basic underlying cells, circuits, and mechanisms, but has both distinct and added bene�ts, including

partially protecting you from some of the negative health e�ects of viewing arti�cial lights late at night.

Here again we start with the SCN. Earlier I described the SCN as a “cluster of neurons,” but that doesn’t really do it justice. A key feature of the SCN is that it contains two oscillators, each following a roughly twenty-four-hour rhythm of electrical activity, but o�set from one another.64 It’s as if they are singing in a round, with peaks happening at di�erent yet speci�c moments within the twenty-four-hour cycle. One peak roughly corresponds to morning and the other to evening, and each can be entrained to sunrise and sunset. And they communicate with one another to be sure neither the morning nor the evening oscillator runs too fast or too slow. That helps generate the SCN’s coherent daily rhythm that all other cells in the body follow. It also allows us to shift our clock forward or back as the lengths of days and nights change across the seasons.

Here’s the best way to think about it: These two oscillators are like bookends buttressing a row of vertically stacked books, making the books less likely to fall over. This is the right analogy given that viewing morning sunlight shifts the phase of our circadian clock forward, making us want to go to sleep earlier and wake up earlier. Viewing late afternoon or early evening sunlight delays the phase of our clock, which, because it shifts the timing of the release of hormones like melatonin, makes us want to go to bed later and wake up later. So viewing both morning and afternoon sunlight thus helps keep us on a regular sleep-wake schedule, because the phase shift e�ects of morning and evening sunlight o�set each other ~~.~~ 65

Another great reason to view sunlight in the late afternoon or early evening is that it helps bu�er us against the negative e�ects of viewing bright arti�cial lights at night ~~.~~ 66 In the morning, we need to see a lot of bright light to train our SCN with the solar cycle, and to elevate our levels of alertness. Unless it’s a 10,000 lux lamp, most arti�cial lights and certainly our phone or computer screens just can’t do the job at that time. After sundown, however, it takes extremely little bright light to quash our melatonin levels, and shift our circadian clock. And even if we can still fall asleep at night, that sleep is not going to be as high quality.

In fact, studies show that as little as �fteen seconds of bright light can signi�cantly shift our circadian clock.67 And while most screens are not as bright as the lights used in these studies, our ipRGCs and SCN work to sum photons —that is, add up all the light we see from various sources. And let’s face it, most people are looking at their phone and other screens for a lot longer than �fteen seconds after sundown.

To recap: In the morning, you need more bright light in your eyes than a screen or conventional home lighting can provide, and at night you want far less light reaching your eyes than typically comes from a phone or computer screen or conventional home lighting. It all has to do with how our eyes are more sensitive to detecting light at di�erent times of day or night. If that seems inconvenient, you’re right; nowadays it is! But the circuits underlying retinal and circadian sensitivity across the twenty-four-hour cycle evolved long before humans had arti�cial lighting, much less the bright, short-wavelength-enriched LED screens and LED bulbs that we use today.

I, like most people, often wake up once in the middle of the night to use the bathroom. If I had things my way, our circadian system would be bu�ered from the phase-shifting e�ects of light at that time, but I wasn’t consulted at the design phase, and our ipRGCs are _exquisitely_ sensitive to bright light in the middle of the night and wee hours of morning. In fact, our ipRGCs and SCN become increasingly responsive to light with every hour after sundown.68 If you’re wondering if �replaces, camp�res, candlelight, or moonlight are too bright to view after dark, the answer is no. Firelight sources emit very long wavelengths, and moonlight is low lux. Candlelight is typically just 1 lux. A bright, full moon is _less_ than 1 lux! Compare those numbers to a typical table lamp, which is 200 to 400 lux, or commonly used overhead indoor LED lighting, which is 500 to 1,000 lux.

So are we to all avoid arti�cial lighting and opt for candlelight or moonlight? Maybe, but more on that later. In the meantime, let’s acknowledge that most people just won’t do that, and even if we opt to at home, we can’t control the lighting of most other environments like o�ce cubicles, restaurants, hotels, and the rest.

That is where this protocol can help. Viewing sunlight in the afternoon reduces the sensitivity of neural circuits in your retinas, so that any arti�cial light you see after dark does not have as strong an e�ect in disrupting melatonin and other circadian-related molecules and processes in your eyes and brain. This protocol is especially important if your mornings and days are mostly spent under arti�cial indoor lights, as that will cause any arti�cial lights you view at night to have an outsized negative e�ect on your sleep and circadian rhythms.69 Think of viewing the sunset as your (partial!) nighttime TV-watching or phonescrolling inoculation. That said, you should still strive to dim the lights in the evening, and make it as dark as possible while you sleep, as discussed in the next protocol.

### Avoid Viewing Bright Lights in the Final Hour Before Bedtime

###### WHAT TO DO:

- After sundown, limit your nighttime light exposure. You have a few options for how to do that. Which you use will depend on where you are and what activities you need to carry out.
  - Option 1: Dim the lights. After sundown, dim the lights in your home or wherever you are in the hours before sleep.

  - Option 2: Use red lights at night. I am a fan of using soft amber or red incandescent (or even amber or red LED lights, which are easier to �nd nowadays) for indoor lighting after dark as they don’t spike cortisol or suppress melatonin as much as many bright white LED lights do ~~.~~ 70 Remember, you want to try to keep your cortisol low in the late evening and especially the �nal few hours before your bedtime at night. You also want your melatonin elevated then. While this protocol might seem extreme, shifting to amber or red lighting in the �nal hours before sleep can make a marked di�erence for some people’s ability to fall and stay deeply asleep, which extends to every aspect of next-day energy, mood, and focus.71
    - _Consider buying a few high-quality red light bulbs._ Bon Charge makes great LED bulbs that are just the right level of brightness to see, but not so bright as to disrupt circadian rhythms and Ra Optics has LED

bulbs that lack the usual �icker of LEDs and can shift between daytime and “candlelight” mode (I have no a�liation with Bon Charge or Ra Optics, but I use these brands at home, and I travel with one or two of their bulbs when on the road and staying in hotels.) SaunaSpace makes a large, red incandescent bulb that is about the size of a shoebox that can illuminate a medium-sized room. I have one in my living room and another in my bedroom. ###### HOW IT WORKS:

Humans are not the strongest or fastest creatures on earth, but we are the best at building technologies. Every technology—the automobile, the smartphone, airplanes, antibiotics—brings the potential for unprecedented power over nature in our daily lives. Arti�cial lights have vanquished darkness. But in the case of LED lights, in particular, this technology also carries a risk to our circadian cycle, our mitochondria, and thus, our health.

Until about ten years ago, most arti�cial lighting used incandescent bulbs, which contain more long-wavelength light and a more even distribution of di�erent wavelengths than LED bulbs. Incandescent bulbs have been largely phased out because they are less energy e�cient than LED bulbs. Nowadays, most indoor lighting comes from LEDs, which emit a disproportionate amount of short-wavelength light that can potently reduce melatonin levels.72 Emerging evidence also points to negative e�ects of LEDs on mitochondrial health (which we’ll go into later, in chapter 5).73

Those are some of the risks. Now let me explain why bright arti�cial light at night may also be a�ecting our mood. Each of us has a brain structure called the habenula that sits at the middle and top part of an egg-shaped brain structure called the thalamus ~~.~~ 74 Your thalamus is a station for routing di�erent types of sensory and motor information to the correct parts of your brain so you can detect and integrate that information into your thoughts and actions. When I was an undergraduate and graduate student taking neuroanatomy, the habenula was listed as having an “unknown function.” Recent studies in rodents, �sh, and humans �nally revealed what it does.75

We now know the habenula is part of a network that controls depressive feelings and disappointment.76 Habenula activation creates those states by altering dopamine and serotonin dynamics in brain areas associated with reward.77 Why would we harbor such a structure and circuit? The answer is that not all behaviors are meant to be rewarded. Some need to be punished so we are

less likely to repeat them. And it turns out that viewing bright light in the “you really should be asleep now” phase of your circadian cycle is one of them. Animal studies and emerging evidence in humans show that viewing bright lights at night causes your ipRGCs to activate a speci�c region called the perihabenula ~~.~~ 78 That leads to elevated levels of cortisol, reductions in dopamine, next-day anxiety, and de�cits in learning—all consequences that appear to be separate from any reductions in total sleep time.79

For most people, the “you really should be asleep now” time is somewhere between the hours of 11:00 p.m. and 4:00 a.m. But of course, neither your SCN nor your habenula knows clock time; they only know circadian time, which follows the circadian body temperature, cortisol, and other twenty-four-hour rhythms I described brie�y earlier in this chapter. Your body temperature starts to rise in the �nal two hours before waking, and continues to rise throughout your morning and day until you reach the mid to late afternoon ~~.~~ 80 At that point, it starts to decline. That decline continues as we sleep, reaching its lowest point, called, unimaginatively, your _temperature minimum time_ about two to three hours prior to waking ~~.~~ 81 So when I say avoid viewing bright lights from LEDs or other sources at night, I am referring to the time about six to eight hours before your temperature minimum time. This may seem overly technical, but knowing your temperature minimum time can be very valuable. And no, you don’t have to measure your body temperature; your temperature minimum is the approximate time in your twenty-four-hour circadian cycle that roughly corresponds to two hours before you typically wake up, alarm clock or no. The exact clock time of course will vary depending on whether you are a morning lark or a night owl, or somewhere in between (more on how to determine that soon). But since most people wake up between 6:00 and 8:00 a.m., their temperature minimum time is between 4:00 and 6:00 a.m. If that’s you, assuming you’d like to fall asleep anytime between 10:00 p.m. and midnight, it means you should avoid viewing bright arti�cial lights between 11:00 p.m. and 4:00 a.m. You would do even better to dim the lights starting around 8:00 or 9:00 p.m. Put simply, to avoid habenula activation and shifting your circadian

clock, avoid bright arti�cial lights in the four to six hours prior to your temperature minimum time.

If you want to �gure out your exact temperature minimum time, simply take the average of your wake-up times over the course of three to four days and subtract two hours. Then strive to avoid viewing bright arti�cial light in the full six-hour period prior to that. I generally wake up at about 6:30 a.m., which means my temperature minimum time is 4:30 a.m., so I avoid viewing bright arti�cial light between 10:30 p.m. and 4:30 a.m.

I know this all sounds technical, but it’s very simple. By doing it, you’ll likely enjoy improvements in your sleep and thus daytime mood, focus, and alertness. I acknowledge that many people can fall asleep after being under bright arti�cial lights in the hours before bedtime, but knowing several such folks, I can assure you even they bene�t by adopting this simple (and incidentally cost-saving) change. Bonus: your home feels cozier at night too.

A bit more on those mood improvements: In 2018, a team of researchers, including noted UCLA psychiatrist Peter Whybrow, reviewed the data on the potential link between LED lighting and mental health. They concluded that exposure to blue light, in particular, posed a risk to sleep and other processes governed by the circadian system ~~.~~ 82 There is also evidence suggesting that the way in which arti�cial lighting at night interferes with this system may lead to depression ~~.~~ 83

These �ndings do not mean we should all throw away our LED lights. However, if you can �nd incandescent lights for your home, they are preferable because they’re less disruptive to the circadian system. In a study from 2020, researchers found that incandescent lighting interfered with the production of melatonin far less often than LED or �uorescent lights ~~.~~ 84 (I cover why this is in chapter 5.) If you can’t �nd incandescent bulbs, consider the Bon Charge or Ra Optics bulbs or ROKA Wind Down or other short wavelength (not just “blue”) blocking glasses.

Experiment with the options in this protocol to see what works best for you. And no matter what bulbs you choose for your home, still dim them before bed, and keep it dark in the six to eight hours prior to your temperature minimum

time. If a light is bright enough, it doesn’t matter if it is an LED or incandescent, it will still alter your circadian cycle.85

hours of sleep.86 But their socialization is vital, too, so you’ll have to strike a balance between encouraging a healthy relationship to arti�cial light, screens, and their social life. That said, if your teen or child is depressed or anxious, it’s important to assess their sleep patterns and relationship to light, especially the amount and timing of screen use.
