###### **SLEEP PROTOCOL**

4

### Find Your Ideal To-Sleep and Wake-Up Times and Strive to Adhere to Them

###### WHAT TO DO:

- Find your chronotype to set your schedule. Some people sleep better when they stay up late and sleep in late; others feel best when they go to bed early and wake up early; and most people fall somewhere in between, preferring to go to sleep somewhere between 10:00 p.m. and midnight and to wake up between 6:00 and 8:00 a.m.

Try to stick to your schedule. As long as you sleep for at least six to eight hours a night, pick a sleep-wake schedule that works for you. Even shifting slightly closer to your chronotype will a�ord you much more restorative sleep.

###### A systematic approach to figuring out your ideal sleep-wake schedule:

Let’s get something out of the way. If you’ve been reading this chapter and thinking, “Hmm, my circadian rhythm is nothing like the one you describe,” then maybe you are a night owl. Or maybe you just think you are. Kenneth Wright, whose lab at the University of Colorado Boulder studies circadian rhythms, wanted to �gure out how much of people’s preference to go to bed long after sundown and sleep in many hours past sunrise was due to a natural inclination, and how much was due to the

in�uence of arti�cial indoor lighting.88 He and several colleagues gave participants wrist monitors that measured the intensity and timing of their light exposure throughout the day, as well as their activity patterns, so that they could know when the participants were sleeping. Next, they measured their melatonin levels every hour to see whether the participants’ bedtimes matched up with their circadian-driven increases in melatonin—which is a reliable measure of circadian clock output. Finally, the participants were sent packing. They went camping for a week, with only the sun and camp�res as their light sources; no �ashlights, screens, or other electronic devices permitted.

That one week was all it took for participants to sync sleep-wake cycles to the rising and setting of the sun. Before the outing, some of the participants were convinced they were morning people and others were convinced they were night owls. After a week in the wilderness, those di�erences faded. They all went to sleep around sunset. The researchers noted that the intensity of the light the participants experienced while camping was four times greater than the intensity of light in their normal lives—a testament to how much time they normally spent indoors. Interestingly, just one weekend spent camping had a similar e�ect of shifting people’s circadian rhythm toward being early risers and people who prefer to go to sleep early. Mind you, those shifts were not just while camping. They persisted _after_ they came back. This study was small and in no way does it mean there is no such thing as a night owl. But the rapidity and degree of the change suggest that arti�cial lighting masks the preference of many people to have a solar-cycle-aligned rhythm.

There are potential health implications tied to shifting toward (or away) from your innate sleep-wake timing. And they suggest that except for bona �de night owls, a more solar-cycle-aligned rhythm is bene�cial. A large-scale 2019 study of nearly 700,000 subjects showed a causal link between being a morning person and better mental health—that’s right: a causal link.89 A di�erent study found a higher risk for cardiovascular disease among people who went to sleep later and slept for a long time.90 Another analysis using

data from 6,258 people in Finland found a link between routine late nights and type 2 diabetes.91 The patterns a night owl keeps have also been linked to depression.92

And there are new data showing that even if you prefer to go to bed and sleep late, shifting to becoming an early riser can improve your health.93 But telling a night owl to become a morning person can be dangerous— people cling to their natural sleep cycles like a pit bull on a rope toy.

Whether you think you’re a night owl or not, by systematically experimenting with your to-sleep and wake-up times a bit and by limiting bright arti�cial light exposure in the �nal hour or two before sleep, you can determine the ideal sleep-wake schedule for you. Few people can do genetic testing or sleep lab analysis to determine their true chronotype, but there is a simpler way and it’s worth exploring.

Here’s how:

Unless you are perfectly happy with your sleep, for one week, try getting into bed by 8:30 to 9:00 p.m. If you’re not ready for bed at that time, read a book or do another non-screen activity, but turn all the lights out by 9:00 to 9:30… maybe 10:00 p.m. at the latest.

Many people who do this wake up at 6:00 a.m. or even 5:00 a.m. the next day feeling more refreshed than ever before. Those who had previously been going to sleep at 11:00 p.m. or 12:00 a.m. and assumed they needed eight or more hours of sleep to feel rested often �nd they can feel great with just six or seven hours of sleep if they just get to sleep a bit earlier.

This process aligns your sleep more accurately with your genetically driven cortisol and melatonin rhythms. The genes that determine chronotype impact what are called clock genes, which are located in your SCN, and in almost every other cell of your body too. Your SCN entrains every cell in your body by changing its patterns of clock gene expression, either directly or indirectly, by altering the timing and type of peptides, hormones, and neural signals those cells receive. It’s a multipronged and highly distributed network that allows your SCN to do that. That is one reason why once people �nd their correct sleep schedule, they often notice

their digestion and immune systems improve, as well as key biomarkers of metabolism, not just their sleep and mood. It’s not unusual to get more deep and REM sleep and awaken feeling substantially more refreshed when you obey your chronotype. Nocturnal growth hormone releas ~~e~~ 94 is strongly regulated by your circadian clock,95 and is released in the �rst hours of sleep. If you are meant to go to sleep between 8:30 and 10:00 p.m. and you stay up late, you miss out on getting some of that growth hormone. And growth hormone is vital for bodily and brain repair, metabolism, and myriad other health functions ~~.~~ 96

A few things to keep in mind as you try this protocol. If you typically have been going to sleep after 10:30 p.m., dim the lights as described in Sleep Protocol 3. Also, remember that it is perfectly normal to wake up once to go to the bathroom in the middle of the night. If you do, I highly recommend that you do not look at a clock or turn on bright lights. Chances are you’ll fall back asleep within thirty minutes or less. No matter when you typically have been going to sleep, eating too close to bedtime and/or drinking ca�eine late in the day will mess up this whole experiment —both lead to more frequent nighttime wakings, so don’t do either ~~.~~ 97 In general, eating your last bite of food at least two to three hours before bedtime is best, provided you are not experiencing gnawing hunger near bedtime, in which case a small snack one hour before is helpful. Yes, eating too close to bedtime may disrupt sleep, but gnawing hunger will keep you awake, so we need to be practical about this whole “don’t eat too close to bedtime” thing.98 And try not to drink ca�eine after 1:00 or 2:00 p.m. (more on the reasons why in Sleep Protocol 11).

If you are not used to going to sleep this early, and you �nd yourself unable to fall asleep even after several nights, you may just be genetically wired to go to sleep between 10:30 p.m. and midnight. True night owls do exist! There is nothing wrong with that, provided your schedule lets you sleep long enough for you to feel rested the next day. Again, this assumes you are not drinking ca�eine after 1:00 or 2:00 p.m., stressed out, or

otherwise generating elevated levels of arousal late in the day, all things that can a�ect your sleep-wake schedule.

Indeed, people prefer di�erent sleep schedules. Approximately 33 percent of people feel great going to sleep between 10:30 p.m. and midnight and waking up between 6:30 and 7:30 a.m ~~.~~ 99 The other 33 percent do best going to sleep between 8:30 and 10:00 p.m. and waking up between 4:30 and 6:30 a.m. The remaining third are bona �de night owls— in the absence of ca�eine or work demands, their genetically driven melatonin rhythms and circadian rhythms cause them to be wide awake until 12:30 a.m., 1:00 a.m., or even 2:00 to 3:00 a.m., and they do best waking up between 9:00 and noon ~~.~~ 100 The point is to determine which group you are in, and to do so while not letting other variables screw up your experiment.

It is oh-so-valuable to know what your body and brain need, and thrive on. If you’re truly an early or late chronotype, perhaps you can delegate tasks to family members or roommates to meet life’s demands. You can select courses and workout times that better match your rhythms. I will even go so far as to say that, because of the way that getting your sleep-wake times right generates outsized positive e�ects on your health and cognition, you might even be wise to try to build your life around it. Tell your boss you’ll have fewer sick days (you will), tell your partner you’ll be a better partner (you will), and if you have kids, a better parent (you will). Feel free to cite me during the negotiations. There are aspects of our biology that we can neglect for a while before it causes issues. Chronotype is not one of them. Of course, we can shift our circadian clock for child-rearing, work, or travel, and this book teaches you how to do that more e�ectively, but we can’t disobey our chronotype for more than a few years before it catches up with us, and often it only takes a few weeks of disobeying it before we start to notice mild to severe malaise, irritability, or poor digestion. Fortunately, the reverse is also true. Align better with your chronotype—even by just an hour or two and you’ll often feel much better within days.

That said, our ideal sleep timing and total sleep needs do change as we age. Some of that is socially driven, but other aspects are related to changes

in our pineal gland—the gland that makes melatonin and other hormones and neurotransmitters.101

Also, when we are sick or recovering from an injury or bout of chronic stress, we need more sleep. The point here is to �gure out the best sleep schedule for you, this year, and know that it may drift a bit over time, or in speci�c circumstances.

Key point 1:

Keep in mind that regardless of your ideal sleep-wake schedule, you bene�t from being consistent with any sleep-wake schedule. That means going to bed and waking up at the same time, plus or minus thirty minutes, six to seven nights out of the week. Consistent does not mean neurotic. Strive, don’t strain, to get things right. Nothing is worse than trying to force yourself to sleep.

Key point 2:

It is very normal to feel very awake about one to three hours before your bedtime. That increase in arousal, sometimes referred to as the “wake maintenance zone,” is thought to be an adaptive mechanism for allowing us to secure our physical surroundings and safety prior to sleep, but that is just speculation. A transient increase in alertness—that for some occurs around sunset and for others around one to three hours before their typical bedtime—also may happen; it’s well documented in sleep studies, although to my knowledge its physiological basis has not yet been explored in detail ~~.~~ 102 Remember, this is a transient increase, so don’t sweat it. Let it pass and embrace the drop in body temperature, the rise in melatonin, and sleepiness that follows.

###### HOW IT WORKS:

The intricacies of what happens when we sleep—the so-called architecture of sleep—deserves a book of its own, and indeed many have been written about it.

Rarely discussed, however, is how the architecture of each sleep-wake cycle in�uences our sleeping _and our waking_ states. We touched on this topic a bit earlier in this chapter. But now, by exploring the architecture of sleep itself, we

can start to understand how the placement of six to eight hours of sleep in each twenty-four-hour cycle, and the consistency of that placement from one day to the next, has a profound e�ect on exactly what happens while we sleep, and how that impacts whether our sleep is maximally restorative.

###### The Stages of Sleep

Many people are familiar with the two major types of sleep: rapid eye movement, or REM, sleep, and non-REM sleep. Non-REM sleep is often referred to as deep or slow-wave sleep, but that’s oversimpli�ed. Non-REM sleep consists of three distinct phases that we enter, one after the other. These are referred to as N1, N2, and N3 sleep, and only in the N3 stage does actual deep or slow-wave sleep occur. Cycling through N1, to N2, to N3, to REM sleep takes, on average, about ninety minutes. So a person who sleeps for three hours might make it through two cycles, a person who sleeps for six hours experiences four cycles, and a person who sleeps 7.5 hours gets �ve cycles, and so on.

We enter N1, or _light sleep_ , �rst and it typically lasts �ve to ten minutes. It is easy to rouse us from N1 sleep. But N1 is not merely a transition stage; during N1, our body starts to generate additional adenosine triphosphate, or ATP, the chemical that fuels all our biological processes. What’s more, proteins that have become misshapen or broken during our waking hours get repaired during N1, and proteins that help build memories by recon�guring our neural circuits are created.103

Next we enter N2 sleep, which lasts about twenty minutes. During N2 our body temperature drops, our heart rate slows down, and our brain produces sleep spindles—surges of transient brain activity that help consolidate information we have learned in the days prior ~~.~~ 104 Sleep spindles are vital for learning new cognitive information and motor skills, which both represent types of neuroplasticity ~~.~~ 105 We explore this in greater detail in chapter 6.

N2 has another intriguing feature: PGO waves, which are surges of large-scale brain activity that travel from the pons (P) of the brainstem, to the geniculate (G), a structure in our thalamus (the sensory waystation we discussed earlier), and then to our occipital (O) cortex, which resides in the back of our brain and is involved in, among other things, visual processing. PGO waves trigger the

release of massive amounts of glutamate, an excitatory neurotransmitter that is a requisite component of the multistage process of learning, such as in the formation and elimination of synapses.106

After N1 and N2 we enter deep sleep, what sleep researchers call _slow-wave sleep_ , or N3. This is an extremely restorative stage of sleep. During N3, our brain waves shift to very high amplitude and low frequency, aka _slow_ ; our heart rate slows way down, and growth hormone is released from our pituitary gland into our bloodstream.107 What’s more, the active repair of our muscle, brain, and other bodily tissues occurs—including our tendons, skin, heart, et cetera.108 That process involves a lot of protein synthesis, or the repair and regeneration of cells and tissues by use of speci�c amino acids.109 Some of that repair and regeneration occurs in response to tissue damage from exercise, but most of it is simple “housekeeping”-based cellular turnover and repair, which is also vital to our health and longevity. N3 is also when _glymphatic washout_ of our brain occurs. 110 This process was discovered just in the past �fteen years or so and involves the pulsing of lymph-like �uid through our brain, thereby removing the waste products caused by normal brain metabolism and any cellular debris that accumulated the previous day ~~.~~ 111 This glymphatic clearance is actively governed by multiple brain regions—including the locus coeruleus—that we will talk about more below and in later chapters.

REM sleep, or rapid eye movement sleep, follows N3, but often we cycle from N3 back to N2 for a few minutes or more before advancing into REM sleep. REM sleep is crucial for sorting through all that waking life brings our way by eliminating or strengthening speci�c neural connections in accordance with what information we need to keep and what we should discard ~~.~~ 112 Thus, think of REM sleep as an experience audit, with only the meaningful experiences surviving the cut.

One more interesting thing about REM: Our body becomes mostly paralyzed during this stage, a phenomenon known as sleep atonia ~~.~~ 113 The most prevalent hypothesis to explain sleep atonia is that it keeps us from acting out our dreams during REM sleep ~~.~~ 114 Our brains are extremely active during REM and the dreams we experience during this stage tend to be vivid and emotionally

laden—often marked by �ying, swimming, being �lled with anxiety or awe, and highly dynamic in how we move through time and space (in the dream of course).115 The idea is that REM-associated atonia prevents us from acting in accordance with what are essentially in-sleep hallucinations, which would put us in danger.

The relative amount of time we spend in REM sleep increases, and the amount spent in deep N3 sleep decreases, as we complete more sleep cycles across a night of sleep. This means our most vivid dreams tend to occur as we approach morning. A baby’s sleep is largely REM sleep, and the amount of REM we experience decreases with age starting in adolescence.116 If we are sleepdeprived, or we do something that reduces the amount of REM sleep we get on a given night—using cannabis, for instance—the next night we experience REM rebound by entering REM sleep sooner in the sleep cycle, and experiencing more REM overall. Chronic cannabis users who stop using cannabis often report vivid dreams in the �rst weeks and months after quitting.117

Alcohol and many prescription drugs reduce the fraction of our sleep that is REM as well. Once someone stops using these, they also experience an REM rebound ~~.~~ 118

REM sleep is fascinating. As stated before, it is characterized by more brain activity than we ever experience in our waking life, and yet we are paralyzed while our brain is in that hyperactive state. And there’s more. REM sleep is also the only time in our lives when our locus coeruleus—the brainstem region that releases norepinephrine and increases our focus and alertness—goes largely dormant. Also, we don’t readily release adrenaline from our adrenals during REM.

Researchers believe that this paradoxical state, during which our brain is highly active but our body is paralyzed, our locus coeruleus is almost silent, and our body can’t easily release adrenaline, serves as a sort of naturally occurring therapy, unloading the emotional burdens from our daytime experiences. Indeed, this general set of conditions parallels many established trauma therapies, in which patients recount a traumatic event while in an intentionally or progressively lowered state of anxiety, so as to detach the body’s and brain’s

emotional responses from the details of the memory. People selectively deprived of REM sleep have a harder time unloading emotional burdens from past experiences, including traumas.119

REM, like some of the other sleep stages, is also a key time for the consolidation of new skills and information that are of a nonemotional nature. We will cover more on that in chapter 6.

###### Health risks of sleep deprivation

Given all this, it becomes clearer and clearer how lack of sleep, but also altered sleep architecture, a�ects our mind and body in a variety of ways. Sleep deprivation is associated with diminished response time, alertness, attention, memory, and executive functioning.120

Additionally, as described at the chapter outset, lack of sleep can bring about longer-term problems as well. Insu�cient REM sleep may increase the risk of dementia. In 2017, a group of researchers published their investigation of links between dementia and sleep architecture.121 They looked at three years of data on thirty-two adults over age sixty with dementia and found that the likelihood of cognitive decline fell in line with a reduction in REM sleep. In fact, with every 1 percent reduction in REM sleep, the risk of dementia rose by about 9 percent. (Non-REM sleep deprivation did not share this connection.) The role of REM in building and consolidating neural connections, thereby protecting against cognitive decline, may also explain why truncating this stage would raise the risk of dementia, but direct evidence for this mechanism in humans is still lacking.

Getting su�cient REM sleep is also connected to overall longevity. In 2020, a group of researchers from multiple institutions reported that less REM sleep is associated with an increased mortality risk. Using data from 4,050 people, they found that for every 5 percent decrease in REM sleep, the mortality rate increased by 13 percent ~~.~~ 122 That held true for most causes of death, including cardiovascular disease.

Ask any sleep researcher “How can I get more REM sleep?” and they will tell you “Sleep in an extra hour or two.” But most people can’t a�ord to sleep in an extra hour or two past their usual wake-up time. The good news is that _when_ we

sleep is almost as important as getting enough of it. If we get to bed and wake up at a time that is in sync with our chronotype, we end up getting more growth hormone release, and we spend less time in light sleep and more time in deep sleep and REM sleep. As a consequence, we tend to need less sleep overall. Our sleep can become more e�cient and restorative ~~.~~ 123

Studies of shift workers tell us what happens if we sleep enough, but at the wrong times of the twenty-four-hour cycle. The short answer is: Bad things happen. Working at nighttime and sleeping in the daytime is associated with greatly elevated risk of type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, depression, and suicide ~~.~~ 124 Shift workers are also susceptible to neurocognitive impairment and at greater risk for substance abuse.125 One large survey from Canada found that executive function is signi�cantly worse among people whose jobs take place outside normal work hours.126 One study found the level of performance impairment to be equal to a blood alcohol concentration of 0.10, which exceeds the legal limit for driving in many places.127

To be clear: Being a night owl is not the same thing as forcing yourself to be nocturnal, so if that’s your chronotype, don’t worry. The health detriments of shift work are likely to be multifactorial—the lack of sunlight, the altered social interactions associated with an inverted schedule, and more. We know that one of the worst types of shift work for one’s health is the swing shift, where people switch back and forth from daytime to nighttime work each week or even within the same week.

How long we sleep, when we sleep, and how consistent we are with our sleepwake schedule a�ect our physical and mental health. That’s why I hope you try the approach outlined here. Figure out what is best for you and then stick with it.

###### COMMON QUESTIONS:

Yes. When we turn the clocks forward an hour to move from standard time to daylight saving time, or back an hour to return to standard time, or when we

change time zones during travel, our circadian clock has to shift.

Changing our clocks forward or back means we have collectively decided that 7:00 a.m. is now 8:00 a.m., or 8:00 a.m. is now 7:00 a.m., but our SCN really doesn’t care about clock time, it only knows time according to the entrainment cues it receives. You already know the most powerful entrainment cue and that’s viewing morning sunlight. Even if we move the clocks just by one hour, the SCN needs a few days to shift its patterns of gene expression and communication with all the cells of the body to get them on schedule. In the meantime, we are groggy at times in the morning when we were perfectly chipper the day before. And a whole host of other systems in our body and brain have to shift before we feel like ourselves again. The dangers of such shifts extend beyond mere irritability. Tra�c accidents increase in the days immediately following seasonal clock changes ~~.~~ 128 So do heart attacks.129 It also makes people more susceptible to depression.130

Jet lag occurs when our sleep-wake cycle no longer matches the solar cycle of our location. Our internal timekeeper may be telling us it’s time for bed when the locals are just eating dinner. Many people �nd that traveling east, into a later time, is harder than traveling west, into an earlier time, because we have to move our circadian clocks forward. It’s often easier to stay up a few hours longer, or even take a brief nap, than to force ourselves to go to bed before we’re ready.

Some people don’t su�er much from jet lag. Others su�er tremendously. For those of you in the latter group, Sleep Protocol 15 o�ers a technique that can help avoid jet lag or at least dampen its impact.

We should all strive to keep a consistent sleep-wake schedule, for the reasons discussed above. That means we should try to get to bed at the same time, plus or minus thirty minutes, on most nights. Same goes for waking up; try to wake up at roughly the same time each day, plus or minus thirty minutes. Larger changes in sleep or wake times every once in a while won’t be too disruptive, because the entrainment of your SCN re�ects the weighted average of inputs from multiple factors, as discussed. So by all means, enjoy that birthday or

wedding or New Year’s celebration and don’t despair about arriving home late. One late night is not something to worry about.

Many people wonder whether wake times should be later after that occasional late night. If you usually go to sleep somewhere between 8:30 and 11:00 p.m. and have a night where you’re up until 1:00 or 2:00 a.m., should you sleep late or wake up at your usual time? In general, it’s best to get enough sleep to feel rested but not to sleep more than one or two hours past your usual wake time. So on those “I stayed up too late last night” mornings, get an extra hour in bed asleep if you can, and try to take a twenty-minute nap, or practice non-sleep deep rest (NSDR) in the afternoon (more on that soon), and then get to bed around your usual time that night. Your SCN—and thus you—thrive on consistency. If you go to bed much later than usual and sleep in much later, too, be sure not to shift your whole schedule forward. It’s still �ne (and encouraged) to view sunlight, exercise, and so on, but be especially mindful not to drink ca�eine much later in the day than usual, or you will soon �nd yourself o� your usual rhythm and it will take three to four or more days to get back to it.

The advice is a little di�erent for young children and teenagers. Babies need to sleep A LOT and enter REM far more frequently and for longer than any other age group. Toddlers and young children should also sleep as much or as often as necessary, or desired, to support their extraordinarily fast brain and bodily growth rates. The amount of neuroplasticity in infants and children, all the way up to adolescence and beyond, is incredible—and sleep is a key part of that process. Limiting their sleep is never recommended but of course once kids are in school, setting a regular schedule (and keeping devices out of their rooms near bedtime and throughout the night) becomes important.

Sleep needs are somewhat di�erent for teenagers. Bedtimes shift during puberty for at least two known reasons. First is what researchers call the homeostatic sleep drive. This term refers to a brain and bodily pressure to sleep that builds up gradually throughout the day, mainly due to adenosine accumulation ~~.~~ 131 The longer we are awake, the more adenosine in our bodies, and the greater the pressure to sleep. Adenosine levels drop while we sleep and

begin to mount again when we wake up for the new day. This pressure to sleep is separate from the circadian clock mechanisms we have discussed a lot thus far. Teenagers (good rebels that they are) resist this pressure and force themselves to stay up late, building up more adenosine and, therefore, the desire to sleep in the 132 next morning ~~.~~

And they often don’t need to force themselves to stay up late; it just happens naturally, as the hormonal testosterone, estrogen, and progesterone surges of puberty shift their circadian clock to a later phase.133 Melatonin production begins later in the teenage brain than in the brains of either adults or younger children.

All of these changes leave the typical sixteen-year-old awake until about 11:00 p.m ~~.~~ 134 And this age group should be sleeping about nine hours per night, making 8:00 a.m. the preferred wake-up time. Studies have found that moving school start times to 8:30 a.m. or later leads to better grades and other measures of academic performance. There is even evidence suggesting that this shift also reduces car crashes among teen drivers.135 It’s bene�cial for teenagers to have days when they can sleep as long as they want, even if that means staying in bed until noon. That doesn’t mean they should never be woken up earlier on a Saturday or Sunday, but parents and caregivers do not need to worry about prolonged sleeping on the weekends. Teenagers, yes, reference this book if you need leverage to sleep in and parents, yes, you still want to encourage them to get sunlight in their eyes once they get up, even though it is midday, and not lowsolar-angle sun.

Current data indicate that teenagers in the US are in the midst of an epidemic of sleep deprivation that is likely having serious consequences for their health. Ideally, young people between the ages of six and twelve years should sleep at least nine hours per night, and thirteen-to-eighteen-year-olds should sleep at least eight hours per night. More than 70 percent of young people do not sleep enough, according to one large survey from the CDC.136 Anxiety, mood disorders, obesity, high-risk behavior, poor academic performance, and substance use have all been tied to sleep deprivation among adolescents ~~.~~ 137 Good practices for teenagers include shutting o� screens at least an hour before

bedtime, keeping the phone (and the laptop, the tablet, etc.) out of the bedroom at night and the room cool and dark, having a consistent bedtime, and, ideally, sleeping for those eight to nine hours per night.

Parsing the changes in sleep that arise in older adults is tricky. Ailments and medications of various kinds impact sleep in many ways. Absent any such interferences, sleep can vary in our later years, but not to a great extent. Older adults sleep a bit less than middle-aged adults by about an hour or so, on average ~~.~~ 138 It can take longer to fall asleep as we move past age �fty, but again, not in a dramatic way. And older adults are able to doze back o� to sleep after a middle of the night waking, just as well as teenagers and younger adults can.

The stages of sleep also shift a bit as we age. The percentage of time we spend in deep sleep and REM decreases, although studies have shown a surge in REM in people between the ages of seventy-�ve and eighty-�ve years ~~.~~ 139 Older people also tend to nap more.

Counting sheep has long been recommended for calming a busy brain before bed. The idea is that by giving ourselves a task, we stop ruminating on the day and going over our to-do lists for tomorrow. It turns out that counting sheep isn’t such a great nighttime activity. Allison Harvey, a psychologist at UC Berkeley, found that counting sheep actually made it more di�cult for people to fall asleep ~~.~~ 140 She concluded that this basic mental imagery was not engaging enough to hold the attention of people lying in bed trying to keep anxieties at bay. Without that focus to help calm our brain, we’re back to ruminating and reviewing to-do lists. A subsequent study in which Harvey instructed participants to deliberately suppress whatever thought was most likely to intrude into their mind before sleep found this didn’t help—predictably, the thought they were supposed to be suppressing just became more preoccupying.141

_Take a mental walk:_ Imagine walking from your bed to your mailbox and then down the street and to a nearby location, then home again by the same or different familiar route.

Occupying a busy brain with an easy and engaging task can help stop ruminating thoughts. Mental walks like these are occupying but not stimulating. And they have the tendency to lull people o� to sleep.

_Move your eyes following the pattern described below:_ Warning: This is going to sound a bit out there, but it works well for many people, and studies are indirectly starting to suggest why.

Lie down in bed and close your eyes. Keep your eyes closed and move your eyes slowly to the right then to the left, then up, then down, then counterclockwise and then clockwise. Then cross them somewhat by directing them gently toward your nose. Finally, do a big inhale and long exhale. Repeat one to three times as needed.

Told you this would sound a bit out there! This trick often helps people fall asleep, because to do so we need to stop thinking about our limb position, or proprioception. Our visual and vestibular systems, or balance, and proprioception systems interact, and the eye movements just described “confuse” those systems. A similar mechanism partially explains why gentle slow rocking and pacing can help babies, and slow rocking of a bed (yes, such beds exist) can help adults improve their sleep metrics ~~.~~ 142 We need more data to understand the mechanism behind this pattern, which is why it’s not its own protocol, but it is reasonable to assume it is related to the eye-to-vestibular circuits involved in, among other things, proprioception and sleep. New eye mask and rocking-bed technologies that trigger this eye movement pattern are designed to cause similar eye movements. I have tried a few of these nascent technologies and confess I fell asleep in less than two minutes! Meanwhile, this technique is free and easy to try. “Next thing I knew it was morning!” is not an uncommon refrain from people with whom I have shared this trick.

###### **SLEEP PROTOCOL**

5

### Lower Your Core Body Temperature at Night

###### WHAT TO DO:

- Lower the temperature of the room you sleep in at night. Cooler ambient temperatures facilitate sleep. Keep your bedroom between 65 and 68 degrees Fahrenheit, and a maximum of 70 degrees.

- Warm your extremities before bed. A hot shower, hot bath, sauna, or even washing your face with very warm water can help induce drowsiness by warming hands and feet and by triggering a drop in core body temperature in compensation for this heating.

- Make sure your feet and hands can be easily exposed from underneath your covers. The skin of these areas is a primary way we shed heat from our body. Exposing them to cool air is one of the most e�ective ways to decrease core body temperature. So untuck your sheets at the foot and sides of the bed.

- Avoid wearing socks while you sleep, especially if you tend to wake in the middle of the night. Socks can stop the natural cooling process that happens through the feet. (People who tend to run very cold at night may want to skip this recommendation.)

###### HOW IT WORKS:

Socks or no socks? Window open or closed? Blanket or just sheets? Feet exposed? We all have our sleep habits and a lot of them revolve around

temperature. That makes sense. Thermoregulation—the maintenance of our core body temperature—and the management of our sleep environment to control our body temperature is crucial for a great night’s sleep, both falling and staying asleep. Indeed, changes in our core body temperature both re�ect and in�uence our circadian rhythm, how much melatonin and other hormones we release, and even the amount of deep and REM sleep we get in a given night.

As I mentioned earlier in this chapter, our core body temperature declines as the day goes on, eventually reaching its lowest point at a speci�c time—we call this temperature minimum time ~~.~~ 143 A decline in body temperature precedes us falling asleep. The rate of temperature reduction, and not just the absolute core temperature value, seems to matter. In one experiment, researchers made the case that people tended to head o� to bed at exactly the time that their temperature was declining fastest ~~.~~ 144 Body temperature starts to increase shortly before we wake up. The relationship between core body temperature and our level of autonomic arousal—which is what sleepiness and alertness re�ect—is causal but is best thought of as “necessary but not su�cient,” meaning we need the change in temperature, but other factors are key too ~~.~~ 145

Research has found that the ideal ambient temperature while we sleep is between approximately 66 and 70 degrees Fahrenheit, which typically brings the microclimate immediately around our skin down to somewhere between 88 and 95 degrees Fahrenheit.146 To fall asleep our core body temperature needs to decrease by about 1 to 2 degrees.

A lower core body temperature facilitates various sleep-related biological processes you are now familiar with. First, research indicates that this reduction may help initiate non-REM sleep ~~,~~ 147 and our lowest body temperature is associated with deep sleep. Melatonin, a hormone that facilitates falling asleep, is released in sync with the nightly drop in body temperature. In one small study of twelve women who were entrained to the solar cycle, the secretion of natural melatonin at night occurred with a simultaneous decline in core body 149 temperature ~~.~~ 148 Other studies have observed a similar coupling.

The stillness of our body during early sleep also plays a role in further dropping our core body temperature. In sleep, our autonomic nervous system

shifts from more sympathetic activity (or tone, as it’s often referred to), which is related to being alert and able to generate movement, to a far more parasympathetic tone, which is associated with calmness, lower heart rate, and less or no bodily movement ~~.~~ 150 All that combined causes our blood to �ow more to our periphery, to our hands and feet, where it “dumps heat,” which in turn leads to a lower core body temperature.

This means that warming up our hands and feet a bit before getting into bed could facilitate falling asleep. That may seem paradoxical: Why would warming up your periphery help at a time when cooling down your core body temperature is the goal? Because heating your periphery acts as a trigger. A hot shower or bath, or a sauna, warms the surface of your body. That causes the preoptic area of your hypothalamus—a brain area that works sort of like a thermostat—to trigger a compensatory response, lowering the core temperature in your body ~~.~~ 151 This process makes it easier to fall asleep, a phenomenon known colloquially as the _warm bath effect_ ~~.~~ 152

Once you get in bed, having your sleeping environment cool is also helpful. Many people sleep best in a cool room but with their whole body under loads of warm blankets. Other people run hot and like to sleep under just a sheet or a light blanket. Try out a few of these recommendations and pick what suits you best.

###### In My Experience

I prefer a comforter and a weighted blanket, but stick my bare feet out from underneath them, which we know helps cool core body temperature. And I keep the room about 68 degrees Fahrenheit. Closer to morning, I �nd that I often bring my feet under the blankets (in my sleep!), which we know can increase the amount of time spent in REM in the �nal few hours before waking.153 Temperature-controlled mattress covers like Eight Sleep make controlling your bed temperature across the night easy, and I use one. (They are a podcast sponsor, and I am a scienti�c advisor to Eight Sleep). But with or without Eight Sleep, it is a good idea to use programmable room temperature controls to help

create that cooler-at-start and warmer-toward-morning sleep environment. Experiment and �nd what works for you.

###### COMMON QUESTIONS:

Some data from animal studies suggest that a slightly elevated body temperature for a few hours in the afternoon may lead to more time spent in N3 sleep at night, when waste products from the brain and spinal cord are cleared away (among other processes) ~~.~~ 154 That’s one reason why many people �nd that doing some moderate to intense exercise in the early or midafternoon improves their sleep, provided they don’t consume a lot of ca�eine before their workout.

It’s best to avoid intense exercise late at night, within three to four hours of sleep. High-intensity exercise raises our core body temperature, which is counterproductive to falling asleep. That said, some people can only exercise at this time, and many learn how to down-shift afterward with a hot bath or shower, and by using some of the tools covered in chapter 3, like deliberate longexhale breathing.

If you consistently �nd it di�cult to fall and stay asleep after exercising hard at night, consider moving your more intense workouts to mornings and doing something lighter in the evening. A review of several randomized clinical trials found that meditative movement like tai chi and qigong improved sleep quality.155

However, if night is the only time of day you can exercise, then it’s more important to get the workout in than to skip it just because it’s late in the day (more on that in chapter 2). In this case, it may help to take some additional steps for ensuring a solid night of sleep: no ca�eine after 1:00 or 2:00 p.m., a nighttime wind-down routine, a hot shower, some breathing exercises to reduce stress, no screens, and dim lighting will all help counteract the energizing e�ects of late evening exercise.

### Increase Your Core Body Temperature in the Final One to Two Hours of Sleep Before You Wake Up

###### WHAT TO DO:

- Program your heating system for the room you sleep in at night. If you have one that can be set to di�erent times, program it to rise one to three degrees above your room temperature, starting one to two hours before your wake-up time. Keep clothing by your bed. If you wake up one to two hours before your preferred wake-up time or in the middle of the night to use the bathroom, try putting on some socks, sweats, or even a knit cap and go back to sleep until your preferred wake-up time. This can increase your core body temperature, which increases the amount of REM sleep you get and will help you wake up feeling energized.

###### HOW IT WORKS:

We touched on this in the previous protocol but given the importance of getting su�cient REM sleep for mental and physical health, and for performance, it’s worth delving into this topic as its own protocol. So here it goes: Just as cooling our core body temperature facilitates falling and staying asleep, warming our core body temperature starting about one to two hours before we wake up can lead us to feel far more refreshed and ready to lean into the day.

Hot temperatures are disruptive to falling and staying asleep.156 Interestingly the body tends not to adapt; even after several days of trying to sleep well in hot temperatures, sleep remains disrupted.157 One theory holds that wakefulness itself is triggered by the need for thermoregulation; in other words, waking up is a way to bring our body temperature back to normal.158

We have less data on the use of temperature in this part of the sleep cycle than we do for the previous protocol. However, we know that our lowest body temperature, or temperature minimum time, occurs at about two hours before we wake up and begins to rise after that ~~.~~ 159 A return to our normal core body temperature accompanies our return to wakefulness, so it stands to reason that supporting the general process of warming up after we reach our temperature minimum helps us wake up feeling energized ~~.~~ 160 (It likely re�ects having had at least two REM-enriched sleep cycles.)

Admittedly, there’s a small problem here. It’s hard to get out of a warm bed into a cold room. Heating the room you sleep in on a timer that increases the temperature one to two hours prior to waking solves that problem. Otherwise you just have to get up and get to the thermostat. As mentioned before, devices such as Eight Sleep mattress covers that can cool at �rst and then heat your sleep environment in the �nal hours of sleep are very e�ective. These can also measure your deep and REM sleep, and use AI to make real-time adjustments to your sleep temperature to help you get the best possible sleep. But these carry a cost that for many could be prohibitive, and most versions don’t travel easily. Anyone can adjust their bedroom temperature and/or use clothes to try to achieve some of the ideal temperature ranges described here.

### Nap (Correctly) to Offset Minor Sleep Deficits

###### WHAT TO DO:

- If you need a nap, make it short. Keep the duration to no more than about twenty minutes, and avoid naps longer than ninety minutes.

- Avoid late-day naps that interfere with your nighttime sleep. Each person can determine what time constitutes “too late” with a bit of experimentation. See how groggy you are in the hours following your nap. Most importantly, note if you can still easily fall asleep at your regular bedtime afterward.

- Know your goal. Nap strategies depend on what you are trying to accomplish.
  - If you need an energy boost to sustain your focus and drive for the rest of the day: Aim for a �fteen-to-twenty-minute nap. Five to ten minutes will give you a mild energy boost and help your focus but it doesn’t last long. After a �fteen to twenty minute nap, concentration, mood, and energy will improve in a way that will sustain you for the remainder of the day.

  - If you are dealing with heavy emotions, say from a loss or a rejection or an argument: Aim for a longer nap, but no longer than ninety minutes. You’ll recall from Sleep Protocol 4 that the REM stage is when emotions are processed, and that stage arrives about sixty to seventy minutes into the sleep cycle. So know you might feel groggy after a nap of forty-�ve minutes or so because sleep is cut o� before the REM

cycle is completed. And know too that when people’s nighttime sleep is altered due to heavy emotions, and they nap in the day, they often go into REM more quickly; that’s the REM rebound e�ect discussed in that same protocol.

If you are sleep-deprived for any reason: It is �ne to nap for thirty, sixty, or even ninety minutes but avoid longer naps as these can alter your circadian rhythm. It can often “split” your circadian rhythm so that you’re asleep from 10:00 p.m. to 2:00 a.m., then awake for a few hours, then asleep again.

Consider other forms of daytime rest besides sleep to replenish mental and physical vigor. Particularly if you have trouble falling asleep at night, napping may not be ideal. Sleep Protocol 8 describes non-sleep deep rest (NSDR), a highly e�ective alternative to napping that can help you feel refreshed without grogginess or impairment to your nighttime sleep. It has other bene�ts as well.

###### HOW IT WORKS:

There are con�icting views on napping among sleep experts ~~.~~ 161 Some say if you are sleepy enough to nap in the daytime, you must be getting less than optimal sleep at night, and you should focus on improving that instead. Others take the stance that napping is �ne, bene�cial even, and not always re�ective of a sleep de�cit. Provided you adhere to a few simple constraints, napping is great. But if you don’t crave naps, there is no need to nap.

And yes, there is a proper way to nap.

First o�, it’s normal to feel a bit sleepy in the afternoon as your body temperature shifts from rising to falling—remember that the rate of core temperature dropping is what initiates the feeling of drowsiness. For people on a conventional schedule of being asleep at night and being awake in the daytime, this dip in early afternoon energy passes. I fall asleep at about 10:30 p.m. most nights and wake up at 6:30 a.m., and I always get a bit sleepy between 2:00 and 3:00 p.m. irrespective of what I eat, how much ca�eine I drink, and so on. After 3:30 p.m. or so, I feel wide awake and energetic again. The point is, you might get a bit tired in the afternoon, but the feeling is temporary. Not everyone

experiences this dip. Some people just barge right through the day, morning until night.

We know that napping can increase our ability to focus and learn. Matthew Walker, a professor of neuroscience and biomedical engineering at the University of Texas in Dallas, conducted a study in which a group of participants learned a new set of facts at midday.162 Half of them napped for ninety minutes afterward; half of them relaxed without sleeping. At 5:00 p.m., they learned a second new set of facts. The group that did not nap experienced a decline in learning capacity. The nap group sustained or even improved their capacity to learn. The di�erence reached about 25 percent, which is meaningful.

The �nding goes back to the role of sleep spindles, which we covered in Sleep Protocol 4. These are the types of brain waves present during N2 sleep, which happens early in the sleep cycle. Even a brief snooze of twenty minutes takes us into N2 ~~.~~ 163 Sleep spindles help us process new learning, but also prepare our brain for more learning after we wake up.

Napping also in�uences our mood. In another study, Walker and his group asked participants to rate the level of emotion they observed in a photograph.164 How angry were the angry faces? How happy were the happy faces? Again, half the subjects napped for about an hour and half did not. Toward the end of the day, the non-nappers were rating the emotions as more extreme; angry people were angrier, and so on. The napping group was more likely to rate faces as happy; the rest time seemed to blunt the normal increase in anger sensitivity across the day. As Walker sometimes puts it, sleep gives us a “rose tint” to our worldview. In this study, the naps were ninety minutes, long enough to get some REM sleep, so the bene�t is likely due to that, which as we discussed, is when we unload the emotional burdens from our daytime experiences. Although, in this case, it wasn’t about the nappers’ emotions; it was about how they perceived the emotions of others.

Finally, there is the simple bene�t of restoring energy. Many people experience what sleep researchers call a postprandial drop, a dip in energy after eating, especially large meals rich in starchy carbohydrates. Aside from modifying your dietary pattern, naps can help get you to the other side of a

postprandial drop if and when you do experience the phenomenon. That said, for anyone who feels tired in the middle of the day and would do better without that sleepiness, I suggest making sure you don’t overeat, and possibly even reduce starchy carbohydrate intake, at lunch. Take a short ten-minute walk afterward; that can help for reasons related to blood sugar, or glucose, regulation (covered in chapter 2). Many people �nd that just reducing the amount of starchy carbs they eat at lunch allows them to go straight through the rest of their day feeling energized and focused. I’ll talk more about the relationship between food and brain states in chapter 4.

###### When Not to Nap (and Why)

A short midday sleep isn’t a good idea for everyone. To understand why, we need to return to adenosine. As you recall, adenosine acts as a neurotransmitter that inhibits neural activity in brain regions involved in strategic planning.165 Sleep actually results from two processes: the circadian clock and sleep pressure from adenosine. Most of the protocols thus far depend on the former. This one has to do with the latter, which you might remember from Sleep Protocol 4. Adenosine is so vital to this process that we ought to explore it a bit further, so here goes.

ATP, or adenosine triphosphate, is the basic unit of energy for all our cellular processes. It is generated during the early stages of sleep. Adenosine is the downstream product of the burning of ATP ~~.~~ 166 It’s a product of metabolism that accrues as we engage in activity over the course of a day. As we move from morning to afternoon to evening, more energy has been spent and therefore more adenosine builds up in our brains, gathering in the space between our cells. As it does, we register a need to sleep. This is, again, called homeostatic sleep drive.

The longer we are awake and the more physical activity and mental activity we engage in over the course of a day, the higher the levels of adenosine we accumulate. On days when we get more exercise, for example, our brains accrue more adenosine. And the more they do, the easier it is to fall and stay asleep. Additionally, greater amounts of adenosine are associated with an increase in deeper slow-wave sleep and a decrease in shallower sleep.

Napping—which is, after all, a form of sleep—reduces the amount of adenosine in our brains.167 It won’t zero it out like a solid eight hours of sleep will, but a forty-�ve-to-ninety-minute nap will clear away a substantial amount of adenosine. For this reason, people who have trouble falling asleep at night should not nap. You want the buildup of adenosine to create enough sleep pressure so that you easily fall and stay asleep at night.

###### How to Nap

Research at NASA back in 1995 found that napping for twenty-six minutes maximizes the bene�ts for alertness, focus, and motivation.168 These became known as _power naps_ , and are frequently used to improve memory, reduce blood pressure, and increase concentration. I don’t believe there is anything magic about twenty-six minutes except that it is less than forty-�ve minutes and more than ten, so set your alarm for a �fteen-to-twenty-minute nap and perhaps hit the �ve-minute snooze button if you don’t feel refreshed the �rst time your alarm goes o�. Just don’t hit it a second time!

A twenty-minute nap shouldn’t make you groggy. That feeling, known as sleep inertia, happens when we wake up in the middle of the deeper stages of non-REM sleep. By keeping the nap to about twenty minutes, you get the bene�ts of N1 and N2 sleep without su�ering from sleep inertia.

Perhaps surprisingly, some people �nd that resting without sleeping is su�cient to restore mental and physical energy. When you do, you can enter a liminal state in which you are still awake but some parts of your brain are in a sleeplike state. Many people �nd that even if they just lie down, elevate their feet on a few pillows or a chair, close their eyes, and rest for ten to �fteen minutes, they get some of the restorative e�ects of a real nap. Elevating your legs and feet slightly in this way promotes a parasympathetic response, increases venous blood �ow to the heart, may lower blood pressure slightly, and—provided you don’t ruminate on stressful topics—can shift your brain’s state toward one of more “relaxation.” No, it’s not a good idea to spend this time tapping or scrolling on your phone, as it will o�set the brain state shift you’re seeking. You need to get your mind into a sort of idling mode. _Idling_ is clearly not neuroscienti�c language. But it’s a good way to describe how our brains shift to a very di�erent

Napping, on the other hand, lets our brain enter N1 and N2 sleep, allowing even lower frequency theta waves (4–8 Hz) to emerge ~~.~~ 169 Experienced meditators can get themselves into a state where theta waves emerge quickly, although that takes practice. Relaxation techniques like those o�ered in the very next protocol can help you rest during the day without interfering with your ability to fall asleep at night.

###### COMMON QUESTIONS:

If you are not tired in the daytime, don’t force yourself to nap. Some people get through a day just �ne without naps.

People with insomnia should generally avoid naps.170 The temptation to sleep during the day can be powerful when coping with poor sleep at night. ###### WHAT TO DO:

- Do non-sleep deep rest (NSDR) if you feel tired and need to restore your mental and physical vigor. NSDR is fast, safe, e�ective, and costs nothing. It has both immediate and long-term bene�ts for your brain state, and there is evidence it can improve focus and learning. It takes as little as ten minutes, although longer versions of twenty, thirty, or even sixty minutes can be even more e�ective. It’s nearly impossible to do NSDR incorrectly (unless you are texting in the middle of a session).
  - Do NSDR �rst thing in the morning if you failed to get enough sleep the night before and want to feel more rested as you enter your day. If you don’t have time just then, I suggest you do NSDR in the midmorning or afternoon. It will still help.

  - Do NSDR at night if you have trouble falling asleep, or if you wake up in the middle of the night and can’t fall back asleep. NSDR is a far better option than tossing and turning and worrying about the sleep you’re not getting.

###### HOW IT WORKS:

First o�, it’s important to emphasize that NSDR is not anything like traditional meditation. NSDR is not breathwork either. Rather, NSDR belongs to a category of techniques that can be broadly thought of as self-directed relaxation. NSDR is also not anything like a nap. A central feature of NSDR is to stay awake (but not focused on planning or action), while simultaneously bringing the body into an extremely relaxed state. It puts you in a unique brain state.172 Meditation often involves holding one’s attention on a speci�c location inside or near one’s body (such as the spot just behind our forehead), or on an external object (a candle �ame, for example), or even on a sensory experience (e.g., the taste of a single almond). These kinds of directed perceptual focus exercises have been shown to improve concentration, reduce stress, strengthen memory and improve mental health.173 When done consistently, meditation techniques can lead to profound shifts in our awareness of our internal thought patterns. And over time, meditation can provide a rich understanding of how our minds work and can even change our temperament.

Self-directed relaxation protocols like NSDR are di�erent. NSDR involves shifting our autonomic nervous system into a more parasympathetic, or relaxed, state by breathing in a manner in which the duration of our exhales is deliberately emphasized.174 NSDR also involves deliberately and systematically moving our focus of attention from one part of our body to another, then to locations far from our body, then closer to us, then away again. The focusing, then defocusing, and moving and resetting of attention over and over keeps the mind active. And because it is done while the body is deeply relaxed, it brings about a somewhat dreamlike state, and yet you are completely aware and alert.

NSDR is a modi�cation of an ancient practice known as yoga nidra, which roughly translates to “yoga sleep.”175 Yoga nidra has been described as creating the experience of moving our mind away “from thinking and doing toward a state of being and feeling”—which is an admittedly vague statement. There is a small but growing body of modern science on the brain and bodily states that yoga nidra and NSDR bring about and their ability to restore mental and physical vigor, improve consolidation of newly learned information, o�set sleep loss, and more.

When I �rst tried yoga nidra in 2017, I found it to be incredibly restorative. Doing this technique for twenty to thirty minutes �rst thing in the morning after a restless or less-than-full night’s sleep left me feeling fully rested, like I’d had the best sleep of my life. I also noticed that incorporating this practice in the morning improved my ability to fall back asleep quickly if I happened to wake up in the middle of the night. That’s right—even though NSDR stands for nonsleep deep rest, and even though it is typically done in the morning or afternoon, something about doing it at that time signi�cantly improved my ability to selfdirect my brain and body into a relaxed state and drift back to sleep at night if ever I needed to. What’s more, if I ever woke up in the middle of the night, listening to a guided NSDR recording beat tossing and turning, and often sent me back to sleep. Challenges with falling asleep and staying asleep are very common, so I was intrigued. I also noticed that replacing an afternoon nap with an NSDR session left me feeling especially reinvigorated and did not alter my nighttime sleep in any negative way.

I wondered how this simple practice really worked. So I dove into the literature and found there wasn’t much known. But the few studies I did �nd were interesting. A 2002 study from Denmark found that doing yoga nidra dramatically increases levels of dopamine in a brain region called the basal ganglia, which are involved in taking, and withholding, action ~~.~~ 176 Yoga nidra also reduced people’s blood pressure and heart rate. Although this and other studies of yoga nidra were small in terms of the number of subjects studied, other investigations indicated that this practice could improve various measures of mental health and help consolidate certain forms of learning ~~.~~ 177

At one point, I decided to devote a portion of my lab to studying yoga nidra as a tool for stress reduction. To do so we needed to keep its core elements— breathing that emphasizes long exhales to slow the heart rate and place us into a more parasympathetic state, the deliberate and systematic movement of one’s perceptual attention to the surface and then the interior of the body, then away from the body, and so on—but we opted to remove the “intentions” and any language pertaining to more spiritual aspects of yoga nidra ~~.~~ 178 This parsing was not an attempt at cultural appropriation of an ancient tradition. Rather, it was a way to examine this powerful tool within the context of Western science, where we seek to understand what works and why, and to then use this knowledge to build more e�cient and e�ective tools. Any aspect of the practice that couldn’t be reliably measured was discarded.

Later, as I moved into public education and spoke about stress mitigation tools, I coined the term _non-sleep deep rest_ , which keeps the key elements related to the physiology of yoga nidra, but removes the subjective aspects that are hard to keep constant from one person to the next.

And eventually, given the wide interest in stress mitigation tools, my podcast team produced various NSDR scripts of short (ten minute), medium (twenty minute), and long (thirty minute) durations and made them freely available online.179

Public feedback has con�rmed the positive e�ects of NSDR, but of course it just follows the thousands of years of people across the world doing this timetested practice. (Later in chapter 3, I’ll get back to what my lab’s studies on stress discovered about the bene�ts of NSDR).

Among all the protocols that I have shared on the _Huberman Lab_ podcast, NSDR is in the top ten of those that people tell me have changed their lives, especially individuals who struggle to sleep enough, to maintain high levels of daytime energy and focus, and also among those struggling with excessive work, school, or other demands. I am the last person in the world to suggest people sleep less than they need to at night, but I will be the �rst to acknowledge how challenging it can often be to get a full seven to nine hours of sleep, especially for parents of young children and those working very long hours. NSDR is a remarkable tool for anyone who simply can’t get enough sleep because they have

to wake up and meet the demands of the day. Or for those who don’t like naps or who can’t nap for whatever reason. We will revisit NSDR several times in this book, but in the meantime, if you’re seeking tools for improving sleep, or even replacing missed sleep, I highly suggest doing NSDR.

Claims that “thirty minutes of yoga nidra is worth two hours of sleep” abound. I’ve also heard that “twenty minutes of meditation twice daily reduces your nighttime sleep needs by several hours.” I am not aware of much laboratory data supporting those statements. It can be hard to get enough sleep, and most of us would love to need less of it to feel fully rested. NSDR won’t necessarily reduce the amount of nighttime sleep you need, but it may very well improve the quality of the sleep you get. So while they weren’t sleeping less, the sleep they were getting was better than before.

The study also found a signi�cant reduction in cortisol following yoga nidra.181 That may be one factor that reduces the total amount of sleep you need because, in theory, lowering your evening cortisol should improve sleep. When it comes to getting optimal sleep, it’s always best to start with behavioral tools and changes to your sleep environment. (Sun)light exposure, adjusting your core body temperature, and NSDR can all be employed to improve sleep. So, too, can exercise and proper nutrition (more on both later). Many people turn to supplements to help improve their sleep. Parsing the scienti�c literature on the e�cacy of over-the-counter, supplement-based sleep aids can be di�cult. The studies are often small, they have con�icting results, and they are too few to provide a signi�cant body of evidence ~~.~~ 183 That being said, enough data exist to indicate that some supplements may be bene�cial and carry a very low risk of harm for most people trying them. In my opinion, these are much safer than the majority of prescription sleep medications.

A major issue when it comes to supplements is that the dose of the pills inside the bottle often does not match the dosage stated on the label ~~.~~ 184 In addition, just because a supplement contains a “natural” ingredient does not mean it is safe. And these ingredients may react badly with a prescribed medication. So a reminder here, again, to talk to your doctor before proceeding, and to only buy supplements from reputable brands. on magnesium bisglycinate than threonate for sleep but these seem to work interchangeably for this purpose.

### Approach Prescription Sleep Drugs with Caution

###### WHAT TO DO:

- Talk to your doctor. If you’re still struggling with sleep after working through the prior sleep protocols, and you have tried the stress-management protocols, too, talk to your doctor. There may be an underlying health condition that needs addressing. Or it may be that your sleep issues warrant more intensive treatment. Cognitive behavioral therapy has shown e�cacy for sustained sleep disturbance.

- Stay away from prescription sleep aids if you can. These are best avoided, unless your physician prescribes them as a last resort. Most can carry side e�ects, like confusion and daytime drowsiness. Some, like Ambien, may harm sleep architecture and glymphatic function.199 That means even if you have more time in bed, sleep might not be doing the “cleaning” job it’s designed to do. Some, like trazodone, and the DORAs (dual orexin receptor antagonists), appear safer than the others, yet it is easy to become dependent on them for sleep once you begin. None are without side e�ects, and withdrawal then carries its own set of side e�ects.

###### HOW IT WORKS:

Below I’ve described the di�erent and more common classes of sleep aids, so you can understand how each works, as well as the potential risks:

- Benzodiazepines: These drugs belong to a class often referred to as hypnotics or sedatives, although they have other e�ects too. They are often prescribed to treat insomnia. They work by increasing the e�ects of GABA.200 They are older medications that can be addictive, and can have other serious side e�ects including confusion, memory problems, unsteadiness, and slurred speech.201 The withdrawal from benzodiazepines is notoriously hard. Non-benzodiazepine hypnotics: These short-term insomnia medications tend to be less disruptive than benzodiazepines ~~.~~ 202 The most well-known is Ambien. However, the FDA has issued a “black box” warning for nonbenzodiazepines following reports of rare but dangerous behavior during sleep, including wandering, driving, and using a stove, and amnesia and other forms of memory alterations after the drug has worn o�.203 And again, Ambien may harm sleep architecture and glymphatic function, the clearance of waste products from the brain at night ~~.~~ 204

- Antidepressants: Drowsiness is a common side e�ect of certain antidepressants, leading to their use as a sleep aid. The American Academy of Sleep Medicine has recommended the use of certain antidepressants as a treatment for insomnia among people with depression, but clinical evidence for this bene�t is limited.205 Trazodone, a serotonin receptor agonist and reuptake inhibitor (SARI) seems to preserve sleep architecture better than other antidepressants when taken speci�cally for sleep.206 Please note that many people who take selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) like Prozac, SARIs like trazodone, or norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitors (NDRIs) like Wellbutrin/bupropion during the daytime for depression, anxiety, or other reasons do not experience altered sleep, and some of these, like bupropion, when taken early in the daytime, can indirectly improve sleep later that night.207 Psychiatrists now will prescribe antidepressants speci�cally for sleep because some can improve sleep.

- Melatonin receptor agonists: This category of medications mimics the action of melatonin and may help with falling asleep faster and improving sleep quality. They do not appear to cause dependency or serious side e�ects.208 However, the e�cacy of melatonin receptor agonists is somewhat unclear.

- Anticonvulsants and dopamine agonist drugs: These may be prescribed to treat restless legs syndrome and other conditions involving nighttime limb movement that can make it di�cult to fall and stay asleep ~~,~~ 209 as well as to treat pain. Examples include gabapentin and cabergoline.

- Dual orexin receptor antagonists (DORAs): Insomnia is characterized by abnormal wakefulness, and orexin, a neuropeptide that helps regulate the sleep-wake cycle and that is altered in narcolepsy, has been found to cause a state of arousal.210 Thus it makes sense to investigate orexin as a potential target for insomnia drugs. That led to the development of the DORAs, which work by reducing the action of orexin and thus wakefulness circuits in the brain rather than by direct sedation ~~.~~ 211 Early evidence of such drugs shows that they do e�ectively block orexin, and indicate a potential role for them in safely treating insomnia.212 A meta-analysis of ten randomized clinical trials that combined a sample of 7,086 individuals with insomnia found these drugs to be generally safe, with a comparably lower incidence of mild side e�ects and with improved sleep compared to a placebo ~~.~~ 213 These new medications are expensive, typically costing about $300 or more per month.214 Generic lower-cost versions are not yet available.

### Adjust Your Caffeine Schedule to Improve Your Sleep

###### WHAT TO DO:

- Avoid caffeine in the eight to ten hours before bed. As it’s a stimulant with a long half-life, ca�eine should be avoided late in the day, especially if you have trouble falling asleep. Some people who are especially ca�eine sensitive may have to avoid ca�eine in the twelve hours before bedtime. Even those who can “fall asleep after drinking co�ee” are likely not getting the best sleep they could. As someone who loves ca�eine, I relate to anyone reluctant to stop drinking ca�eine in the afternoon. As painful as it can be, I personally avoid it after 2:00 p.m. most days.

- If you tend to experience an energy crash in the afternoon despite sleeping well, consider delaying drinking caffeine until thirty to ninety minutes after waking up. This slight adjustment to your ca�eine schedule may help you have more sustained energy levels throughout the day and may help you avoid the need to drink ca�eine after 2:00 p.m.

###### HOW IT WORKS:

Remember adenosine, from Sleep Protocol 7? It’s a chemical that builds up in our brains as we go throughout our day, eventually making us want to sleep through a process called homeostatic sleep drive.215

Our scienti�c understanding of adenosine is deeply intertwined with that of ca�eine ~~.~~ 216 The research history dates back to 1911, when Coca-Cola asked a psychologist named Harry Levi Hollingworth to investigate the e�ects of ca�eine on human behavior because the US government was suing the company for including what it considered to be a drug with a “poisonous tendency” in the soda. (The cocaine that had once been a major ingredient of Coca-Cola had been removed years earlier. ~~)~~ 217 The company wanted reliable evidence on exactly how ca�eine altered human behavior. Hollingworth agreed as long as the company did not include his study results in its advertisements. He also insisted that the results be published regardless of what they revealed.

Hollingworth’s investigation is often cited as the �rst time that the doubleblind, placebo-controlled study design entered psychological research.218 Although some may argue whether it was indeed a double-blind study, it is considered a landmark for its introduction of rigor into the process, and for its �ndings. Sixteen participants consumed ca�eine daily at a range of doses (at amounts re�ecting drinking a daily soda) or a placebo. They then completed various tasks that examined their alertness, coordination, and other mental skills. Ca�eine undeniably improved their capacity in all these domains. The �ndings were favorable toward Coca-Cola because the chemical in question seemed to only help people, not hurt them, at least in the context of what was measured. But Coca-Cola wasn’t interested in sleep. (If you were wondering, the US government’s case was dismissed on a technicality when the company argued that ca�eine wasn’t added to the beverage but rather was naturally occurring.)

According to Hollingworth’s report, published in the _American Journal of Psychology_ in 1912, a few grains of ca�eine taken on successive days were enough to impair sleep.219 The connection relied on self-reporting and each individual recording their impression about the quality of their sleep following each study day. But the �ndings were consistent.

Decades later we know how that happens: Ca�eine leads to longer sleep latency (that is, the time it takes to fall asleep) and more nighttime waking, thus leading to reduced wakefulness the next day.220 We also now know that ca�eine can alter sleep architecture, including less time spent in REM.221

Hollingworth’s study was the �rst of many to come. Today we understand a great deal about how ca�eine stimulates brain activity. It’s a psychoactive stimulant that increases the actions of epinephrine and dopamine, in part by increasing the availability of dopamine receptors, the sites on cells where it can attach and thereby initiate its e�ects.222 Ca�eine also increases the activity of certain neural circuits and brain areas associated with alertness, such as the locus coeruleus, which we discussed earlier in this chapter.223 We also understand now how it interferes with sleep. That brings us back to adenosine.

Ca�eine is what is called an adenosine antagonist ~~.~~ 224 It parks in adenosine receptors, which prevents adenosine from exerting its normal fatigue-inducing activity in the brain. As sleep expert Matthew Walker describes it, “Ca�eine keeps pulling out the chairs from under adenosine.”225 So even though adenosine is building up with each hour we are awake and increasingly so when we are very alert or active, our brains don’t register that fatigue or the number of hours we’ve been awake accurately ~~.~~ 226 Ca�eine dampens the communication between adenosine and the brain.

This process explains the phenomenon many of us know of as the ca�eine crash. This all sounds rough, but I want to reiterate: I love ca�eine and I have no plans to give it up. The data say ca�eine in moderation is �ne… and may even be good for us. A recent large-scale study involving over 100,000 subjects found that daily intake of approximately two to three cups of ca�einated co�ee or tea can reduce risks of stroke and dementia ~~.~~ 227

“What is moderation?” you may be wondering. One or two cups of strong co�ee, a few twelve-ounce diet sodas (we can debate arti�cial sweeteners later, in chapter 4, but we should all probably avoid the sugar in regular soda), or my

Ca�eine is hard to study.
