### Avoid Alcohol Within Eight Hours Before Sleep

###### WHAT NOT TO DO:

- Alcohol should not be used as a sleep aid. Alcohol severely disrupts the elegantly sequential architecture of sleep, and reduces both the total amount of deep sleep and REM sleep, so even if it helps you drift o� and you sleep for seven to eight hours, it will negatively a�ect the quality of your sleep.

- If you drink, avoid alcohol within eight hours of the time you plan to be asleep. This timing reduces the amount of alcohol in your body by the time you go to bed.

The “What Alcohol Does to Your Body, Brain & Health” episode of the _Huberman Lab_ podcast remains one of the top downloaded and shared podcast episodes of all time, across all podcasts. It makes clear that the data show zero to two drinks per week is �ne for nonalcoholic adults without confounding medical issues. However, zero is better than any, and there is growing data on the increased risk of cancer associated with alcohol consumption ~~.~~ 237

I am not anti-alcohol! I know some people enjoy a drink now and again and that is my motivation for the inclusion of this protocol. I subscribe to a “do as you like, but know what you’re doing” philosophy. I personally don’t drink but I have never liked the taste or e�ects of alcohol.

But there’s a key question for everyone that has not been addressed: Are many of the negative e�ects of alcohol the consequence of the negative e�ects of alcohol on sleep? This has not been systematically studied, but for those that like a drink now and again (and also for those who abstain), keep that question in the back of your mind as you read the section below.

###### HOW IT WORKS:

Alcohol is a sedative that a�ects the neural pathways associated with sleep in multiple ways. Alcohol decreases the amount of time it takes us to fall asleep.238 But what happens next is not good. During the �rst half of the night, the presence of alcohol in the body suppresses REM sleep and it takes longer for us to reach whatever REM sleep we do manage to achieve.239 Remember that each sleep stage is like a gate to the next, so the reduced REM means less deep sleep, and less REM in the next cycle. As discussed earlier in this chapter, REM sleep is critical to our cognitive functioning, to consolidating new information, and to daytime emotional regulation. So missing out on any amount of REM is a problem. And alcohol is a potent REM suppressor.

Alcohol has also been found to decrease the amount of growth hormone and testosterone released during the night—hormones critical for vitality and metabolism for both men and women ~~.~~ 240 Normally, growth hormone is released relatively soon after falling asleep, and testosterone is released before and during REM sleep.241 The negative e�ects of alcohol on REM and these hormones happen acutely, meaning after even just a single night of drinking or for those who are alcohol sensitive, even one drink. Only if we metabolize the alcohol prior to bedtime do we avoid some of these consequences, which is why this protocol recommends a speci�c timing.

Chronic drinking is even more problematic for sleep. Insomnia and alcohol dependency frequently coexist, for example.242 The cycle is self-perpetuating in that poor sleep leads to increased ca�eine and other stimulant use during the day and into the afternoon and evening, which leads to di�culty sleeping at night, which leads to alcohol intake as a sleep aid. Beyond the changes one or two drinks can make on REM sleep, people with alcohol dependency tend to have

decreased amounts of both N2 and N3 sleep, the non-REM period when we sink into a deep sleep ~~.~~ 243 These alterations in sleep architecture can persist for some time even after a person stops drinking. Frequent drinking also interferes with our circadian rhythm, disrupting or even decreasing the amount of melatonin our brains produce.244

Adolescents are at particular risk of turning to alcohol intake as a sleep aid. In 2008, public health researchers at the University of Texas Health Science Center reported their �ndings from a large, yearlong study of insomnia among youth between the ages of eleven and seventeen years. They collected data on 3,134 people in this age range from a baseline date and then twelve months later and found that chronic insomnia heightened the risk of alcohol use.245 That’s concerning because insomnia is the most common sleep disorder among young people, and because nighttime phone use, which is very common in this age group, also interferes with sleep quality and duration ~~.~~ 246 Phone use at night has been linked to insomnia.247

That means there are two major risks to this age group when it comes to good sleep, not to mention the chronic stress that kids at that age face. We’ll discuss phone use in Sleep Protocol 14.

It’s not practical to avoid alcohol within eight hours of sleep because any drinking I do<br>happens at night. How can I compensate for the negative effects of consuming alcohol close<br>to bedtime?<br><!-- End of picture text -->

For most people, social drinking happens well within eight hours of going to sleep. What’s important here is that drinking this way every night, multiple times per week, or even once per week will disrupt sleep, and thereby health, in detrimental ways. Occasional alcohol use closer to bedtime, say once a month or less, is very unlikely to cause long-term problems, unless it’s excessive during that once-a-month night out.

If you drink in the eight hours before sleep, make sure you also consume su�cient water before going to sleep and after waking. Take electrolytes too if you can, and emphasize other behaviors that support great sleep, as well as a healthy microbiome, to try to o�set the e�ects of alcohol.

To be clear, it’s good to enjoy life. If having a few drinks during a celebration or a night out now and again is how you do, you’re not alone. The important considerations are that this isn’t happening too often, that you’re not driving, that you’re not experiencing any kind of dependency, and that you’re not too young to drink (the negative e�ects of alcohol are much worse for the developing brain compared to the adult brain) ~~.~~ 248

Not with respect to the negative e�ects on sleep and the microbiome. As mentioned above, no alcohol is better than any alcohol. Although many studies have been done on the potential bene�ts of red wine, conclusive evidence of this link does not exist.249 The amount of red wine you would need to drink to get bene�ts from grape skin, for example, would require consumption of enough alcohol to far outweigh any bene�ts. ### Avoid Cannabis as a Sleep Aid

###### WHAT TO DO:

- Do not use cannabis specifically for sleep. Cannabis should not be used to facilitate falling asleep or returning to sleep after night wakings. It potently reduces REM sleep.

- Understand CBD’s impact on sleep. Some evidence exists on the bene�t of CBD for sleep but those e�ects are mainly due to the reduced anxiety it causes ~~.~~ 250 At higher dosages (e.g., 160 mg or more), CBD is more of a sedative. The dosage of CBD that makes it an e�ective sleep aid varies depending on weight and other factors ~~.~~ 251

###### HOW IT WORKS:

Cannabis is a psychoactive drug that comes from the cannabis plant. The main chemical behind its psychoactive e�ects is THC (delta-9tetrahydrocannabinol) ~~.~~ 252 CBD, or cannabidiol, is another well-known component of the cannabis plant; this chemical technically is psychoactive, too, because it impacts the brain, but it’s not responsible for the “high” that people are usually seeking when they use cannabis. THC can impair cognitive or behavioral functioning; CBD doesn’t appear to do so ~~.~~ 253 When present with THC in the cannabis plant or in an edible, CBD can modify the way that THC works in the brain, so their ratios can determine the subjective e�ects of the drug ~~.~~ 254

THC potently reduces the amount of REM sleep even at low doses.255 THC is often used as an aid for falling asleep, as its psychoactive properties are often accompanied by, or followed by, drowsiness. As with alcohol, people often come to depend on THC to fall asleep, which disrupts the sleep-wake cycle, and can put them at risk for the physical and mental health issues associated with a de�ciency in REM sleep, including depression and cardiovascular disease, among other issues ~~.~~ 256 Not everyone who uses cannabis experiences these challenges of course but the link between REM sleep and health is solid: THC reduces REM. Ask people who have used cannabis regularly and then stopped and you’ll often hear about the wild dreams they experience afterward. That is the REM-rebound compensation for the lack of REM they experienced while using cannabis.257

A multidisciplinary team at McMaster University, in Canada, conducted a review of the scienti�c literature on the link between cannabinoids and sleep.258 One of their most noteworthy �ndings was that the direct e�ects of both THC and CBD on sleep are lacking data because most clinical studies of cannabis have focused on various health conditions, such as pain, post-traumatic stress disorder, or glaucoma. The researchers did identify data showing that cannabinoids could have a positive impact on sleep. But the small size of these studies and the fact that examining this connection was not the main objective of the investigations somewhat limits the usefulness of the �ndings. Furthermore, THC and CBD are vastly di�erent, which makes any reference to _cannabinoids_ confusing and unhelpful.

A survey of 4,637 ninth through twelfth graders in Colorado found that those who consumed cannabis through edibles or vaping tended to sleep fewer than seven hours per night.259 Another study of adolescents found that the sedative e�ects of THC were followed by increased wakefulness at night and impaired memory the next day, which could have been directly due to the THC, which is known to impair memory, lack of sleep, or both ~~.~~ 260

Researchers have also found a potential link between use of cannabis among pregnant mothers and poor sleep habits among their children during adolescence.261 You might be asking, “How many pregnant women use

cannabis?” A recent report said that anywhere from 4 to 12 percent of pregnant mothers in the US said they’d used cannabis during pregnancy, usually by edible and usually in the �rst trimester prior to learning they were pregnant.262 Cannabis use during pregnancy has reportedly increased in recent years, from 3.4 percent in 2002 to 7 percent in 2017.263 Smoking or ingesting cannabis during pregnancy has been tied to lower birth weight, possibly due to THCinduced changes to the placenta.264 Rates of neonatal and infant death are higher with cannabis use during pregnancy compared to no such use (and combining cannabis with nicotine raises this risk even higher).265

Many people use CBD to try to induce sleep, but rigorous evidence of a direct bene�t to sleep is currently insu�cient. Chances are any positive e�ects of CBD on sleep are due to its anxiety-lowering e�ects. CBD may help people to stop ruminating—a prerequisite to falling asleep. As such, there are populations for whom CBD may be useful. In one study, �fty-seven of seventy-two adults with anxiety reported improved sleep with the use of CBD, although this study was retrospective, meaning the participants were reporting their recall of possible e�ects from memory rather than measuring them directly.266 A 2025 review of twenty-nine studies identi�ed a potential for CBD to reduce sleep disruptions but emphasized that research on this link has su�ered from a lack of standardization.267 There certainly is enough evidence to warrant continued study of CBD in this context and no known negative e�ects of CBD that would preclude trying it for sleep if you feel stressed at night. That said, in January 2024, a team from Australia published the results of a small, randomized, placebo-controlled study in which �fteen people received 150 milligrams of CBD and �fteen people received a placebo as a sleep aid to combat insomnia.268 The investigators observed no di�erence between the two groups in the time it took to fall asleep, the e�ciency of their sleep, the duration of sleep, or overall severity of insomnia. There were some signs of an improved mood upon waking among the CBD group, and that group had fewer night wakings after two weeks of treatment.

One more thing: An increasing number of studies report a potential for THC (but not CBD) to induce psychosis in certain individuals.269

If your goal is to improve your sleep, there are better tools covered in the other protocols of this chapter. The same goes for stress management—more reliable tools exist (and these can improve sleep too), which I’ll explain in a later chapter.

### Avoid Screens Within an Hour or More Before Bedtime

###### WHAT TO DO:

- Avoid screens in the bedroom at night. This includes phones, laptops, tablets, and TV screens.

- Avoid consuming information on an electronic device within an hour (at least) of bedtime. Light from phones and other screens can disrupt your circadian clock.

- If you opt to read or watch content on a screen in the hour before sleep, dim the screen. I suggest lowering the brightness and/or activating the “red” screen function. You can also wear blue and green (short wavelength) blocking glasses.

###### HOW IT WORKS:

In 2011, the National Sleep Foundation conducted a poll ~~.~~ 270 They asked 1,508 Americans about their sleep habits, whether any technology was around them in the hour before bed, and if so, what it was and how they used it. Ninety percent of respondents said they used some kind of screen device at this time; for those under thirty, that percentage climbed to 96! Adolescent and young adult respondents were more likely to use cell phones or play video games before bed compared to adults over thirty, and the same went for computers and digital music players. I strongly suspect those percentages have either held constant or increased in the last decade and a half. In 2011, watching television was the most

common activity among the entire sample. Others included doing homework, using social media, using a smartphone, sending work emails, and other activities. The researchers also asked about reading printed books and magazines before bed, which about half of respondents reported doing.

More than half the respondents—63 percent, to be exact—said they didn’t get enough sleep on weeknights. And nearly all the people who reported insu�cient sleep said it negatively a�ected both their personal and professional lives. The high rates of late-night technology use and insu�cient sleep seen in the survey responses didn’t automatically mean the two were related, so the researchers conducted some statistical analyses to check for such a link. They found that di�culty falling asleep rose in keeping with the amount of technology people used in the hour before bed. More passive devices like e- readers were less problematic than interactive devices like game consoles, cell phones, and laptops.

These screens are illuminated by LEDs, and as we’ve discussed in this chapter, this type of lighting is disruptive to our circadian rhythm. Evidence suggests that LED screens can interrupt melatonin production, which, as you now know, is essential for sleep. In 2014, a group of sleep researchers at Harvard Medical School reported that people who read on an e-book at night with a dim bedside light took longer to fall asleep, were less sleepy, had lower levels of melatonin, and were less alert the next morning compared to people who read a printed book with a dim bedside light before bed.271

And there’s more. In 2018, a team of researchers, including UCLA psychiatrist Peter Whybrow, reviewed the data on the potential link between LED lighting and mental health ~~.~~ 272 They concluded that exposure to blue light, in particular, posed a risk to sleep and other processes governed by the circadian system. There is also evidence suggesting that the way in which arti�cial lighting at night interferes with this system may lead to depression ~~.~~ 273

The problem with devices at bedtime is not solely due to the type of lighting. Technology, particularly interactive technology, stimulates our brains in a way that counters the calm that we need in order to fall asleep. For example, the devices in the 2018 study were most strongly linked to di�culty falling asleep

and to poor sleep quality. Also, people who sleep with their phones in their rooms with the ringer on contributed to the numbers reported in the study, indicating that the problem isn’t just about late-night scrolling.

We have known since at least the 1970s that the bedroom should be reserved for sleep and intimacy.274 The evidence linking various stimuli to insomnia is well established. Yet decades later, here we are, with about 1,350 out of 1,508 randomly selected Americans ignoring this basic practice.

Believe it or not (believe it!), this protocol is one of the most potent in this chapter. It’s also one of the most di�cult to stick to for many people. Sleepbased apps and the use of smartphones as alarm clocks don’t make it any easier. Still: I highly suggest you try it.

### A Tip Sheet for Avoiding Jet Lag

Some people experience terrible jet lag, others far less so. This changes as we age. And it depends on where we �y—which direction and if we need to push ourselves to wake earlier or stay awake later than usual. The latter is always easier for people.

Five factors allow you to shift your circadian clock. Knowing these can help you switch to a new time zone quickly, which allows you to be more e�ective on work trips and enjoy vacations more fully. The factors you use to entrain your SCN to a new local light-dark cycle are, in descending order of in�uence:

- Light

- Temperature

- Meal times

- Exercise

- Social factors

You might think: Can’t I just hop on the local schedule? Alas, that’s hard because your SCN is entrained to wherever you have been for the prior week or so before your trip. So for instance if you �y from California to London and arrive at 5:00 p.m. and you view the sunset, your SCN thinks it’s morning sunlight and it wakes you up. But there is a way to overcome this. I’ll explain.

###### WHAT TO DO:

###### BEFORE YOU TRAVEL EAST

Eastward travel is typically more challenging for the body. Why? Most people �nd it easier to stay awake later than to fall asleep earlier. But you can prepare for your trip and partially adjust your circadian rhythm before you leave:

- Get early bright light exposure, but be careful when. When traveling east, you need to shift to waking up earlier than you normally would. Starting two days before you leave, try waking up thirty to forty-�ve minutes prior to your usual wake-up time and view bright sunlight or bright arti�cial light as soon as you wake up.

- Drink caffeine early. This will help promote alertness early in the day and make it much easier to shift to your new time zone when you travel.

- Get moving. Within sixty minutes of your new, earlier wake-up time, exercise. Even just some light jogging will help if you can’t do a full workout.

These three levers—light, ca�eine, and exercise—will help adjust your circadian clock to your new eastward-of-typical location, fast.

###### BEFORE YOU TRAVEL WEST

As mentioned earlier, westward travel tends to be easier for most people. That said, it can still help to adjust your circadian rhythm before you leave by using light, exercise, and ca�eine. In this case, however, you’ll want to shift everything thirty to forty-�ve minutes later in the day as opposed to earlier. A slightly later wake-up time, a slightly later ca�eine intake in the morning and early afternoon (but still avoid ca�eine in the eight to ten hours prior to bedtime), and a slightly later workout—even just by forty-�ve minutes—will all help.

You’ll also want to make sure that you view bright light from arti�cial lights one to two hours after sunset. Remember, you’re trying to prepare to stay up later as you soon �y westward.

WHEN YOU ARRIVE AT YOUR NEW DESTINATION (REGARDLESS OF WHETHER YOU FLEW EAST OR WEST)

- Eat like a local. Adopting the local meal schedule when you arrive—eating breakfast, lunch, and dinner more or less at the same times as the locals, even if you’re not hungry—will help you shift your circadian clock to the new time zone. Personally, I hate to eat when I’m not hungry (and love to eat when I am!), so I opt out of this protocol. If it works for you, go for it. The sooner you can get on the local meal schedule, the better. Many �nd it e�ective to fast for a period of fourteen to sixteen hours before the local breakfast time so they are very hungry when that time arrives.

Time your light exposure correctly by knowing your temperature minimum. This is the real power tool to shift your circadian clock fast, but it involves learning your _temperature minimum_ �rst. See Sleep Protocol 3 and Sleep Protocol 5 for more on that topic. For now, know that it occurs approximately two hours before your usual wake-up time. If you typically wake up at 7:00 a.m., your temperature minimum is very likely to be between 4:30 a.m. and 5:30 a.m. Here’s the key: If you get bright light exposure in the one to two hours after your temperature minimum, you will adjust your circadian clock such that it will make you want to go to sleep earlier on the subsequent nights and wake up earlier on the subsequent mornings. Perfect for traveling east. Conversely, if you get bright light exposure in the one to two hours before your temperature minimum, you will shift your circadian clock such that it will make you want to go to sleep later on the subsequent nights and wake up later on the subsequent mornings. Perfect for traveling west.

But remember we are referring to the time of your temperature minimum before you leave! This is vital to understand. Get it right and you’ll shift fast across time zones. Get it wrong and it can be a mess.

Why? Well, think about this. Imagine you �y from San Francisco to London (+8 hours). You land in the morning London time and the sun is out. I said get morning sunlight in your eyes, right? Yes, but for the �rst two to three days in London before you adjust your clock, viewing that London morning sunlight is the same to your brain’s clock as getting a

giant blast of light in your eyes at midnight San Francisco time. So you just made your body want to go to bed much later and wake up later. You got it backward. Many people sleep well their �rst night after �ying east, wake up, see sunlight, and the second night is a mess. They can’t sleep! It would be better to wear dark sunglasses during the two to three hours before your temperature minimum for the �rst two days in London. After those �rst two or three days, just view sunlight per the recommendations earlier in this chapter.

Obviously, I am just using London as an example. You must �gure it out based on your own travel destination. I know it sounds complicated, but if you know the time of your temperature minimum back home, and follow the instructions above, you’ll nail this protocol easily.

Use artificial light and blue and green (short wavelength) blocking glasses as tools. Of course, it’s often very cloudy, or you may land at night, and we can’t control the time of sunrise and sunset—though if you can, please contact me.

What you can do, however, is travel with a portable bright light device (you’ll want one with 5,000- to 10,000-lux brightness) to shift your circadian clock. Several are the size of a book and thin enough to �t in a carry-on bag. I have no a�liation with any companies that make these, but I use the Verilux Happy Light when I travel. They cost about $50. At home I use a larger countertop unit, the Carex Daylight (also no a�liation) and Ra Optics or Bon Charge full-spectrum LED bulbs in the daytime, as discussed earlier. Remember that even when it is cloudy, sunlight through cloud cover is still almost always far brighter than arti�cial lighting. Get outside and view that sunlight at the correct times and you’ll shift your circadian clock fast. Then, you can return to the standard protocols to stay on the local schedule.

One more thing we can all control is the brightness of our evening and nighttime environment. As you get ready for bed, reduce exposure to bright lights—especially blue and green, or short-wavelength, light. Alas, as you now know, all LED lights are rich in blue and green wavelengths. For that reason, I wear blue and green (short wavelength) blocking glasses

after sundown to help adjust to the local schedule. This protocol is known to protect against the melatonin-reducing e�ects of bright light and to prevent the cortisol-increasing e�ects of bright light.

Maintain a regular exercise schedule. While traveling, try to maintain a consistent early-in-the-day exercise routine (adjusted to the local

schedule). That, too, helps shift your circadian clock.

- A final tip. For trips that last fewer than two days, staying on (or near) your home sleep-wake, eating, and exercise schedule can be bene�cial to minimize disruptions to your circadian rhythm.

These tips will help you quickly overcome any jet lag in your future travels—they’ve certainly helped me over the years, as well as people in the military, medical professions working night shifts, and more.

The cardiovascular exercise group walked for increasing durations of time, reaching a

And they did three sessions per week. The participants continued with that regimen for a year. According to the results, the hippocampus—a brain region associated with learning and memory—increased in volume by about 2 percent among the cardiovascular group, whereas it shrank by about 1.4 percent among the stretching-only group. While that might not seem like a lot, these �ndings are noteworthy because a shrinking hippocampus is linked to memory impairments during the later decades of life. A rather simple low-intensity exercise intervention seems to not only prevent brain deterioration but also trigger brain growth. Other studies, including those exploring higherintensity exercise and resistance training show similar—and in some cases greater —neuroplasticity brought about by exercise.12

It perhaps shouldn’t surprise us that exercise can open the gates for learning in the brain. A disproportionate amount of our brain’s volume is devoted to generating our movements. Rodolfo Llinás, MD, PhD, a neuroscientist at NYU School of Medicine, cites an odd but telling example of the sea squirt, a spineless marine creature ~~.~~ 13 Young sea squirts swim freely until they are fully grown. The adults then stick themselves onto a rock and become �lter feeders, catching whatever happens to �oat by. When this transition from swimming to sedentary occurs, sea squirts eat their own brains, leaving only what is necessary for their new passive style of feeding. Llinás’s story about a distantly related animal is relevant to us for two reasons. First, it provides a warning to humans with an overly sedentary lifestyle. As humans age and become less mobile, their brains degenerate too, albeit not as dramatically as does the sea squirt brain.14 Second, people who continue to exercise—in particular those who do exercise that is challenging (but safe) for them, o�set much of typical age-related brain loss that is otherwise observed. This has real implications, allowing them to maintain youthful cognitive function well into their later years, possibly through neurogenesis, the addition of new brain neurons ~~.~~ 15 Deliberate, repetitive, e�ortful movements that elicit the short-term stress responses (discussed throughout this chapter) trigger a battery of chemical and neural feedback

signals to the brain, which both supports the existing brain cells and the connections we would otherwise lose over time, as well as releases signals that cause neurons to grow new connections. This makes sense if you think about the sea squirt anecdote once more. Our brain is the most metabolically demanding organ in our body. Much of that organ is devoted to our ability to generate movement ~~.~~ 16 If we don’t move, much of our brain is less active too. Am I telling you that we must exercise just to maintain the brain capacity we have? Indeed I am. Exercise—provided it is of su�cient intensity—makes us cognitively resilient.

The bene�ts of exercise to brain health and neuroplasticity turn out to be robust at every age, for women, for men, for people vulnerable to age-related cognitive decline, and for both neurologically healthy and unhealthy people alike. Resistance training and cardiovascular training both impart huge bene�ts, but their combination (typically in separate workouts) turns out to be the most e�ective stimulus for brain health and neuroplasticity ~~.~~ 17 And when mobility and �exibility, and walking, are added in, the positive results increase signi�cantly.

Some of the e�ects of exercise on brain health and neuroplasticity are the result of something called brain-derived neurotrophic factor, or BDNF, a protein our brain makes that can exert a powerful role on learning and memory by virtue of its ability to sculpt and reinforce new neural circuit connections.18 Numerous studies have found that exercise leads to elevated levels of BDNF in the brain ~~.~~ 19 These elevations are temporary,20 but enough to open the window for neuroplasticity for several hours after the exercise has ceased. Exercise also increases the release of catecholamines:21 that dopamine, epinephrine, norepinephrine trio that we discussed in the chapter on sleep and that we will revisit throughout this book. When that trio is deployed in the body and brain, our levels of alertness and focus are increased, allowing us to access the memories, skills, and cognitive abilities we harbor in our neural circuits. As neuromodulators, the catecholamines also can open the opportunity for neuroplasticity. (I explain this process in more detail in chapter 6.)

The way to think about the e�ects of exercise on brain health and neuroplasticity, therefore, is that moderate-to-intense exercise reinforces and

maintains the brain functions we already have and lets us access the best of our attentional systems for focus and memory. It also opens the window for you to learn at an accelerated rate after the exercise session. Exercise alone won’t make you smarter, but it opens the door for you to become smarter, should you decide to put in the e�ort to do so. (Chapter 6 explains the best and fastest way to do that.)

It’s important to remember that any learning facilitated by elevated levels of BDNF is not con�ned to the neural circuits involved in the exercise that triggered it. Rather, BDNF will facilitate whatever learning we pursue while its levels are elevated. As one of many examples, just six minutes of intense running improved the ability of twenty-seven healthy adults to learn new words.22 The improvements in learning and retention were tied to elevated levels of BDNF, along with elevated catecholamines: dopamine and epinephrine. Moderate-tohigh-intensity exercise is arguably the best type of workout to trigger this process. People will debate whether resistance training is as e�ective at increasing neuroplasticity as cardiovascular training is. The key variable seems to be the intensity of training; it has to be su�ciently high. When done correctly, resistance training can be at least as taxing as intense cardiovascular training when viewed through the lens of neurological demand, and perhaps more ~~.~~ 23

Another way that exercise supports our brain and body is that it markedly improves sleep quality and duration.24 Remember from chapter 1: Morning workouts appear to shorten the amount of time it takes to fall asleep at night, and regular exercise has been found to improve the overall quality of sleep for adults. In a study including forty-eight adults with insomnia, moderate aerobic exercise improved sleep, and helped the participants feel less stressed ~~.~~ 25

One caveat. If exercise is very intense and done too close to your desired bedtime, it can be detrimental to sleep. (We cover this more in chapter 1 and chapter 3.) It’s best to either avoid intense exercise in the hours prior to sleep, or if you can’t, to make sure you engage in some deliberate downregulation practices, such as a few minutes of long-exhale breathing or a hot shower, so that it does not negatively impact your sleep.

There are many reasons why appropriately timed exercise improves sleep. As discussed in chapter 1, the chemical adenosine, which not only builds up in the brain and body throughout the day but is also further increased with exercise, creates an increasing pressure to sleep.26 So exercise helps promote great sleep and reduces factors that lead to poor sleep. Regular physical activity also appears to increase the amount of time we spend in restorative slow-wave deep sleep, regardless of what time of day we exercise, and that translates to us feeling more rested when we wake ~~.~~ 27

Then there is the bene�t of moderate to intense exercise on our subjective waking experience, speci�cally on our feelings of well-being. Although “wellbeing” might sound nonscienti�c, for a lot of people it’s an important barometer they use to gauge their quality of life. People who don’t like exercise often look at me askance when I say that exercise improves mood, and not just because it helps us sleep better. But it’s true: Exercise makes us happy.28 And relaxed ~~.~~ 29 A moderate to intense workout is a proven, excellent way to snap ourselves out of a slump.30 Exercise reduces our baseline levels of stress,31 increases our capacity to show resilience in a wide range of circumstances,32 and reduces anger.33 These mood enhancements of exercise come from several di�erent chemicals: dopamine, which increases motivation, focus, energy, and cognitive function;34 and serotonin, which does many things, including help make us more resistant to challenges.

And here’s a fun fact: The lactate your body produces during high-intensity exercise can physically modify—or lactylate—proteins in the brain, altering how neurons communicate. A recent study found that lactate production spurred by exercise reduced anxiety-related behaviors in mice, apparently by supporting the molecular machinery present at synapses between neurons in the prefrontal cortex. 35 The prefrontal cortex has many parts and functions, but will come up repeatedly in this book in the context of reducing impulsivity, decreasing anxiety, and learning new information and skills.36

There’s more. Exercise has a surprising e�ect on our energy levels. The relationship between exercise and energy is key to understand, especially for those who feel they don’t have the energy to exercise. After all, exercise requires

energy, right? Right. For those who don’t enjoy it or who have a ton of demands on their schedule and may not be sleeping well or enough, that’s especially true. Add in a bit of low-level or major depression, anxiety about �nances or the state of the world, or challenges with relationships in your life and, voila: You have a person who quite understandably does not want to exercise, and very likely won’t exercise, no matter how many studies about its bene�ts or inspirational tales they see and hear. If this is you or someone you know, I hope what I’m about to share will help.

Yes, exercise requires energy to initiate and to complete, but it also gives us energy. I’m not just referring to energy in the psychological sense. I mean it gives us _actual chemical energy_ and it does so by changing the electrical state of your nervous system. Work from neuroscientist Peter Strick’s laboratory, at the University of Pittsburgh, identi�ed three sets of brain areas that, when activated, communicate with our adrenal glands to cause them to release adrenaline.37 In turn, this adrenaline activates receptors on our vagus nerve, which is a dense neural pathway that bidirectionally connects our body and brain. Our vagus nerve then triggers the release of norepinephrine from the locus coeruleus, which in turn can increase release of dopamine, acetylcholine, and other neuromodulators in other brain centers.38 Other research found that exercise enhances a group of neurons in the hypothalamus—known as VMH SF1 neurons—whose activity is required in order for endurance-speci�c adaptations to occur. 39 Meaning, the brain is what actually coordinates the speci�c bodily adaptations that e�ective exercise triggers. Put di�erently, your body changes because your brain tells it to.

While the abilities of our brain to energize and change our body are incredible, the key practical questions are: “What are the magical brain areas that, when made active, �ick the �rst domino in this brain–adrenals–vagus– locus coeruleus/basal ganglia circuit? And how do we activate those brain areas?” The answer, Strick found, is a set of brain regions that control voluntary movement of the major muscles of the limbs—and the core muscles; yes, your abdominals, or abs, but also the sheets of muscles below and all around them, such as the rectus abdominis and obliques. Translation: Deliberate movement of

your limbs and your core muscles creates chemical energy that activates your brain to _want_ to further move your body, and gives you heightened levels of motivation to continue doing so.

We can use that exercise-induced energy not just to exercise more or harder. It can be directed toward cognitive activities in the hours after you exercise or simply to go about the tasks of your day with more motivation and focus. Provided we don’t exercise to the point of exhaustion, exercise markedly improves our brain function, psychological state, and overall energy levels. Yes, it involves hormones. Yes, it involves endorphins (everyone seems to know this based on the notion of a “runner’s high”). But it also involves a shift in brain state.

And exercise a�ects more than just our brain. There’s perhaps the most familiar bene�t: our heart health. In 1986 researchers from Stanford and Harvard reported their �ndings from sixteen years of tracking physical activity and the causes of death of nearly seventeen thousand people between the ages of thirty-�ve and seventy-four ~~.~~ 40 They found that the more a person walked, climbed stairs, or played sports, the less likely they were to die of heart disease. And the correlation was linear: The more physically active someone was, the lower the risk. This connection existed regardless of smoking status, weight, or having a parent who’d died young (a potential indicator of an inherited condition). The report, led by noted epidemiologist Ralph Pa�enbarger, MD, and published in the _New England Journal of Medicine_ , was considered a landmark—proof that exercise improved longevity, largely by preventing cardiovascular illnesses.

Research since con�rms this �nding. In one study, researchers followed 3,307 people with heart disease from 1985 to 2014 ~~.~~ 41 Everyone in the study had been encouraged to exercise and lose weight. After thirty years, the researchers could see that while weight loss alone did not reduce the risk of death, exercise did. Other data con�rm exercise’s signi�cance, even when people have other risk factors. One group of researchers described this link starkly, back in 1996.42 “Low �tness is an important precursor of mortality,” they wrote. To put that in plain language: People who aren’t active are more likely to die young.

One mechanism behind this link is increased insulin sensitivity.43 Insulin is a hormone made and released from your pancreas that is essential for keeping your blood sugar, or glucose, levels within a particular range. Almost every cell in the body, including our neurons, requires glucose to function. Glucose comes from the food we eat and stored sources of energy, such as glycogen in our muscles and liver and adipose tissue, what is commonly referred to as body fat. Resistance to insulin leads to a buildup of glucose in our blood, which damages the endothelial cells that make up our capillaries, veins, and arteries, and deprives all cells of the glucose they need, impairing their functioning. It thus can cause cardiovascular disease and cerebrovascular diseases such as stroke and dementia. Exercise increases insulin sensitivity and can even improve the expression of genes that regulate insulin and glucose over long time spans which means more stable energy levels and reduced cellular in�ammation and other symptoms of metabolic disorders.44 People with diabetes are more sensitive to insulin after exercising,45 too, and nondiabetics derive additional bene�ts from exerciseinduced insulin sensitivity. Such bene�ts can be seen even after just one moderate workout.

What’s more, exercise can make your muscles become much better at pulling glucose out of the bloodstream, which ultimately helps your body handle carbohydrates more e�ciently.46

Finally (although I could go on!), there’s this: As you now know from everything you’ve just read, exercise can make you healthier and happier, and it can allow you to get smarter too. It will also extend your life.

One analysis examined data from thirteen studies that directly compared life expectancy among active and inactive people ~~.~~ 47 Eight of those studies included both men and women, and the results showed an average increase of 3.7 years of life among people who exercised regularly compared to those who did not. While it’s great to have a physically active job or lifestyle, the bene�ts of structured exercise are independent. You need both of these in your life.

And you don’t need to have been a longtime �tness devotee either. A Swedish study of 2,205 middle-aged men found that people who started to exercise between the ages of �fty and sixty experienced the same life-extending bene�t as

men who’d been working out all their lives and continued to do so as they got older ~~.~~ 48 There are also now studies of people who started resistance training in their mid-sixties, seventies, and even eighties, and all made excellent progress in strength and derived many other general health and lifestyle bene�ts. In fact, the group in their eighties made the same degree of progress in muscle mass and strength compared to people who had been exercising regularly for decades ~~!~~ 49

There is a lot more to say about exercise and longevity, but the e�ects are multifaceted. Some of them arrive via improved metabolic health and fuel utilization. Some via improved sleep, and improved immune system functioning —again, assuming we don’t chronically exhaust ourselves with over-exercising. The point is: Exercise gives us life—literally.

So by now I hope you’re on board with the “why.” We can move on to the “how.”

###### How should I exercise?

As I’ve mentioned, there is no one best way to exercise but there is, I believe, a best way to structure an e�ective exercise program. ### Walk as Much as Possible Each Day

###### WHAT TO DO:

- Incorporate walking into your daily life. Also, in these instances in particular, if you can:
  - Walk for �ve to ten minutes after meals, when health bene�ts of this activity are ampli�ed.

  - Walk or pace for at least �ve minutes for every thirty minutes of sitting or standing.

- Consider a walk-and-work desk. If you need to be at a desk for work for long stretches of time, a sit-stand desk may be a good investment. Even better is a walk-and-work desk, with a treadmill that �ts below.

- Seven thousand steps per day is a good goal, and ten thousand is even better.

- Accelerometers, step counters, or even your phone can help you keep track, but are not necessary.

###### HOW IT WORKS:

This isn’t that foundational �tness program I discussed; it’s something even more essential. While walking isn’t the only exercise we need to do, it’s listed as the �rst protocol in this section because it should not be thought of as an addon. Rather, it is at the bedrock of a healthy lifestyle, just as viewing morning sunlight is the basis of a good sleep routine. Simply walking for at least an hour a

day (total, not even all at once) is one of the best things you can do to protect yourself against illness and improve your overall health. The data show us why.

A group of researchers from across the US recruited 2,110 people between the ages of thirty-eight and �fty years to wear an accelerometer, or a step counter, for one year.50 The researchers then collected health data on these individuals for the next ten years (on average). Their analysis, published in _JAMA Network Open_ in 2021, showed that people who took at least seven thousand steps per day during the decade of the study had a signi�cantly lower mortality risk compared to people who took fewer steps.

In 2023, researchers from Kyoto University, in Japan, and UCLA published their study of 3,101 adults who took eight thousand steps three to seven days per week, eight thousand steps one to two days per week, or fewer than eight thousand steps on any one day in their week.51 Health data were collected over the ten years following study enrollment. Like the earlier report, this one found that taking eight thousand steps or more correlated with a signi�cantly lower risk of death from all causes, including heart disease. The bene�t appeared to plateau at three to four days per week of eight thousand steps.

And walking protects against more than heart disease. Researchers from Denmark and Australia investigated the link between walking and dementia risk.52 They monitored 78,340 adults for an average of seven years and, like the studies above, saw a link between walking and a lower risk for dementia. They noted that the optimal “dose” of walking to reduce the risk of dementia was just shy of 10,000 steps per day. Walking has also been tied to reduced risks of depression ~~,~~ 53 diabetes,54 cardiovascular disease,55 and the incidence of some cancers ~~,~~ 56 as well as increased survival after certain cancer diagnoses.

A paper published in _Nature Medicine_ in 2022 found that walking 8,200 steps or more per day had a preventive e�ect against obesity, sleep apnea, gastroesophageal re�ux disease, and major depressive disorder ~~.~~ 57 That is a remarkable set of bene�ts for such a simple, zero-equipment, zero-cost activity. In other words: We should all be walking. A lot. If not every day, then almost every day.

A primary reason why walking is so bene�cial is that it requires repeated muscular contractions. This activates an enzyme called AMPK. A 2018 paper by researchers at the Salk Institute for Biological Studies called AMPK the “guardian of metabolism,” and with good reason ~~.~~ 58 This enzyme has multiple roles. It is involved in the process of stimulating glucose uptake into muscle cells. Animal research indicates that AMPK is also involved in generating more mitochondria through its interactions with PGC-1alpha, helps counter in�ammation and improves vasodilation to help lower blood pressure and deliver more nutrients to cells, and under some conditions, can remove debris from them ~~.~~ 59 Taking enough steps each day is therefore bene�cial for health in numerous ways that extend way beyond just the calories burned by walking.

Data also support the value of interrupting long bouts of sitting with short bouts of walking. A large review from 2022 gathered data from seven studies that examined the health bene�ts of interrupting long bouts of sitting with either standing or walking.60 According to the analysis, standing between long stretches of sitting helps gradually lower glucose levels, but walking is far more e�ective.

Speci�cally, those researchers wanted to see which change is better at lowering glucose levels after meals. Walking is particularly e�ective right after a meal because glucose levels tend to increase at this time and preventing that rapid rise can help lower the risk of diabetes and heart disease ~~.~~ 61 (High glucose levels are linked to both.) A review of eight randomized studies examining thirty di�erent interventions in 116 people found that walking within thirty minutes after a meal lowers glucose levels more e�ectively than walking before a meal or after a break ~~.~~ 62 That’s because we use glucose as energy… to walk. Moving therefore helps clear glucose out of the bloodstream, which is both protective to our vascular cells—our arteries, veins, and capillaries—and is bene�cial for all the cells of our body by making them more e�ective energy utilizing machines, as described above. There is no need to rest right after eating. Just head straight out for that walk, even for just �ve minutes, although ten to twenty or even thirty minutes would be better.

We are talking about walking, not a workout. Just low-level, repeated muscle contractions. In fact, these contractions don’t even have to be created by walking: A 2022 study from the University of Houston found that repeated contractions of the soleus muscle, the deep muscle of our calf, signi�cantly improve glucose regulation.63 Remarkably, this was found to be the case even if people remained seated and repeatedly raised their heel o� the �oor. It seems that even though the soleus is only about 1 percent of our total musculature, it has an outsized (positive) e�ect in regulating our glucose levels when it is repeatedly contracted by walking or “soleus pushups.” Of course, doing repeated soleus contractions while seated throughout the day, while possible, is not terribly compatible with daily life. Most people would not be able to concentrate on that while doing their work. But I include this recent �nding here to emphasize just how powerful low-impact-repetitive muscle contractions can be. And of course, people who spend hours in meetings all day may want to consider doing calf raises while they’re con�ned to a desk. It’s not a replacement for walking, but it is certainly better than sitting still for long amounts of time.

What about standing still for long stretches of time? The study just described tells us that standing breaks are bene�cial. Maybe you have a standing desk at your o�ce, and that can be a great way to stretch your legs throughout the day. But walking is de�nitely better. A walk-and-work desk—where a treadmill �ts underneath—can be a great way for some people to walk more ~~.~~ 64

Curiosity about the health bene�ts of walking has generated a tremendous amount of data. As mentioned above, we now have studies showing that walking reduces the risk of heart disease, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, cancer, cognitive impairment, death by pneumonia, poor sleep, mental health issues, stress, hormonal imbalances tied to aging, and more ~~.~~ 65 Glucose regulation is certainly a part of it, but a deep dive into the molecular mechanisms behind all these e�ects is beyond the scope of this book. For those who are interested, a multidisciplinary team of researchers published a comprehensive review of the cellular mechanisms behind this wide range of e�ects.

There’s one more useful but nonobvious bene�t to walking that I’d like to mention here. Walking induces optic �ow, the state of having the visual image of

the world slide past us. We are usually unaware of what this does to our nervous system. When we ambulate—nerd-speak for “walk”—a stream of visual input �ows past us, an e�ect called global motion.66 Human and animal studies have found that forward ambulation causes re�exive lateral and repetitive (right-leftright…) eye movements that serve to stabilize the visual image on the eyes. Perhaps surprisingly, such eye movements signi�cantly reduce neural activity in the amygdala, a region of our brain involved in threat detection ~~.~~ 67 In fact repetitive lateralized eye movements are the cornerstone of trauma therapies such as EMDR (eye movement desensitization and reprocessing), which pairs left-right-left-right repetitive eye movements with the recounting of challenging experiences to uncouple their memory from the anxiety response ~~.~~ 68 EMDR is done in a therapist’s o�ce but was developed by psychologist Francine Shapiro, PhD, after she noticed that recounting traumatic experiences was made less stressful when the recounting took place on a walk.69 EMDR is still considered somewhat controversial in the therapy community. Some believe EMDR’s bene�ts come from the hypnosis-like state it can cause—and clinical hypnosis has well-established e�ects on mental health and brain rewiring.70 Others believe EMDR has its own direct e�ects on relief from trauma and depression ~~.~~ 71 We need more data to parse all that. For now, however, it is interesting to note that walking makes the amygdala less active, thereby reducing stress and anxiety ~~.~~ 72

Alas, this bene�t of walking won’t happen if you’re staring at your phone while doing it. That prevents the forward-ambulation-induced eye movements discussed here. The suppression of amygdala activity only occurs if we’re looking forward and around. I believe this phenomenon is one reason why spending time simply walking or hiking in nature is so tied to well-being ~~.~~ 73 And also why walking or running on a treadmill—while better than not exercising—is less stress reducing than doing the same activity outdoors. The link between optic �ow and stress reduction is an understudied area. However, walking outdoors is a zero-risk, zero-cost intervention that seems to translate to powerful results for your body and mental state.

###### In My Experience

I have a step tracker on both my phone and my WHOOP band (I’m an advisor for WHOOP). I track my steps every day but I don’t look at the data every day. I check it every few days to make sure I’m “hitting my numbers.” I know I get about seven thousand to ten thousand steps on average. More importantly, I am always seeking ways to take more steps. I make a point to pace indoors or walk outdoors whenever I take a phone call that doesn’t require me to be in front of my computer. I take stairs rather than escalators or elevators whenever I can. I see stairs as an opportunity, not a task, especially on travel days when I am going to be sitting a lot on the plane. I always strive to take two short walks of twenty to thirty minutes each during the day, usually one in the morning and one in the evening. If I miss the �rst one, I make the evening walk longer. I often take work calls, check in with friends or family, or listen to books or podcasts while I do. Every time we �nish recording a podcast with a guest, our whole team takes a walk together (in the direction of the sun of course). If I have to sit a lot on a given day, I make it a point to walk a lot more the next day. I have an indoor treadmill for days when I can’t get outside to walk much due to work or weather.

I almost always use my standing desk to work at home. When I travel, I simply put my laptop on a box or stack of books on the desk or co�ee table in the hotel room. It’s low-tech but it works, and I can rotate it toward the window to get more natural light. You need to �nd what works for you, of course.

###### COMMON QUESTIONS

Any walking is better than no walking and brisk walking is better than slow walking.74 Taking all studies discussed above into account, walking briskly for at least thirty minutes per day and ideally forty to sixty minutes should be the goal. Walking at least �ve days a week and making an e�ort to take stairs, et cetera, appears to be su�cient activity to meet current recommended guidelines ~~.~~ 75

Again, walking is not “working out,” but it is the basis of any good exercise program. Think of it as necessary for your health. We were made to move.

Getting steps each day is essential and should be part of your life. You can weave it into time in the yard, time with friends, time on the phone, and so on. And when you are stuck in a meeting or on a plane and can’t walk, try the calf raises discussed above. It’s discreet enough that you’re unlikely to get any strange looks.

Seven thousand steps are roughly an hour of walking, as I recommend, though obviously this will di�er somewhat depending on the length of a person’s stride, the terrain, and walking speed. And, again, these steps do not need to be done all at once but rather can be spread throughout the day.

Aim to speed up as you incorporate walking more into your life. If you already walk often, then try to walk a little faster. Faster walking obtains health bene�ts in less time.

Yes and no. All movement is good movement, provided you don’t get injured. Doing ten air squats—going from standing to a seated position with your thighs parallel to the ground, then standing up again, and repeating that ten times— every forty-�ve minutes throughout the day for an 8.5-hour period has been shown to have even better glucose-lowering e�ects than thirty minutes of walking, which makes it a decent alternative when you can’t walk, like on really stormy days or on a long (or even a short) �ight.76 The ten-air-squats-everyforty-�ve-minutes approach obviously does not provide all the bene�ts that walking outside does (like optic �ow, fresh air, sunlight, etc.).

There are other types of low-impact, continuous physical activity to explore. Tai chi is great for balance and is often done near sunrise and outdoors, adding to the bene�t for reasons discussed in both chapter 1 and chapter 5, and it’s typically done in groups, which has a positive social component. And tai chi certainly improves lower leg strength, balance, and coordination.77 That’s just one idea, but of course there are many others.

Everyone needs to �nd a low-impact, continuous physical activity that works for them in terms of enjoyment, and compatibility with lifestyle.

That being said, I’ll come back to walking. Walking is a movement that draws on many di�erent aspects of our anatomy: It puts weight on our skeletal structure, which is good for helping maintain our bone density and strength; it engages the soleus, which as mentioned before has a positive e�ect on glucose regulation; and it has the added bonus of optic �ow for mental health. Add walking into your life wherever and whenever possible. Again, don’t think of it as _exercise_ , think of it as nonnegotiable movement that is foundational to a healthy day. Does that mean walking is the only thing we need to do? Of course not. In the context of physical activity, and to use scienti�c jargon, it is “necessary but not su�cient” for your health. So let’s now discuss the things to do in addition to walking, starting with three times per week resistance training. Done properly.
