###### **EXERCISE PROTOCOL**

3

### Do Cardiovascular Training Three Times per Week

###### WHAT TO DO:

- Elevate your heart rate for anywhere from six to seventy-five minutes, three times per week. Plan three sessions, each focused on stimulating a di�erent speci�c adaptation: a long, a medium, and a brief cardiovascular workout, scaling the intensity inversely with the duration of each session. That means the long cardio workout should be of low intensity, the brief cardio workout should be of high intensity. Here is how to incorporate cardio into the overall program:
  - Day 1: Cardiovascular training, 45–75 minutes (low intensity/long duration) Day 2: Resistance training (legs: calves, quadriceps, hamstrings, glutes) Day 3: Rest day

  - Day 4: Resistance training (torso: chest, back, abdominals/core; optional neck)

Day 5: Cardiovascular training, 25–30 minutes (moderate intensity/moderate duration)

Day 6: Cardiovascular training, 6–17 minutes (high intensity/brief duration) Day 7: Resistance training (shoulders, biceps, triceps, abdominals/core; optional forearms and/or neck)

The first cardio workout each week marks the �rst day of the foundational �tness program schedule. It should be relatively low intensity, and long duration. And it should be continuous. Your goal is to sustain a steady output of e�ort for forty-�ve to seventy-�ve minutes without any pauses except perhaps to drink some water or wait for a stoplight to change so you can cross the street. This falls into the category of classic endurance work. The primary adaptation you’re stimulating with this workout is to increase your heart’s _stroke volume_ , which is the amount of blood your heart pumps with each beat. This means the heart can pump more blood per beat, and thus does not have to beat as fast to deliver the same amount of oxygen. The consequences of that for your health are manifold, including a lower resting heart rate when not exercising.108 This workout also stimulates a number of metabolic pathways related to utilizing fat for fuel and for vascular growth and even lymphatic health.109 It indirectly improves mood and sleep too.110

The challenge of this workout resides in its duration, not its intensity, and for many people the most challenging aspect is refraining from going faster and harder as they complete it. The forty-�ve to seventy-�ve minute duration is intentionally broad. In fact, if you’re out of shape when starting this program, I suggest you begin with just �fteen to twenty minutes, and add a few minutes to that each week, until you’re doing forty-�ve to seventy-�ve minutes of continuous movement. In my observation, most people �nd that sixty minutes is about the upper limit of their psychological tolerance for this sort of exercise, unless they really love the activity or it’s made social, like a hike or bike ride with family or friends. In any case, your goal pace throughout should be such that you can just barely hold a conversation. It’s quite all right if you must pause your speech here and there to catch your breath, but the idea is to exert yourself at a level that, were you to push yourself any faster or harder, holding a conversation would be impossible.

Another way to calibrate to that goal pace is to push as hard as you can while still breathing in and out only through your nose. No mouth breathing whatsoever, unless you are talking. As soon as you feel you have to gasp to get air through your mouth, you know you’re pushing too hard.

In the language of percentage of maximum heart rate this cardio session is done at 60 to 70 percent of your maximum heart rate (HR), but ideally closer to 70 percent. Your max HR can be estimated by this formula: 220 – your age = your approximate max HR. That’s not a perfect measurement but it’s close, and for most it’s more than su�cient to use here. If you want to be more precise about it, max HR is better approximated by the following formula: for men, you take 208 beats per minute – (0.7 × your age in years); and for women, it’s 206 beats per minute – (0.88 × your age in years).111 Once you have determined your approximate max HR, multiply that by 0.6 and 0.7 to get the lower and upper range, respectively, of your target heart rate for this cardio session. I’ve shared this formula because some people like to use an HR monitor while training to be sure they stay in that target HR zone. I prefer to use the “upper limit of e�ort while maintaining nasal breathing” approach, because whenever I have measured my HR while running and restricting myself to nasal breathing, it lands at about 70 percent (+/–5 percent) of my max HR. I have nothing against HR monitors. I just prefer not to use one when doing this workout. I like to let my mind wander or to listen to a book or podcast or music but if you like tracking your HR in real time, go for it.

A few other things to consider for this workout: Some people refer to this as Zone 2 cardio, which is a term that describes the intensity of the exercise with regard to heart rate training zones. But on that scale, I consider it more Zone ⅔ because it’s done at the high end of Zone 2 and the low end of Zone 3.112

Ideally you would get outside to do this workout so that you’re getting all the bene�ts that come with being outdoors. This raises the issue of what type of exercise is best for this. That’s an easy one to answer. Select any activity you can do for the speci�ed duration and intensity without getting hurt. That means do what is safe for your joints, works for your skill level, doesn’t stress any of your injuries, and can be completed in safe conditions. I love running and much prefer doing it outside on a trail or city streets to all other forms of cardio, but many people loathe running, or it hurts their knees, or it’s not safe for them to run in a given area. You don’t have to run! You can opt for cycling, or use the elliptical machine or a stair climber, or hike with a weight vest or a rucksack or, heck, even a backpack with a one-gallon jug of water in it. The possibilities are

nearly in�nite, and many of these cost very little. If I don’t run, I’ll sometimes swim laps in a pool or swim parallel to shore in the ocean. If the weather is bad, I’ll occasionally run on a treadmill or use a stationary bike.

Pick your poison and deliver it slow and steady for forty-�ve to seventy-�ve minutes. Many people �nd this workout meditative and learn to enjoy it. While you can of course go longer than seventy-�ve minutes, remember you’re training your legs the next day.

The second cardio workout each week is done three days after your leg workout (day �ve of the program). By then, your legs should be feeling mostly or completely recovered. This second cardio workout should be moderately fastpaced. It should have you breathing fairly hard but not gasping for air or needing to stop to recover. I suggest you start with �ve minutes of low-intensity movement to warm up and then shift to twenty-�ve to thirty minutes of “work” where your heart rate is kept between about 75 and 85 percent of your maximum heart rate.

Using the heart rate training zones, this workout falls in the high Zone 3 and low Zone 4 range.

Notably, although this workout is more intense than the �rst cardio session, it generally leaves you feeling energized and focused for many hours afterward. The key is to not push overly hard at any one time of that approximately twenty�ve to thirty minutes. You want to stay roughly in that “75 to 85 percent of max HR” range. That said, it’s perfectly all right to move between high and low within this range by pushing harder at times, and pulling back at times. Say, for example, you’re climbing a hill or you’re just feeling strong on your bike for a stretch and want to push yourself. Your pace and your heart rate don’t have to be perfectly constant throughout. Remember: It’s not a sprint! You don’t want to overly tax your body. The third cardio workout is the one that is intense. Luckily, it’s brief too.

The third cardio workout each week lands four days following your leg workout. If you still have a bit of residual leg soreness, no big deal: Proceed anyway. Some people refer to this type of workout as Zone 5 training or HIIT (high-intensity interval training), but I like to refer to it as “max heart rate training” or simply “intense cardio” because there are non-interval ways to do it, and—for reasons

that will become clear in a minute—getting your heart pumping near your maximum heart rate is highly bene�cial.

There are a few variations in the “classic” versions of this workout. All begin with �ve to ten minutes of warming up at an easy to moderate pace. HIIT has you modulating between near-all-out e�orts that put you at 90 to 95 percent of your max HR, interspersed with bouts of lower intensity e�ort where you let your HR fall a bit before repeating the sequence.113 Another approach is to start at an easy e�ort and build in a continuous and progressive manner—for example, increasing the level of resistance to your e�ort (think: increasing treadmill speed and incline)—until your e�ort plateaus, or starts to drop. (That actually mirrors how a VO2 max test, a measure of �tness and endurance, is conducted.) There are many ways to do max heart rate training but the total time spent at near-all-out e�ort is always pretty brief: as short as about six minutes, and up to about sixteen minutes. Either works for this third cardio session.

What form of exercise you choose can vary. For example, you could hop on an assault bike—those stationary bikes with a fan and handles that you pump forward and back while you pedal. You’ll soon realize that the fan is there to increase the resistance, not just to cool you down. Or you could use a stationary bike that lets you adjust the resistance of the pedals. You could also go sprint at a track or on a trail, or swim in a pool. The important thing is to do something in which you can really exert yourself without getting injured.

A “fun” HIIT session is this: brief �ve- to ten-minute warm-up, then pedal (or run, row, or swim, etc.) as hard and fast as you can for thirty seconds, then rest or slow down for sixty seconds, then another thirty seconds of all-out e�ort, then back again to sixty seconds of rest or low e�ort, and so on, for a total of six to twelve rounds of alternations. I do this on the assault bike once a week. I lovehate it.

You will quickly realize that with each round of all-out e�ort it gets tougher and tougher to recover, such that by rounds six to twelve, those sixty seconds of rest will seem to go by _extremely_ fast. There is actually a neuroscienti�c basis for the warping of time perception we experience under stress that I discuss in the next chapter. The good news is, even though this workout is intense, the whole

thing, including the warm-up, only takes about twenty-�ve minutes. At the end, you will feel fatigued, but remarkably, within �ve to ten minutes after stopping you will likely feel extra energized from all the adrenaline and norepinephrine you generated in your body and brain ~~.~~ 114 You will also have provided a great stimulus to improve your VO2 max, and max HR, the importance of which I cover below.

Other options for this workout include the Cooper test, where you see how far you can go (run, swim, cycle, etc.) in twelve minutes of steady, hard e�ort.115 That is a “fun” one too.

Or you can try to run your best mile time. This is something performance coach, author, and former elite runner Steve Magness has emphasized as being a terri�c correlate of VO2 max.116 It’s one of my favorite workouts. Here is how to do it properly:

First �nd a 400-meter track. Start by warming up with an easy jog of four to six laps slowly interspersing the occasional faster-paced 100 meters—not all out but just quickening your pace to about 60 to 70 percent of your subjective “run for your life” speed. Perhaps do that on one straight-track segment between turns on each warm-up lap. Once you feel properly warmed up, run four laps (which is 1,600 meters—about 9 meters shy of 1 mile). It’s a skill to run the mile and pace everything just right for your best time. But you’re not aiming to be a competitive miler here. So set out at a pace you can maintain for three laps— about 85 percent of “running for your life” speed, then push it harder on the last lap, or 95 percent of “running for your life” speed. The key is to pace yourself so you’re not sprinting laps one to three and then forced to walk or jog the remainder. It can take a bit of practice but within a few weeks you’ll know the pace to take for each lap. Almost everyone likes to really push the �nal 200 meters or so.

I test my approximate best mile time about once every two months lately. I’m not training to be a competitive miler but it’s nice to have one version of the short intense cardio workout where I can track my progress across the year. I doubt I’ll beat my best time from high school ever again, but it’s fun to have an

“a bit faster than last month” run. My goal is to maintain or reduce my mile time each time I run it.

And there is the Norwegian 4×4, if you want to try it.117 That’s where you warm up, and then run, bike, or row hard for four minutes, then rest or slow down for four minutes. Repeat this cycle for a total of four work-rest rounds.

As you can see with all these examples, the exact work-to-rest ratio and total time can vary dramatically, and yet all can be e�ective. What’s key is that during the work periods, you’re truly working hard. That is because, during the rest periods, you’re allowing enough time for recovery so that you can again come back to a truly hard e�ort. Don’t be overly caught up in the exact protocols. You can alter them if you like and still get the same results.

I’m recommending three di�erent types of cardio training sessions every week because this variation is typically what delivers the best results over time for improving your VO2 max. We’re trying to balance duration and intensity in this program. It’s best to emphasize both. You want longer moderate e�orts and you want brief and very intense e�orts. And while the shorter, intense e�orts are extremely e�ective (and time e�cient), they take longer to recover from compared to the longer, moderate e�orts. Given that you’re also balancing this cardio training with the resistance training, a blend of longer/lower, moderate, and brief/high intensity cardio training sessions is what works best for results across the board.

###### HOW IT WORKS:

The cardio workouts described above each help trigger bene�cial adaptations. They all increase your heart’s e�ciency in delivering blood (and thus oxygen and vital nutrients) to the rest of the body.118 They trigger capillary growth in your muscles, which allows more oxygen to move through these vessels during all activities. 119 They stimulate an increase in the number, size, and e�ciency of your mitochondria, the energy producing organelles in our cells known to be critical for preventing chronic disease and premature aging. Further, they all acutely elevate levels of the catecholamines: dopamine, epinephrine, and norepinephrine ~~.~~ 120 Also, because they rely on a mixture of aerobic (oxygen

dependent) and anaerobic (oxygen independent) processes, cardio of the types in this program increases metabolic �exibility, or your body’s ability to rely on di�erent fuel sources for energy. And that’s just a small sampling of the many bene�cial adaptations.121

The extent to which brief, high-intensity or longer, lower-intensity cardio triggers these di�erent adaptations varies, but there is also synergy between them ~~.~~ 122 Those brief, intense cardio training sessions will allow you to move faster but with less e�ort on your long and medium cardio days, not unlike how getting stronger with low repetition heavy sets in the gym equates to you being able to move more weight on your higher repetition sets once you get stronger.

So, while people often debate which form of cardiovascular exercise is best for overall health and longevity, that’s not the lens through which to look at it. I suggest a practical lens. (And you know by now, I don’t believe in any best type of exercise; only the best way to structure an e�ective exercise program.) For instance, consider that your one-mile time is a good re�ection of your VO2 max ~~.~~ 123 Does that mean you should only do one mile distances for cardio? No. In fact, whether you’re a competitive miler or simply using the one-mile time test as a fun workout and barometer of your VO2 max, doing some longer/lower, moderate, and brief/high intensity cardio workouts across the week is how to get faster at the mile.

In science we love to isolate variables, so people have done the “which cardio exercise is best?” experiment. That research made clear that if you have to choose one type, you want to opt for brief/high intensity cardio rather than, say, three thirty- to forty-�ve-minute Zone ⅔ sessions ~~.~~ 124 But doing a mix of durations and intensities is recommended, and for the reasons mentioned above, it meshes well with your resistance training. A Zone ⅔ jog or hike for an hour the day before you train your legs with weights is no problem. Sprinting the day after leg training to failure? Not a good idea. The injury risk is too high.

Doing these three cardio training sessions also means you’re logging a total of about two hours per week of cardio. Considering the immediate and long-term health bene�ts, that’s a great return on investment.

We hear all the time about “�tness” and it re�ects many things. But from a health perspective consider that two studies—one published in 2018 and another in 2022—both showed essentially the same thing, which is that as you move from the lowest to the higher tiers of cardiorespiratory �tness (one measure of that is your VO2 max), your mortality risk drops ~~.~~ 125 These are meaningful shifts in life expectancy too. One of the studies states, “Those with the highest �tness had roughly �ve times lower mortality than the least �t.”

Resistance training is less about cardiorespiratory �tness, but its e�ects in maintaining (or increasing) muscle mass and bone density, promoting cognitive function and healthy body recomposition, make a combination of resistance training and cardio training two of the three vital interlocking puzzle pieces for excellent physical health.

###### COMMON QUESTIONS:

To be clear: If your goal is purely to put on as much muscle as possible, or to do an endurance event like a half marathon or marathon as fast as possible, there are better training programs for those speci�c goals. When splitting your time across both building muscle and building endurance, there’s going to be a performance trade-o�. You can’t _maximize_ for both at the same time because of so-called interference e�ects.126

That said, for vitality, health, longevity, aesthetics, and all-around �tness, you want to do both resistance training and cardio training. Research indicates that the interference e�ects are minimal when done on separate days at the duration and intensities similar to those in this foundational program.127

If you’re training for a competition or a race, or you play a sport like soccer or tennis or basketball, and you play hard for an hour or more one to two times per week, the program here is still great. You may want to do the lower number of work sets, and you’ll really need to tend to your recovery and nutrition by

making sure you get enough hours of quality sleep and calories—including, yes, enough quality protein, but also starches and fats.

Again, the program here will get you the most all-around �t as possible at any age. That does not mean you won’t gain strength and muscle—you will. You will also burn fat. You’ll increase your endurance too. And once you learn how di�erent exercises impact your body, you can emphasize some and reduce others, per the suggestions I describe in this protocol. Exercise done correctly is very potent in that way. Assuming you pay attention to the points I make about recovery too—that is, eat well and sleep well—I’m certain you’ll achieve remarkable results with this program.

If you are healthy, and you happen to have had a bad night’s sleep—by which I mean only one to two hours less sleep than usual—then try to stick with your workout. There is a growing amount of data that say it can help o�set some of the short-term cognitive disturbances from sleep loss.128

Just be careful not to push too hard in the gym (or in life) after a poor night’s sleep as injuries happen more often when people have not slept enough ~~.~~ 129 And don’t make it a regular thing to get less than enough sleep, and expect to remedy that with exercise. You’ll end up sick, injured, or both. Maybe do some non-sleep deep rest (NSDR) (see Sleep Protocol 8) and then push through the workout. If you have had a really bad night’s sleep for two or more nights in a row, for whatever reason, I suggest you get back on track with your sleep before exercising again. Consider some deliberate heat exposure (sauna or a hot bath, for example), and if you feel you _must_ exercise, try a restorative activity, like stretching, light yoga, or just walking.

There is no clear rule here. Personally, I prefer to train in the morning on an empty stomach. Figure out what works for you. It may be best to eat prior to training if you wake up hungry and you know that hunger will distract you during your workout, or you get dizzy or nauseous training on an empty stomach. Some people may �nd that eating about sixty to ninety minutes prior

to exercise gives them an energy boost without the discomfort of feeling full. It’s highly individual. Experiment with your timing of your workouts and meals.

It’s hard to answer this one because… it depends. However, I would not change the order of your resistance or cardio training sessions across the week because the schedule starts to fall like dominoes, and it’s hard to get back on track. But maybe something comes up and you can’t do the long, slow cardio day as planned. I would not recommend moving that workout to the same day you train legs. I would simply skip the long cardio day and train your legs on schedule. Skipping leg day is a bad idea. You do three days of cardio per week, so having to miss one every now and again is not a huge deal. But you only train your legs directly once a week, and done correctly as outlined above it creates major positive systemic shifts in your brain and body. So when people say, “Don’t skip leg day,” it’s not just about aesthetics. In fact, if I could only train once per week in the gym and do one cardio training session—not what I recommend, but if I _had_ to—I would do leg day and I would do some sprints followed by light jogging four or �ve days later. That’s just to illustrate a point about the potency of those two workouts. I recommend the full program described in this chapter.

Let’s say you can’t do the moderate cardio training session for whatever reason. You could, in theory, shift it to immediately after your arms workout that same day. But remember, you’re scheduled to do the long, slow cardio session the very next day, and you don’t want your legs to feel like noodles when you wake up the following morning for leg day! So think ahead a bit about your recovery.

I suggest you stick to the schedule as best you can, missing days here and there or doubling up when there is no other option. Plan your workouts, follow through, and if people get curious about how you’re getting such great results, teach them the principles, or even better, share the program. No one owns this or any exercise program; they are all derivatives of each other anyway, and based on what science says works.

###### **EXERCISE PROTOCOL**

4

### Incorporate Brief Mobility and Flexibility Work Two to Four Times per Week

###### WHAT TO DO:

- Do four specific movements to improve your mobility, two to four times a week.

- Refer to the instructions below to target areas susceptible to injury as you do these movements. Wrist, back, knee, hip, and shoulder injuries are common. The movements described here will ensure mobility in these areas. They aren’t a guarantee against injuries, but they can help tremendously.

###### HOW IT WORKS:

First, I’m not giving you yet another workout to do. The current program— about three hours a week of resistance training, about two hours of cardio—is not terribly time-consuming, considering the years (literally!) it can add to your life. Still, I acknowledge that people’s time is limited. That is why I suggest incorporating just a few minutes of mobility exercise two to four times per week. It can be done at the end of one of your other workouts, or any time of day really. It does not take long at all, only about ten minutes per session.

That might seem woefully inadequate to the mobility experts out there. I get it. I would love to add two thirty-minute mobility workouts to my own schedule but alas “my dance card is full,” as they say. I’m assuming yours is too.

The good news is that some aspects of the training suggested in the earlier protocols in this chapter are pro-mobility and pro-�exibility too. Remember the

emphasis on using a full range of motion for resistance training sets, as described in Exercise Protocol 2? Doing that will not only build your strength and muscles but can also enhance your �exibility and mobility. In fact, some studies �nd that full-range resistance training can be as e�ective as static stretching, a type of stretching in which you hold a muscle in a stretched, or elongated, position and gradually deepen the stretch using body weight. Controlling the eccentric, or lowering, phase in full-range resistance training may be critical for this e�ect, which makes sense as that is when the muscle is elongating ~~.~~ 130

There are easy ways to get even more �exibility from resistance training too. In the resistance training video tutorials at <u>protocolsbook.com/videos, I also</u> emphasize some exercises that are hardest for a given muscle when the muscle is in the elongated, stretched position, as well as exercises where the tension is greatest when the muscle is in its shortened, contracted position. Consider a sti�-legged deadlift or similar variation for your hamstrings, glutes, and lower back—the so-called posterior chain. It involves holding a barbell or dumbbells and moving from standing to something resembling a toe-touch (or an attempt to) by lowering the weight under control toward the ground, and then standing up again. You can imagine the stretch to your hamstrings and lower back that movement provides if you use a full range of motion. Including some movements that are most challenging for a given muscle group when it is in the elongated position can help build �exibility and can help you remain “strong in any position,” which assists mobility too ~~.~~ 131 Again, if any of this is confusing, I provide a gallery of movements to choose from at protocolsbook.com/videos.

I also hope you’ll include the direct mobility exercises that I describe below in your weekly routine but even if you don’t, by training the way I describe above, most people will improve their mobility, and �exibility too. We’re talking about the ability to touch your toes while keeping your legs straight or just slightly bent, to hang from a bar with no pain, to twist around to look behind you while seated in a chair, to sit in a deep squat for one to two minutes (and be able to stand up at the end!), and so on. You can develop those basic abilities through resistance training with a full range of motion, and focusing on the relevant muscles at all positions in each rep.

There are many great ways to improve mobility. Here I have created what I believe is the minimal effective dose of it. And if you want to do more mobility work, please do!

At least two to four times a week, take ten minutes and do the following four movements. You can do these most any place and at any time.

###### 1 Deep sumo squat, torso twist, point, and look up

Set your feet a few inches wider than your shoulders, then squat down as far as you can.

Put your elbows against the insides of your knees and your palms and �ngers together in “prayer” position, and push out gently with your elbows until you feel a stretch in your hips and inner thighs. Then raise one arm and, with your index �nger, point directly up at the ceiling (or as high overhead as you can) while keeping your other elbow against the inside of your knee. Let your gaze follow your �nger, which will naturally have you twist your torso and turn your neck to raise that arm. Look directly up at your index �nger for three to ten seconds. Inhale and exhale.

Then put your arm down, reset to the �rst squat position with both elbows against the insides of your knees. Place your hands in prayer position for three to ten seconds, and then raise your other arm up to point at the ceiling. Twist your torso and look up at your index �nger for three to ten seconds. Repeat three times for each side. You may have to stand up between sets. That is �ne.

This is a great movement because it gets you squatting deep, it improves your thoracic spine and neck mobility, and you’ll also feel a decent stretch in your inner thighs and hips. It will also reveal if you have any asymmetries in your mobility (perhaps one side versus the other) which is common.

I demonstrate this movement here: <u>protocolsbook.com/videos.</u>

Note: _If you can’t point and/or look all the way up to directly overhead, start by pointing and looking up at a lower angle. Gradually progress to pointing and looking directly overhead._

###### 2 Get your knees behind your glutes, one at a time

This is one I learned from mobility expert Kelly Starrett whom I mentioned earlier in this chapter. Since it may not be easy for most people to envision, try this: Start in a standing lunge by placing one foot in front of you and the other foot behind you. Bend your front knee and keep your rear leg straight or a bit bent. Now nudge the foot in front of you slightly farther out. Bend that front knee more and focus on stretching the hip �exors at the top of your back leg. You may need to lean your torso back a bit to really feel the hip �exor stretch. Okay, notice the knee of your back leg is now behind your glutes? That is what I mean by “get your knee behind your glutes.” Slowly ease into this hip �exor stretch for ten to thirty seconds while exhaling. It’s �ne to reach up and look overhead while doing this, as that will help extend the hip �exor, but keep your attention on the back leg. Your front leg is there for stability and you can bend it to provide more rear-placed-leg hip stretch. Repeat for each side three times. I demonstrate this movement here: protocolsbook.com/videos.

Next, you’re going to kneel on both knees. Then put one knee up in front of you (the foot of that same leg is thus �at on the ground). The shin of your rear leg is parallel to the ground. That means your back foot will be sole-facing-up. Place your hand on that raised front knee for stability and gently extend the back leg until you feel a stretch in your hip �exor. Again, think “I need to get my knee behind my glutes.” Keep your torso upright, your eyes forward or up, and even lean slightly back at the waist. Hold the stretch for ten to thirty seconds. Repeat three to four times. Don’t forget to breathe.

I demonstrate these movements here: protocolsbook.com/videos.

The reason to do this: Your hip �exors are located where your leg meets your pelvis. When you sit, your hip �exors are partially �exing. When you run, bike, or walk up a set of stairs, your hip �exors are repeatedly �exing as you bring your knee up and forward. Modern life has us �exing our hip �exors all the time. A key step toward good mobility is to make sure you can extend your hips. Hip extension is the opposite of hip �exion—it moves your knee away from the front of your pelvis, to a location _behind_ you. Hence the directive here. Once you experience how good it feels during (and after!) this stretch, you’ll be looking for ways to do it more often.

###### 3 Get into a reverse tabletop position

Sit on the �oor with your feet in front of you, the soles of your feet and butt on the ground, and with your knees bent. Place your hands at your sides a few inches away from your hips, with your palms down. Turn your hands so your �ngers point away from you out to each side.

See if you can slowly push your pelvis up so that the tops of your legs and torso are parallel to the �oor, and your knees are at a 90 degree right angle. Many people �nd they can’t get into this “reverse tabletop” position for very long, if at all, but some can. See if you can hold that position for ten seconds.

If you can’t do this, practice doing this each week for three sets of however long you can hold it until you can easily remain in this position for ten seconds. Once you can do that, move to the following progression:

Sit on the �oor with your feet in front of you, with the soles of your feet and butt on the ground, and your knees bent. Place your hands just behind your hips, with your palms down. Turn your hands so your �ngers point backward. See if you can _slowly_ push your pelvis up so that the tops of your legs and torso are parallel to the �oor, and your knees are at a 90 degree right angle.

Once again, the goal is to get into the �at reverse tabletop position and hold for ten seconds. For some people this will take a while to achieve. For others it will be easy depending on your level of shoulder mobility. These movements are also great for wrist mobility, too, by the way.

Once that �nal “reverse tabletop” variation is achievable, then you can start to experiment SLOWLY with this next movement. Sit on the �oor with your legs straight in front of you, heels on the ground and the soles of your feet facing forward. Place your hands �at on the ground just behind you, with your �ngers pointed backward. Keep them there as you gently and slowly scoot your glutes forward. Remember, your hands stay �at on the ground and �xed in place. Keep scooting forward until you feel a stretch in your biceps and shoulders. Exhale, and see if you can ease into it another centimeter or so. Once you can extend your shoulders back behind you with the edges of your hands touching, you are getting to quite mobile shoulder status.

The reason to do this: Tight shoulders can arise from many sources, but often there will be people who can raise their arms to the front or to the side

without issue but who don’t have the mobility to raise their arms up behind them, meaning they don’t have much shoulder _extension_ mobility. This is made worse by desk work, and the chin-down/forward-leaning posture that is nearly ubiquitous nowadays, thanks to excessive amounts of time texting and scrolling on our phones. Shoulder tightness and neck and back pain are often linked too. Improving your shoulder extension mobility is straightforward. It just requires a willingness to work through these progressions.

Wrist, back, knee, hip, and shoulder injuries are super common and many can be avoided by a quality strength training program and by including some basic mobility exercises like the ones in this protocol. Some quick movements you can incorporate in your routine are the “face pulls,” which strengthen these and other areas, as well as neck training a few times a week, as described in Exercise Protocol 2 and shown at protocolsbook.com/videos. You will be amazed at how strong, mobile, and stable your shoulders, neck, and upper back will be if you do.

Do not push too fast when it comes to mobility work! Work through the progressions listed above over the course of months or more. Make it painless but deliberate, and you will build and maintain much greater shoulder, hip, knee, back, and wrist mobility.

###### 4 Practice the Founder pose

The �nal mobility exercise is the Founder pose, made popular by chiropractor Eric Goodman, who has served as a conditioning coach for numerous top athletes in sports ranging from cycling to sur�ng to water polo. I was referred to his work by friends who previously had back pain and shoulder pain, and who sit a lot of the day. “You have to try this thing called Founder pose,” I kept hearing. Mind you, in my role, I hear that about a thousand times per day about a variety of things, so I’m not easily moved to try them. But I heard this decompresses the spine and trains your musculature to work properly as a functional unit.

I tried Eric’s Founder pose and, wow, it’s great. Not just because it feels good while you do it but your posture improves. And it de�nitely made me more �exible.

So what is it? It’s similar to the “chair pose” in yoga but while that mainly emphasizes the musculature of the front of the body, the Founder pose emphasizes mobility of your posterior and lateral chains: your hamstrings, glutes, lower and upper back, and thoracic muscles.

Here is how you do it: Stand with your feet a bit wider than your shoulders, toes pointing slightly out.

Stand as tall as you can by pressing your heels down and lifting your head up, as if a string were tied to the top of your head but your heels were fastened down to the ground.

Hinge your hips so you lean slightly forward at the waist—almost as though you’re about to sit in a chair but freeze only about a third of the way down into the movement. Your hips and glutes are back behind your heels, and your knees are just slightly bent. Keep your head as far away from your glutes as possible. You should feel a stretch in your lower back and hamstrings. If not, lean farther forward at the waist until you do.

Raise your chest, and with your arms at your sides, turn your thumbs out and away from the midline of your body (away from your belly button).

Keeping your thumbs rotated out, start to slowly lift your arms. Stop when you feel more stretching in your lower back and/or the backs of your legs.

Now move your hips back a few inches more. And raise your chest and head, aka “make your spine long,” still pressing your heels down.

- Raise your arms a bit more if you can (thumbs still pointed away from your

- navel in external rotation), all the while pushing your heels down. Hold this position for �ve more seconds then stand up straight.

- Repeat that one to two times, as often as every day or even just a few times a

- week.
  - Thank me later. No, thank Eric Goodman!

I, like everyone else, don’t like the feeling of being stressed, but I have grown accustomed to the idea that life inevitably involves stress. The problem was that when I looked to see what the science said about stress, it was uniformly negative. It made clear that stress wasn’t just uncomfortable, it was damaging to the brain and body. I always appreciate when science shows up in a conversation, but I confess phrases like “�ght or �ight” make me shake my head. And research has shown that the beliefs we hold about stress can change how

Stress is an area I’ve thought a lot about from a neuroscience perspective. My lab has studied it in animals and humans. Decades into my career, I now know that there is, in fact, a good way to address it. There are excellent stress management tools based in science. So, given how pervasive stress is, I am especially excited to share the information in this chapter.

First let’s begin with the facts. Forget saber-toothed tigers. Many of the same situations that stress us out now have been stressing out humans for thousands of years. An argument with a loved one, a persistent pain of unknown cause, a worry about a child, a looming payment, and on and on. Scenarios like these are not unique to modern times.

A good way to think about stress is this: Stress is nature’s attempt to create a single solution to all matters that might be, or actually are, urgent. I’ll say that again. Stress is nature’s attempt to create a single solution to all matters that might be, or actually are, urgent.

So no matter what the stressor (and there are an in�nite number of them out there), the basic architecture of the stress response—that is, what happens to our brain and body when we perceive a stressor—is the same. Cortisol and other hormones, including the catecholamine neuromodulators adrenaline and norepinephrine, �ood our system. Adrenaline, or epinephrine, as well as cortisol are released from our adrenal glands. Norepinephrine is released from speci�c locations in the brain including the locus coeruleus, which we discussed in chapter 1 and chapter 2. Dopamine is released in the brain and in the body too. All of these chemicals change the activity level of speci�c neuronal circuits and, in doing so, initiate a coordinated shift in the ways our organs function, and thus in our overall state of mind and body. We often hear about the increase in heart rate, breathing, and blood pressure that stress brings about. Less discussed, however, are the perceptual changes. Stress changes our visual �eld and narrows our mental attention ~~.~~ 2 We become �xated on the events related to the stressor: “How did this happen? How can I undo this?!” Stress causes our perception of time to slow down. Seconds start to feel like minutes, minutes like hours, hours like days… Meanwhile, our rate of thinking—the sheer number of thoughts we

have per second—seems to speed up. And yet, our cognitive �exibility is reduced. We default to simple black-and-white thinking. Nuance evaporates. Mild-tomoderate stress makes us feel jittery whereas intense stress can cause us to freeze. At its extreme, it can make people feel as if they have left their body, as if they are viewing themselves from above.3

While that all sounds dreadful, we must remember that the stress response is adaptive. The purpose of it is to put our brain and body into a state that gives us the best chance of addressing the problem at hand. A single solution. In an ideal world, the degree of stress response would perfectly match the stressor we face. Running late? A little bit more arousal to help us focus on the key items we need to get out the door with grace would be perfect. See our toddler running toward the tra�c? A huge surge in energy to quickly grab them is what we want! In fact, the parts of our nervous system that govern stress—called the autonomic nervous system—can be calibrated to generally match our stress level to the stressor we face, from mild to severe, from brief to ongoing.4 But nowadays, the many comforts most people enjoy thanks to technology—indoor heating and air conditioning, abundant food and shelter, and all in all our general lack of actual survival stressors—have our autonomic nervous systems uncalibrated. We are far more labile under the constant barrage of minor psychological stressors all day and night, and a lot of people are in a constant state of stress related to things they simply cannot control or in�uence even slightly. The occasional bout of stress lasting a few hours or less is no big deal, and even a few days is something our bodies can handle without longterm consequences. We’ve all heard the laundry list of things that stress harms: our hormones, memory, mood, and decision-making ability, as well as the many diseases it makes worse or can bring about to our heart, brain, gut, and liver. Eliminating stress from our lives is unrealistic. So our goal with stress should be twofold. First, we need to be able to adjust the intensity and the duration of our stress response so we can better handle stress in the moment. Second, many of us need to increase our stress threshold—that is, the subjective point at which events and thoughts trigger large amounts of adrenaline release in our body—so our stress response is calibrated to any stressors we may encounter. Ahem, I mean, that we _will_ encounter. When adrenaline release occurs as the consequence of tiny things, that is not good. It negatively a�ects our physical health and relationships, including our relationship with ourselves. Do you like being around you when you’re stressed? Didn’t think so. We can change our relationship to stress through cognitive reframing, but an e�ective approach is to learn to quickly control our stress response once it hits, and to periodically reset our stress threshold to a level that best serves us. We can’t always control what life throws at us, but we can indeed control our stress response, and we can raise our stress threshold. That’s what this chapter is all about.

And those are great qualities. The examples—both historical and contemporary—of people being gritty and resilient and mentally tough are there to remind us that humans harbor within them an enormous capacity to manage and even channel their stress.

While there is a lot known about the neural circuits and hormones that control the stress response, I speci�cally wanted to understand the mechanisms that determine its intensity and duration. I was able to �nd some data about stress inoculation,8 including some studies supporting the idea that certain forms of early-life stress can set the stage for resilience later in life by virtue of how they tune the physiology of the stress response to better match the intensity of a stressor.9 But it was hard to �nd evidence for speci�c tools that kids or adults could reliably apply to recalibrate the stress response across di�erent circumstances. I wanted to �nd mechanistic data that could be translated broadly and that were accessible for the average person.

I continued my search. I found studies on the bene�ts of positive self-talk10 but just as many studies on its lack of e�ectiveness.11 Despite the fact that we are all born with the same biological stu�—adrenals that release adrenaline, locus coeruleus neurons that release norepinephrine, and prefrontal cortices that can exert top-down control over our impulses and feeling states—I just couldn’t �nd any really convincing studies in humans that pointed to tools people could use to improve their capacity to manage stress. Meanwhile, we know that slogans like “Just do it” and mantras like “Embrace the suck,” or telling ourselves “You got this,” can be good for pushing us through a stressor we have chosen to face— a long run, the �nal reps of a hard set in the gym, a study session or big exam— but most people would agree that self-talk fails the vast majority of the time when the stressor isn’t one we’ve chosen, or when our e�orts have us falling short of our goals. And at some point, real life brings the sorts of stressors we simply cannot control, like a medical emergency or the loss of a beloved friend or family member. In those circumstances, “Just do it” just doesn’t do it.

Of course, much has been researched and written about what I call o�ine practices to manage stress. Meditation, massages, vacations, hot baths, deep breaths, talk therapy. Great! Who doesn’t love a massage at the end of a hard day? Meditation is powerful as a tool to bu�er against the stress response; a randomized clinical trial conducted by researchers at Georgetown University found that people with generalized anxiety disorder who meditated experienced a noteworthy reduction in pro-in�ammatory cytokines—chemical messengers

But I wanted to know how people can navigate stress while they are in the throes of the stress response. When their pulse is racing, their vision is blurry, their hands are shaking, and all they can think about is the stressor and the potential bad outcomes from it. That’s when the capacity to manage stress matters most. Not o�ine, but in the moment.

As I pointed out above, the stress response is universal. Whatever the speci�c stressor might be, the stress response is the same. It varies in degree, not kind. This suggests that if we have reliable tools to reduce the stress response in one context, we ought to be able to reduce it in another. The problem? No one had dissected the universal features of stress control, only the stress response.

One valuable thing everyone should know about the stress response, though, is that it is asymmetric: It starts extremely fast and turns o� relatively slowly. The adrenaline release that is the �rst domino of the stress response happens in seconds or less and can continue for several minutes after we perceive a stressor. 15 Think of a time when you were groggy from just waking up and you picked up your phone to see a disturbing text. BOOM! You are wide awake and ready to move in an instant. That’s the speed of adrenaline in action.

Then, even after the stressor is resolved, the stress response persists. Imagine getting a text that says, “I think Mom was on the �ight that just crashed,” and ten minutes later, “I just spoke to her, she wasn’t on there. She’s �ne.” Your feeling of relief will no doubt outpace how quickly your body settles down. That’s an extreme example, but the same thing applies when someone almost sideswipes you while driving, and you swerve just in time to avoid a collision. A shot of adrenaline wicks out through your body in an instant, and almost as fast, norepinephrine is released to ramp up attentional circuits in your brain. Cognitively, you realize you’re safe almost as quickly as you thought you were

about to get hit, but your body and mind don’t relax immediately. More often than not, we plummet into the stress response and it takes time to return to baseline. And that’s when everything turns out okay. When stressors persist, you experience wave after wave of adrenaline. And while the basic circuits for stress are the same in everyone, seldom discussed is that not everyone has the same threshold, or trigger point, for a stress response to kick o�. For some people it’s as if that �rst domino is �xed in cement. Such people are rare. For most people, however, the domino falls too easily. I wanted to understand this aspect of stress too, in order to develop tools anyone can use to raise their stress threshold, to allow them to calibrate their autonomic set point. That is, the balance point that our nervous system works to maintain—so that the stress response happens when it’s needed and not when it isn’t. I also wanted to develop tools that do not rely on practice, like cognitive behavioral therapy, which is great but can take a fair amount of time to maste ~~r~~ 16 and doesn’t always translate across stressors very well; there is evidence both for and against generalizability.17 Like all protocols in this book, I wanted tools for stress management that could be e�ective the �rst time and every time because they are anchored in hardwired circuits and processes we all possess. ###### The Seesaw Model

Think about the stress response as existing somewhere along a spectrum of arousal, with very low arousal at one end of the spectrum and very high arousal at the other. At the extremely low arousal end is a comatose state. Slightly more aroused than that would be deep sleep, then light sleep. Then toward the middle of the spectrum is a state in which we are alert but calm (which incidentally is the ideal state for most of our waking activities). As we progress further along

toward the highest arousal end of the spectrum, we enter mild stress, then severe stress, and �nally, full-blown panic. When we think about stress on a spectrum of low-to-high arousal, we realize that arousal—and what increases or decreases arousal—is the thing to focus on if we wish to deliberately lessen the stress response.

Where we happen to be on the spectrum of arousal at any given moment re�ects the level of activity in our autonomic nervous system. Our autonomic nervous system regulates involuntary functions like our heart rate, digestion, blood pressure, and breathing. It also controls our level of alertness, and thus our ability to focus. It is comprised of two sets (sometimes called “arms”) of neural circuits: the parasympathetic nervous system (PNS) and the sympathetic nervous system (SNS). These function more or less independently of one another, but their balance of activities combines to determine our arousal level, and thus our overall brain and bodily state ~~.~~ 18

But what sets the balance between these two systems? Or, to put it another way, what regulates our autonomic nervous system? There are three main categories of autonomic regulators. The �rst is our twenty-four-hour circadian rhythm ~~.~~ 19 If you follow a typical diurnal schedule—awake in the daytime and asleep for a major portion of the night—then your SNS activity levels will dominate in the daylight hours and your PNS will dominate at night. In fact, the incredible impact your circadian rhythm has on your ability to reason ~~,~~ 20 exert physical e�ort ~~,~~ 21 and resist infection ~~s~~ 22 stems from how it controls the balance of SNS versus PNS activity. In the morning and early daytime, elevated SNS activity (sometimes called “sympathetic tone”) caused by a natural and healthy increase in our baseline levels of cortisol makes us physically stronger and better able to focus, whereas in the later evening and at night, when our baseline cortisol levels are markedly lower, our parasympathetic tone is elevated, and we become mentally and physically weaker, and our immune system becomes far less capable of warding o� infections ~~.~~ 23 (Circadian variation in the expression of speci�c genes and the actions of various molecules—neuromodulators, hormones, peptides, etc.—are what underlie those dramatic morning-versusnighttime variations in autonomic tone, as discussed in chapter 1.)

The second category of things that control our autonomic nervous system, and thus our level of arousal, are the sensory inputs—or stimuli, as neuroscientists call them—that we experience. For example, our level of physical comfort or pain, how well-fed or hungry we happen to be (not surprisingly, hunger makes us more alert), whether we are in a brightly lit or dim environment, the environment is quiet or loud, et cetera. And, of course, by the presence or absence of psychological stressors. In general, when we are hungry, thirsty, tired, or otherwise in need of basic sustenance, our arousal levels increase and, with that, our propensity to think and move increases. It should be obvious why that is adaptive. (It helps us seek out food, water, etc.)

The third category of things that control our autonomic nervous system is pharmacologic. Ca�eine and other stimulants are sympathomimetic, meaning they stimulate the SNS and increase arousal.24 Other drugs promote PNS activation, and thus decrease arousal levels. For example, alcohol and barbiturates indirectly increase PNS circuit activity ~~,~~ 25 as does the molecule apigenin, which is found in chamomile tea.26 By the way, if you’re wondering why alcohol initially makes people more talkative and alert before it makes them drowsy or has them pass out, it’s because before it reduces central nervous system activity and lowers arousal, alcohol �rst transiently stimulates the SNS. “It lifts you up before it drops you,” as they say.

_Autonomic_ means “automatic” and indeed our sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems are, for the most part, not under our direct conscious control. We of course can adjust them indirectly. We just discussed three categories of ways to do that. The pathways and mechanisms by which di�erent activities like exercise,27 or mechanical inputs like massage or a warm bath,28 or drugs like ca�eine29 elevate or lower arousal by adjusting the activity of our SNS or PNS are fairly well known, but again, it’s crucial to note these are all indirect ways of adjusting autonomic arousal. As such, they tend to be slow and hard to titrate—meaning hard to get just right. Moreover, some, like barbiturates or prescription stimulants, have addictive potential and/or are costly.

There is, however, one major exception to all of this: one lever by which we can quickly, directly, and reliably change our level of autonomic arousal by shifting the balance of SNS versus PNS activity. That lever is our respiration pattern, aka our breathing.

Why? Because the neural circuits that control our breathing are part of our autonomic nervous system. In fact, they are the one (and only!) component of it that is both autonomic—breathing works just �ne without us having to think about it—but that we can also consciously and directly control at any moment we choose. The same cannot be said about our heart rate, digestion, or immune system. As my colleague at Stanford, David Spiegel, MD, has described it to me, breathing and the neural centers that control breathing represent a bridge between our conscious and unconscious mind. We will return to this idea shortly, but to understand the speci�c patterns of breathing that allow us to consciously and directly control our stress response, and to understand the best tools for adjusting our stress threshold, we need to take the autonomic spectrum —that continuum spanning from deep states of calm to intense states of panic I described earlier—and turn it into a seesaw.

A seesaw? Correct. The simplest model for understanding how to control stress is a seesaw: parasympathetic at one end and sympathetic at the other. When the seesaw is tilted toward the parasympathetic end, we feel calm and relaxed. Tilt it further in that direction and we start drifting o� to sleep. A �at, balanced seesaw represents when we are alert, but calm. Tilt it a bit in the other direction, toward the sympathetic end, and we feel more alert and energized. Tilt it further, and we feel stressed. At its steepest tilt, we are in full-blown panic. Reducing the intensity or duration of the stress response can be accomplished either by increasing the load on the parasympathetic side, by reducing the load on the sympathetic side, or both. How do you do that? We just need to understand a bit about the neural circuits and physiology of the SNS and PNS. And how breathing impacts each of these.

Because it turns out that inhales and exhales modulate the activity of our autonomic nervous system. Inhales reduce PNS activity, leading to relatively more SNS activity and thus, arousal. Exhales directly increase PNS activity. This means your heart rate is faster during inhales than during exhales—which

incidentally is the basis of heart rate variability (HRV). Higher HRV in sleep and throughout your day is better than lower HRV, because it means PNS activity is periodically slowing your heart rate down. It’s a good marker of your body controlling its own level of arousal, and keeping stress in check ~~.~~ 30 More on all that later but for now, it’s going to be helpful to understand what “feeling stressed” is about at a neurochemical level. If you are stressed, that likely means that adrenaline and cortisol have been released and are circulating in your body at higher-than-typical levels, and that norepinephrine has been released at higher-than-typical levels ~~.~~ 31 You can’t just make those molecules go away with positive self-talk. Also, when stress hits, your prefrontal cortex changes its pattern of electrical �ring in a way that limits the range of solutions you can come up with to a problem ~~.~~ 32 It even changes your ability to link previous experiences in insightful ways ~~.~~ 33 Most of us are familiar with this stress-induced black-and-white thinking. These facts should help alleviate some of the frustration you may experience when someone tells you to “just relax,” and you can’t. Or when someone says, “Don’t worry, this too shall pass.” The �rst form of encouragement ignores that we must actively do something to our _physiology_ to relax. You can’t out-think adrenaline. The latter encouragement is spot on, as stress does indeed hinder our ability to see the big picture, but it’s not particularly helpful in the moment. It’s sort of like telling you that the splitting headache you’re su�ering from right now won’t suck in the future. Fortunately, there is a way to get right to the physiology of the stress response. Rather than try to directly reduce sympathetic tone, you need to instead tilt the seesaw back toward the parasympathetic side by increasing the activity of your PNS. That is going to be the fastest way to calm down in real time whenever you are feeling stressed.

###### Resilience defined

If you think about it, this is a big part of what resilience is really about. It’s not our ability to tolerate or eliminate the stress response but rather our ability to reduce its intensity quickly and in real time, when our arousal exceeds a useful level, so that we can move forward. Resilience is our ability to control stress.

Sometimes that means going from extreme stress to very alert and energized, so we can perform a task and quickly problem-solve under intense pressure. Other times it means taking ourselves from endlessly looping thoughts to deep sleep. Resilience is also about an ability to deliberately increase our stress threshold, so life’s minor stressors don’t disproportionally hijack our mind and body. Once you learn how to do those two things, then you will truly be in the driver’s seat.

Maybe that all sounds overly simplistic. Easy to say but harder to do. Well, it turns out there are science-supported tools to adjust your stress response in real time and to raise your stress threshold, and they work exceedingly well—and fast. They can also work the �rst time, and every time, because they are grounded in biological mechanisms and circuits that you already have inside you and can access. Some involve adopting a speci�c pattern of breathing, but they are not breathwork. After all, when we �nd ourselves in a high stress situation, we can’t run o� and do �ve minutes of box breathing! Other protocols don’t involve breathing at all. I’ve been blessed to play a partial role in the discovery and application of several of these stress control protocols, although like so many other scienti�c “discoveries,” aspects of them were known about and used by nonscientists in other contexts �rst. None of us gets the patent. The following pages explain what they are, how they work, and how to use them.

###### **STRESS CONTROL PROTOCOL**

1

### Do One to Three Physiological Sighs to Reduce Stress Fast

###### WHAT TO DO:

- Breathe in the pattern known as the physiological sigh. Inhale deeply through your nose until your lungs are full (your belly should expand out while you inhale), then sharply inhale a second time, also through your nose, to maximally in�ate your lungs. Then slowly exhale through your mouth until your lungs are empty of air. Repeat this in-in-out breathing pattern up to three times, in succession, as needed to reduce your stress level (meaning, your level of autonomic arousal) fast.

###### HOW IT WORKS:

Physiological sighs are, to my knowledge, the fastest and most e�ective way there is to deliberately calm yourself down. Often just one physiological sigh does the trick.

That’s because our state of mind and body changes our breathing but our breathing also changes our state of mind and body ~~.~~ 34 Remember the locus coeruleus that releases norepinephrine to make us alert? Well, speci�c populations of neurons involved in speci�c patterns of breathing connect directly to and modulate this release from the locus coeruleus.35

The conversation between the neurons in your brainstem that control breathing also extends downward, into your spinal cord, which contains

neurons that in turn control the muscles between your ribs (called the intercostals) and a dome-shaped muscle attached to the bottom of your rib cage called the diaphragm that actively in�ates and de�ates your lungs.36

When we inhale, oxygen enters our body, �lls our lungs, then passes from our lungs into our bloodstream. That only happens because our lungs are not just two big, hollow bags; they contain hundreds of millions of tiny sacs called alveoli, which in�ate with air as we inhale. The walls of the alveoli are extremely thin—about 1/2000<sup>th</sup> of a millimeter (!)—and yet rich with capillaries, the smallest diameter blood vessels. Together, they allow oxygen to move from the air-�lled alveoli into the bloodstream. Having hundreds of millions of alveoli greatly increases the surface area through which oxygen can pass into our blood, and thus increases the amount of oxygen we absorb with each breath. (As wild as it sounds, you have approximately 70 to 100 square meters—about the size of a regulation tennis court—of alveolar surface area packed inside your lungs.) Big, deep breaths in�ate more alveoli and the more alveoli that in�ate, the more oxygen passes into your bloodstream to get delivered to your organs, including your brain ~~.~~ 37

Carbon dioxide from the bloodstream passes into the alveoli—again through capillaries—and then is expelled from your body when you exhale. We need both oxygen and carbon dioxide, but we need them in the right balance. If we breathe too little, carbon dioxide builds up in our brain and bloodstream, leading to headaches and tiredness ~~.~~ 38 If we breathe too much—rapidly inhaling and exhaling, or what we typically call hyperventilation—we expel too much carbon dioxide, which is problematic because carbon dioxide is crucial for making sure oxygen gets to our brain cells. If you’ve ever wondered why it’s advised to breathe into a paper bag if you’re having a panic attack, it’s to recapture some of the carbon dioxide that would otherwise be expelled. In this chapter you’ll learn faster and better ways to calm down, but the logic is the same. Overbreathing causes anxiety, dizziness, confusion, poor sleep, and even muscle spasms ~~.~~ 39

As mentioned in the introduction to this chapter, the neurons in our brainstem that control our breathing represent a bridge between our conscious and unconscious mind. They are equipped to sense the ratio of oxygen to

carbon dioxide in our blood, which prompts any necessary alterations in our breathing pattern to keep us alive and well. That happens regardless of whether we are exercising hard or deeply relaxed—it even happens while we sleep.40 Unlike other autonomic neural circuitry, however, we can take immediate conscious control of these neurons. We can decide “I’m going to extend my next exhale a bit” or “I’m going to take one more inhale before holding my breath” and—voila!—we can make that happen. We just don’t have that level of conscious control over any other autonomic function. There are some reported examples of people who used biofeedback to learn to directly control their heart rate or the size of the pupils of their eyes, but that requires a fair amount of training.41 Extended exhales and physiological sighs are something that anyone can do.

Certain internal states are associated with certain respiratory patterns. And by deliberately changing how we breathe, we can shift our internal state. That’s a big deal and something I wish they had taught us in grade school. Alas, it wasn’t until recently that Western science embraced controlled studies of respiration and, in doing so, revealed what had been known in Eastern traditions for thousands of years. We owe it to a small set of dedicated researchers, mostly neuroscientist Jack Feldman’s lab at UCLA, for discovering how the brain controls breathing, both our unconscious re�exive breathing and deliberate breathing, and how they impact our emotional and cognitive states.42 Before and during our discussion on the _Huberman Lab_ podcast, Jack told me stories of setting out to study this topic in the early 2000s, and a luminary of neuroscience making fun of him at meetings. He would jab: “Why would you study something as boring as breathing? Why don’t you study something important, like memory?”43 (That guy studied memory.) Jack knew to ignore him and follow his intuition. His work ignited a �eld that is now positively impacting the mental and physical health of people of all ages. Detecting and modifying certain breathing patterns also turns out to be important for predicting heart attacks ~~,~~ 44 strokes ~~,~~ 45 and seizures,46 and for preventing sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS) ~~.~~ 47 Some of his recent work has also shed light on the fact that some opioid drugs can lead to death because of how they change

the �ring patterns of the neurons that control breathing ~~.~~ 48 It is fair to say that Jack’s work has literally saved lives.

Breathing isn’t just about getting oxygen into your lungs; it also helps control heart rate. While you can’t directly control your heart rate, you can leverage the fact above and use your breathing to control it indirectly. Deliberately inhaling more vigorously or longer (or both) increases your heart rate, whereas deliberately exhaling more vigorously or for longer slows your heart rate down, through a process called respiratory sinus arrhythmia. Exhales also activate a speci�c branch of the vagus nerve, which is part of the PNS, which in turn reduces the rate of electrical activity in neurons of the sinoatrial node of the heart, your heart’s natural pacemaker. So deliberately emphasizing the intensity and/or duration of your exhales for a few breathing cycles will caaaaalm youuuu dooooown. The breathing pattern described in this protocol does just that.

Once you learn the relationship between breathing and heart rate, and deploy the physiological sigh to reduce your heart rate on the spot, it gives you a signi�cant feeling of con�dence in dealing with stress, and uncertain circumstances too. You no longer have to be afraid you will get stuck in an anxiety response in a key moment, or any moment for that matter. You also realize that what most people say to themselves or others when stress hits —“Take a deep breath”—is the exact _opposite_ of what we need to do! When stress hits we should do a big exhale. It is when we really draw out that exhale that our heart rate starts to slow down.

So why am I recommending “Do one to three physiological sighs to calm down fast” and not just “Do a big exhale”? And why aren’t I suggesting box breathing, a popular breathing pattern that asks you to inhale-hold-exhale-hold, each in equal duration? Because some breathing techniques are far more potent and fast acting than others for stress reduction. And physiological sighs are particularly powerful for that purpose, because they capitalize on a hardwired set of neural circuits and neuromuscular pathways, which at once slow our heart rate down and adjust our oxygen–to–carbon-dioxide ratio in our brain and our bloodstream. The �rst two steps of the physiological sigh—the long inhale, followed by the quick inhale—are vital because of those hundreds of millions of alveoli we discussed. The insides of alveoli are a bit damp, not unlike a de�ated

balloon that once held water. And they tend to stick together due to surface tension. The long inhale in�ates many alveoli, and the second quick inhale that immediately follows helps generate the force needed to rein�ate alveoli that would otherwise stay de�ated. This is especially e�ective when you inhale through your nose, because nasal breathing generates more resistance than mouth breathing and thus more force to rein�ate those alveoli. Doing a physiological sigh also stimulates a collateral (meaning a branch of a neural pathway) that emerges from the brainstem area controlling your breathing and reaches other brain areas important for emotional and cognitive control.49 Thus, physiological sighs, unlike just a big exhale or box breathing, are a three-pronged tool to quickly (1) slow your heart rate, (2) reestablish proper oxygen–to– carbon–dioxide ratios in your brain and bloodstream, and (3) engage brain areas that let you think logically about your situation. It’s adaptive biological engineering at its best and works to calm you down.

Infants do physiological sighs re�exively ~~.~~ 50 Animals do too.51 Observe a dog right before it goes down for a nap. You’ll see that double inhale, long exhale pattern. Rats physiological sigh when placed into a claustrophobic environment ~~.~~ 52 People re�exively do physiological sighs about once every few minutes when workin ~~g~~ 53 and even in their sleep to reset their oxygen–to– carbon-dioxide ratio.54

In fact, you have dedicated sets of neurons in your brainstem for generating physiological sighs.55 Nature just doesn’t create discrete neural pathways by accident; that’s how important this breathing pattern is. One respiratory region, the pre-Bötzinger complex, controls your rhythmic breathing, the regular alternation of inhales and exhales.56 But a second region, the parafacial nucleus, controls breathing that involves double inhales, double exhales, or any combination of inhales and exhales in ratios other than the 1:1 inhale-exhale pattern.57 The parafacial nucleus does things other than generate physiological sighs but that’s one of its primary functions.

I’d like to clarify that physiological sighs are not breathwork. _Breathwork_ refers to setting aside �ve to twenty minutes to do a speci�c breathing pattern (or designated sequence of patterns) to get you into a speci�c state of mind and

body. Physiological sighs are a naturally occurring breathing cycle that we can deliberately recreate. And they are the fastest way to consciously tilt your seesaw to the parasympathetic side of your autonomic nervous system.

Do it before public speaking or a hard conversation. Do it when you’re stuck in tra�c or late to an important meeting and starting to feel your tension level rise. Do it to stop yourself from overreacting to an o�hand comment. It won’t guarantee that you’ll always do the right thing in response, but it will put you in a better frame of body and mind, so that you have the best chance of navigating the stress that comes from these or similar situations.

There are data showing that doing physiological sighs outside of stressful moments can help bu�er you against future stress too ~~.~~ 58 Several years ago, my lab collaborated with psychiatrist David Spiegel to investigate just that ~~.~~ 59 We conducted a study that randomized 108 participants to one of four groups. One group did �ve minutes per day of cyclic physiological sighing: Inhale, inhale, long exhale, repeat, and so on for �ve minutes. The second group did �ve minutes per day of box breathing, a breathing technique I’ve mentioned before, which follows a pattern of inhale-hold-exhale-hold-repeat, where each inhalation and exhalation, and the holds, are the same duration, until �ve minutes have elapsed. The third group did �ve minutes per day of cyclic hyperventilation: You take a big deep breath in through the nose and a shorter exhale through the mouth, putting more vigor into the inhalation than the exhalation. A fourth group did �ve minutes per day of meditation, seated with eyes closed, and focusing their attention on their breath but with no speci�c instructions about breathing pattern.

Most participants, regardless of their group, reported an improvement in mood and outlook. But cyclic physiological sighing had a notably bigger e�ect. We also observed improvements in resting heart rate, improved sleep, and other metrics of well-being related to autonomic function. In other words, doing one to three physiological sighs is a great tool for when stress hits and doing �ve minutes of physiological sighs on repeat can help bu�er us further against the inevitable stress of life. Given what you now know about exhales slowing heart rate, oxygen and carbon dioxide levels, and the autonomic seesaw, it should make sense as to why this works. Your brain and body were literally built to do this.
