###### **STRESS CONTROL PROTOCOL**

2

### Use Deliberate Cold Exposure to Raise Your Stress Threshold

###### WHAT TO DO:

- Put yourself in uncomfortably cold water three to seven times per week. This can be as simple as a cold shower, or as involved as an ice bath. For the duration, choose one of these options:
  - Timed protocol: One to three minutes per session.

  - Count “walls of adrenaline” protocol: Rather than committing to a speci�c amount of time, try committing to a speci�c number of mental “walls” to climb over. When you feel the impulse to avoid or exit the cold but you stay, that’s one wall you’ve scaled. Decide in advance how many times you will encounter this impulse and keep going. You do not have to always increase the number of walls. There are days when you will decide to “go over” �ve walls and other days where two walls will be enough.

The water should be uncomfortably cold. This means it should immediately trigger your impulse to get out, but it should be warm enough that you can safely stay in the water for up to three minutes. Why do I suggest using such annoyingly subjective criteria? Because the speci�cs will di�er by person, the time of day, the ambient temperature, how well rested you are, and on and on. It should be cold enough to require you to overcome some mental resistance to get in. And once you get in, it should be cold enough to cause your breathing to quicken. It should make you want to raise your shoulders.

If the water is so cold that it burns or gives you a headache, however, it’s probably too cold. For most people, somewhere between 40 and 50 degrees Fahrenheit works great.

###### HOW IT WORKS:

The previous protocol will help reduce the intensity and the duration of your stress response. This one takes a di�erent approach to stress control by increasing your stress threshold.

But let’s �rst address some of the common myths about deliberate cold exposure. You may have heard that it can increase your metabolism. In my view, the data are not strong enough to support those claims, at least not by doing a typical one-to-three-minute cold shower or cold immersion (and staying in the cold much longer than that could be unsafe).

You also may have heard to avoid deliberate cold exposure after any resistance training session aimed at increasing muscle growth and/or strength. That counsel is legitimate. Deliberate cold exposure in the six to eight hours after resistance training can prevent some of the strength and hypertrophy adaptations that would otherwise occur. (Chapter 2 explains more about those adaptations, and how to achieve them.) That inhibition of muscle growth is likely due to the vasoconstriction the cold causes, which limits both nutrient delivery and waste removal from the recently trained muscles and also blunts protein synthesis ~~.~~ 60 Wait at least six hours after resistance training to do deliberate cold exposure, or do it before you train, or just save it for another day. Or do it any time relative to your resistance training, but be sure to end with a hot shower or bath to reestablish perfusion of the muscles to correct for this. One study argued that deliberate cold exposure done in the �rst six hours after resistance training does not prevent strength adaptations, but most of the work on this issue indicates that deliberate cold exposure done in the six hours or so after resistance training will signi�cantly reduce any hypertrophy or strength increases that would otherwise occur.61 So it is best to simply do it before resistance training, or on rest days. Or allow six or more hours to elapse after resistance training before deliberate cold exposure.

Another common myth is that deliberate cold exposure is harmful for people wishing to limit their cortisol levels. You often hear that people should avoid deliberate cold exposure to keep their cortisol levels low too. Yet the cortisol increases caused by deliberate cold exposure, while signi�cant, are transient and small compared to the dramatic increase that a moderate intensity exercise session triggers ~~.~~ 62 You won’t hear that people should avoid exercise to keep cortisol low because the cortisol increase caused by exercise is, again, transient and, what’s more, bene�cial. (Indeed, it is a key aspect of the speci�c and general adaptation triggers we discussed in chapter 2).

Many of the “cold exposure is bad for you” stories involve people going into the cold for very long periods of time at excruciatingly cold temperatures, or combining deliberate cold exposure with hyperventilation breathwork and/or jumping or diving under ice. All of which are dangerous and should be avoided.

Now that those points are out of the way, let’s look at why deliberate cold exposure is bene�cial. Done correctly, deliberate cold exposure is a powerful, safe, and reliable tool for rapidly adjusting your internal state and stress threshold. There are two key phases, each with distinct bene�ts. First, the state shift that occurs during the cold exposure itself. Second, the state shift that occurs for many hours afterward. Anyone who has done deliberate cold exposure consistently—that is, three to seven times per week—will tell you there is a third phase too, which is the change in your subjective experience of stress and your ability to navigate other forms of stress.

When you enter the cold, it sharply tilts your autonomic nervous system toward the sympathetic end of the seesaw. It does this the �rst time and every time, and it happens fast, within one to two seconds upon entering the cold. Then, once you get out of the cold, you tend to remain in a very “alert but calm” state—meaning (in the context of the model I described) with an evenly balanced autonomic seesaw—for many hours afterward.

Deliberate cold exposure increases the levels of circulating catecholamines in your brain and body: adrenaline, norepinephrine, and dopamine, and increases in the hormone cortisol too.63 Some, including dopamine in particular, remain elevated long after you dry o� and warm up.64 These catecholamines increase

mood, energy, and alertness. They also can increase your stress threshold; more on that below.65 But �rst I want to pause for a moment because you may be asking this: Why would I want to trigger the release of these “stress” chemicals? Won’t that make me feel more, not less, stressed? Yes, but that’s what this protocol is all about.

We need to challenge the notion that stress is always bad for us.

In fact, when we have control over when, how much, and especially for what purpose we experience stress, the impact of that stress can switch from being health-perturbing to health-promoting, and this reshapes the body’s response to all forms of stress.66 This is not “mind over matter,” it’s leveraging the brain circuits that convert the arousal response we call stress into something called eustress—a term coined by Swiss physiologist Hans Selye ~~.~~ 67 (You may remember him from the previous chapter.) He was nominated for the Nobel Prize seventeen times for his work on this and related topics ~~,~~ 68 long before we knew what the underlying mechanisms were, but as those mechanisms have become elucidated, many of his theories have largely been deemed correct.

We now know that your prefrontal cortex—that patch of brain real estate involved in context-dependent decision-making (as well as “top-down” inhibition of impulsive actions) is also a key component of our limbic system, which is involved in di�erent arousal-based responses.69 Usually when people talk about the limbic system, they focus on the amygdala, a brain structure often touted as our fear center. They also talk about our reptilian brain, which is pop neuroscience language for structures like our hypothalamus, which contains dozens of subareas involved in regulating hunger, thirst, aggression, mating, and much more. The hypothalamus and amygdala are often placed conceptually opposite “more evolved” or “higher” brain centers like the prefrontal cortex. But alas, that framework is a gross misrepresentation of the way our brain actually works.

Human brains don’t have one system for positive arousal and another entirely di�erent system for negative arousal. We simply have a system for autonomic arousal that is linked to, and impacted by, areas of the brain that evaluate the context of our experiences and then help us make adaptive

decisions. Think about it: There are an in�nite number of di�erent contexts in which arousal could be good, and just as many where it could be bad. Your prefrontal cortex carries out the basic analysis when arousal happens, asking questions like, “Did I choose this situation?” “Can I control how long and/or how intense this arousal is?” and most importantly, “Is this state of elevated autonomic arousal good or bad for me?” Of course, the answers to those questions depend on the context. And your prior experiences and knowledge.

In fact, our knowledge about stress—not just our memories of stressful circumstances we have been in before, but what we believe to be true about stress—a�ects how we respond to it. Work from Alia Crum’s lab at Stanford shows that humans who learn about some of the (true) positive e�ects of stressrelated arousal on physical health and mental performance experience those positive e�ects when they are subjected to stress.70 Her lab also showed that if people learn a bunch of (also true) information about how stress can make us physically unhealthy and cognitively impaired, well, that’s what happens to them when they get stressed ~~!~~ 71 We can thank our prefrontal cortex for that ability to reframe stress in ways that change its actual e�ects on us. It’s not just a decrease in its negative e�ect but an inversion from deleterious to bene�cial. There’s more that shapes our experience of stress as good or bad. Perhaps one of the most interesting things that determines the outcome is whether the stressor has a known end point and resolution that we control.72 With that in mind, it should now make perfect sense why deliberate cold exposure meets all the criteria of eustress, and why I coined it _deliberate_ . If you are the one who elected it, and you control its duration, and you understand how it is good for you, you can turn stress into eustress.

So how, exactly, is it good for you? Two ways. First, the stress of deliberate cold exposure helps us become better at handling other moments of stress. That’s sometimes called cross adaptation. It’s often studied in the context of physical stress, where exposure to one type of stress—say, exercising in extreme heat—prepares a person to tolerate another type of stress, such as thriving in environments with low oxygen levels.73 The idea is that we can precondition ourselves to cope with challenges by seeking out situations that draw on similar

aspects of our physiology. Cold water swimming has been proposed as a way to improve surgical outcomes,74 for example, because the stress of the former helps patients better handle the stress of the latter.

Controlled studies showing that cross adaptation focused on physical stress can prepare us to face emotional stress are slowly accruing. In one study of eighty-six people, combining cold exposure with breathing techniques changed the participants’ perception of stress in their everyday lives.75 Participants rated statements such as “You feel calm” and “You enjoy yourself” following a few minutes of vigorous breathwork and a quick cold shower every morning for a period of two weeks. And participants who did both during that period reported a greater sense of control over irritations, and stronger feelings that life was going their way and that they were on top of things, compared to participants who did only the breathwork or the cold exposure, or neither.

Some data are more tangential in nature. For example, cold exposure appears to improve the body’s response over time to hypoxia, or low oxygen levels in the blood, which is relevant because hypoxia can rapidly set in when we hit a state of anxiety or panic ~~.~~ 76 Some preliminary evidence has pointed to a possible role for cold exposure in the treatment of depression, not as a replacement for medication but as an accompaniment ~~.~~ 77 In 2018, a group of researchers from the UK reported that a twenty-four-year-old woman who had been treated for major depressive disorder and anxiety since the age of seventeen with little to no relief began weekly sessions of cold water swimming in an attempt to �nd something that could diminish, or negate, the need for medication after she became a mother. The intervention worked for her. Within four months, she no longer required drug treatment.78 That was a case study of just one person, but interesting nonetheless.

A 2023 review of fourteen studies on the mental health bene�ts of outdoor cold-water swimming found this practice to be associated with stress reduction, mood improvement, and a positive outlook.79 That result is not necessarily entirely tied to cold; being outdoors and part of a community (many people do winter swims in groups or with friends) certainly contributes, but cold exposure is responsible for at least some of this bene�t. Other work has also shown a

connection between winter swimming and well-being ~~.~~ 80 In one study, �fty-three people in the UK who participated in eight weekly sea swims reported a reduction in both depression and anxiety.81 Interestingly, “confronting a challenge” was commonly reported as a reason why the experience was rewarding. In another investigation, forty-two undergraduates at the University of Chichester, in the UK, completed a mood pro�le questionnaire before and after cold immersion, with an additional twenty-two students completing the questionnaire twice but without cold immersion in between ~~.~~ 82 Energy and selfesteem increased signi�cantly in the experimental group, which also experienced a decrease in tension, anger, and depression. No comparable changes were observed in the control group.

The overarching concept here is really about the intentional discomfort brought about from doing deliberate cold exposure. As Mike Tipton, a sports and exercise scientist who has studied cold exposure extensively at the University of Portsmouth, has noted, the kind of discomfort stemming from a cold bath was once a commonplace occurrence.83 Humans have been exposed to cold for a very long time, and modern living has eliminated it. As a result, we are never forced to move out of homeostasis, which means our various systems are rarely challenged. “The dynamic equilibrium that underpins homeostasis needs to be perturbed,” Tipton wrote in an editorial �rst published in 2018. Stanford University psychiatrist Anna Lembke, author of _Dopamine Nation_ , has also spoken about the role of deliberate pain exposure to combat addictions. As she explained it, we are living in the midst of a “�re hose of dopamine,” triggered by our phones, ca�eine, sugar, and other aspects of modern life.84 And part of the way out of this is to temporarily abstain from pleasure and to intentionally seek pain—not life-threatening pain, not anything dangerous, but discomfort ~~.~~ 85 We need to learn to cope with stress, not just eliminate it. Stress is a part of life, and we are capable of withstanding it. Cold immersion shows us how.

The second way deliberate cold exposure is good for us is the state it puts us in after it’s over. And no, I’m not just talking about a state of relief—although it is fair to say that nearly everyone enjoys getting out of the cold plunge or cold shower more than getting into it. In all seriousness, very few people actually

enjoy deliberate cold exposure while they are in the cold. It is a potent stressor and no amount of learning about eustress will change that. In fact, I often �nd myself cursing Selye when I’m in the cold. But once we get out, ahhh, that’s when the real magic starts. The sharp increase in adrenaline, norepinephrine, and cortisol we just triggered also sets in motion a dramatic and prolonged increase in dopamine—the molecule that, as we will discuss more in chapter 6, induces a heightened sense of motivation and focus and, with the pain of the cold now gone, buzz. Dopamine doesn’t act alone to create the post-deliberatecold state, but it is a central player in that neuroendocrine cocktail. It’s the perfect state for a work session, for exercising, socializing, pretty much any activity that requires us to be alert and focused.

If the way I’m describing the post-cold state sounds almost drug-like, it is. Only better. One study found that full-body (up to the neck) immersion in water at about 57 degrees Fahrenheit for one hour triggered a more than �vefold increase in norepinephrine levels compared to baseline ~~.~~ 86 It also produced a rise in dopamine levels in the body, raising them more than twofold for hours afterward. We call this peripheral dopamine, because it was measured from the body. We don’t yet know the exact relationship between dopamine levels in the body and in the brain, but we do know they tend to increase and decrease in parallel. And there is emerging evidence that when peripheral dopamine is elevated, it increases dopamine in reward and motivation circuits in the brain in a dose-dependent manner.87 When adrenaline is released in the body, it doesn’t cross the blood-brain barrier but it does activate receptors in the vagus nerve that project from the body to the brain. In doing so, it causes the locus coeruleus to release norepinephrine, which increases alertness in the brain. So there is reason to assume that peripheral increases in catecholamines triggered by deliberate cold exposure are mirrored by similar increases in the brain.

It is worth noting that drugs known to sharply increase dopamine and epinephrine, such as amphetamines or cocaine, also produce fast, large increases in catecholamines but with the important caveat that they cause levels of the catecholamines to rise so fast and then drop so fast, that they plummet below pre-drug levels. That is part of what, as Anna Lembke, MD, explained in _Dopamine Nation_ , puts people in a state of psychological and physical

discomfort, and leaves them craving more of those drugs right away, which partially explains why they are addictive ~~.~~ 88

Deliberate cold exposure then seems an almost perfect way to signi�cantly increase and maintain elevated levels of catecholamines. You get the mental focus and mood bene�ts they provide, and you also raise your stress threshold.

Most of us don’t have an hour available to spend sitting in chilly water, however. Fortunately, you can use colder temperatures for much shorter periods of time to get the same e�ect. Studies show that even thirty seconds can work.89 Yet I suggest one to three minutes or two to ten “walls.” As mentioned above, pinpointing an exact temperature for every reader isn’t possible because it will vary according to di�erences in the amount of body fat, time of day, tolerance for cold, and other factors. That being said, adrenaline levels reliably increase when we expose our body surface to temperatures below 59 degrees Fahrenheit (15°C) and the colder the water, the faster and larger the resulting catecholamine response will be. This relationship isn’t linear. We cannot say, “Sit in this temperature water for this long and you’ll get this much more adrenaline and dopamine released.” It doesn’t work like that. We don’t work like that. Nor can we say that x number of minutes in x degrees water will elevate our dopamine x amount for x number of hours after.

That’s why, although I refer to deliberate cold exposure as a protocol, like resistance training or cardio, you will need to consider what number of sets, so to speak, works best for you. It is best thought of as a time to practice triggering speci�c types of adaptations to build resilience. Some people say you should try to relax and breathe slowly during deliberate cold exposure. Others suggest distracting yourself with mental arithmetic or singing a song. I disagree and view both those approaches as the loss of a valuable opportunity to focus on stress control. You can take this time to learn to steer your mind and body through the stress response.

Resilience, grit, and mental toughness are really about the ability to stay in control of your thoughts, words, and actions when you experience that stress response. When you get into the cold, your prefrontal cortex experiences a surge in norepinephrine input, which causes a disruption in its communication with

subcortical areas ~~.~~ 90 This is true of any stressful circumstance, whether deliberate or involuntary. With your prefrontal cortex function essentially impaired for the �rst thirty seconds after you get in the cold, all your thoughts and actions initially will default to removing the stressor. It’s where the immediate “I want out!” response comes from. The key is to remind yourself that it is normal to feel like that. You’re in what I call “pure impulse” mode. Do this: Try to consciously watch your mind shift from “I want out!” to “I’ve got this,” which will likely happen again and again very rapidly in that �rst thirty or so seconds. By observing that phase and not trying to grind your way through it, you are actively engaging your prefrontal cortex in a way that is not typical of someone going through a mild cold-shock response. That’s an extremely valuable skill, to be able to observe your own mind during stress. It’s not about passively observing or dissociating, nor is it about getting hijacked by stress. It’s about learning adaptive self-control during stressful moments.

The �rst time you try this, it’s hard, but most people �nd that within a few sessions the mind racing starts to lessen, and pretty soon, they feel in control of their thoughts and actions from the start. Few people have mastered this valuable skill in any domain of life, but anyone can learn it. Deliberate cold provides a safe way to practice.

I believe the walls approach mentioned above is the best way to practice this skill, whose bene�ts translate to other forms of stress. When we measure time elapsed in the cold, we focus, not surprisingly, on its passage. As you learned in the introduction to this chapter, high arousal states tend to slow our perception of that. We count, we wonder why time seems to be moving so slowly—a known function of stress—and we focus on it… 3, 2, 1, okay, done! Real-life stressors are very di�erent. Some hit when we least expect it (e.g., an accident or crisis), others are stressful in large part because we know they are coming (e.g., a public talk we need to give, a medical appointment we would sooner avoid, etc.). The way to train for real-life stress in the cold is therefore to learn to sense the increases in adrenaline that occur as we approach, enter, stay in, and exit it. Each of these can be the walls you need to climb over. If you think like that, you’ll notice something very useful: Stress is not constant. It’s not, as we say, a step function.

It oscillates, often very quickly and irregularly. The walls appear, and then disappear and reappear with unpredictable frequency.

If you dread the cold, remember that adrenaline is released merely from the anticipation of getting in. Congratulations! That’s the �rst wall. And as we lower ourselves into the cold, that’s another wall; next comes the �rst “I want out!” wall, then it passes… then comes the next wall, the next, and the next. Importantly, the time between walls is variable. This is also important to notice, as that is exactly how real-life stress feels. We often can’t predict when the next stressful event is coming.

Basically I’m suggesting you approach deliberate cold exposure as resilience training. And by doing it you’ll become mentally stronger in the face of nonvoluntary stress. Just be sure you don’t stay in the cold longer than �ve minutes. Stick to the one to three minutes recommended here, or “go over” two to eight walls. Then get out and go about the rest of your day. Some people, myself included, like to take a hot shower after deliberate cold exposure. People debate whether it’s better to end on cold or not. I don’t care. I like a hot shower after and, in my experience, it does not seem to diminish any of the bene�ts. Find what works for you.

As a �nal point, you actually have more moment-to-moment control over the temperature of the water than you may think. While you can’t quickly make the water temperature change, you can dynamically adjust your experience of it. If you hug your arms around your body, raise your shoulders toward your ears and bring your knees up toward your chest, you will feel slightly warmer. Conversely if you keep your arms and legs extended and move them around, you’ll break up the thermal layer of heated water around your body, making the experience much colder. Want it even colder? Make sure to let the cold water reach as high as your armpits and keep your hands and feet under. You’ll want to remind yourself that this is all very good for you now, and in the hours to come. Cursing Selye, as I do, or cursing me (feel free), is allowed and encouraged.

###### COMMON QUESTIONS:

Cold exposure can be dangerous if the water is exceedingly cold. Exercise caution and prudence with this tool. If you are new to cold immersion, start o� slowly, with short exposures in temperatures that are outside your comfort zone but not extremely so. Try a cold shower, which allows you to adjust the temperature higher or lower quickly. Alas, there is not much data on deliberate cold exposure for pregnant women so if you’re concerned about potential negative outcomes, avoid this. Don’t do it when sick with a cold, the �u, or other respiratory illnesses. Regardless of what you may see online, it’s likely to make your illness worse. Here’s a good set of guidelines for nonpregnant individuals with no serious health issues:

Start with water around 50 degrees Fahrenheit the �rst time, maybe in the mid- to high 40s. Test the water temperature with your hand or foot before getting in; it should feel cold and make you think, “Whoa, that’s cold!” but it should not “burn.”

- If the water triggers a re�ex to raise your shoulders and huddle your arms when you get in, then it’s cold enough. If your breathing involuntarily quickens, it’s cold enough.

- Get in up to your neck with your feet under. Put your hands under last. If you opt for a cold shower, back into the water until your whole body and head are underneath the stream.

- Expect your mind to start racing with thoughts like, “I want out! Why am I doing this?!” Congratulations, you have a functional autonomic nervous system.

Note: _Never, ever jump or dive into very cold water. Lower yourself in while holding something reliably stationary like a ladder or the sides of a cold plunge, or back into a cold shower. I recommend against deliberate cold exposure in cold or frozen outdoor bodies of water unless you have an expert with you, know the location well, and there are real safety measures in place. There is a video on the internet of a woman who drowned after jumping into an ice hole; unbeknownst to her, there was a rapid current under the ice and she was swept under. Her husband allegedly went in after her and also drowned. I have a professor friend who nearly drowned doing deliberate cold exposure in a river. He had done at-home cold plunges many_

_times before but hadn’t realized how cold the river was until he swam out a few feet from shore. He couldn’t breathe properly in a shocked state and he was alone. Have someone with you and decide on a nonverbal signal for “Save me!” before you get in._

_Never—never, ever!—combine immersion in cold water with any type of deliberate hyperventilation before or during. Your breathing will naturally quicken when you get in cold water, but what I am referring to is deliberate hyperventilation_ (Wim Hof _or_ Tummo _breathing, as it is sometimes called). This breathing method causes the lowering of carbon dioxide and will delay the gasp reflex, potentially leading you to black out and drown; sadly, people have died this way._

_Deliberate cold exposure is easy to do safely. Almost all deaths from it occur because people were reckless in some way or combined it with hyperventilation. Don’t be reckless._

A study from metabolic scientist Susanna Søberg, at the University of Copenhagen, and colleagues showed that if people did eleven minutes total per week of deliberate cold exposure, divided into two to four sessions, they enhanced the amount of brown fat in their bodies, a healthy, mitochondria-rich fat that surrounds the heart, neck, and clavicles ~~.~~ 91 That additional brown fat allowed them to feel more comfortable in other cold environments, because when the sympathetic nervous system is active it causes brown fat to burn fatty acids and glucose, which generates heat in the process. In that way, brown fat is like an internal furnace. So if you’re someone who is often cold, deliberate cold exposure can help shift your thermal set point. This is connected to the metabolic bene�ts of cold immersion, which are outside the scope of this protocol. (Note that the participants didn’t gain weight; they just added this special—and bene�cial—type of fat.)

Yes. As an alternative to deliberate cold exposure, you can do three to �ve minutes of cyclic hyperventilation _away from water_ , which reliably raises adrenaline levels. Cyclic hyperventilation, as the name suggests, involves taking

long, vigorous inhales through your nose and passively exhaling through your mouth—think of it as letting the air fall out rather than forcing it out—over and over. It’s not easy to keep up this breathing for several minutes. You’ll �nd it makes you quite agitated and a bit lightheaded.

Data suggest that cyclic hyperventilation works similarly to cold exposure.92 Adrenaline rises. Your heart rate increases. Your limbs will feel like they want to move. And your brain will ask “Why am I doing this?!” It’s normal to feel some light burning in your nostrils as well. It feels uncomfortable while you’re doing it, but it can improve mood and sleep afterward. Also, you can back o� the intensity and/or duration of the inhales and thereby modulate your stress response as you go, an advantage that cold exposure doesn’t o�er.

So if you really hate the cold or if you don’t have access to it, cyclic hyperventilation is the next-best alternative. Just never do it in combination with deliberate cold exposure as, again, you can pass out and drown. People have died combining cyclic hyperventilation with cold immersion; that’s why I’m repeating the warning here yet again. And of course never do cyclic hyperventilation while driving or operating machinery, or other activities that demand your attention. Just sit or lie down somewhere safe for a few minutes to use this tool.

### Do Non-Sleep Deep Rest (NSDR) to Buffer Against Stress

###### WHAT TO DO:

- Do a non-sleep deep rest (NSDR) session for 10 to 30 minutes. Sit or, ideally, lie down in a quiet place and listen to a scripted NSDR session. Guided NSDRs in di�erent voices are available online (hubermanlab.com/nsdr) for zero cost and can be downloaded to use o�ine (also at no cost). NSDR is especially useful in high-stress times lasting weeks or longer, such as intense work or school periods, or when facing deadlines and life transitions, such as raising young kids or caring for an elder. Ideally you do NSDR once per day but it is bene�cial to reduce stress at any point. I do it at least once a week, depending on my schedule.

###### HOW IT WORKS:

I talked about NSDR earlier in this book (remember Sleep Protocol 8?). It is impossible to overstate what an extraordinarily potent tool NSDR can be for mental and physical health. In chapter 1, I covered NSDR’s ability to restore mental and physical energy without creating sleep inertia grogginess. But it is particularly potent when it comes to limiting unhealthy stress. I was �rst introduced to this tool nearly ten years ago. I often get asked “What is something you wish you had known when you were younger?” and my answer is always, “I wish I had known about yoga nidra (aka NSDR).”

NSDR has so many bene�ts. It replenishes your mental and physical 94 it energy ~~,~~ 93 it can o�set many of the negative e�ects of sleep deprivation ~~,~~ improves the depth and continuity of your sleep at night ~~,~~ 95 and it bu�ers you against the harmful e�ects of both acute and chronic stress.96 To get the most out of this practice, I’ll make a few things clear. First, NSDR is not a nap. Nor is it hypnosis. Nor is it meditation, as I explained in chapter 1. Rather, NSDR belongs to a category of techniques that can be broadly thought of as selfdirected relaxation. You shift your brain and bodily state from one of “alert and ready to move” to “alert yet deeply relaxed.” It emphasizes parasympathetic nervous system (PNS) activity, or increases your parasympathetic tone, tilting you toward that calmer side of the autonomic seesaw that I described in the introduction to this chapter. Sounds like a shallow nap… but it’s not. Because you deliberately stay awake during this practice, your sympathetic nervous system remains engaged too. It’s a unique brain state that has important implications.

Research shows that during NSDR, parts of your brain enter sleeplike states, while other brain areas remain in a state of alertness ~~.~~ 97 We don’t quite know what to call the overall brain state that NSDR creates, but we know that it’s selfdirected and has signi�cant stress-reducing and energy-replenishing e�ects ~~.~~ 98 We also know that people typically emerge from NSDR in an alert-but-calm state of mind and body, that center of the seesaw. When one considers that it costs nothing but ten to thirty minutes of time, that is quite a return on investment!

As discussed in chapter 1, NSDR involves shifting one’s focus throughout the session, which for some people makes it easier than meditations that demand you anchor your focus or “clear your mind.” NSDR asks that you shift from thinking, doing, and planning, to being and feeling—I know, that sounds super New Agey. But the instruction is based in physiology, not mysticism. Here is why: Turning o� our thoughts is really hard. In fact, we can’t do it. Even in sleep, we dream. Even in REM sleep people can solve and respond to math problems.99 (If you’re wondering how the experimenters knew that, given people are paralyzed during REM, the subjects signaled correct answers to

simple subtraction problems using eye movements.) So forget trying to destress by not thinking. It just won’t happen.

We can, however, easily shift our immediate experience from planning and analyzing to just experiencing physical sensations. NSDR has us do that. We deliberately shift our attention from one aspect of our sensations in that moment—for instance from our toes to our �ngers, then to a location away from our body such as to sounds in the room, then to sounds far away, then back to a speci�c location on our body, and so forth. This regular and deliberate shifting of our focus on di�erent aspects of our perception both eliminates the strain of trying to continually focus on one thing, and the tendency of our mind to default to planning and analyzing. With NSDR, your mind drifts from one sensation to the next in an intentional but relaxed way. When you do that, your mind goes into an atypical, almost liminal state, the one described above— somewhere between that of deep sleep and being awake. Cortisol levels drop, discrete brain areas fall asleep while others remain active ~~.~~ 100 Because NSDR is done lying down with eyes closed, from the outside it appears you are napping but you’re not. You’re in self-directed reset mode.

If you’ve never done yoga nidra or NSDR before, this may all sound a bit abstract, but it’s really very concrete. It is grounded in what we know about selfdirected brain states. And it’s very easy to do. One of the biggest advantages of NSDR is that, in contrast to mindfulness meditation—which is a skill you build up gradually over time and that requires daily (or near daily) practice to maintain the positive e�ects—NSDR can work the �rst time, and every time.

You lie down, listen to the instructions, and voila! Ten to thirty minutes later you emerge feeling renewed and rested. Most everyone who tries it marvels at the immediate positive e�ects. It’s starting to be used in schools, by elite military operators, professional athletes, Fortune 500 CEOs, and many other men and women around the world as a tool for managing stress and even as a means to accelerate recovery from illness and injury, to o�set some of the negative symptoms of menopause, sleep deprivation, trauma, and more.101 I encourage everyone to try it a few times and experience the bene�ts for themselves.

###### COMMON QUESTIONS:

This is the most common question I get about NSDR. You can do it ANY time. In the morning if you wake up and don’t feel fully rested and don’t have time to get another hour or more of sleep. In the afternoon instead of a nap and if you know you’ll be working harder or longer than usual that day. Before a workout if you’re feeling less-than-motivated or lacking energy. In the evening if you get home and want to destress from the day. In the middle of the night if you wake up and can’t fall back asleep. (In that case, get out of bed and do an NSDR then get back into bed; a return to sleep will arrive easier.)

The simple answer I default to whenever asked “When should I do NSDR?” is “First thing in the morning, or in the afternoon, or any time of night…” It is that versatile and that useful.

### Do a Micro Meditation Immediately After Waking Up

###### WHAT TO DO:

- Incorporate a simple, five-minute daily meditation into your routine. Any time of day can be bene�cial, but doing it before getting out of bed each morning ensures you don’t have to carve out time later and may o�er distinct bene�ts as well.

- If you feel an urgency to get out of bed before five minutes have elapsed, stay put. Contrary to how it is usually framed, meditation is one of the best forms of resilience training. So see this as an opportunity to practice resilience. This meditation is not about clearing the mind. It’s about building the capacity to sit with the stress that even micro meditation can trigger. This will help you better deal with real-life stressors once your day starts.

###### HOW IT WORKS:

Plenty of evidence exists that mindfulness-based meditation practices bu�er us against stress, and even brief daily sessions reduce anxiety ~~.~~ 102 I mention both stress and anxiety here, because there’s a di�erence. Some say stress has an identi�able cause, or a known stressor, whereas anxiety does not. That’s a good working distinction. But the fact that meditation protects us against both highlights that each experience is based in the same thing: an elevated sympathetic tone that exceeds the demands of the stressor.

Meditation can adjust your autonomic seesaw, bringing you back to the center. But just how may surprise you.

Most everyone assumes the goal of a meditation practice is to quiet the mind and that it involves cultivating a sense of peace during the practice. In some sense that’s true. One study found that four consecutive days of a meditation practice reduced anxiety and increased mindfulness, a broad term encompassing a sense of awareness, calm, and being in the present moment.103 A 2019 report by New York University neuroscientist Wendy Suzuki and colleagues found that doing eight weeks of thirteen-minute daily meditation notably decreased anxiety ~~.~~ 104

But data also show that meditation can make us more resilient by allowing us to observe stress when it hits without reacting to it. When psychologist Richard Davidson—one of the world’s foremost experts on the science of meditation— appeared on my podcast, he described that his lab saw a statistically signi�cant increase (!) in people’s anxiety levels in the �rst week that they started doing a regular meditation practice.105 Wait, what? Meditation increases anxiety? Yes. Because it can be maddening to force yourself to focus and refocus on your breathing over and over for �ve minutes when you wake up and you have to dive into your day. Your mind wants to shift to planning and doing. In that way, meditation can serve as a way to increase your stress threshold. Not unlike learning to stay in uncomfortably cold water.

This is as hard as it sounds, but well worth it. Regular meditation teaches us to observe, rather than act on, our autonomic arousal. It also reduces the likelihood that real-life stressors will hijack our mind. Just like Stress Control Protocol 2.

One study found that the intensity of the emotions people experienced while viewing potentially disturbing pictures was reduced when people did so from a “mindful” state, indicating that meditation promotes a kind of awareness that makes a person’s autonomic nervous system less subject to outside stimuli.106 Indeed, neuroimaging studies have con�rmed that meditation consistently alters brain regions connected to both body awareness and mental awareness, as well as emotional regulation.107 The underlying mechanism appears to be connected to the production of GABA, an inhibitory neurotransmitter—meaning a chemical

that generally suppresses the �ring of other neurons. People with panic disorders and anxiety tend to have decreased GABA activity in particular regions of the brain.108 Researchers have theorized that the increased blood �ow to the prefrontal cortex that seems to occur during certain types of meditation may, in turn, lead to increased GABA activity, along with improved top-down inhibition of brain areas that generate re�exive thoughts and actions, and this equates to a general sense of relaxation ~~.~~ 109

A bit more on the format of the micro meditation: stay in bed or, if you must, get up and use the bathroom �rst, and then set a �ve-minute timer, sit or lie down, and stay as still as you can while you focus on your breathing. Observe where your mind goes. If it wanders—which is completely normal by the way— redirect your focus back to your breath. Slow nasal-only inhales and exhales are best. But the most important thing is to do it, and on days when you feel stressed, do it anyway. In fact, that’s a bonus opportunity. The bene�ts to your ability to observe your stress rather than have it engulf you that come from a daily �ve-minute meditation are well worth it. And of course, if you want to do a longer meditation, go for it.

As simple as this protocol may sound, I and countless others can attest to the fact that it provides immediate bene�ts, and bene�ts that extend throughout the day. And one more thing: We don’t yet understand the science of exactly how, but it also seems to create the ability to “see” when stress is coming your way. Perhaps it sensitizes the brain circuits that respond to autonomic arousal. Perhaps it leads to better recognition of adrenaline in our body rising, or our heart rate starting to increase. After all, a �ve-minute meditation will gradually have you feeling more anxious as you progress from start to �nish; it’s very di�erent from getting into cold water, which causes a big spike in adrenaline right at the start. But that ability to sense approaching stress is a game changer, as it can reduce your reactivity and improve your ability to make decisions about what to do and say—and in many cases, what not to do and say—when the inevitable stressors of life appear.

### Boost Your Morning Cortisol and Catecholamine Peak

###### WHAT TO DO:

  - Get bright light, ideally sunlight, in your eyes for about ten minutes, as soon as possible after waking. If you wake before the sun is up, you’ll either have to wait for the sun to rise or use a 10,000 lux light for this trigger. (I cover how in detail in Sleep Protocol 1.)

ten minutes. While not a full-�edged workout, it will help stimulate the morning cortisol and catecholamine increase you’re after.

Do one of the deliberate cold exposure protocols discussed in this chapter.

As an ALTERNATIVE to deliberate cold exposure, try cyclic hyperventilation: Do a cycle of twenty-�ve to thirty deep, vigorous inhales through your nose, with each inhale followed by a passive exhale—meaning just let the air fall out of your lungs via your mouth. Afterward, you’ll feel a bit lightheaded. That is a normal response. Exhale all your air and hold your breath for thirty to sixty seconds. You should no longer feel lightheaded. You can repeat this process for two to three more rounds. Note: NEVER do cyclic hyperventilation before or during deliberate cold exposure, anywhere near water, while driving, operating machinery, or performing other activities that demand your attention. You may recall from those protocols that deliberate cold exposure doesn’t spike cortisol all that much, but it does signi�cantly increase the other catecholamines. And that is bene�cial here. Consider occasional (once or twice per week) use of low-dose licorice root containing glycyrrhizin or consume grapefruit in the first one to three hours of your day. Both have been shown to signi�cantly increase cortisol and the duration of cortisol action. Subjectively, they can increase feelings of morning and daytime energy and focus. Warning: Despite licorice and grapefruit sounding natural (and they are), their e�ects can be very potent. They can increase blood pressure and/or �uid retention at high doses, so use the minimal e�ective dose and, as with all supplements discussed in this book, consult your doctor �rst.

###### HOW IT WORKS:

Cortisol and the catecholamines adrenaline and norepinephrine, but especially cortisol, are often thought of purely as stress chemicals. The third catecholamine —dopamine—escaped this reputation but is usually thought of (also incorrectly) as purely a pleasure chemical. And while cortisol is involved in the

stress response, thinking about it as purely a stress chemical is wrong. I wish I could banner this across the sky: _Cortisol Is Not a Stress Hormone!_

In fact, if I could impart just one message about how to improve your health, it would be this: Strive to get your morning cortisol high (yes, high!) and your nighttime cortisol low.

The main function of cortisol is to ensure there is enough energy in the form of glucose, or blood sugar, for you to meet life’s demands. Yes, that can include overcoming stressors, but it also includes simply waking up each morning with the physical and mental energy required for work, school, family, and exercise. Cortisol causes glucose (as well as fats) to get released into the bloodstream, and it also stimulates the liver to make more glucose ~~.~~ 111

Cortisol and adrenaline play additional key roles in our body’s everyday functioning. They improve our immune system’s ability to ward o� infections, they elevate our mood, they allow for our capacity to form new memories, and they increase metabolism… so just forget the idea that cortisol and adrenaline are only about stress.

A gradual rise in your cortisol levels starts three to four hours before you wake up each morning and its levels eventually hit a threshold level, at which point you wake up, open your eyes, and get out of bed. Keep in mind that cortisol doesn’t act alone to rouse you from sleep; a parallel rise in body temperature and clearance of the sleepiness-inducing molecule adenosine follows a similar schedule. Nonetheless, scientists call this rise the “cortisol awakening response” or CAR. Now that makes it sound like a medical problem of some sort, but CAR is a normal and (provided it is timed correctly) healthpromoting aspect of our biology.112 And it helps bu�er you against unhealthy stress.

Cortisol �rst starts to rise as a result of a signal from your SCN, your brain’s master circadian clock that we discussed in chapter 1. For most people, that rise starts somewhere around �ve hours into their night’s sleep and continues sharply over the subsequent two to three hours until it reaches a threshold level and bam! You wake up. Even if you use an alarm clock, you can be sure your cortisol levels were rising as you approached the start of your day. Now, once you’re awake, cortisol _continues_ to increase until it hits its peak for that twenty-

four-hour cycle. For most people, that peak occurs anywhere from 0.5 to 1.5 hours after waking up.

Then cortisol levels slowly start to decline—a process that continues into the late afternoon and evening. Assuming you encounter no major stressors, your cortisol levels continue to drop in the hours before you fall asleep and reach their lowest level about three to four hours after you doze o�, and then slowly start to rise again to eventually trigger the next morning’s CAR, and so on. This is the ideal cortisol pattern for mental and physical health, energy, and resilience to stress.

Night shift workers deal with a very disrupted sleep-wake schedule, and their cortisol pattern gets fragmented, with multiple peaks and troughs throughout the day. For some, the pattern inverts to match their wake-sleep schedule. Although that might seem like not that big of a deal if they are still getting enough sleep, it’s known to cause serious and long-lasting health issues. Indeed, many of the known health detriments of nocturnal schedules are due primarily to alterations in the pattern of cortisol release and its downstream e�ects. I cover what shift workers can do to partially o�set those negative e�ects in chapter 1 and chapter 5 ~~.~~ 113

Most people, even night owls or those staying up too late on their phones, are not completely inverting their sleep-wake schedule, and yet there is reason to believe that they have less than ideal cortisol patterns. I say “most people” because the vast majority of questions I get are about wanting better sleep, more energy, improved focus, and less stress and anxiety. And when I inquire about the structure of their days, I learn that very few people are doing the few simple things to ensure high cortisol in the morning and low cortisol at night. This sets them up for health problems and lowered resilience to stress.

Numerous studies show that if your cortisol levels fall too slowly as you approach the later hours of your day—a so-called “�attening of the diurnal cortisol rhythm”—or if your cortisol is spiked by stress or bright light in the evening, you can experience that as increased anxiety, and sleep can su�er too.114 If this happens once in a while, it’s no big deal. Acute stressors—an argument, a small crisis at work, and so on—are part of life. They spike our cortisol and catecholamines. But these levels ordinarily return to baseline a few minutes or

hours later. So don’t freak out about a bit of stress here or there even late in the day! The stress management tools discussed elsewhere in this chapter will assist in helping you navigate those events.

If, however, your cortisol undergoes stress-induced peaks in the late evening or nighttime, or if your morning cortisol is too low or declines too slowly, that �attening of the cortisol curve is what puts you into a state of chronic stress.115 This can cause a cascade of detrimental events in your body and brain. Diabetes, hypertension, depression, and weight gain can result, as can physical imbalance, leaving a person feeling unsteady on their feet ~~.~~ 116 Studies have also linked abnormally high cortisol levels later in the day and into the night to acne, irregular menstrual cycles, and digestion issues ~~.~~ 117 High cortisol at night has been linked to insomnia and reduced amounts of REM sleep ~~.~~ 118 Given this, everyone would do well to try to anchor and amplify their cortisol and catecholamine peak in the �rst hours after waking to start their day and limit their cortisol and catecholamine levels at night. That simple framework goes a long way toward limiting your chronic stress. And that’s what this protocol is all about.

Let’s start with what to do at night, because how you prepare for bed a�ects your cortisol and catecholamine levels the next day. Some of what you’re about to read will be familiar to you from chapter 1. Before bed, implement a winddown routine of dimming the lights, maybe taking a hot shower or bath or even washing your face with hot water. If you’re feeling stressed from the day, take a few moments to do some physiological sighs to lower your heart rate, and/or do a ten- to thirty-minute NSDR session. Don’t drink too many �uids or eat in the two to three hours before sleep, and de�nitely try to avoid ca�eine in the eight to ten hours prior to bedtime. Viewing bright overhead LED lights (of the sort that are in many bathrooms) is a quick way to spike your cortisol and quash your melatonin, and checking your email or the news in the last hour before sleep is de�nitely a risky move if you want to keep your cortisol low at night (see chapter 1 for details). And to be clear: Low cortisol at night should be your goal!

If you happen to wake up in the middle of the night for whatever reason, avoid viewing bright lights or looking at your phone. Again, do some

physiological sighs to help keep your heart rate low, and let yourself drift back to sleep. If you can’t fall back asleep, listen to an NSDR session. Or try the weird eye-movement trick I shared in chapter 1.

By the way, if you exercise in the evening or at night, that does signi�cantly increase late-day cortisol. It’s better to exercise than not to, if you have a workout planned. To help keep your cortisol and catecholamine rhythms on a diurnal schedule, you can reduce the intensity of your evening training a bit and/or be sure to include a wind-down routine afterward. Andy Galpin, an exercise physiologist, encourages this after all workouts, but especially nighttime ones. Even moderate-intensity exercise can cause a large increase in cortisol (as discussed in chapter 2), especially if you consume ca�eine �rst ~~.~~ 119 That is one more reason to drink ca�eine before moderate to intense exercise in the morning, but also to avoid it before moderate to intense exercise at night.

I don’t want to demonize late-day exercise. Better to do it than not do it. But just know that if you exercise intensely within four to six hours of bedtime, your next-day waking cortisol may be lower due to the negative feedback regulation of cortisol.120 That’s a mechanism you often see with hormones in the body, like cortisol or testosterone: When those hormones reach a certain high level, it signals speci�c brain areas and glands, such as the hypothalamus and pituitary and adrenals, to reduce their release of those hormones. Just another reason why spiking your morning cortisol is a good thing. It not only sets you up for the day, it helps keep cortisol levels low at night.121 So if you exercise at night and wonder why you’re dragging a bit the next morning, this may very well be why. Be diligent about using the tools in this protocol and you’ll be A-OK.

What about spiking your cortisol and catecholamines in the morning—how best to do that? There too you have options: Viewing bright light can boost your morning cortisol peak by 50 percent, making it a very easy, e�ective and bene�cial practice (see Sleep Protocol 1 for more). Sunlight is ideal, but a 10,000 lux light works too ~~.~~ 122 Hydration, ca�eine, moderate to intense exercise, deliberate cold exposure, maybe cyclic hyperventilation (but never with deliberate cold exposure): Doing one of these is better than none, two is better than one, and so on. If I had to place them in order of e�ectiveness, I would say:

sunlight viewing, exercise, and ca�eine are the big levers here, but don’t worry about the order. Let logic be your guide. Obviously hydrate before and during your exercise, drink ca�eine for an energy boost, get the sunlight before or during exercise if you can, but if the sun isn’t up and you’re ready to train, train! Don’t wait for the sun to rise, thinking that it has to come �rst because it’s a big lever. The cortisol and catecholamine systems are primed for release in the early hours of your day and will synergize without the need to get the relative timing (of all the things that cause their release) perfect.

When people ask me, “Who has time for all this?” I respond that it takes mere seconds to drink 16 ounces of water, a few minutes to make a ca�einated beverage and step outside into the sun while you drink it, and then depending on your schedule, exercise. Do not obsess over the details of relative timing of these tools.

A number of people have asked me over the years: “Given the importance of ensuring elevated morning cortisol, is there anything I can take to boost it besides ca�eine?”

In chapter 6, I cover the many prescription drugs and supplements that can increase dopamine and norepinephrine, but when it comes to things that boost cortisol there are two that are particularly useful. And they are inexpensive. And commonplace. You may even have one of them in your kitchen right now.

They are grapefruit and licorice root extract. Not licorice candy, but licorice plant root extract ~~.~~ 123

Each can increase the size and duration of your morning cortisol peak and thereby increase your level of alertness and the other subjective e�ects associated with elevated sympathetic tone. How is this possible? Well…

Grapefruit impacts cortisol levels by two known mechanisms. First, it inhibits the enzyme (11β-HSD2) that blocks cortisol to cortisone conversion—cortisol being the chemical that imparts the functions we’ve been talking about so far in this protocol. Slower conversion means more active cortisol stays in our system for longer to impart its e�ects. Second, grapefruit inhibits the enzyme CYP3A4, which blocks the liver’s metabolism of cortisol, the net e�ect of which is to increase cortisol’s duration of action.

Licorice root extract contains something called glycyrrhizin (pronounced glycer-ry-zin) that potently inhibits the same abovementioned enzyme 11β-HSD2.

You may be thinking, _Grapefruit and licorice?! Is he serious?!_ Yes, quite serious. At high doses it can raise blood pressure, cause �uid retention, and even a�ect the metabolism of certain pharmaceutical drugs and potassium because of the many roles of the abovementioned enzymes in the liver.

I make sure to use a version containing glycyrrhizin, and I take it with my morning ca�eine usually before a hard workout that I need to start earlier than is typical for me. The energy-increasing e�ect is very noticeable. On very rare occasions I will take it around noon to try to extend my window of elevated cortisol to work for an especially long day, or to exercise hard midday. Again, I use it as a sometimes tool, not a regular tool, to boost cortisol in the morning.

Overall, grapefruit and grapefruit juice have a milder, but still meaningful, impact on cortisol’s duration of action. Most people can consume these without an adverse e�ect. But they can interact with various medications, so be sure to consult your doctor before taking. If you’d like to try incorporating grapefruit as a cortisol-boosting tool in your routine, perhaps eat a grapefruit or drink a small glass of grapefruit juice in the morning (pink or conventional is �ne; it doesn’t matter). See how that a�ects your energy throughout the day. I would avoid these at night for obvious reasons.

One more thing to note here is that it is hard to �nd very-low-dose licorice root extract with glycyrrhizin. Most are 400 milligrams or more, and even at 200 milligrams it works very well to increase energy, so I empty half a 400 milligrams capsule into water or my co�ee, and drink that. It tastes good. Remember: It raises blood pressure, and taking glycyrrhizin every day can lead to serious problems over time, so if you experiment with it, try a low dose—even if it means having to open up a capsule to remove a portion of the contents. I can’t end this protocol without one more reminder about ca�eine: If you consume ca�eine in the late afternoon, too, don’t overdo it. I get it; I love yerba maté in the morning, and I love, love, love the taste of co�ee in the afternoon. But if you’re an afternoon ca�eine drinker and having sleep issues or trouble getting going in the mornings, you can bet it’s at least partially because the ca�eine levels in your bloodstream are still too high from your afternoon co�ee or tea. Try to drink only decaf after 2:00 p.m., or limit yourself to roughly 60 milligrams of ca�eine (that’s about 3 to 4 ounces of regular co�ee, or an espresso shot), and do your best to avoid it altogether within eight hours of bed (refer to Sleep Protocol 11 for more guidance). You could also opt to ditch the afternoon ca�eine and instead to take 300 to 900 milligrams of alpha-GPC, which is a short-acting stimulant that can increase energy and focus and may actually improve REM sleep at night if taken six to ten hours before bedtime. This protocol includes several tools, so to recap: By increasing the slope and height of your morning cortisol and catecholamine peak, you bu�er yourself against later-day stress in several ways. First, you’re likely to experience improved energy and focus for many hours afterward. Viewing bright light ~~,~~ 124 consuming ca�eine ~~,~~ 125 exercise ~~,~~ 126 and cold exposure127 all increase cortisol and/or catecholamine release. This helps us keep our reactions proportional to any stressors we may encounter later. By starting your day in a state of focus and readiness, if a stressful situation arises you don’t need to produce more cortisol to confront it e�ectively. Researchers who have examined the link between morning cortisol and stress call this connection the CAR anticipation

hypothesis.128 It suggests that a big cortisol peak in the morning isn’t just to wake us up; it also prepares us for whatever stressors lie ahead ~~.~~ 129 And just remember this: You _want_ your cortisol and catecholamines relatively high in the morning and daytime, and you want them low in the evening and at night.
