###### **STRESS CONTROL PROTOCOL**

6

### Consider Specific Supplements to Help Offset Excessive Stress

###### WHAT TO DO:

- Find a combination of supplements that might help you combat severe or prolonged periods of stress. Remember: Behavioral protocols are the foundation of mental and physical health and performance, and that is especially true when it comes to stress control. It’s also true that if your sleep duration and quality are not su�cient, no amount of pharmacology will help, at least not for long. Refer to chapter 1 for more on that topic. With that said, below is a list of supplements that have shown some e�cacy for reducing various aspects of the stress response:
  - Ashwagandha: 200–300 mg, 1 to 2 times per 24 hours, but taken only in the afternoon and/or evening.

  - L-theanine: 100 mg or 200 mg, 1 to 3 times per day; if you drink ca�eine regularly or are in a period of unusually high stress, take theanine with your ca�eine.

  - Phosphatidylserine: 400–800 mg, once per day anytime after 4:00 p.m. _Rhodiola rosea:_ 200 mg, once or twice per day

- Proceed with caution. As always when discussing supplements or medication, it is important to consult with a physician. You need to be sure that you are not risking a dangerous interaction, that the product is reliable, and that a

medical professional has information about what may be symptoms of an underlying health issue.

###### HOW IT WORKS:

Certain supplements can help in times of excessive stress, such as when you are dealing with two or three nights of poor sleep due to an emotionally challenging circumstance, or if you’ve made behavioral changes but are still �nding it hard to balance that autonomic seesaw. Alternatively, changes that occur with age can cause hormone surges or other shifts that can make you more vulnerable to stress.

On these occasions, certain supplements, taken alone or in combination, can help. The supplements in this protocol can increase parasympathetic nervous system activation and reduce sympathetic nervous system activation, either directly or indirectly, helping you to tilt that seesaw in the direction that is most bene�cial to you. The studies described below are selected from the body of research on each supplement. These summaries are not comprehensive but provide an overview of the evidence.

If you decide to explore supplements for limiting stress, I would suggest taking one of them and seeing how it works for you before adding another. That is going to be the most informative and cost-e�ective approach. (I am well aware that some people will opt to just dive in and take all four because they hate stress that much. Try to hold back.)

###### Ashwagandha:

Ashwagandha, also known as Indian ginseng or winter cherry, is used as an adaptogen—a term that broadly refers to substances that improve a person’s resistance to stress. A large review published in 2021 that included forty-one total studies in humans included seven that focused on stress and anxiety, enrolling a total of 491 adults who either reported being under high stress or were diagnosed with an anxiety disorder.130 Ashwagandha dosages varied from 240 milligrams per day to 1,250 milligrams per day for an extract and up to 6,000 milligrams when administered as a powdered root. (Most ashwagandha capsules sold over the counter in the US contain 200–600 mg per capsule.)

Taken together, these studies showed that ashwagandha reduced stress and anxiety when compared to a placebo, and also reduced sleeplessness and fatigue. Cortisol levels in the blood were also lower among people taking this supplement, and it appeared that the cortisol-lowering e�ect of ashwagandha is likely the major basis of its e�ect on lowering stress and anxiety. A study of sixty adults found that those who took 225 milligrams or 400 milligrams per day of ashwagandha reported reductions in anxiety, depression, and food cravings compared to people randomized to a placebo ~~.~~ 131 One study found that men and women taking ashwagandha had a 22 percent and 25 percent reduction in cortisol, respectively, when they took ashwagandha for sixty days versus taking a placebo for sixty days ~~.~~ 132

Research has identi�ed several components that could contribute to the stress-reducing e�ects of ashwagandha. Most likely the e�ect is due to a “cocktail” of several di�erent compounds in ashwagandha that work in parallel on various aspects of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, which, as you may remember from Sleep Protocol 1, is our main biological circuitry for mobilizing a physiological response to a stressor. The most potent of these mechanisms is the suppression of the signaling pathway for corticotropin (ACTH), a hormone that acts to stimulate the release of cortisol from your adrenals.133 The ashwagandha-suppression of corticotropin (ACTH) happens through a multistep process that begins with compounds called withanolides (naturally occurring plant hormones). These compounds can lower corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) in the hypothalamus.134 Limiting the amount of CRH in turn dampens the signaling that would normally trigger the release of cortisol. The fact that ashwagandha works “upstream” from the adrenal glands has a potential downside: Namely, it is likely to impact all the biology connected to CRH, which includes the gut and the immune system, among others. That’s one of several reasons why I suggest not taking ashwagandha at dosages higher than 600 milligrams per day for more than a few weeks before taking at least a few weeks o�. There is at least one report of someone taking a high dose (950 mg) of ashwagandha daily for a year and developing adrenal insu�ciency ~~.~~ 135 People seem to vary quite a bit in their sensitivity to ashwagandha, so if you decide to

try it in times of excess stress, I suggest starting with one dose per day, taken in the evening or an hour before bedtime at a dose of about 100 to 200 milligrams, and only increase the dosage, if needed, to �nd the minimal e�ective dose for you. Importantly, you don’t want to suppress cortisol in the early part of your day. If you decide to take more, take ashwagandha in the afternoon around 3:00 to 4:00 p.m., and perhaps again an hour before bedtime in a dosage of 200 to 300 milligrams each.

As mentioned above, I suggest you do not take ashwagandha at doses exceeding 600 milligrams per day for periods of longer than a couple of weeks. While the reports are largely anecdotal, some people taking high doses of ashwagandha (700–1,200 mg) per day experience apathy, starting about three to four weeks after continuous intake. The reasons for this are not clear and may be similar to the case report mentioned above, but because e�cacy has been shown at lower doses of 300 to 600 milligrams per day, I suggest people use it as a tool to augment stress reduction by taking about 300 milligrams on a regular basis as described above, or reserve its use to high-stress periods and take higher dosages (greater than 600 mg/day) only during those times. And don’t let up on the behavioral practices for stress reduction.

A quick note about sourcing ashwagandha and other herbal adaptogens: The herbal supplement world is full of fake and contaminated products, perhaps even more so than for other types of supplements. Stick to major brands with third-party testing, especially ones that test for and remove metals from their products and ensure purity. Gaia Herbs has a good reputation for doing this and sells single-ingredient formulations. Barlow Herbals is another. I have no a�liation to either.

###### L-theanine:

L-theanine is an amino acid present in green tea and has been recognized as one of its active compounds, alongside ca�eine, catechins, and other molecules.136 Many studies of green tea have investigated a potential protective bene�t against cancer and other chronic diseases ~~,~~ 137 with the evidence from laboratory and animal studies indicating that it may reduce the risk of obesity and type 2 diabetes, as well as heart disease138 and breast cancer.139

Large-scale clinical trials exploring the e�cacy of theanine in humans are still lacking. It’s unlikely such studies will ever happen given their high cost and the fact that theanine is unlikely to be made into a pharmaceutical drug. That’s just how it goes with most naturally occurring compounds.

The reason L-theanine is in this chapter is that it is widely used to reduce arousal. That’s why nowadays L-theanine is sometimes added to energy drinks, and even to some co�ee blends, to o�set the jitters associated with drinking too much ca�eine—presumably a clever trick on the part of the manufacturers that allows people to drink more of these beverages without feeling too strung out.

In one small, blinded, randomized study, thirty participants between the ages of thirty-six and sixty took L-theanine 200 milligrams per day or a placebo for four weeks ~~.~~ 140 The investigators, a team from Japan, used several standard measures to gauge depression, anxiety, and sleep quality. They reported that the group taking L-theanine had signi�cantly fewer stress-related symptoms.

In another study, a group of researchers in Australia and the Netherlands enrolled thirty-four adults between the ages of eighteen and forty in a blinded study to measure stress response in reaction to a series of cognitive tests involving mental arithmetic, memory, and coordination.141 Tasks like these can trigger stress because they challenge us. The tasks were presented following consumption of either a placebo or L-theanine as a nutrient drink. They found that the stress response, measured through the amount of salivary cortisol, was reduced compared to the placebo, an e�ect that appeared to last for several hours. In addition, the L-theanine group showed an increase in alpha brain waves, suggesting a more relaxed state of mind. That being said, cognitive performance was no di�erent between the L-theanine and placebo groups. The reduced stress reaction may be bene�cial for other reasons, but it’s useful to know that theanine didn’t make people better at the tasks they were given.

In terms of the underlying mechanisms, L-theanine research has found that this compound indirectly increases GABA—the major inhibitory neurotransmitter in the brain—and dopamine.142

Theanine taken in the hour before bedtime is part of the sleep stack I describe in chapter 1. There, I warned that people who have especially vivid dreams _not_

take theanine. I suggest that people who want to try theanine to reduce their stress do so by taking about 200 milligrams of it in the early afternoon and perhaps another 100 to 200 milligrams again in the evening, especially if you had ca�eine in the early afternoon.

###### Phosphatidylserine:

Phosphatidylserine is a type of phospholipid. It is naturally found in the membranes of neurons, and comprises about 10 to 20 percent of the total phospholipid content of the brain—an enormous percentage when one considers that much of the nonliquid content of the brain is phospholipids. Naturally occurring phosphatidylserine plays a role in cognitive function,143 and the loss of phosphatidylserine in neurons known to occur in later adulthood may partially explain age-related (non-dementia) cognitive decline.

What’s more, in its natural state in our brains, this compound is known to decrease the stress response ~~.~~ 144 As a supplement, phosphatidylserine has shown some bene�t in older adults who experience chronic stress. There is some evidence phosphatidylserine taken late in the day may preferentially reduce evening and nighttime cortisol ~~,~~ 145 which may explain how it indirectly supports sleep.

In one investigation, from 2004, participants took a phosphatidylserine supplement at a dose of 400 milligrams, 600 milligrams, or 800 milligrams, or a placebo (twenty people per group) and then completed a type of social stress test that involves performing in front of an audience ~~.~~ 146 Data collected on biological indicators of the stress response revealed a signi�cant decrease in these symptoms among the 400-milligram group, but not among those taking the higher doses (or the placebo). It’s hard to interpret the e�ect of higher doses, but this is not uncommon in pharmacology studies. Many studies of stress and cognitive performance show an inverted U-shaped response, where low- and high-dose conditions yield similar or no e�ects, but mid-range dosages do. Such are the complexities of biology. Another study found no link between phosphatidylserine and measures of a stress response across all sixty participants, but the researchers did observe an e�ect among participants with high chronic

stress levels.147 Initially, this group had a diminished cortisol rise in response to a social stress test. That may sound like a good thing but it’s not. A blunted cortisol response is often a sign of underlying issues, such as depression.148 Treatment with phosphatidylserine appeared to restore the healthy rise in cortisol in response to the test, meaning it seemed to recalibrate the stress response rather than stop it. I say all this not to confuse you but to remind you that though the best model for your autonomic nervous system might be a seesaw, we need to consider the “hinge” of that seesaw (metaphorically speaking). How it bends, or sticks, matters. And compounds like phosphatidylserine may change people’s stress response by adjusting mechanisms analogous to how you might treat a hinge, rather than merely increasing or decreasing cortisol or adrenaline. Finally, in a six-week study from 2014 of seventy-�ve men randomized to phosphatidylserine (at a dose of 200 or 400 mg per day) or a placebo, the higher dose of the supplement appeared to lower the stress response among participants with chronic high stress.149

If you opt to try phosphatidylserine for stress control, I recommend starting with a low dose of 100 to 200 milligrams, taken a few hours before bedtime, and increasing the dose only as needed. I know many people who like its e�ects on lowering stress late in the day, and for sleep.

_Rhodiola rosea_ is a yellow-�owered plant that grows in northern regions of Europe and Asia and on the Atlantic coast of North America. It’s long been part of traditional medicine practices in Europe and Asia, used to address fatigue, mild anxiety, and symptoms of burnout ~~.~~ 150 It is considered an adaptogen, because it alters the subjective experience of e�ort, apparently by adjusting the threshold for perceived e�ort, and by increasing e�ort endurance in physical and mental exertion. Subjectively, people taking _Rhodiola rosea_ report less postphysical-exertion-related fatigue and that mental stressors feel less stressful, meaning they can lean into sustained e�ort without feeling exhausted. Indeed, _Rhodiola rosea_ has been shown to reduce the symptoms of burnout, which is a multidimensional feature of chronic stress that includes the “wired but tired”

feeling that is a common consequence of prolonged periods (days, weeks, etc.) of stress and altered sleep-wake cycles. European medical authorities approved the use of _Rhodiola rosea_ for short-term relief of stress in 2012151 and data on this connection have been slowly accruing.

One study examined the e�ects of _Rhodiola rosea_ among �fty-six physicians working night shifts for fourteen days ~~.~~ 152 Signs of mental fatigue were tested before and after the night shift for three two-week stretches. The investigators reported an improvement in tests examining memory, concentration, perception, and other aspects of brain function during the �rst two-week administration of _Rhodiola rosea_ .

Another trial, from Russia, randomized 161 military cadets to one dose of _Rhodiola rosea_ per day at either 370 milligrams or 555 milligrams, or placebo, and found a reduction in fatigue among both supplement groups.153 And in another investigation, a phase 3 clinical trial at Uppsala University, in Sweden, sixty people were randomized to receive four daily doses of _Rhodiola rosea_ , for a total of 576 milligrams per day, or four placebo tablets.154 The participants completed several questionnaires gauging quality of life, depression, fatigue, and attention. Both groups experienced improvements in overall mental health and reduced feelings of burnout. But in the group taking _Rhodiola rosea_ , the reduction in fatigue was more pronounced, and linked to improvements in performance and concentration.

_Rhodiola rosea_ is among the better-studied supplements for stress control, and we have copious evidence pointing to its usefulness in this context. With regard to the underlying mechanism, _Rhodiola rosea_ contains numerous phytochemicals (compounds made by plants) that could contribute to its bene�ts, including by interacting with cortisol pathway ~~s~~ 155 and by activating heat-shock proteins ~~,~~ 156 which our cells make in response to stressful conditions such as the excessive heat or cold, the presence of heavy metals, or an infection. Researchers are still investigating the exact mechanisms tied to the stressreducing e�ects, as well as its apparent contribution to physical strength and endurance ~~.~~ 157 The picture emerging is that _Rhodiola rosea_ bu�ers against stress

by calibrating the amount of adrenaline that is released in moments of high physical exertion and high emotional stress.

I recommend one of two approaches to trying _Rhodiola rosea_ . The �rst is to take it thirty to sixty minutes before a known stressor, like a hard workout or big exam or study session or public speaking engagement—basically any event that you know will require an intense and prolonged e�ort. I take 120 to 240 milligrams of _Rhodiola rosea_ before hard resistance training workouts, which is per the standard protocol used in most peer-reviewed studies of _Rhodiola rosea_ for physical exertion. The second way to take _Rhodiola rosea_ is during periods of chronic stress, when you can’t get as much sleep as you would like and/or when your output is greater than usual. Think �nal exam week, the days of long work hours before a vacation, the vacation with your in-laws where you are coordinating everything, et cetera. In those times, I suggest taking 100 to 120 milligrams (the typical capsule dose of _Rhodiola rosea_ in most supplements) three times daily (morning, afternoon, and evening). It can be taken with or without food. I would not suggest taking _Rhodiola rosea_ multiple times throughout the day for more than three to four weeks without taking a break of at least two weeks, as all the biological pathways _Rhodiola rosea_ is known to impact are subject to feedback loops and downregulation. Use 100-milligramsplus daily dosages of _Rhodiola rosea_ as a short-term tool to combat stress and burnout, not as a mainstay of your supplement regimen. And I know I sound like a broken record, but don’t just pile on supplements for managing stress. You need—and now have—multiple behavioral tools to reduce stress. Use them!
