### 90 Percent or More of the Food You Eat Should Be Unprocessed or Minimally Processed

###### WHAT TO DO:

- Eat and cook with single-ingredient, non-processed foods. These include meat, �sh, eggs, poultry, fruit, vegetables, rice, lentils, beans, oatmeal, pasta, olive oil, avocado oil, and even butter (albeit in small portions). They can be consumed alone or combined in recipes, and of course you can use spices, seasonings, and salt as well.

- Avoid ready-to-eat packed foods or packaged multi-ingredient foods. Most prepackaged sauces and condiments should be avoided; these typically contain a fair amount of added sugar. Read nutrition labels to check.

- Consume nut butters in moderation. These can be healthy, but some contain processed oils and even added sugar. Even when nuts and salt are the only ingredients, all have a very high calorie-to-protein ratio. If you’re trying to lose body fat, then it’s best to abstain from nut butters entirely.

- Consume full-fat yogurt and cottage cheese and other forms of dairy, but in plain flavors only. Here too added sugars should be avoided. Add fruit, a drizzle of honey, or a pinch of cinnamon for taste if you don’t like these foods plain.

###### HOW IT WORKS:

Food is amazing. Despite the debates, I think we can all agree on that. We eat for the building blocks food supplies our brain and body, as described in the introduction to this chapter, and of course for the pleasure of it. For many people, food is one of their biggest joys. I count myself among people who love to eat.

But the type of food we eat is probably second only to sleep and exercise for its importance to our long-term health. Centering our meal and snack choices on whole (that is minimally or non-processed) foods has so many bene�ts— disease prevention, longevity, cognition, mood, energy, reduced in�ammation, healthy weight management, and more. The increasing concerns about processed foods stem from the plethora of data linking them to obesity, high blood pressure, heart disease, gastrointestinal disorders, cancer, and other serious ailments.77 Chemical additives used to color, preserve, texturize, and �avor these products have been linked to potential health hazards ~~.~~ 78 Processed foods also tend to contain high amounts of sugar, even in products that would seem to not require it. And excessive sugar consumption is tied to diabetes, heart disease, cancer, and an increased risk of early death ~~.~~ 79 All of which is to say, we need to make it a point to eliminate, or at least vastly reduce, processed foods.

The good news is that eating healthily is not complicated or expensive. We can all make incredible tasting meals and snacks using whole foods, if we learn just a bit about how to prepare them. Think: a perfectly cooked steak and carrots roasted with olive oil, salt, and some spices. In some cases, these foods need no preparation at all. Like a juicy orange or fresh berries. If these sound bland or overly simple, chances are your taste circuits in your brain and body need some recalibration.

If you have grown accustomed to eating processed foods, this recalibration can seem di�cult. Processed foods alter our brain and gut to make us perceive other, more nutritious foods as less appetizing. It’s because of how sugar, certain starch-sugar, and starch-sugar-fat combinations are metabolized in our gut, and how they change our brain’s reward pathways. You’ll be happy to know, however, that the cells in your gut and brain are perfectly happy to rewire to

make healthy, unprocessed foods literally taste better. It doesn’t take long, and it will make eating healthy most of the time re�exive.

This protocol looks at the gut-brain axis, the connection between the cells in our digestive tract and speci�c areas of our brain. That connection is the key to understanding how processed foods a�ect us.

Our gut talks to our brain via two main parallel pathways. The �rst involves the cells in our gut communicating with our brain using a neural pathway called the vagus nerve, a bidirectional superhighway linking the organs of our body and our brain. You may remember the vagus from chapter 3.

Our body and our brain are connected by a second pathway, through secreted hormones and small proteins called peptides (in general, the vagus pathway is the faster of the two). The hunger sensation arises, in part, because our stomach produces a hormone called ghreli ~~n~~ 80 in amounts proportional to how much time has elapsed since our last meal. Ghrelin travels to our hypothalamus, a marble-sized brain region located over the roof of our mouth, where it activates our drive to seek food ~~.~~ 81 Other hormones and peptides made by both our gut and our brain make us want to eat less; for example, the peptide GLP-1 gives us a feeling of fullness, which is why GLP-1 analogs are used as drugs to treat obesity. (The gut microbiome, the trillions of bacteria living in our digestive system, also in�uences hunger—more on that in Nutrition Protocol 6.)82

At the same time, speci�c nutrients in the foods we eat—most notably sugars, but also fatty acids and amino acids—activate cells in our gut called neuropod cells that communicate with the brain via the vagus nerve, leading to the release of dopamine.83 And while dopamine does many di�erent things in the brain and body, when it is stimulated in this context, it can drive the urge to consume more of that food. It’s an elegant mechanism if you think about it, because the taste of food in our mouth is not a great indication of the actual nutrients in a given food. Taste is more of a guess, a correlate. The cells in our gut, on the other hand, are poised to respond to the broken-down components of food, letting the rest of our body and brain know what we ate and what to eat more (or less) of. Amazingly, all this happens below our conscious awareness.

Given how sugar drives the urge to consume more, it’s no mystery why it’s in so many foods. Processed food manufacturers add sugar to foods so we buy and consume more of these foods. That’s why sugar can be found in everything from packaged mac-and-cheese to frozen pizza, and most everything else on the supermarket shelves. Even tortilla and potato chips can have added sugar. So does most store-bought pasta sauce. And salad dressings. And condiments. Which is why so many people crave sugary food all the time.

You get the idea. It’s a clever, albeit diabolical, tactic.

As mentioned in the introduction to this chapter, sugar that gets added to food is considered a simple carbohydrate. Typically it is added as sucrose, but sometimes as high-fructose corn syrup, or something similar. The exact form doesn’t really matter however. Our brains are hardwired to detect simple carbohydrates. Studies in both mice and humans show that even when we are unable to taste sweetness, we still show a strong preference for sugary foods and beverages, indicating that the brain can detect sugar by a pathway other than 84 conscious taste.

Here’s a simple and fun experiment you can try; it’s something that Anna Lembke, MD, a world expert in dopamine and its role in craving and addiction, taught me. Eat one small piece of chocolate or one spoonful of your favorite ice cream. Both have sugar and fat, a combination known to trigger a lot of dopamine compared to eating either one alone. Pay attention to how it tastes, but then also notice your thoughts as you swallow. You’ll notice how quickly they move from “mmm, yum” to “I want more.” The immediate sense of craving that overlaps with pleasure is the power of dopamine in action. Sugar, in particular, ampli�es that response, even after the �avor experience has passed, by activating the gut-to-brain pathway ~~.~~ 85 It even works for sugary foods that don’t taste that good! And it’s why processed foods that we don’t even think of as sweet often contain added sugar.

Again, I want to be clear that I do not subscribe to the view that all sugar is inherently bad. A homemade dessert, chocolate, or ice cream once in a while… all can de�nitely �t within a healthy diet. But I do think we should limit these foods and avoid, as much as possible, consuming non-dessert foods that have added

sugar, as well as any highly processed foods, except on rare occasions or out of true necessity.

Maybe you’re wondering about fruit, which as I mentioned contains a sugar called fructose. Fruit contains a lot of water, �ber, valuable nutrients, and polyphenols, compounds found in plants that have various bene�cial properties. All these components contribute to the prevention of heart disease, cancer, and other serious health issues.86 And the high �ber content of most fruits slows down the absorption of sugar, which makes them less stimulating than desserts, sweets, or highly processed foods. But there are a few fruits that contain more fructose than others—like grapes. Note, too, that dried fruits, without their water content, now contain concentrated amounts of sugar. Fruit juices, like orange juice, are generally best avoided. They are high in sugar and calories, too, and the absence of �ber means that the sugar contained there is easily absorbed into the body, which means it spikes blood sugar quickly. Because that spike leads to a subsequent crash in blood sugar,87 consuming it often can lead, in the short run, to fatigue, sugar cravings ~~,~~ 88 and, in the long term, an increased risk of diabete ~~s~~ 89 and heart disease.90

Then there are arti�cial and low-calorie sweeteners. The data show that arti�cial and low-calorie sweeteners do not drive the same craving typical simple sugars do. Stevia for instance, is safe, and may even have some health bene�ts.91 Aspartame appears to be safe too ~~.~~ 92 Saccharin and sucralose, though, may negatively impact the gut microbiome ~~.~~ 93 And there’s interesting data on diet sodas. In a randomized controlled trial from 2024, people who consumed diet sodas lost more weight than people who drank equivalent amounts of water.94 The underlying reasons include less hunger among soda drinkers and more cravings for sweetness among the water drinkers. At the same time, people who consume a lot of arti�cial sweeteners often experience increased overall appetite, perhaps due to glucose and insulin disruption ~~.~~ 95 There isn’t a broad rule that applies to all arti�cial and low-calorie sweeteners. For some people, they seem to help with weight loss, whereas for other people, they stimulate hunger in ways that may make it harder to keep from overeating. You have to �gure out which group you are in.

If a few diet sodas a day help quell your sugar cravings at a time when you’re trying to lose weight, then great. If you don’t like diet sodas, there is no reason to consume them. I drink beverages containing stevia and occasionally enjoy an aspartame-sweetened diet soda. When developing the zero-sugar cold brew yerba maté for Mateina (as noted, a company I partially own), I chose to include a small amount of stevia. I drink that for much of the early part of the day. I avoid sucralose and saccharin.

### Stay Hydrated

###### WHAT TO DO:

Regardless of what and when you choose to eat:

- Consume 18 to 24 ounces of water upon waking. Try to do this �rst thing in the morning before drinking or eating anything else, including co�ee or other forms of ca�eine.

- Aim to consume about 80 ounces of water across the first ten hours of the day. That’s about 2.4 liters. It is not necessary to consume 8 ounces each hour, but try to spread it out in a way that works for you. The earlier in the day you drink it the better. It’s typically best to avoid a lot of water in the hours before bedtime, since you want to wake as infrequently as possible to use the bathroom.

- For optimal performance during exercise, consume water according to this equation: Your body weight in pounds divided by 30 equals the number of ounces to drink for every 15 to 20 minutes of your workout time. This calculation originates with the work of human performance expert Andy Galpin, director of the Human Performance Center at Parker University, and is referred to below as the “Galpin Equation.”
  - Example: Total body weight of 150 pounds ÷ 30 = 5 ounces every 15 to 20 minutes, which means 15 to 20 ounces consumed during an hour-long workout. You can sip water throughout, drink at regular or non-regular intervals. Your pattern of consumption during exercise will of course be

dictated by the type of exercise you’re doing: running, cycling, swimming, et cetera.

###### HOW IT WORKS:

Your body is made mostly of water. By one estimate, obtained by sending a weak electric current through the body, an adult human is about 62 percent water, with that percentage starting to decrease around sixty years of age.97 Water is essential for every biological process that we need in order to live and function.98 If there is one protocol that is most overlooked and that can immediately and signi�cantly improve your energy levels, focus, and general feeling of well-being, it is this: Hydrate properly. It is rarely discussed. When we do hear about hydration, the message is typically a warning against dehydration, not the great bene�ts of hydration.

So let’s talk about what hydration is, and why it’s so powerful.

Hydration is the process of providing the cells of our body with the water they need for all those biological processes. Some hydration is achieved by breathing, some is produced through metabolism, and some comes through the foods we eat. Most hydration comes from the liquids we consume. The water we take in through eating and drinking enters our gut and is absorbed into our bloodstream and �nally our cells.

Proper hydration is crucial to both the body and the brain. Hydration helps prevent injuries, improves recovery, and is also important for maintaining body temperature during and following exercise ~~.~~ 99 It reduces the risk of kidney stones. 100 Drinking water stimulates the sympathetic branch of your autonomic nervous system, the circuitry that increases your alertness and focus. (See chapter 3 for more on this.) Research indicates that drinking water can trigger the release of norepinephrine, the hormone that helps keep us focused and alert.101 In a study of �fteen children, proper hydration was tied to improved performance on tasks involving motor skills and memory.102 Similar �ndings have been observed in adults.

Dehydration, on the other hand, quickly becomes problematic. It’s also common. This is unfortunate because even slightly insu�cient amounts of

water in your body can diminish your concentration, alertness, short-term memory, visual perception, and other cognitive functions.103 Mild dehydration can cause low-level confusion, fatigue, depression, and irritability.104 One review found that a 2-percent decrease in body mass due to dehydration was enough to diminish mood, increase fatigue, and reduce alertness. That is remarkable because most people do not consume enough water to maintain hydration, and spend much of their day su�ering the ill e�ects of mild dehydration… without even realizing it.

A mildly dehydrated state can reduce brain volume and alter the activity of neural pathways associated with motor output and cognition ~~.~~ 105 It also reduces blood �ow, which in turn diminishes the supply of oxygen to the brain. What’s more, it can cause headaches and lethargy, and of course a dry mouth and thirst ~~.~~ 106 It’s important to note amidst all this that we can be dehydrated without registering thirst.

People engaging in intense exercise need to be especially vigilant about hydration, and not just in hot and/or dry environments either. In one study, eight trained cyclists rode for two hours on a stationary bike, consuming either 2.4 liters of an energy drink or 0.4 liters of water plus sports gel to equal the carbohydrates in the energy drink. The low-hydration riders became exhausted sooner and exerted less energy as they rode ~~.~~ 107 In a study of seven experienced resistance trainers (all male), insu�cient hydration decreased performance during exercise.108 These studies are small but are representative of what happens when we exercise.

The quantities provided in this protocol do not need to be followed to the precise ounce or milliliter. They are general guidelines to help ensure su�cient hydration.

One reason to focus on getting about 80 ounces of �uid in the �rst ten hours of the day is that this time is when our kidneys function at their best. Our kidneys �lter �uid and produce hormones to regulate water and salt balance, among other things, and their e�ciency at doing so is strongly governed by our circadian cloc ~~k~~ 109 (see Sleep Protocol 1 for more on the circadian clock). Our kidneys are simply much better at �ltering water and other �uids we drink in the

morning and daytime than at night; their function tends to peak in midafternoon and is slowest around midnight ~~.~~ 110 Focusing most of your water intake to the time of day when �uid �ltration by the kidneys is at its most e�cient will also help prevent, or at least reduce, having to get up in the middle of the night to use the bathroom, which is among the more common causes of sleep disturbance.

The quantity of 80 ounces across the �rst ten hours of the day gives us a solid metric to aim for. Simply make sure to drink 8 to 16 ounces of water (one to two glasses) upon waking, and again approximately every waking hour during the day. That will get you in the ballpark of 80 ounces in the �rst ten hours. Individuals living in hot environments tend to need more water. So do people who move around a lot, even if that’s in a temperature-controlled o�ce or home.

But if you’re exercising, that’s where the Galpin Equation enters the picture. If you want to improve your exercise performance, hydrate according to this calculation. You’ll be amazed by the di�erence it makes. Again, anyone living in hot environments will tend to need a bit more water here too; so increase the amount from the equation by a few extra ounces every �fteen to twenty minutes.

Beyond these three points, just remember: Stay hydrated. Hydration sounds boring but it’s actually really powerful when it comes to improving health and performance and again, it’s one of the more overlooked tools out there. It’s important for your brain, for your skin and appearance, for your digestion, and for your mood. You will notice the di�erence in all these areas after starting to follow this protocol.

There are so many myths around this. Among the more popular ones is that clear urine indicates su�cient hydration. Wrong. Many factors impact urine color besides hydration status. Your urine can be yellow and you can still be plenty hydrated. Another: If you pinch the skin on your hand, it should retract

in less than two seconds. Wrong again. This response depends on age, skin thickness, and other factors. It’s true that if you pinch the skin on the top of your hand and it does not return to its original state within three to �ve seconds, then there’s a decent chance you’re dehydrated. - urination.

### Eat High CP:C Ratio Protein at Each Full Meal

###### WHAT TO DO:

- Aim to include 30 to 50 grams of high complete-protein-to-calorie ratio foods at each meal or snack. Your daily goal should be around 1 gram per pound of body weight. This is the cornerstone of your diet.

- The number of calories from those foods will depend on what you select. Poultry, lean red meat, �sh, and shell�sh are the best high CP:C ratio sources of protein for those who eat animal-based products. Eggs are great as well, but they do have a relatively high calorie-to-protein ratio. Whey protein and plain full-fat Greek yogurt and cottage cheese too. Plant-based complete protein sources include beans and rice (together), lentils, soy, seitan, and some grains, such as quinoa. Just be aware that these have a less-than-favorable protein-tocalorie ratio.

Nuts, nut butters, and most cheeses are not high-quality protein sources. And all of them are very calorie dense. Peanut, almond, and other nut butters are mostly fat, and most nut butters on the grocery shelf often also contain added sugar and/or seed oils. If you’re going to eat nut butters, limit them to a few tablespoons a week and be sure they contain only nuts and salt. No sugar or added oils. It would be better to avoid nut butters and eat whole seeds and actual whole nuts. But these are mostly fats; they are not high CP:C ratio proteins.

- If you are someone who tends to overeat, whichever foods you choose, eat your high CP:C ratio proteins first. Then any starches, then your �brous vegetables. You’ll enjoy more satiety, better appetite regulation, and better digestion because apparently the French have it right about “salad last.”

###### HOW IT WORKS:

I know it’s not much fun to see a delicious steak and think “amino acids,” but that’s what your body does. If you took apart any protein, you would �nd an array of amino acids.

As I explained in the introduction to this chapter, all living things need amino acids to make protein. The human body needs twenty di�erent amino acids. Nine of these are impossible for our body to make on its own. We get them through the proteins we eat. The proteins that have all nine are considered complete proteins, and we want to consume these proteins, because the body uses them to maintain a healthy immune system, produce certain hormones, and maintain and increase muscle mass, among other functions ~~.~~ 112 You might be amazed to learn that most of your organs, not just your muscles, are made of proteins that are remade every few weeks to months. And it’s these nine essential amino acids that allow for this to occur. Your spleen, your heart, your liver, your muscles—the protein we consume allows them to keep working as they should.

Your body is smart. While you might think you eat for pleasure, it’s actually how your body keeps you seeking the food it needs to maintain these processes —that is, seeking those nine essential amino acids.

Whole grains, vegetables, seeds, and legumes do not contain all nine amino acids, but it is entirely possible to obtain all nine by consuming a variety of these plant-based proteins. Whether you eat meat or not, you are foraging for amino acids as you choose your proteins each day. That’s why we feel so satis�ed after we eat complete protein; it’s because the feeling of satiety is strongly linked to obtaining enough essential amino acids.113

And there is one particular amino acid we prioritize in that foraging, even if we are not consciously aware of it. An expanding body of evidence indicates that leucine, one of those nine essential amino acids, is especially impactful.114 Rising leucine levels in a cell launch a signaling pathway associated with the protein

mTOR (I mentioned it in the introduction to this chapter), which in turn triggers the body to make muscle.115 This amino acid also has several other known e�ects. Research has found links to improved immune function, for example ~~,~~ 116 as well as increased muscle mass among older individuals ~~.~~ 117

As discussed earlier, mTOR has been linked with aging and cancer. One mutant strain of mice lived three times longer than usual after treatment with the drug that lowers mTOR, called rapamycin ~~.~~ 118 But again, those results don’t appear to translate to humans, and in fact they have translated to far less dramatic results in normal mice. There is currently no evidence that stimulating mTOR has a life-shortening e�ect on humans. Rather, eating complete protein foods, and especially those rich in leucine such as lean meat, �sh, and eggs, should be the cornerstone of your diet.

And not to belabor the point, but once again, we are less likely to overeat when we consume su�cient protein because it leaves us feeling full and satis�ed ~~.~~ 119

###### COMMON QUESTIONS:

Most people who strive to eat 1 gram of protein per pound of body weight do feel better than they did before adopting that habit. From time to time, though, someone will tell me they just don’t feel “right” eating so much protein, and that they feel that they must force themselves to do so, even if their overall caloric intake is in proper range for them. We don’t have the exact knowledge to know why that might be. I notice my protein hunger follows the intensity and amount of exercise I do, and while that makes sense based on how protein synthesis works, we don’t have any formal studies on training and protein hunger, so take my experience as what it is: anecdotal.

For those of you who struggle to eat 1 gram of quality protein per pound of body weight, there are a few things to consider: Make sure you’re eating highprotein foods without excess fat or preservatives. If that does not eliminate the discomfort, then try replacing about a fourth of your protein calories with clean

starches, like rice, and with �brous foods, like salad, broccoli, or apples, while keeping your overall calories approximately the same. Starches are calorie dense, so it won’t take much to o�set the slightly lower protein intake. Then, make adjustments until you arrive at a way of eating that is sustainable, and makes you feel good.

CICO—calories in, calories out—is a universal law of nutrition. Well, that and we all do need adequate protein and essential fatty acids to survive (which is what this protocol is all about). Other than that, �gure out what works for you. And what works best for you may even change over time. I have long made it a point to eat enough protein daily, but I need to eat more vegetables now than I did when I was younger to feel my best.

### Choose Fibrous Vegetables and (Some) Fruit as Your Major Sources of Carbohydrates

###### WHAT TO DO:

- Vegetables should form the second major brick in the foundation of your diet and fruit, the third. If protein is the cornerstone, these foods build on it by helping to ensure enough vitamin, mineral, and other micronutrient intake.

- These foods are also essential for our fiber intake. Men should aim for at least 35 grams per day, and women at least 25 grams per day.

###### HOW IT WORKS:

Many readers know already why vegetables and fruits are so important: They contain vitamins, minerals, and other micronutrients like �avonoids, all of which our bodies need to function optimally.120 Once you understand how nutrient-rich vegetables and fruits are, you won’t think about them the same way again. Eating vegetables isn’t a chore; it’s a gift.

The �ber in vegetables and fruits is also important ~~.~~ 121 A bit about �ber: It provides support structure for the plants that produce it, be that in the roots, the stems, or the leaves. And it’s the part we can’t digest when we consume them. Fiber can be insoluble (will not dissolve in water), soluble (will dissolve in water), or prebiotic (feeds bacteria).

We need all three. Insoluble �ber, present in root vegetables and fruits with edible seeds, helps with stool formation. Soluble �ber, present in foods such as avocados, carrots, and Brussels sprouts, collects waste products as it travels through the body, helping to eliminate them. Prebiotic �ber, present in apples, asparagus, onions, and garlic, provides sustenance for the bene�cial bacteria in our gut microbiome, which promote intestinal health and also healthy brain functioning via the gut-brain axis ~~.~~ 122 (The foods noted above are just a few examples from each category.)

And they do a lot more. Studies also indicate that dietary �ber reduces the risk of metabolic syndrome, a cluster of symptoms that increase the risk of heart disease and diabetes. The heart-protecting bene�ts of �ber are widely known. A study that followed 9,776 US men and women for an average of nineteen years found that those who ate the least dietary �ber had a signi�cantly higher risk of coronary heart disease compared to those who ate the most dietary �ber.123 A review of eleven meta-analyses, which each included several studies, con�rmed the link between high �ber consumption and a reduced risk of several cancers, including ovarian, prostate, colon, breast, and pancreatic.124

Consuming �ber can also leave us feeling full, simply from the physical bulk of the food in our gut and the slowed gastric emptying that results.125 It also leaves us less fatigued. That’s because consuming adequate �ber helps adjust what’s called the postprandial glucose response, the entry of sugar (and fat) into the bloodstream, which can otherwise cause “brain fog” and tiredness. Fiber also blunts post-meal in�ammation that often follows eating a dish high in fat and carbs. That in�ammation, in which levels of some proteins and hormones rise in the body, can contribute to the risk of heart disease if it occurs with any regularity.

How much �ber should we get? Men should get at least 35 grams per day and women 25 grams per day. Very few people actually do that. In fact, an estimated 95 percent of Americans do not consume recommended amounts of �ber.126

Some people fear adding more �ber to their diet because it can cause gas and/or bloating. It’s true that a sudden increase in daily �ber intake may temporarily result in both. But once you’re eating enough �ber on a regular

basis, this usually becomes a non-issue. In one study on the link between bloating, sodium, and a high-�ber diet, the researchers found that while this diet did increase bloating to some extent, an accompanying decrease in sodium lessened that side e�ect, pointing to the idea that it’s often what we add to vegetables that becomes the problem, not the vegetables themselves.127

And at risk of sounding like your mother, vegetables require more chewing. You need to slow down and chew them well for them to digest properly, and for you to reap their full bene�ts.

A few notes on fruit: Some people �nd that eating fruit at the end of a meal causes some digestive discomfort. Others have no such issue. If you experience this problem, try eating fruit alone, before a meal, or as a snack rather than to cap o� a full meal. It may help.

Beyond �ber, these foods contain, as I mentioned, essential vitamins, minerals, and other micronutrients. The words _vitamins and minerals_ are thrown around a lot (I did it above). But knowing which ones tend to be lacking in most people’s diets, and knowing how to get more of these from food, can make a real di�erence to our health. Magnesium is largely an under-discussed, bene�cial component of many foods. This mineral, the eighth most abundant element on earth,128 is used by the body for energy production, bone development, making DNA, muscle contraction, nerve impulses, and even for regulating our heartbeat.129 In fact, it’s involved in more than three hundred systems in our body and thousands of crucial biological processes. Yet most people don’t get enough of it. It’s easy to rectify, and I’m sure you can guess how: by eating enough fruits and especially enough vegetables.

Studies of the so-called Paleo diet, which focuses on fruits, vegetables, lean meat, �sh, eggs, and nuts (in other words, foods that likely re�ect the diet of a hunter-gatherer living in the Paleolithic era) indicate that we once had a magnesium intake of about 600 milligrams per day, leading researchers to theorize that human metabolism is adjusted to this high level.130 Health authorities currently recommend 420 milligrams of magnesium daily for adult males and 320 milligrams daily for adult females. Available data indicate that most people consume less than that already low recommended amount. For

Americans, the average is about 323 milligrams per day for males and 228 milligrams per day for females. This level is due, in part, to not eating enough foods containing magnesium, but likely also because many foods that would be high in magnesium are grown in soil depleted of this mineral due to modern farming methods.131 Major or persistent magnesium de�ciency can cause heart problems, neurological problems, and also dangerous reductions in calcium and potassium.132 And we don’t know how moderate de�ciencies over time may more subtly diminish our health and vitality.

Vegetables and some �sh, such as salmon and mackerel, are excellent sources of magnesium. Avocados (technically a fruit) and certain dairy products, such as milk and cheese, also contain magnesium. Among the foods with the highest amount of magnesium are pumpkin seeds, almonds, black beans, and soybeans. And I know it can be hard to feel excited about kale, spinach, and chard, but a few minutes spent enlightening yourself about magnesium will likely change that. Dark, leafy greens are an excellent source of it and very low in calories; one cup of cooked spinach contains more than a third of the recommended daily intake and fewer than 50 calories.

And there are more vitamins and minerals that vegetables o�er. Potassium (beets, tomatoes, butternut squash) is integral to muscle contraction and nerve impulses ~~.~~ 133 Calcium (broccoli, kale, edamame, leafy greens) is crucial for our bones and our teeth.134 Flavonoids, a category that includes a wide number of compounds present in the plant world, can reduce in�ammation; the risk of diabetes, heart disease, and breast cancer; antibiotic resistance; the formation of free radicals (atoms that can damage cells and can contribute to cancer formation); oxidative stress, which can contribute to various diseases and conditions including neurodegenerative disorders; and the risk of viral, bacterial, and fungal infections ~~.~~ 135

We could continue talking about the bene�ts of high-quality protein, vegetables, and fruits until the cows (and cauli�ower) come home. In fact, cruciferous vegetables such as cauli�ower and broccoli o�er numerous additional bene�ts such as sulforaphane, which can help scavenge and detoxify endocrine disruptors and generally supports healthy reproductive hormones in

women and men,136 and on and on. I hope that all we’ve covered in this protocol has inspired you to �ll half your lunch or dinner plate with vegetables. Perhaps even add some spinach and tomatoes (though, again, technically a fruit) to your breakfast too.

Though one last note on fruit: Most people, unless they are very lean (less than 10 percent body fat for men and less than 15 percent for women) should probably not be eating more than three servings of fruit per day, especially if they are trying to lose body fat. Too much fruit, despite its �ber and water content, can stimulate hunger. Don’t get me wrong, fruit is amazing, and is always a part of a healthy diet. Enjoy it, but don’t overdo it.

### Consume Healthy Fats as Part of Most Meals and Snacks

###### WHAT TO DO:

- Most of your fat intake should come from unsaturated fats. These are present in olives, avocados, olive oil, and avocado oil, among other foods. Cook with olive oil, and use it for your salad dressing. If you need an oil with a higher smoke point for certain recipes, avocado oil is a good choice.

- Consume omega-3 polyunsaturated fats. These are present in fatty ocean �sh, like salmon with the skin, and in various �sh oil and krill supplements. (More on the bene�ts of omega-3 in Nutrition Protocol 7 of this chapter.)

###### HOW IT WORKS:

Perhaps no category of food is as feared, misunderstood, and maligned as fat. Part of the problem is terminology: The fact that we call dietary lipids fats brings to mind body fat. The two are not the same but they are easy to con�ate.

I want you to create a healthy relationship with fat. The purpose of this protocol is to do that, based on science.

We all need some fat in our diet. The question is not if, but which and how much. Which? It turns out there are quite a few to choose from. And how much? As you learned earlier in this chapter, it depends on the other macronutrients you are eating, or avoiding, according to your overall diet (keto, clean omnivore, vegan, and so on).

And yet we have become wary of this macronutrient. This fear is based less on science than on history. Concerns about a link between fat and heart disease date back to the 1940s and grew in the ensuing decades.137 In 1990, the USDA Dietary Guidelines recommended that Americans limit fat to 30 percent or less of their total calories and saturated fat to just 10 percent of their total calories, a recommendation that led to a proliferation of low-fat and nonfat products ~~.~~ 138 It soon became clear that these foods, often ultra-processed, were much worse for us than the fat we were now avoiding. These guidelines scared many people away from highly nutritious, high-quality protein foods that also contain some fat, like red meat and eggs. Moreover, we were then living without two crucial bene�ts that consuming fat provides: the way it slows the rise of glucose in the bloodstream and the way it increases satiety between meals. And Americans, on average, gained weight and su�ered from rising rates of heart disease in the following years.

More recently, the pendulum swung the other way with rising interest in ketogenic diets, which involve eating mostly fat, some protein, and extremely few carbohydrates.139 Interestingly, this diet �rst originated as a treatment for some forms of epilepsy in the 1920s. It’s also been studied as a treatment for schizophreni ~~a~~ 140 and bipolar disorder ~~.~~ 141 As a daily routine, the ketogenic diet is hard to stick with. But this and similar trends helped spread the awareness that many fats, such as monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats, are good for us.

How can we move forward? Again, by looking at the science. Though a comprehensive review of all types of fat is beyond the scope of this book, a few things are helpful to this discussion. Above we established that fats are made from fatty acids. The body breaks down the fat we eat into these component parts, which are then absorbed into the blood. Once inside the body, fatty acids contribute to the structure and function of cell membranes, help regulate metabolism, and in�uence hormone production, among other roles ~~.~~ 142 Yes, dietary fat can be more readily converted into body fat, and it’s higher in calories per gram than carbs or protein—but at the end of the day, if we are burning as much or more of the calories we eat for energy to meet our metabolic needs, then it doesn’t matter if the calories we eat come from fat, carbs, or proteins.

We covered the main types of dietary fat in the introduction to this chapter: monounsaturated, polyunsaturated, saturated. There is also trans fat. A bit more detail on all is warranted. The terms _saturated_ and _unsaturated_ , and the reason the former are solid at room temp and the latter are not, have to do with their di�erent chemical bonds inside the chains of fatty acids.

The lack of double bonds in saturated fats makes the molecules stack on each other more easily, which makes the fat more stable; this is why products like butter stay solid at room temperature. These fats are hard to digest, which can leave us feeling tired. They can also increase certain forms of cholesterol.

Unsaturated fats are kinked in their structure. When you want to consume fat, these are the ones to prioritize. They contain fatty acids, which trigger circuitries involved with many bodily processes mentioned above ~~.~~ 143 Some fatty acids are directly involved in neuroplasticity, which we can loosely de�ne as the continued ability to learn and form new memories and skills ~~.~~ 144 Fatty acids are also integral to regulating appetite. The presence of fat triggers communication along the gut-brain axis, which prompts the brain to release chemicals that deliver a sense of satiety. In addition, fat in our body releases a hormone called leptin, which activates neural circuitries primarily in the hypothalamus that also result in the feeling of fullness.145 Leptin is also involved in the signaling pathways related to the menstrual cycle and sperm production.146 It is one reason why having enough body fat, but not too much, is needed for libido and fertility. It’s the signal from the body to the brain that food resources exist in su�cient abundance to potentially bring another member of our species into the world.

The fourth kind of fats, trans fats, are unsaturated, but the type of chemical bond is di�erent from those in the other unsaturated fats. Although trans fats that occur naturally in some foods like meat and some dairy are relatively neutral or even bene�cial to our health, when we hear about trans fats it usually refers to industrial-made versions.147 These types of trans fats negatively impact cardiometabolic health, and were banned from the US food supply in 2018.148 When you hear about partially hydrogenated vegetable oil, that is an industrial trans fat. Prior to 2018, many commercial products, such as margarine,

processed meat, microwave popcorn, and packaged baked goods, made in the US contained trans fat, but no more. Health authorities recommend restricting industrial trans fats to 1 percent of total calories consumed—20 calories of a 2,000-calories-per-day diet, which is less than even one tablespoon. If you travel or live outside the US you’ll need to see if industrial trans fats are still used in foods there.

As I note in this protocol, ideally choose monounsaturated fats. Also include some amount of saturated fat.149 Although some studies have found that switching from saturated fats to polyunsaturated fats reduces the risk of heart disease somewhat ~~,~~ 150 other studies have not con�rmed this connection.151 And a common challenge that can arise when eliminating saturated fat from the diet is that it can lead to an increased consumption of ultra-processed carbohydrates and added sugar (we reach for a processed snack instead of, say, some cheese or full-fat yogurt), which is also detrimental to health.152 This often happens when someone decides to eliminate meat, and ends up eating more packaged foods to reduce the e�ort required to prepare high-protein meals. Ultra-processed foods often contain a lot of calories and little to no �ber. I believe it is better to have a little bit of satisfying saturated fat than to replace it with foods that do not trigger a satiety response from the brain, that the body cannot digest e�ectively, or that lead to overconsumption.

If you’re at this part of the protocol still wondering exactly how much fat to incorporate into your diet: Aim for 10 percent or less of your diet to consist of saturated fat. Keeping your overall fat intake to about 30 to 35 percent of your diet will help enable you to receive the bene�ts of this macronutrient without weight gain. Learn to love the right fats and your hormones, connective tissues, heart, and palate will all thank you.

###### COMMON QUESTIONS:

No. Assuming you’re eating 30 percent or so of your calories from fat, and that fat is a mix of saturated fats from high CP:C ratio proteins, and otherwise unsaturated fats such as avocados, olive oil or avocado oil, and some nuts and

seeds, there is no reason to spike or drop your fat intake. If anything, we need to increase our clean starch intake, not our fat intake, on days we exercise. That’s because intense exercise depletes us of glycogen, a sugar that the body makes as a way to store energy, which eating clean starch can replace.

Recent research suggests that our microbiome starts forming before we are even born ~~.~~ 156 Bacteria we are exposed to during the birth process and in the early

The mere act of lacing up our muddy running shoes helps build our microbiome. And it’s important to have that bene�cial bacteria present there. Studies have found connections between the content of our gut microbiome and many digestive disorders, such as irritable bowel disease and colorectal cancer.

The gut microbiome also appears to in�uence mood and mental health through the gut-brain axis (introduced in Nutrition Protocol 1) ~~.~~ 161 A 2022 review of twenty-four observational studies and nineteen experimental trials, totaling about four thousand participants, identi�ed di�erences in the beta diversity—which measures how dissimilar the various bacteria types present are to one another—between individuals who had been diagnosed with major depressive disorder and those who had not.162 Researchers theorize that disruptions to the gut microbiome alter the release of serotonin and dopamine, setting o� a cascade that ultimately ends with the release of cytokines, proteins

that trigger the immune system into action and heighten in�ammation.163 Speci�c in�ammatory cytokines have been linked to depression.164

On the positive side, we know that when our gut bacteria are provided with su�cient L-tryptophan (the amino acid precursor to serotonin) and short-chain fatty acids, they can readily help synthesize serotonin and signal for our brain to do the same, via our vagus nerve.

The Human Microbiome Project, the American Gut Project, the British Gut Project, and other ongoing large collaborative studies are continuing to uncover the function of the gut microbiome—both its role in healthy biological processes and its in�uence on chronic and acute ailments. Studies also seek to �gure out which speci�c species of microbiota are bene�cial and which are not. As a general rule, diversity is the most important feature of a healthy gut microbiome.165 Diet plays a huge role in ensuring that our gut hosts a wide range of healthy bacteria ~~.~~ 166 Fiber has long been a focus in this endeavor to ensure a healthy microbiome (more about how to prioritize �ber in Nutrition Protocol 4).167 But fermented foods appear to play an equally if not more signi�cant role as well. Hence this protocol.

Take the study led by Stanford University biologist Justin Sonnenburg comparing how dietary �ber and fermented foods a�ected the microbiome of thirty-six participants ~~.~~ 168 Half of the individuals consumed a high-�ber diet for ten weeks, increasing their intake of soluble and insoluble �ber by eating more fruits, vegetables, legumes, grains, nuts, and seeds. They also consumed more vegetable protein and decreased the quantity of animal protein and salt. The other half upped their intake of fermented low-sugar foods like yogurt and ke�r and also consumed fermented vegetables (sauerkraut, kimchi) and beverages (kombucha and vegetable brine). Analyses of the blood and stool samples revealed that the group focused on fermented foods experienced a signi�cant decrease in nineteen markers of

in�ammation, including the cytokines interleukin-6, interleukin-10, and interleukin-12b. Of all the science I’ve studied over the years—as a research neuroscientist, in my role hosting many of the world’s most quali�ed doctors and scientists on my podcast, and in my own real-world experience—light, and the incredible in�uence it has on every aspect of our health, is the subject that has thrilled and surprised me the most.

As a master’s student I worked on the visual pathways that control circadian rhythms, and in graduate school and during my postdoc fellowship, and in my own lab, I researched visual circuits that convert light energy—photons, that is —into conscious visual perception, or what is commonly referred to as eyesight. My lab also spent a few years exploring the connections between our eyes and the cerebellum. Turns out, our eyes and our cerebellum—or “mini brain”—are in an ongoing dialogue that helps us orient in space. We will get back to the cerebellum later when we discuss learning in chapter 6.

But as my lab explored the visual system, papers kept coming out showing how light either supports or damages the health of our cells. In some cases these �ndings were about how light a�ects the skin. In other cases, it was about how light impacts our health via our eyes in ways that are separate from eyesight. Given that so much of my training centered around our visual system, that research intrigued me. Not just because it was in my wheelhouse but also because of how actionable it was. It could be applied easily to daily life, and impact health in potent ways. So I voraciously read every one of those studies. I also knew one of the pioneers in this �eld. Glen Je�ery, PhD, at the University College London, a former colleague of mine from the �eld of visual system development, began to study how particular types and sources of light either help or hurt human physiology. His lab also studied how light a�ected longevity ~~.~~ 1 I connected with him periodically to get a sense of what was on the horizon. While his is not the only lab working on the relationship between light and health, Glen is a leader in the formal study of this topic. We have him to thank for taking what were largely anecdotal observations put forth by niche

###### What Is Light?

First we need to discuss what light is, exactly.

Obviously, light makes things visible. Any light source, be it the sun, a lamp, a candle �ame, or the glow from a phone screen makes things visible because it emits energy. Light sources vary by type and amount of energy; that’s what makes them di�erent from one another.

Recall from chapter 1 that light is comprised of a broad range of wavelengths, from very short wavelengths to very long ones. Some of these wavelengths are visible to humans—they make up what we call the visible spectrum of red, green, blue, and so on. Other wavelengths of light, such as ultraviolet and infrared, are invisible to us.

Short wavelengths of light are, as their name suggests, waves of energy where the peaks and the troughs of the wave are very close together. Long wavelengths of light are the opposite; the peaks and troughs of long wavelength light are relatively far apart.

The sun emits an extremely broad range of short, medium, and long wavelengths. The entire visible spectrum is held inside sunlight. That’s why sunlight through a prism comes through as a rainbow on the other side. The prism slows down and bends the light, and each wavelength exits at a di�erent angle, spreading the light into the full visible spectrum of red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, and violet.

Green, blue, and purple light are shorter in wavelength compared to yellow, orange, and red light, which are longer. Sunlight (in the absence of a prism) appears white or pale yellow. The sky turns colorful at dawn and dusk because, as you may recall from chapter 1, when the sun is low in the sky, components of the atmosphere reduce the amount of shorter wavelengths reaching our eyes—a process called Rayleigh scattering—leaving us primarily seeing the longer wavelengths of red, orange, and yellow. The sun of course always emits the same wavelengths of energy regardless of where it happens to be in the sky. Which visible wavelengths arrive at our eyes is what determines how the sun appears to us, and the e�ect it will have on us.

Then there are the invisible wavelengths. Sunlight includes wavelengths shorter than blue or violet that are (unimaginatively) called ultraviolet (UV)

light. We can’t perceive UV light but it’s there, radiating down on us all day. (Though interesting to note that bees can see UV, and squirrels can see it too, possibly to help them detect predators at night. Some species of �ying squirrels actually have UV �uorescence that causes their bellies to glow a bubblegum pink.)15 The sun also emits wavelengths longer than red light, appropriately called infrared (IR) light. We humans can’t see IR, but we can feel it as warmth. Though we have engineered technologies to see IR emissions—that’s what night vision goggles do.

The sun also emits small amounts of X-ray energy, which is made up of very short wavelength radiation, even shorter than UV. And, like with UV and IR, we can’t see X-rays, but they are there. X-rays pass through our skin but are absorbed by our bones, teeth, and other dense tissues. That’s how X-ray machines work: They are designed to send out concentrated X-rays so their patterns of absorption can be captured on �lm or by a digital sensor, allowing your doctor or dentist to see di�erent structures inside your body that absorb those X-rays to varying degrees.

Whether visible or invisible, these wavelengths travel in a similar pattern— not as a line but, well, as a wave, moving up and down, up and down. Shorter wavelengths of light go through many more up-down-up-down cycles as they travel from one point to another; longer wavelengths go through fewer. Thus, we often refer to short wavelengths of light as high frequency light and long wavelengths of light as low frequency.

Mentions of UV light can trigger concerns, so let me address that now. Whether light exposure is harmful, bene�cial, or benign depends on the type, intensity, duration, and timing. All light energy is radiation. Often when people hear the word _radiation_ they think _radioactive_ . The radiation from visible light is not harmful because it doesn’t have enough energy to perturb the atoms in our body. But here’s where type, duration, and the other factors matter. Some forms of non-ionizing light radiation can disrupt our cells if we are exposed to too much of it. For example, we need some UV light exposure each day. But excessive exposure can cause genetic mutations in our cells by causing the formation of abnormal bonds in our DNA.16

Wavelength and intensity of light are inversely related to one another. Put in practical terms, you can be exposed to a lot of long wavelength light, like red or IR light, without damaging your skin. It takes comparatively less exposure to short wavelength UV light to cause a sunburn. But that doesn’t mean short wavelength, high frequency light is inherently bad for us. Again, we come back to this core idea: Dosage matters. We all need some UV light from the sun to reach our skin, where it sets o� a cascade of reactions that results in the production of vitamin D, which is critical for calcium absorption, bone health, immune health, and more.17 But too much UV exposure can lead to a sunburn, as I mentioned above, and cause premature aging of your skin, as well as DNA mutations that lead to certain skin cancers.18 And because long wavelength IR is so low energy (remember, wavelength and intensity are inversely related), we need relatively long sun exposure times to enjoy its bene�ts. The challenge is getting enough IR and NIR (infrared and near-infrared) light from the sun without also getting excessive UV exposure, but it can be done. There’s a protocol for it.

I’m aware that none of what I’ve shared with you thus far tells you exactly _how_ light can change your cells. As wavelengths travel through space, in that upand-down cycle, they hit various surfaces, big and small: a mountain range, a tree, this page, your hand. These surfaces absorb or re�ect wavelengths. But sometimes they pass right through. Light can pass right through your body, for example, and as it does it can change the molecular properties of the cells it encounters and the components within them, such as in the example of excessive UV-altering DNA structure of, say, skin cells. Here are two more examples, this time with light playing positive roles in cellular function: Studies suggest that red, NIR, and IR light can enhance the functioning of your mitochondria, the energy producing organelles in your cells ~~.~~ 19 Data suggest that NIR and IR may also trigger the release of a gas called nitric oxide that acts on your vascular and lymphatic cells and causes them to dilate, allowing for more lymph �uid and blood to move through them ~~.~~ 20

There are more examples in the protocols that follow. You’ll learn how to use light—in some cases sunlight, and in other cases arti�cial light of speci�c

wavelengths—to improve your physical and mental health. Also here are recommendations for in-home lighting and light devices that emit or block speci�c wavelengths of light, which you can use to achieve speci�c bene�ts, such as increased morning and daytime energy levels, better glucose regulation, and even better eyesight. In chapter 1, we explored how light helps with sleep; now it’s time to see its immediate e�ects on other important aspects of our health.

As you read these protocols, remember this: While it might seem fantastical that light can do so many positive things for our brain and body, it actually makes perfect sense. Light is energy that the cells in our body can absorb and use. The very �rst law of thermodynamics is that energy can’t be destroyed or created de novo; it can only be converted from one form to another. So let’s discuss the ways you can convert light energy into cellular energy, which leads to improvements in physical energy, vision, skin, mood, and heart health… and more.

###### The Natural Cortisol Cycle

Sleep Protocol 1 explains the science behind how viewing morning sunlight impacts your circadian rhythm. As a brief reminder: When you view sunlight, or a 10,000 lux light, it activates cells in your eyes that convert light into electrical signals. Those signals are relayed to the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), your master circadian clock, located above the roof of your mouth in your hypothalamus. The SCN in turn releases chemical and electrical signals that

coordinate the activities of the trillions of twenty-four-hour clocks found in every cell and organ of your body into a coherent set of rhythms. The physiological and psychological bene�ts that circadian coordination brings about are many.

But the SCN is not a one-trick pony. It serves another crucial role that is seldom discussed but, frankly, just as important. Your SCN can also stimulate a signi�cant increase in your cortisol levels in the �rst sixty minutes after you wake up. It’s time restricted, meaning it can only occur in this short window. If you miss it, it’s gone—at least until the next day.

This is not a window you want to miss! Because whereas surges in cortisol are generally not advantageous if they occur in the afternoon, the evening, or at night, as I’ve mentioned, you actually want your cortisol levels to be very high in the �rst hours of your day.

Cortisol has gotten a bad rap. It’s been labeled the stress hormone and indeed, this hormone made in your adrenal glands is released during times of stress. But cortisol is also released when you wake up each morning. More accurately, you wake up each morning because cortisol is released. You read that right. Cortisol is the hormone that ensures you have the energy to get out of bed and lean into your daily activities. That is because cortisol’s fundamental role is to cause the release of stored fuels in your liver and muscles, which shifts the state of your brain and body from sleep to one of physical and mental readiness. The technical term for this process, which you might remember from chapter 3, is called the cortisol awakening response (CAR). Cortisol is not just a stress hormone. It’s an energy-releasing hormone. (See Stress Control Protocol 5 if you’d like a reminder.)

When we view cortisol in this way, we start to understand that it’s not something to be avoided at all. Rather, it is something to harness and use to our advantage. Our body has designated pathways and mechanisms to do just that. It allows for what’s called the healthy twenty-four-hour cortisol curve, which follows the pattern below:

- 1 Very low in the 1 to 2 hours prior to bedtime

- 2 At its absolute lowest in the �rst half of your night’s sleep

- 3 Rising slowly in the second half of your night’s sleep

- 4 Rising sharply in the 30 minutes prior to your desired wake-up time

- 5 Rising sharply even more in the �rst 1 to 2 hours after you wake up

- 6 Peaking about 30 minutes to 3 hours after waking

- 7 Gradually decreasing across the early and late afternoon

- 8 Repeat…

Countless studies now show that allowing this natural cycle to operate without disruption helps optimize our sleep, cognition, and energy levels as well as mood and immune system function ~~.~~ 22 By contrast, altering this cycle such that evening or nighttime cortisol levels are too high (or morning cortisol levels are too low) can lead to problems in all these areas. This �attening causes anxiety, sleep disturbances, low daytime energy, and mood disruptions as well as impaired immune resistance to viral, bacterial, and other infections ~~.~~ 24

###### Cortisol and Stress

Keep in mind that just because we are framing cortisol as not purely a stress hormone does not mean it is not related to stress. It is. Stress triggers the release of cortisol.25 If you experience stress at any point during the day or night, you can and should expect a spike in your cortisol to occur. That’s perfectly normal, healthy, and adaptive—because that spike will provide you with the immediate physical and mental energy you need to deal with whatever stressor you might face.26 Stress-triggered cortisol levels typically return to baseline within about one hour or so. In fact, you can experience a lot of cortisol spikes above baseline per day (or night) before it ever becomes problematic for your health. I’m not suggesting you seek out stress, but as we discussed in chapter 3, humans evolved to deal with it in a variety of forms. Raising kids, tra�c, di�cult people, the pressures of work, school, or athletics, the state of the world… many of these are indeed stressful at times, and cortisol makes sure you have the fuel to deal with each one.

Cortisol spikes that occur shortly before sleep are where problems begin. That increase is often what prevents people from falling asleep, and what causes the classic stress-induced sleep disturbance of waking up at 3:00 a.m. and not falling back asleep. One night of that happening, no biggie. Two nights in a row? Hard, but manageable. However, three or more nights of stress-induced sleep disturbances really start to take a toll on your mental and physical health.

Here are the basics of how it works, plus some additional information pertinent to the twenty-four-hour cortisol cycle. Your cortisol level at any one moment, and your overall twenty-four-hour cortisol cycle, are controlled via the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, which we discussed in chapter 3. Neurons in an area of your hypothalamus called the PVN (paraventricular nucleus) extend wirelike projections into your pituitary, a gland that resembles two small marbles in a sock hanging out the base of your brain.27 One of those marbles sits in front of the other, and this is called the anterior pituitary. Your PVN neurons release corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) to cause your anterior pituitary cells to release adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) into your bloodstream. Next, the ACTH travels to your adrenal glands and stimulates the release of cortisol into your bloodstream. Voila! Cortisol then causes energy to be released from various organs and cells in your body. Cortisol does many other things, but one more that’s relevant here: Unlike adrenaline, which is also released from your adrenal glands and increases your energy level,

The PVN also detects when cortisol levels in your blood get high. It then _reduces_ its release of CRH, which in turn reduces ACTH release, which results in less cortisol release. This is called a negative feedback loop; when the level of cortisol reaching the brain is very high, less cortisol is triggered to be released. In that way, it is like how many home thermostats work. For example, if the temperature in a room becomes too high from the level you’ve set, the thermostat shuts the heat o�.

Cortisol surges at 9:00 p.m. for a few nights in a row and the next thing you know, your nextmorning levels are lower than they should be _and_ your PVN is then primed to release _more_ cortisol later that night.

- View sunlight in the afternoon and early evening, for five to thirty minutes. Follow the same general guidelines as for Light Protocol 1. Simply go outside, take o� your sunglasses (eyeglasses and contacts are �ne), and face in the direction of the setting sun. Don’t wear a brimmed hat. And again, don’t stare at the sun; blink as needed.

- Do not replace late afternoon/evening sunlight viewing with a 10,000 lux artificial light. It’s too bright, and the wavelengths these devices emit can mess up your sleep-wake cycle.

###### HOW IT WORKS:

As discussed in Sleep Protocol 2, melatonin, which facilitates falling and staying asleep, begins to increase in the late afternoon and early evening and sharply rises in the hour before your natural bedtime (which, by the way, tends to arrive about �fteen to sixteen hours after your morning sunlight viewing). It continues to rise into the night, before gradually decreasing as morning approaches. Melatonin levels are lowest in the morning and highest at night. In other words,

when cortisol is high, melatonin is low, and when cortisol is low, melatonin is high ~~.~~ 33

Bright light robustly suppresses melatonin, and it causes the release of cortisol as explained in chapter 3.34 Blue lights, screen lights, and LEDs, all of which emit lots of short wavelengths, are especially potent at suppressing melatonin. Bright LEDs, commonly used in bathrooms, bedrooms, and hallways, are short-wavelength enriched. It takes less than thirty seconds of bright LED exposure to the eyes to signi�cantly reduce your melatonin levels. So if you pick up your phone at night, or �ip on the lights… you’re exposing yourself to the kind of light that will suppress melatonin. Late afternoon and early evening sunlight viewing helps mitigate these negative e�ects.

Why do I suggest you not use a 10,000 lux arti�cial light as a replacement for evening sunlight, when I already suggested it as a replacement for morning sunlight in the previous protocol? The reason has to do with wavelengths, discussed earlier in this chapter. Low solar angle sunlight is lower in UV and the short visible wavelengths, which is why sunrises and sunsets often appear orange, pink, or even deep red. Those longer wavelengths help inform your brain that night is coming, and it should prepare for sleep. Too much short wavelength light—especially if it’s bright, and 10,000 lux is bright—will alter your sleepwake cycle.

You’ll notice, just as in the previous protocol, that I’m not suggesting speci�c times to view late afternoon or early evening sunlight. Again, that is because schedules vary from person to person, and the time of day when the sun sets varies according to your location and the time of year. Luckily, you can get the desired e�ect without being overly precise about the timing. Just aim to view sunlight at some point after the sun is directly overhead and before it sets.

This doesn’t mean that you should avoid sunlight or arti�cial light during other parts of the day. Researchers from Rush University ran a small study where, for one week, people experienced bright light exposure for up to �ve hours by combining outdoor exposure to sunlight and indoor exposure to 10,000 lux light during the day.35 They called it “the bright week.” The following week, the light exposure was dimmer; people spent two and a half

hours outdoors at most, and wore light-obscuring goggles when they did. That was “the dim week.” The researchers found that light-induced melatonin suppression at night was greater during the dim week than during the bright week (though some participants showed greater di�erences than others). Bright light exposure during the day partially prevented light-induced melatonin suppression at night.

Seems paradoxical, given that light suppresses melatonin, right? Yes, until we look at another mechanism at work here. Another small study from the Netherlands measured melatonin levels, body temperature, and skin blood �ow (all markers of circadian rhythmicity) of twelve women and noted how sleepy they reported feeling, according to when they viewed light in the evening and at night.36 They divided subjects into three groups. One group viewed dim light at night. Another group also viewed dim light at night but also viewed bright lights beforehand, late in the evening. The third group viewed bright light in the early evening, and then dim lights at night. All three groups saw some reduction in melatonin, which is not surprising given that light viewing suppresses melatonin production any time of day or night. But the third group—the group that saw early evening bright light _plus_ late-night dim light—had a less dramatic melatonin drop. This again supports the idea that early evening light exposure can partially inoculate us against the negative e�ects of bright light at night.

These studies may be small, but they point to the importance of viewing sunlight in the late afternoon and early evening, and avoiding bright light exposure at night. It’s worth noting that it may be especially important for adolescents to avoid bright light at night, as one study showed that early evening sunlight exposure did not protect them against the melatonin-reducing e�ects of bright light as it did for adults.37 This may also mean that adolescents are particularly sensitive to the negative e�ects of bright arti�cial lights and screens at night.

The reasons to try to o�set the negative e�ects of bright light at night are not just related to sleep. Animal studies have shown that bright light exposure to the eyes late at night activates pro-depression circuitries ~~.~~ 38 And as we’ve already covered, human studies have shown strong links between nighttime bright light

exposure, cortisol increases, melatonin suppression, and mood disturbances. If you or your child happens to view bright light in the hours before sleep now and again, perhaps from a movie or a night out, that’s no cause for concern. If you make a habit of keeping bright arti�cial lights on late at night, however, and you notice your moods are shifting for the worse, that could be why.

As you’re probably realizing, modern life—with all its lighting options and screens everywhere—is not oriented around daylight �uctuations in the way it once was. Humans used to wake up and go to sleep with the sun. We had no choice but to be attuned to the solar cycle. The advent of arti�cial lighting changed everything, and the shift from incandescent to lower cost LED lighting further exacerbated the issues. In fact, in the last ten years, the amount and type of arti�cial light exposure humans experience has changed so dramatically that we can honestly say that, as a species, our whole relationship to light has been altered. Yet our biology hasn’t changed one bit in thousands of years. Hence this chapter.

###### COMMON QUESTIONS:

There is no need to be obsessive about this—it doesn’t have to interfere with your life. Still, by making some concerted e�ort toward viewing sunlight (or a 10,000 lux lamp) in the mornings, and sunlight in the late afternoons or early evenings, and avoiding bright light at night, you can dramatically improve your mood and energy levels, metabolism, and sleep—which of course bolsters all the rest. So try to get outdoors at these times if you can. Better yet, take a walk in the direction of the sun. ### Avoid Viewing Bright Light One Hour Before Your Bedtime

###### WHAT TO DO:

- In the one hour before your bedtime, use only as much artificial light as necessary to safely carry out your nighttime activities. That recommendation holds until you wake up the next morning to begin your day.

- Be especially mindful to avoid viewing bright short wavelength light at this time. Avoid not just lights that appear blue, but also bright “white” LED lights, �uorescent lights, and screens, because they emit a lot of short wavelengths that stimulate cortisol release and inhibit melatonin.

In the �rst hour of your day, it takes a lot of bright light to stimulate cortisol release and activate the neural pathways in your brain and body that increase wakefulness. By comparison, in the �nal hour of your day, it takes very little bright light to wake you up. Moreover, melatonin, the hormone that promotes sleepiness, is potently inhibited by viewing bright light at any time of day or night. That’s why viewing bright light at night is a double whammy to your

system: It makes you more alert and it makes you less sleepy by at least two di�erent pathways.

The whole light-sensing and cortisol-releasing system is just not the same in the morning and at night.39 If you have ever felt that you are a vastly di�erent person in the morning and at night, indeed you are. The key to using light as a tool to enhance your health is to understand this dynamic.

It all boils down to knowing when you woke up that morning and how many hours it has been since. Here’s a reference you can follow:

A Day in the Light

Phase 1: 0–1 hour after waking: You need to see a lot of bright light (Light Protocol 1).

Phase 2: 6–10 hours after waking: Get some late afternoon or early evening sunlight in your eyes (Light Protocol 2).

Phase 3: 10–14 hours after waking: Start dimming the lights, avoid bright light exposure to your eyes (this protocol).

Phase 4: And �nally, sleep…

Though by now you may be asking (or shouting), “What is all this ‘0–1 hour after waking, 6–10 hours after waking, and 1–2 hours before sleep’ stu�? No one lives this way! Why can’t you just give me a clock time?”

I’ve said this before, and I’ll say it again here: People follow di�erent sleepwake schedules, with some sleeping from 8:00 p.m. to 4:00 a.m. and others sleeping from 11:00 p.m. to 7:00 a.m. Still others work the night shift. Variation in people’s schedules makes it impossible for me to say, “Dim the lights and avoid viewing LED screens between 10:00 p.m. and 5:00 a.m.” or even “View bright light within an hour of sunrise.”

Also, the length of days varies according to location and time of year, and things like daylight further complicate matters. So I suggest you frame your sleep-wake schedule according to four phases. Once you try this approach to your days, and use light (or avoid it) accordingly, I’m certain it will improve your health and well-being.

It’s worth noting again that the clock times corresponding to the four phases will change if you were to, say, sleep in an extra hour or two, or wake up an hour earlier than is typical, or go to sleep an hour earlier or later. In case any of this is confusing, here is how I use this system to structure my days (and nights).

###### My Phase 4:

This phase spans from the period starting fourteen hours after waking until the next morning when the new day starts. Today for me that meant from 9:00 p.m. on. For some time now, I have made it a practice to dim the lights in the �nal hours before I go to sleep. As I mentioned earlier in this chapter, people vary in their visual sensitivity to light.
