Often I wear them at home too, as I �nd they simplify this process.

Take note that phase 4 is where most people make seemingly small mistakes that cost them dearly in terms of health and well-being. There are two main reasons. With the advent of smartphones, and an endless stream of news, content, and the many other hooks that technology o�ers, it’s very easy to turn to a device. It’s also because most homes and hotels use LED lights nowadays, which emit short wavelengths that disrupt sleep. A bit later in the chapter, I’ll explain how to help with this. In the meantime, here are some ways to make phase 4 much easier and more e�ective:

Keep it low and keep it dim. I suggest that any lighting you use in the �nal hours before you go to sleep come from desk lamps or �oor lamps, that is, low light sources, and that, if possible, you avoid using overhead lights. The neurons in your eyes that signal to your brain that it is daytime are arranged across your neural retina (the light sensing tissue in the back of your eye) and they view

the upper visual �eld, meaning the sky when you are outside and the ceiling when you are indoors ~~.~~ 40 Many people �nd that using low, dim light sources in the one to two hours before bed makes it much easier to fall and stay asleep.41 This is pretty easy to do, and can make a big di�erence.

You can go further still and use bulbs without short wavelengths, which thus appear yellow-orange, or even go with bulbs that emit purely long wavelengths, and thus appear red. Keep in mind this is not red light therapy. Red light therapy (explained later in this chapter) can be very bene�cial for certain aspects of health but is altogether di�erent from what we are discussing here. Medium-wavelength-only bulbs are relatively inexpensive and provide a nice yellow-amber glow. Admittedly, using long-wavelengthonly bulbs will make your home look a little space age, but they are a great tool to help you sleep better. Either way, using dim, non-overhead lights without short wavelengths in the last one to two hours before bedtime reduces the activation of the retinal neurons that signal your brain to suppress melatonin and boost cortisol.42

As mentioned above, several companies have conveniently engineered bulbs that are full-spectrum-emitting (white) for the daytime, and with a simple �ick of the light switch, become medium and long wavelength only emitting (yellow-amber or red). Incandescent versions of these exist too and are best, but they use more energy than LEDs, don’t last nearly as long, and are more costly. They are also a bit hard to �nd.

Wear eyeglasses that filter out all short wavelength light. This approach is very convenient if you don’t want to change the lights in your home, or if you don’t have control over the lighting conditions in a certain environment, such as on planes, in hotels or airports, out with friends, et cetera. I designed the ROKA Wind Down glasses for use during the �nal hours before sleep, and I use them at home and when I travel. They di�er from traditional blue blockers because they prevent all short wavelength light, not just blue light, from reaching your eyes. (Don’t wear them while driving because they make anything that is blue or green much harder to see or even invisible, and that could cause an accident.)

Don’t worry about moonlight. You may be wondering if bright moonlight or even a roaring �re will stimulate the wakefulness pathways in your brain. The answer is, perhaps surprisingly, no. Although these are concentrated light sources, a bright full moon is less than 1 lux and while candles, �replaces, and bon�res mostly emit medium and short wavelength light, it doesn’t radiate very far. If you have ever been camping and turned around from a roaring camp�re, you’ve noticed that as soon as you are just a few paces away from it, you need a �ashlight in order to see. We discussed the physics of this in chapter 1. So while �re and candles are great nighttime light sources from a cortisol-limiting and melatonin-preserving perspective, they are not very practical. Of course, if you’d like to read by candlelight or gather around a �re with friends, great. Just make sure the �ames are extinguished when you’re �nished. Be careful not to start a �re.

You may be wondering if all this attention to avoiding bright light in the hours before sleep is silly, neurotic biohacking. After all, you can �nd studies showing that blocking blue light improves people’s sleep to varying degrees,43 and you may be one of those people who can pass out with the TV or computer still at full brightness right in front of you. Indeed, there is considerable variation in the degree to which short wavelength light exposure alters people’s sleep.44 That said, having even just a dim 100 lux overhead light on while you sleep can alter the next-morning glucose levels.45 And that’s while sleeping, with eyes closed. The point is, altered sleep is not the only reason to avoid bright light in phase 4. Nighttime bright light exposure increases blood pressure46 and heart rate, and has been linked to weight gain and even a risk of obesity.47 Studies have found nighttime bright light to negatively impact next-day cognitive function48 and mood49 independent of bright light’s negative e�ects on sleep.

None of this is surprising to biologists who have studied the so-called nonimage-forming visual system or the many opsins other than melanopsin that are present in our skin and other tissues for the last three decades ~~.~~ 50 Myself included. We know, for instance, that the retinal neurons that respond to bright short wavelength light connect not only to your SCN but also to areas of your hypothalamus, such as the supraoptic nucleus, that are directly involved in sleep

regulation. (I know, supraoptic sounds like suprachiasmatic but please don’t blame me, I didn’t name either one.) Your eyes also connect to your thalamus’s perihabenular nucleus, which has been nicknamed the anti-reward or disappointment center ~~,~~ 51 given it actively inhibits dopamine release and is thought to increase feelings of depression when activated at night by, you guessed it, bright light.

The broader �eld of medicine is starting to incorporate these discoveries. Disrupting the light-dark cycle can a�ect lifespan. An international team of researchers conducted an enormous study in which 88,905 people enrolled in the UK Biobank, a database for collecting long-term health information, were given wearable light sensors for one week.52 The participants wore these wrist sensors for seven days, during which they went about their normal routine. The sensors recorded light exposure around the clock. At the end of the week, the researchers had data on 13 million hours of light exposure.

They grouped all the data according to daytime and night, categorizing participants according to light exposure during the day (between the hours of 7:30 a.m. and 8:30 p.m.) and light exposure during the night (between the hours of 12:30 a.m. and 6:00 a.m.). They then collected health data over a follow-up period of about eight years. For the 3,750 participants who died during the follow-up period, the researchers categorized mortality data according to cause of death.

They found that the brighter the night and the darker the day, the higher the risk of death; the link was dose dependent! The risk of death by any cause was up to 34 percent higher among those who got the most light exposure at night, compared to those with the least light exposure at night. The reverse was also true. The risk of death (by any cause) was up to 34 percent lower among the participants with the most light exposure during the day compared to those with the least. This connection held despite any other traits including age, sex, physical activity, smoking, drinking, and cardiovascular health.

There’s more. The analysis zoomed in on nighttime light exposure, grouping it into half hour increments and matching those increments with mortality data. The brightest lighting between 1:00 a.m. and 6:00 a.m. carried a risk of death by any cause that was 11 to 39 percent higher compared to the darkest lighting

during this stretch of time. The risk of death due to cardiometabolic issues (heart attack, stroke, diabetes, nonalcoholic fatty liver disease) was 20 to 67 percent higher for the brightest lighting compared to the darkest lighting during this stretch of the night. The time frame here di�ers slightly from the one described in this protocol, but the exact times aren’t the point; the point is that viewing bright light at night is disruptive to your immediate and long-term health.

It’s true that this was a relatively brief study, using just a week’s worth of light exposure data. However, about three thousand participants repeated the study up to four times and the light exposure patterns were the same. Several other studies have found similar links.53 And the sheer volume of light exposure data in this one makes a persuasive case. As the researchers wrote in the 2024 publication of their study in the _Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences_ , “Across the general population, avoiding night light and seeking daylight may lead to reduction in disease burden, especially cardiometabolic diseases, and may increase longevity.”

In another large study, published in _Nature Mental Health_ in 2023, researchers at the University of Manchester cross-referenced data on mental health with data on light, sleep, and physical activity from 86,722 individuals.54 Their analysis revealed a link between greater nighttime light exposure and higher risk for several mental health issues, including major depressive disorder, anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder, and self-harm behavior. Greater daytime light exposure correlated with a reduced risk of these issues. They also found that people who experienced darker nights had fewer mental health symptoms, an e�ect that occurred independent of daytime light exposure. That is, brightlight-�lled mornings and days and dark nights independently and additively promoted better mental health.

These large datasets deliver a clear and important message, one that typically goes unmentioned: Keeping the lights o� during the late hours of your night is not just about getting great sleep; it is fundamentally important for your health and well-being.

###### **LIGHT PROTOCOL**

4

### Expose Your Upper and Lower Body Skin to Sunlight During the Day

###### WHAT TO DO:

Get twenty to thirty minutes of outdoor sunlight exposure to your skin at least three times per week, and ideally every day. Wear the minimum amount of clothing that allows you to be comfortable and that is appropriate for your environment, without covering your entire body (for example, shirtless with shorts, or shorts and a tank top, or a swimsuit. In some cases, jeans and a short-sleeved T-shirt may be what’s called for). It is best that you do not wear a hat during this time. I discuss cold weather options below.

###### HOW IT WORKS:

There is no substitute for sunlight. You could turn on every light in your home in the morning and daytime, make sure they are full-spectrum incandescent bulbs or wavelength-balanced full spectrum LEDs, view a 10,000 lux arti�cial light within an hour of waking up, and it still would not replace sunlight.

Each of those technologies can serve as a health-promoting supplement on days when you can’t get enough sunlight, and they can help boost the e�ects of sunlight, but they should not be used as an everyday replacement for sunlight. Think of them the same way you would supplements relative to nutritious food; they can help bridge de�ciencies, and in some cases they can a�ord you a real mental or physical performance advantage. Yet no rational person would ever

replace all their food with supplements on a consistent basis. Alas, because most people don’t understand how powerful light is as a tool for health, and that sunlight is a uniquely bene�cial form of it, they engage with light in a way that is analogous to trying to live solely on supplements.

Actually, in many cases it’s even worse than that. People are spending the �rst hours of their day in sunless, dark, or dim indoor environments, viewing screens, and then continuing their days under arti�cial lights that seem bright but that are actually dim compared to sunlight. After sundown, they stay under those same lights, which are now far too bright for what is needed at night, and many view mostly short wavelength emitting screens. This is, in no uncertain terms, as bad as living on highly processed junk food. And it’s making a lot of people sick, mentally and physically.

Getting sunlight on our skin is as much a cornerstone of health as sleep, exercise, or nutrition. It’s hard for most people to fully grasp this, especially given that we all have heard how damaging UV light is for our skin. Yet, we need to embrace what is special and bene�cial about sunlight and incorporate it into our daily lives. And no, you do not have to live in California, or run around shirtless or in a bathing suit outside. You simply need to know how the energy present in sunlight impacts _every_ cell in your body: your brain, hair, skin, liver, heart, your hormones, neurotransmitters, immune system, and on and on.

And so, on to the science.

Sunlight is the absolute best source of long wavelength light, from the red end of the visible spectrum into non-visible near-infrared and IR wavelengths. It is di�cult to overstate how important these longer wavelengths are for our health, in particular for our mitochondria, the energy producing organelles within our cells. (I’ll cover the uses of LWL devices that purely emit red, NIR, and IR light in the next protocol.)

Sunlight contains short wavelength UV light, which as we discussed earlier in this chapter, triggers the production of vitamin D in the skin. Although this vitamin (which also acts as a hormone) is available in some foods, supplements can replace sunlight as a stimulus for vitamin D,55 yet our bodies evolved to use sun-induced vitamin D in multiple ways that supplements may not mimic.

For example, vitamin D is important for hormone health and the reproductive system. A multi-institution study on mice and humans looked at the e�ects speci�cally of UVB (the ultraviolet wavelength that penetrates the skin) on reproductive-related hormones and behavior ~~.~~ 56 They found that mice exposed to UVB light for one hour per day showed enhanced mating behavior and physiology—greater attraction for one another, larger ovaries, and more testosterone—in both the male and female mice. Moreover, male mice showed a greater attraction to UVB-treated female mice, likely due to how elevated testosterone and estrogen levels in females impacted their appearance and scent, making them more attractive. More interestingly, the researchers saw similar patterns in people. According to their �ndings, published in _Cell Reports_ in 2021, participants reported increased romantic interest in others following time in the sun. The data also showed heightened testosterone levels linked to this exposure in both men and women. Testosterone and estrogen levels—both of which impact romantic desire and feelings of well-being in men and women— were highest in the longer days of spring and summer relative to shorter winter and fall days.

This e�ect appears to relate to a molecule called p53 expressed in a type of skin cell called keratinocytes. Mice in which p53 had been removed did not exhibit the same changes following UVB exposure. This detail emphasizes the importance of having sunlight reach not only our eyes, but also our skin.

Here’s another: UV light from sunlight also reduces physical pain. In 2017, a group of researchers reported a study in which they exposed mice to UVB (midrange ultraviolet light, abundant in sunlight) radiation and then tested various parameters relating to the HPA axis ~~.~~ 57 This brain pathway is the core mechanism behind our stress response (as discussed in chapters 1 and 3) ~~.~~ 58 They found a link between UVB radiation and the stimulation of corticotropinreleasing hormone, which helps us cope with social stress ~~,~~ 59 and endogenous beta endorphins, a type of opioid our body naturally produces in response to psychological distress ~~.~~ 60 Although this work focused on mice, the results point toward a potentially crucial and unappreciated role for sunlight, in particular

UV light—which most people generally think of as the aspect of sunlight to be avoided.

Excessive UV light exposure will cause sunburn and increase your risk for certain forms of skin cancer. So, while UV light from the sun has many bene�ts, it is still important to avoid too much exposure and sunburn.

###### A Word About Sunscreen

Of course, no one wants a sunburn. One’s risk of sunburn and skin cancer varies depending on factors such as skin tone and inherited susceptibility to skin cancer. All dermatologists agree that any amount of sunburn is bad for us, so bear that in mind. And all agree that excessive exposure to sunlight leads to more rapid aging of the skin too. Excessive skin exposure to UV light, in particular, mutates our skin cell DNA and destroys keratinocytes, which give skin its suppleness. So the takeaway message is to avoid sunburn at all costs.

I don’t burn easily but if I am going to be outside at a time of day when the UV index is high, I either rely on a physical barrier—hat and long sleeves—or I apply a mineral-based sunscreen that uses zinc oxide (not nano zinc) as the only active ingredient. People debate whether chemical-based sunscreens are bad for hormone health and my read of the literature is yes, they can be; but that debate aside, no one argues whether physical barriers or mineral-based-only sunscreen are useful and safe. _for_ FOCUS, MOTIVATION, _and_ LEARNING

Our ability to get and stay motivated, to focus, and to learn new things is at the heart of what it is to be successful in life. Not just in school and work, but in creative endeavors and athletics. Consider the e�ort it takes to study for a big test or remember the material needed for a big presentation, or even stick with a new approach to a painting or new musical instrument practice, or try to respond to a social situation in a new way.

The question then becomes, “How?” How can we get motivated when our energy or natural impulses pull us toward apathy, overthinking, or procrastination? How can we tap into heightened focus, on demand? How can we learn faster and more e�ectively?

It turns out these are states of mind and body that we can learn to deliberately access.

My second year of college is when I �rst started to discover this. I learned that motivation can happen automatically as the consequence of, say, being excited or intrigued by something but it can also be deliberately fostered.

As I mentioned a bit in the introduction, I went from being a good student in my early life to falling behind my peers in high school. I touched on why that happened, but I make no excuses. Those were ultimately my own choices and actions. And those challenges both in and out of school, and watching my peers face those challenges too—seeing some soar and thrive while others struggled— would all become a blessing in many ways. It forced me to realize that no one was coming to save me and that I had to change things on my own. That realization scared me, but it’s what motivated me to turn my life around. I never quite had the exact words for what went through my head at that moment until recently, when a very wise friend and mentor said something and I thought, “THAT! That’s what I was hearing in my head! THAT!”

I can’t say I came up with it, but it’s something that I have heard in my head in fragments, over and over since I was nineteen. I still remind myself of it every day:

_Losers take the negative things that happen to them and the feelings that come from things that suck… and they wallow and they use it for self- or outward destruction._

_Winners however take whatever they feel—even if it sucks—and they transmute those feelings into actions that are good for themselves and for the world._

I chose to do something. And through that choice, I learned that while motivation can result in action, it’s possible for action to result in motivation too.

As a sophomore in college, I decided to study as if my life depended on it. I didn’t care if I liked the subject. I decided it made no di�erence, that eventually I would �nd the right path if I kept moving forward but I was going to move forward no matter what. Sure enough, my motivation to learn grew more and more, and morphed into a desire to get a PhD in a topic I fell in love with, to run a lab, to teach, and to build a career in science. Somewhere early along the way that fear I described dissipated. My love of certain topics and lab skills grew, but it often came _after_ I had forced myself to learn them. Sure, sometimes it was there prior—I’ve always had a love for biology for example—but often it was only after I immersed myself in a subject that I truly fell in love with it. The hardest courses I took in college turned out to be the ones I loved the most, and years later those subjects would be among the major focuses of my lab. The most useful thing I learned back then was that I realized that I could access the state of urgency that we call motivation whether I loved something or not. Reason and persistence, not excitement, anchored my e�ort.

And the act of being able to access a state of motivation gave me con�dence to tackle what I wanted to go after or what was placed in front of me. I wasn’t a grade-chasing automaton; I had a sense of agency over my life and that kept me going.

Just as my motivation grew, so too did my ability to focus and learn. At �rst, I had to take drastic measures to force myself to do both. While studying biology in university, I would set a timer for several hours and force myself to study without breaks until the timer went o�. Having been so checked out in high school, I had a lot of catching up to do. This was extremely di�cult at �rst. Long

bouts of studying required a level of focus I did not have back then. But over time, my ability to focus got better—and kept getting better.

I later came to discover that the early stages of focus and learning are supposed to include agitation. That feeling comes from the shift in your brain and body’s neurochemical milieu that sets the stage for learning to take place. You are asking your brain to change, and your brain doesn’t want to change. Changing is very energetically demanding for brains. This uncomfortable feeling is something I often refer to as “limbic friction.” It’s not an o�cial scienti�c term, but it refers to a state of elevated autonomic arousal where you’re funneling into focus, and it takes constant or near-constant e�ort to get there and stay there. It’s a mental edge of sorts. Once I understood that this limbic friction was not only normal, but essential, focus and learning became easier. I started seeking it out. And it felt good. I share this backstory simply to help illustrate that motivation, focus, and learning are states of mind and body. They have neural and hormonal underpinnings, much in the same way that REM sleep has its neural and hormonal underpinnings, as does stress, and so on. And that’s good news, because it makes what might otherwise be nebulous, clear. We know what to aim for.

This is a physiology-�rst approach to focus, motivation, and learning. It’s rooted in how we work, which is why the approach works.

In this chapter you’ll learn how to enhance your ability to focus by leveraging that. You’ll also learn a powerful tool for “getting motivated” that is unlike all others you’ve likely seen before. And you’ll �nally get the truth about neuroplasticity—the rewiring of neural circuits that underlies all forms of learning (and forgetting), and that is often referred to simply as _plasticity_ . Most everyone has heard of plasticity but honestly, most of the ways I’ve seen it discussed publicly are �at-out wrong.

Perhaps you’ve heard that “Every experience you have changes your brain.” That is not true. Or “It takes twenty-one days to form a new habit.” Wrong again. It can take a few days or a year, based on your level of motivation. Perhaps you’ve heard that “Your brain makes new neurons for your entire life.” (The o�cial term for that is neurogenesis.) Alas, barely any new neurons are added to the brain after puberty except for in your olfactory system, which allows you to

smell, and those are mostly to replace neurons you’ve lost. Starting to get depressed? Well don’t, because despite these myths, we all possess a tremendous ability to rewire our brains and to learn at any age.

The key is to understand the _type_ of plasticity you’re after. What we’re talking about here—the rewiring of our brains that occurs as part of learning at any age —is a process that involves _a specific set of steps that must be completed in a specific sequence for learning to occur_ .

I call these steps self-directed adaptive plasticity (SDAP). Mastering these steps opens the doors to learning pretty much anything you set your mind to. And that’s what this chapter is about.

The Steps and Sequence of SDAP Let’s start with an overview of how SDAP occurs:

Get alert.

SDAP requires you to focus on the material at hand. Alertness sets the stage for focus; it’s a precursor. I’ll explain all this in the pages ahead.

So get alert and…

###### Get and stay focused.

Focused on what? On implementing a speci�c strategy during your learning bout.

As you go…

###### Maintain a state of urgency.

Your internal state really matters as you learn. You can’t be too relaxed, but you can’t be stressed either. I de�ne a state of urgency as simply a state of persistent motivation. It’s the state to aim for because it has you stay alert but not too alert and…

###### Embrace errors.

Errors that arise from genuine attempts to do something are key signals for triggering plasticity. Your nervous system is stimulated to rewire largely based on what you fail to do, not what you do correctly.

###### Rest.

Sleep is when neural rewiring actually occurs, especially during REM sleep the �rst night after a learning bout. There are other ways you can incorporate rest—like non-sleep deep rest (NSDR) and short breaks—to improve performance.

###### Repeat.

Consolidate newly learned material or skills through repeat performance, either through physical repetition or taking yourself through the material or skill using your imagination (seriously). Mental self-testing is especially e�ective for reinforcing newly formed brain connections.

Each of these six steps is valuable in its own right, and can be applied to various areas of life. Thus, although this chapter is framed in the context of plasticity, each of the protocols has other important applications too. I’ll explain more as we go.

###### Types of Neuroplasticity

Before we explore each step of SDAP, let’s get clear on what we’re talking about when we talk about plasticity.

All sustained behavioral and cognitive change is the result of plasticity. These changes come in two broad types: adaptive and maladaptive. Adaptive changes are desirable—this is the plasticity that accompanies learning a new language or a new artistic or athletic skill. Maladaptive changes are the ones that make life harder. Consider when a brain injury renders someone unable to produce coherent speech, or a traumatic event leaves someone stricken with PTSD. That’s still plasticity but obviously not the sort you want.

These two types of plasticity happen in di�erent ways. Maladaptive plasticity, as in the brain injury I described above, tends to occur fast and is hard to undo. Adaptive plasticity, like learning that new language, takes more e�ort, and reverts somewhat easily, at least at �rst. I realize that’s not convenient but the sooner we accept that reality, the further along we can all be in our e�orts to learn new things.

Understanding why and how maladaptive brain changes occur will help illustrate how to get the adaptive brain changes that you want, and make them happen more quickly. Psychologically traumatic events trigger astonishingly fast and stable changes to nervous system wiring.1 This rewiring happens not just in the brain but in the patterns of brain-to-body and body-to-brain connections, and hormone-control pathways.2 The duration of a traumatic event can be very brief—no more than a few seconds—yet bring about persistent or recurring anxiety, sleep disturbances, and physical challenges, like chronic pain ~~,~~ 3 rashes ~~,~~ 4 gut issues ~~,~~ 5 and more, that last for years.

This is essentially _one trial learning_ . Something happens and we are (seemingly) forever changed. The evolutionary logic is straightforward: One trial learning from traumatic events helps ensure we avoid similar circumstances in the future. It keeps us safe.

How one trial learning happens brings us back to an analogy discussed in chapter 3. Remember the autonomic seesaw? A stress-inducing event or thought causes your autonomic nervous system to increase your sympathetic tone, which makes you alert. That sharpens your focus. If sympathetic tone is too high, however, it feels like anxiety or panic.

When we experience a traumatic event, our brains quickly trigger the release of a lot of adrenaline into our bodies and a lot of norepinephrine in our brains ~~.~~ 6 Together, these two neuromodulators create all the necessary conditions for plasticity to occur. We’re not talking about a bit of normal life stress. We’re talking about something you perceive as really scary that causes a large and rapid shift in the neurochemical milieu of the body and brain. This shift during a traumatic event may sound like a good thing, because it helps you move away from the person or thing stressing you out, but in the long run many times it’s not. If the stress response is too big, it triggers the rapid modi�cation of multiple brain circuitries all at once and can result in an unhealthily low stress threshold going forward.7 In some cases, one’s stress threshold becomes set so low that anxiety and panic arise from innocuous events of everyday life. Undoing the kind of rewiring that results from traumatic events takes dedicated e�ort. Fortunately, it is possible. I discuss one way to do that in the next chapter.

The conditions experienced during this kind of one-trial learning are also at play in SDAP. “Uh-oh,” you may be thinking, “is he going to suggest that I get stressed out to learn?” No. In fact, if you’re too stressed, and your sympathetic tone is too elevated, you won’t be able to focus, and you absolutely need to focus in order to learn. But you do need to be alert. My point here is that a shift in neurochemical milieu is crucial to achieving that state—alert but calm. Not stressed.

###### Conditions for Neuroplasticity

SDAP is all about desired forms of learning: a new musical instrument, a new language, a new physical skill, a new healthy habit, et cetera. For SDAP to occur, you must focus intensely on what you are trying to learn. To focus intensely on what you are trying to learn, you have to be alert. And to be alert, your autonomic nervous system has to be in a somewhat sympathetic-dominant state.

That seesaw shift in the nervous system signals to the relevant circuits in your brain and body that what is happening is unique and important, and that they need to change to become better equipped for similar circumstances in the future. Another useful way to think about it is that your brain must get the message that there is a gap between its current con�guration and the demands you’re facing—a de�cit of sorts that it needs to overcome. The de�cit is resolved by making new brain connections.

Now of course your neurons don’t talk to each other in words. They don’t say, “This is important, and we have a de�cit between where we’re at and where we need to be, so we need to change.” Neurons communicate in the language of chemicals and electricity. So this message is communicated electrochemically, as a shift in your brain and body’s neurochemical milieu that in turn alters the amount of �ring in the brain circuits that need to change for the desired learning to occur. And when it comes to shifting neurochemical milieus—that is largely the job of neuromodulators.

The neuromodulators dopamine, serotonin, adrenaline, norepinephrine, and acetylcholine each serve di�erent purposes, depending on where they are released in your brain or body.8 It’s incorrect to say that dopamine alone drives motivation, for instance, or that serotonin controls mood. It’s far more varied

and nuanced than that. In terms of plasticity, all these neuromodulators can alter the level of electrochemical activity in the circuits I just described. In other words, these neuromodulators can change the amount and the volume that neurons “talk” to each other.

In fact, in the context of plasticity, you can think of a neuromodulator as a microphone lowered over a speci�c conversation in a crowded stadium. Like a stadium on game day, brains are noisy. They are busy carrying out all kinds of everyday electrochemical duties. The “microphone” makes a conversation louder against the background noise. This is one common way plasticity occurs. The faster and greater the shift in the activity of a given circuit relative to its previous levels, and relative to the background (more electrochemically active), the more likely that circuit will alter its structure and connections—in other words, the more likely plasticity of the circuit will occur. It’s also true that if neural circuits are quieter (less electrochemically active) against the chatter of usual background brain activity, they can weaken.

Di�erent contexts spike the release of di�erent neuromodulators alone or in combination, which ampli�es the conversation of the neural circuits active in that context. For example, dopamine is a major neuromodulator released in response to novelty and surprise, which facilitates plasticity for learning and memory ~~.~~ 9 And acetylcholine is released at high levels under conditions of heightened focus, but not all over the brain; rather, it’s released speci�cally at the sites in neural circuits that are active.10

Regardless of which neuromodulator or combination of neuromodulators is released, what happens next is largely the same. Since the brain is homeostatic— that is, it seeks balance—rather than maintain high levels of activity, the neurons that are part of a given conversation modify themselves so they become more easily active should that context occur again. They may add more receptors to render themselves capable of capturing more neurotransmitters or they may sprout a tiny neurite, an axonal (output) or dendritic (input) branch that becomes part of a new set of synaptic connections with other nearby neurons.11 All this changes the threshold for activation of that circuit going forward, and on and on.12 Voila! That is learning-driven plasticity. Other forms of plasticity

involve similar cellular and molecular changes but the conditions that create them are di�erent.

SDAP is about creating this situation of speci�c neural circuits rewiring in speci�c ways on purpose. The steps involved in this process are designed to help you do just that.

###### Where to Begin

Above, I noted that the �rst step of SDAP is getting alert and the second is getting focused. These two work together in a positive feedback loop.

The cool thing is even the mere act of trying to focus shifts us into a slightly more elevated sympathetic tone, which causes our levels of alertness to increase, which then causes activity in the circuits for focusing to increase, which further causes levels of alertness to, you guessed it, increase. For those who struggle with focus, take solace in the fact that the circuits involved with focus are amenable to plasticity too. As you move through the SDAP process described in this chapter, and practice the various protocols here, you’ll learn new things, but you’ll also get better at focusing, which will help you to learn more new things, and so on.

There are multiple ways to create the increase in alertness and focus needed for SDAP. I’ll cover all your options—behavioral, supplement based, pharmacologic—below.

But remember this: Alertness and focus are necessary but not su�cient for plasticity and learning. To trigger learning, you’re also going to have to make errors from genuine attempts, what I refer to as repetitions, or reps. Not deliberate errors, and not half-baked e�orts, but rather, errors that emerge from truly exerting yourself to learn new information, new movements, even new modes of thinking. Consider this: If your nervous system can already generate the activity patterns that enable you to do a certain task—perform a dance step, for example, or order co�ee in a foreign language—why would it change? It doesn’t need to! You’re already equipped with the neural circuits to accomplish that task. You need to try, and fail, and try again. This is tough to accept, especially for perfectionists, but all who embrace it thrive. Especially those who come to recognize limbic friction, the slight agitation that accompanies e�ective learning, as a state to seek, not shy away from.

The importance of making mistakes and trying again doesn’t mean you have to toil endlessly. SDAP can be enjoyable. You’ll likely experience some limbic friction but guess what? Once you learn to expect it, and you realize that it helps not hinders your ability to learn, you too will be seeking it out.

You may be wondering “Why all these conditions for plasticity? Isn’t there a plasticity pill?” No. As I mentioned earlier in this introduction, plasticity is energetically expensive. Strengthening and reshaping neural circuits requires a lot of ATP, the energy our cells need to function.

And this process applies to everyone. It’s true that when it comes to neuroplasticity, children have it easier than adults. Their brains are more malleable because almost every experience is novel to them. In fact, many aspects of developmental plasticity emerge with no e�ort or need to deliberately focus at all. Good examples include the way that a baby’s visual and auditory systems are shaped by their early visual and sound experiences. Those things just happen. The automaticity of plasticity in our youth isn’t always a blessing however. If a child has a temporary eye injury or if a child’s eyes are misaligned due to an imbalance in the muscles that help move the eyes, it can cause longstanding maladaptive changes in brain wiring.

Yet even at an early age, many forms of plasticity still require focus. Cognitive skills like language and motor skills like walking or eating with utensils all take deliberate focus to learn. In that sense, the process for motor and cognitive skill learning is inherently the same for all ages. Your states of mind and body, alongside the agitation you experience from errors while making genuine attempts to learn, are what ensure that your brain gets the message: This thing happening right now is unique and important; we’re going to have to rewire.

###### As You Proceed

An important point for anyone wishing to establish new brain patterns is that following each step of the SDAP process in its proper sequence is more important than any one tool listed here. This will be an important reframing for a lot of people.

I mentioned that there wasn’t a pill for plasticity, but people love to think about what they can take to increase neuromodulator levels to heighten focus.

Adderall, energy drinks, nicotine, moda�nil, microdoses of psilocybin, et cetera, are used by many people working in business, tech, sports performance, �nance circles, and beyond to try to focus and learn better. The use of such stimulants is widespread on college campuses and among high school students in the US,13 and millions of adults use them daily too.

Their widespread use merely speaks to how hard most people �nd it to focus intensely enough and push through limbic friction. I’m not judging anyone. For example, I, like most adults in the US,14 use ca�eine daily to increase focus. I occasionally rely on other pharmacologic tools for focus too. In this chapter, I’ll cover the popular as well as the rarely discussed ones.

That all being said, the main focus here is behavioral tools. They may not seem as sexy, but many rival the pharmacologic tools.

It truly doesn’t matter what you use to get alert and focused, as long as it’s safe. If you opt to use nicotine or moda�nil or meditation or good ol’ sleep and hydration, those obviously have di�erent safety pro�les. You can use white noise or various sound tones.15 These all have data to support them in the context of focus and learning. You can cycle di�erent tools in and out, by the day or by the month. The point is: You have choices. Think of them as tools in your SDAP arsenal.

###### Stick with It

We know a lot more about plasticity now than we did twenty-�ve or even just �ve years ago. Prior to the 2000s the widely held belief—even among neuroscience researchers—was that the opportunity for adaptive plasticity mostly closes after age twenty-�ve.16

That idea is now dead. We know people can rewire their brains and learn throughout their lifespans ~~.~~ 17 Also mostly dead is the idea that learningassociated plasticity involves the addition of new neurons. Plasticity in humans is almost exclusively the consequence of changes to existing neural circuits, not adding new neurons to those circuits ~~.~~ 18 And yet, the results you can achieve when you incorporate the best of what we know about SDAP can be extraordinary.

Here is an overview of SDAP, once more:

- Get alert.

- Get and stay focused.

- Maintain a state of urgency.

- Embrace errors that arise from genuine attempts.

- Rest.

- Repeat your performance.

I’ve listed these again because the steps and the sequence are non-negotiable. Not because I say so, but because that’s how our neuroplasticity works. There are things you can do to accelerate the process: all the tools I mentioned above (and more), along with micro-pauses, post-learning-bout NSDR, adjusted sleep protocols, and hypnosis. I cover all these in the pages that follow.

I began this chapter with this basic process because it can be applied to learning anything.

Similar to exercise, SDAP is not easy. But with time, each step becomes familiar. If you think of SDAP this way—as a process that consistently leads to a desired end—it can become a pleasure.

###### **LEARNING PROTOCOL**

1

### Shift into a State of Alertness and Focus

###### WHAT TO DO:

- Getting alert and focused is the first step in SDAP. You have to be in a state of elevated autonomic (sympathetic) arousal, but not stressed.

Use tools to help you achieve this state. Such tools are many and varied, and fall into three general categories:

- Foundational

- Behavioral

- Pharmacological

Put your phone away. You may think you have an issue with getting focused, but it’s likely that you are distracted by something in your surroundings—the smartphone being the major culprit. Studies show that even just having your phone in the same room in a bag behind or under your chair reduces your ability to focus on cognitive tasks and/or increases the energy that it takes.19

###### HOW IT WORKS:

You might be thinking “Why would anyone need a protocol for focus?”

Fair question. Most people can easily get (and stay) focused on texting, scrolling social media, playing a video game, or watching their favorite sports team or TV show for an hour or more, with no protocol required.

But when it comes to SDAP—pushing your brain to understand or do that which it currently cannot understand or do—focusing is hard for most people,

young or old.20 One recent, albeit small, study of �fteen people engaged in a work-related task found that their focus wavered every 3.5 minutes, on average.21 The latest data say that most people switch tasks every couple of minutes, or even less ~~.~~ 22 And that number drops further when people are trying to focus on challenging material. That is why I refer to a dedicated session of trying to learn something as a learning bout. It is a �ght—with the material you’re trying to learn, and with yourself as you try to stave o� frustration and resist the temptation to quit.

Yet it’s in that state of mild agitation that plasticity is sparked. But only if we focus intensely on what it is we are trying to learn.

We can all take solace in the fact that getting and staying focused has always been hard. History shows that we humans have long sought tools to make it easier. In the early 1900s an inventor by the name of Hugo Gernsback designed the Isolator—a metal helmet that covered the entire head and face, with eyeholes and a breathing tube cut into the front ~~.~~ 23 It resembled the helmet of an oldschool scuba diving suit. The rationale was simple: Block peripheral vision and outside noise to help people focus. The Isolator did not become popular, but 117 years later it inspired the Helmfon, an oversized motorcycle helmet designed to be worn while seated at a desk, created by industrial design company Hochu rayu ~~.~~ 24 The rationale was the same, all that time later: Block out peripheral vision and outside noise to help people focus. The Helmfon, as you might imagine, also did not gain traction. Even if it had, the advent of social media and other online activities essentially moved the outside noise of the entire world directly into one’s central �eld of view. So much for helmets.

Other long-used tools include non-amphetamine stimulants such as ca�eine, which blocks adenosine receptors in the brain that would otherwise trigger sleepiness, and nicotine, which triggers the release of several neuromodulators discussed in the introduction to this chapter. The use of ca�eine in the form of tea or co�ee dates back more than two thousand years. But co�ee and tea didn’t become popular in Europe until the seventeenth century, the result of invasions and trade ~~.~~ 25 Today, approximately 90 percent of the world’s adults—that’s estimated as more than �ve billion people (!)—drink ca�eine every single day.

Later I’ll explain how to use ca�eine speci�cally to enhance focus, but meanwhile those stats reveal that ca�eine is the most popular drug on the planet by a huge margin. (If you’re wondering, alcohol and nicotine are in a distant second and third place, respectively.)

Nicotine, mostly in oral forms like pouches, gum, and mints, has made a big comeback as a focus aid in recent years. I recently gave a talk to several thousand undergraduate men and women at an East Coast university and asked the auditorium for a show of hands of “who in here takes nicotine daily?” About 30 percent of them raised their hands. (In a more private setting—a smaller group of about �fty male students—about two-thirds said they use nicotine two or more times per day every day.) This is obviously not a controlled study, nor did I count each hand, but even if these are arti�cially high estimates, it’s still pretty shocking. Or is it? Nicotine is an unusual stimulant because it makes people alert but calm—a highly desirable state for learning. Unless smoked, vaped, dipped, or snu�ed, nicotine does not cause cancer, but it is highly addictive and it raises blood pressure.26 Later, I’ll explain how, assuming you’re okay with the risks, nicotine can be used to enhance focus. There are a few safer alternatives, some of which work through the same mechanisms.

And there are the amphetamines. First synthesized in Romania in the late 1880s, amphetamines are compounds that increase levels of some of the key neuromodulators discussed in the introduction to this chapter, like norepinephrine and dopamine.27 These stimulants were initially marketed in the 1930s as a treatment for narcolepsy, but soon hit the college scene when research showed a link with increased scores on intelligence tests ~~.~~ 28 They were also investigated for the treatment of attention de�cit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and as appetite suppressants starting even back then ~~.~~ 29 A decade later, both German and Allied forces used amphetamines during World War II to stay awake and alert.30 Recreational use of amphetamines exploded in general popularity starting in the 1950s, partly due to a surplus from World War II. By the 1960s, there was an epidemic of amphetamine dependency and abuse in the United States.31 They were made illegal for non-prescription use in the early 1970s, classi�ed in the same way as cocaine and morphine, and their use

dropped. That is, until the FDA approved amphetamines for the treatment of ADHD in 1996 ~~.~~ 32 Drugs marketed for ADHD like Adderall, Vyvanse, et cetera, are amphetamines, and they work quite well to increase alertness and focus. Current exact rates are hard to come by, but it seems that up to 35 percent of college students use stimulants at some point during their undergraduate years ~~.~~ 33 For people without a genuine clinical need for amphetamines, their use can be problematic. They are e�ective for helping people complete work that relies on skills they already have, but far less e�ective for learning new skills. They are lousy for contemplative thinking, too, and creative endeavors. And they are very habit forming, and in many cases addictive.

That’s the history. And while getting and staying focused has always been hard, it seems it’s now harder than ever.

The good news is that accessing a state of focus necessary for SDAP is possible for anyone. It starts with understanding the states of mind and body you’re after. You’ll recall that negative experiences automatically set o� the learning process. No co�ee, no tutor, no motivational video or mantra required. The fast, massive increase in sympathetic tone caused by adrenaline and norepinephrine ramps up activity in relevant brain circuits. It’s proof that if the right electrochemical systems get triggered, we all have the capacity to focus. Again, I’m not saying seek out stressful situations. But this points to adrenaline and norepinephrine as potent pro-focus and pro-plasticity molecules. That is knowledge we can use.

Work in the 1990s from neuroscientists James McGaugh and Larry Cahill at UC Irvine showed that if adrenaline and norepinephrine are elevated using drugs, exposure to cold water, or emotionally activating visual images, the resulting increase in sympathetic tone opens the door for the learning process.34 Interestingly, the beta-blocker propranolol, which prevents an increase in sympathetic tone, impairs learning and memory of emotional events.35 Conversely, if sympathetic tone is arti�cially increased before, during, or even immediately after a learning bout, memory is enhanced ~~.~~ 36 And not just for emotional events or information.37

Importantly, the relationship between autonomic arousal and learning follows an inverted U-shape curve, a �nding �rst documented in 1908 and recon�rmed since ~~.~~ 38 If autonomic arousal is too low, learning doesn’t occur. If autonomic arousal is too high, learning also doesn’t occur. Only if autonomic arousal is somewhere on the top of the inverted U-shape curve does learning occur.

Keep this in mind anytime you begin SDAP. The key is to enter a learning bout alert but calm, then to move through it in such a way that your level of autonomic arousal continues to increase—but never to the point where you start to feel overly stressed.

The best way I can describe that level of autonomic arousal is if I ask you to imagine the kids’ game sometimes called “hot hands.” It’s where one person places their hands out, palms up, and you put your hands on theirs, palms down. The person with palms up �ips their hands over to try and tap the top of your hands before you can pull away. You don’t know when they will make their move. You’re alert and focused, anticipating something will happen. Learn to recognize that state. That’s the ideal level of autonomic arousal for a learning bout. With a bit of practice you’ll be able to sense when your autonomic arousal is climbing too high or dropping too low, and keep yourself in that ideal state. In other words, you learn to get better at entering the learning process.

###### Is Being Focused the Same as Being in a Flow State?

No. Don’t confuse this state with a �ow state. In �ow states we forget the rest of the world (and even ourselves), and we do things as if on autopilot.39 Flow states are ideal for task performance—executing cognitive and motor skills we have already mastered. We don’t learn in �ow states, we implement what we already learned.

The person who �rst described �ow states—the Hungarian psychologist Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi—accurately described this feeling as when the challenge of a task is matched with your existing skill level, not too easy, nor too hard… just challenging enough to engage you and “an absolute sense of control.”40 That last part—“an absolute sense of control”—means your brain already has the neural circuits in place that it needs to execute the task. And as

we discussed above, that means no rewiring… no plasticity is triggered, and no learning occurs.

To trigger plasticity and start learning, you must push past your current abilities. You have to get stumped, miss the mark, and most importantly, you have to feel the agitation of making errors. Recognize that as limbic friction, and seek it out.

Ask any elite performer how they got so good at their craft and they will tell you, “Practice, lots of practice.” But there are two kinds of practice. There are the hours upon hours spent drilling what we already know how to do and there is the practice of pushing ourselves to learn new skills. The latter is accomplished by making errors through genuine attempts. As the great Twyla Tharp, worldrenowned choreographer and dancer, put it, “The more you fail in private, the less you will fail in public.”41 Twyla understands that elite performance requires genuine attempts—failing and failing again (and again), until the gap between one’s goal and actual performance is reduced to zero.

###### The Learning State

The experiments that perhaps best illustrate the vital role of focused attention in learning come from the work of neuroscientist Mike Merzenich, PhD, and his lab at University of California, San Francisco.42 The studies were done in the 1990s using monkeys and later adapted to studies in humans. The monkeys were trained to place their �ngers on a rotating cylinder that had both coarse and �ne bumps laid out in rows across its surface.43

The monkeys quickly learned that if they detected a di�erence between the coarse bumps and the �ne bumps, they earned a reward. To signal when they noticed that di�erence, they used their other hand to move a joystick. Over time, the researchers made the task harder by making the di�erence in the bumps progressively smaller, which required more focus from the monkeys. Not only did the monkeys learn to perform the harder task, but the researchers observed signi�cant changes in the brain areas representing sensations in the �ngers that were touching the cylinder. In other words, they observed plasticity associated with that learning. These were adult monkeys, too, showing that plasticity was not just con�ned to developmental critical periods as had long been believed.

That was interesting but it was just the beginning of the story. In other studies from Merzenich, monkeys had to learn to discriminate between di�erent sound tones. In that case the regions of the brain responsible for hearing changed. Perhaps not surprising, except that the monkeys were experiencing bumps on their �ngers at the same time they heard the tones. So why did only the auditory areas of the brain change? Because the monkeys received rewards only for learning sound tones, so that’s what they focused on. Together, these two sets of experiments showed that mere experience doesn’t cause neuroplasticity. Learning-associated brain plasticity only occurs in the circuits associated with where our attention is placed.

Since those landmark studies, there have been thousands of experiments exploring the conditions required for learning and plasticity. Consider the oftencited studies from neuroscientist Eleanor Maguire, PhD, and colleagues of London taxi drivers, who must learn to navigate the complex streets of their city by memory (this was prior to the advent of GPS and Google Maps, mind you).44 They found that, compared to bus drivers, taxi drivers had larger hippocampi, a key brain area for encoding new memories. Then there is the study showing more concentrated patterns of brain activation among professional violinists for �nger movements compared to amateurs.45 And there are studies showing signi�cant brain circuit changes as people learn to juggle ~~,~~ 46 as well as reversion of those newly formed circuits if people don’t practice in the �rst weeks afterward.47

All these studies—the taxi drivers, the violinists, the jugglers—suggest that intense focus is a foundational need in order for SDAP to occur. But suggestions aren’t proof. There is, however, one study that really hammers home the relationship between focus and plasticity in humans. In 1993, two researchers from Hebrew University in Israel asked people to practice detecting a slight shift in the angle of a line relative to the angles of a bunch of surrounding lines. The people got better at that task ~~.~~ 48 Not surprising. Also not surprising was that when participants were asked to detect a slight shift in the angles of _all_ the lines, they got better at that task too. What is surprising is that performance on one task did not improve performance on the other task, despite the fact that what

they saw in both tasks was exactly the same. The only di�erence between the two conditions was what the participants were instructed to pay attention to. The �nding leads to a profound insight: that the plasticity they experienced was tied to the act of _looking_ for something and not solely to the success of _finding_ that something. As the authors concluded, “Learning will occur only in those neurons that are activated by the stimulus and that are at the same time relevant for the task. Which neurons are relevant [for neuroplasticity] is dictated by the mechanism or strategy used for task performance (and not merely a stimulusresponse correlation).”

These results, along with the earlier studies mentioned here, point to the crucial role of focus in plasticity and learning.

Which brings us to the common saying “�re together, wire together.”49 People often use this phrase to capture the idea that habits form from neurons being activated at nearly the exact same time. The thinking goes that neurons �ring simultaneously or one after the other causes them to become wired together, which will lead them to readily �re together in the future. But the term “�re together, wire together” is actually unrelated to the kind of learning we are talking about in this chapter—achieving new skills, developing new behavioral patterns, et cetera. This is not a trivial point. This phrase is often attached to the false notion that people can learn when in passive or semi-engaged states. It implies that we can simply expose kids to music to enrich their brain. Not so. It also implies that simply reading or doing something repeatedly is enough to create new brain patterns. Alas, not so. Oh and the “�re together, wire together” phrase is constantly misattributed to psychologist Donald Hebb when in fact it was Carla Shatz, the developmental neurobiologist, who said it �rst—in the context of developmental brain wiring, not learning.50 The point is this: Whether young or old, if we want to learn, we need to focus intensely on new information, or in the case of cognitive or motor skills, on our attempt to perform them. The good news is that with the right tools and a little practice, anyone can access focus… and learn.

###### Tools for Focus

As I mentioned in the introduction to this protocol, we humans have long sought tools to make this endeavor easier. Here’s where science puts us today. There are three categories of tools to get alert and focused.

- 1 Foundational

- 2 Behavioral

- 3 Pharmacological

The tools o�ered here can be used for learning bouts, as described above, or even for what I call work sessions—time when you’re not necessarily tackling new information or skills, but grappling with some work or physical challenge that simply requires intense focus.

###### FOUNDATIONAL TOOLS FOR FOCUS

These tools are the bedrock upon which all the other suggestions in this protocol depend. Without them, the rest of the tools in this protocol will be far less e�ective. Get the foundational tools right, and you’ll greatly amplify the potency of all others you opt to use.

###### Foundational Tool 1: Sleep

In chapter 1 when I said that sleep is the foundation of mental health, physical health, and performance, that included learning of all kinds. When we do not get enough quality sleep, or if our sleep timing is altered by more than an hour or two from our normal schedule, our levels of alertness get harder to regulate and so focusing becomes an even bigger challenge. Thus, aim to get adequate sleep using the protocols in chapter 1. (See Sleep Protocols 1–6 for a reminder on the basics.)

###### Foundational Tool 2: NSDR

If you’ve had less than adequate sleep and you’re trying to lock in on a learning bout, consider doing ten, twenty, or, if possible, thirty minutes of non-sleep deep rest (NSDR) at some point prior to starting that learning bout. NSDR, while not a replacement for sleep, is your best bet to restore mental and physical

vigor if you didn’t get enough sleep. As mentioned in Sleep Protocol 8, NSDR is preferable to naps, because it doesn’t create sleep inertia so you won’t �nish a session feeling groggy, nor does it disrupt your normal sleep schedule. A short nap of thirty minutes or less can also restore mental and physical vigor, but midday napping for more than thirty minutes can really mess up your nighttime sleep. Refer to Sleep Protocol 7 for best practices.

###### Foundational Tool 3: Stress Control

The other key to an e�ective learning bout is to make sure you don’t show up in a state of excessively high sympathetic tone, or what we commonly call stress. Stressing about something other than what you’re trying to learn steals your focus. If you’re worrying about your to-do list, it’s hard to focus on learning a new song on the guitar. And stressing about what you’re trying to learn prevents you from staying in the alert but calm state you’re after. Chapter 3 provides tools you can use “o�ine”—meaning when you aren’t actively engaged in a learning bout—as well as tools you can use during a learning bout, such as the physiological sigh. Both types of tools are e�ective to help maintain your level of arousal near the peak of the inverted U-shape curve that is ideal for learning.

###### Foundational Tool 4: Nutrition

If you’re even mildly dehydrated, your focus won’t be at its best.51 Drink water and, if you need to, add some electrolytes, which aids the rehydration process. The same goes for your blood sugar levels—make sure yours are relatively stable by not reaching for sugary foods when you know you want to be focused.

Chapter 4 described how to eat to fuel your body for all types of activity, and that includes learning bouts and work sessions. Those protocols o�ered guidelines, but there are options for how you adapt them for your schedule when it comes to learning. For example, in the �rst two to three hours of my day, I focus best if I’m fasted. I make sure I’m hydrated, and that I’m ca�einated, too, but unless I wake up especially hungry (a rarity for me), I don’t eat yet. If I already exercised that morning, however, I eat, and then I start work.

You don’t want to be distracted by hunger or thirst during a learning bout, nor do you want to be lethargic from an overly large or starch-and-fat-laden

meal. Figure out what is best for you. And don’t burn valuable mental energy trying to get conditions perfect. That e�ort can easily use up the self-control available to us, which tends to be �nite. If we’re mentally exhausted from trying to be perfect, we’ll have nothing left for the actual task, a state that psychologists sometimes refer to as ego depletion ~~.~~ 52 Studies show that if people do a lot of decision-making prior to a mental task, they perform less well on the task compared to those who don’t.53 That means no obsessing over your pre-learning nutrition. You’ll short-circuit your ability to learn. (See chapter 4 to make sure you’re hydrating and eating right.)

###### BEHAVIORAL TOOLS FOR FOCUS

The ability to deliberately set and maintain focus is a superpower. It is a skill that carries over to all sorts of professional, educational, physical health, and relational activities, not just to plasticity and learning. That said, one of the best ways to get better at focusing is to engage in learning bouts.

The act of continually adjusting your state of autonomic arousal so it’s not too high and not too low, while engaging with new information or new skills is work. It involves a lot of top-down control as neuroscientists say, which as discussed in chapter 3, is a loose reference to how your prefrontal cortex repeatedly directs and redirects your mental attention. And while no magic pill or ninja move will instantly give you that superpower, there are behavioral tools that can signi�cantly improve your ability to focus. Some assist the transition into a state of focus, and others help you stay there.

###### Behavioral Tool 1: Meditation

Meditation can take many forms. One shown to improve focus is as follows: Set aside about ten to twenty minutes, sit or lie down, close your eyes, and direct your mental attention to the location between your eyes, or concentrate on your breathing, or both. As you strive to maintain those points of focus, thoughts, sensations, and outside noises inevitably distract you. Keep redirecting your attention back to the location between your eyes and/or breathing, over and over again, as many times as needed until the allotted time elapses.

From novice to expert, no one is expected to maintain perfect focus for the whole session. It’s the redirecting of your attention that is the key component. It’s analogous to the �nal few repetitions of a weight lifting set. It’s what drives the nervous system changes that make it easier to focus the next time you meditate, or in any other activity. It’s training; it’s what is meant by the phrase “meditation is a practice.”

A study by researchers at New York University found that meditating in this way for just thirteen minutes per day improved participants’ ability to deliberately focus and to regulate their emotions, two strong indications that this behavioral tool can enhance and speed up learning that requires concentration ~~.~~ 54 Shorter meditations of �ve minutes per day have also been shown to help.55 You may be thinking this seems like the micro meditation described in Stress Control Protocol 4, or any other meditation… and you would be right. All meditation is perceptual exercise where you intentionally limit what you pay attention to. Remember the Isolator? That was a perceptual �lter designed to restrict your visual �eld—that is, intentionally limit what you pay attention to. Knowing that, it should make sense that what you elect to focus on during a meditation is less important than the act of directing, and redirecting, your attention back to the same place. You can close your eyes and focus on the top of your head, your feet, your lower belly, and your breathing, or you can open your eyes and focus on a point on a wall in front of you (allow yourself to blink as needed, of course).

Studies show improvements in focus stem from all such meditations, because meditation is a perceptual exercise for improving focus.56 It just so happens that it also helps reduce stress ~~,~~ 57 boost mood ~~,~~ 58 and improve sleep ~~.~~ 59 A recent study even showed that meditation can induce a similar glymphatic washout process— that is, the removal of metabolic waste from the brain—as observed during sleep —albeit to a lesser degree ~~.~~ 60 With a year or more of experience, meditation can allow for profound insights into how our thoughts arise (and pass) and for some people it can be transformative for understanding consciousness, but those are not the immediate bene�ts. Nor should anyone wanting to improve focus shy away from meditation thinking they have to experience those sorts of major

insights for it to “work.” Meditation done simply as a perceptual exercise is powerful. And the e�ects show up fast: less procrastination, less impulsivity, and better learning.

If you are very limited on time, here’s a simple ten-breath meditation to try immediately upon waking, while still lying in bed: Keep your eyes closed and focus on your breathing for ten slow breaths. If your mind wanders before you reach ten, restart at one, and do that as many times as needed until you reach ten focused breaths. Then get up.

After a few days, you’ll notice improvement. Of course, �ve minutes, as described in Stress Control Protocol 4, and eventually ten, �fteen, or twenty minutes of meditation would be even more bene�cial. I’ve heard from many people who do this regularly—meaning three to seven times per week—that they can focus better, and redirect their focus if it wanders. You’ll experience the other positive e�ects of meditation explained above, such as stress reduction and improved sleep too. My lab found that just �ve minutes a day of meditation provided these bene�ts.61

What time of day or night you meditate is far less important than if you do it regularly. In fact, there is no bad time to meditate as long as you’re in a safe location. If your back or knees ache from sitting cross-legged on the �oor, remember that you don’t have to do that. Make yourself comfortable. Sit in a chair or lie down in bed.

In my experience, it is the rare person who adheres to a daily meditation practice consistently over many years. Most become the “I used to meditate every day, I need to get back to it” people, not unlike the “I used to work out every day, I need to get back to it” people. I believe that happens because we shoot for ten to twenty minutes of meditation every day right out the gate. We make progress but then stop when life gets too busy, and the bene�ts of meditation disappear slowly so we don’t notice until the habit is broken that we are struggling to focus.

That is why I suggest you set a _very_ low bar, just ten breaths. Do that every morning for two weeks, then shift to doing �ve minutes of meditation as described in Stress Control Protocol 4. Do that three to seven days per week for a month, then increase the duration to ten minutes, still aiming for three to seven

days per week for the next month. Then increase it to �fteen minutes three to seven days per week for the following month, then twenty minutes three to seven days per week… inde�nitely. Mark the days you do it on your calendar to keep track of your progress.

Or just stick with �ve minutes if that feels right. Be the person who sticks to things rather than the person talking about all the healthy stu� they used to do.

For the time investment needed, what meditation provides in terms of ability to focus, along with stress reduction, better mood, and improved sleep is extraordinary.

###### Behavioral Tool 2: Hypnosis

Hypnosis. I know the word alone might cause some readers to hesitate before continuing. But keep reading. Maybe the word hypnosis makes you picture people squawking like a chicken, unaware their friends are laughing until they emerge from a trance. But that is stage hypnosis. Clinical hypnosis is completely di�erent. I wish it was called _directed neuroplasticity_ instead of hypnosis.

Clinical hypnosis is supported by solid research as a tool to treat chronic pain, and to help with smoking cessation, sleep challenges, anxiety, even gut health issues. 62 Through decades of research, including brain imaging and randomized controlled trials, Stanford University psychiatrist David Spiegel and his lab discovered that clinical hypnosis stimulates speci�c types of plasticity that allow for better autonomic self-regulation ~~.~~ 63 For example, hypnosis appears to reduce activity in the part of the brain called the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex, indicating diminished self-monitoring. An accompanying increase in connection between the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and the insula indicates that the brain is doing a better job of regulating the body. These and other �ndings point to a state in which people are simultaneously less self-conscious and yet better at selfregulating.

Hypnosis won’t allow you to immediately speak a new language or perform the perfect golf swing, but it is very e�ective for teaching people how to access otherwise inaccessible brain and bodily states, such that they can more easily reaccess those states once hypnosis is over. For example, someone with an intense fear of public speaking can experience being alert but calm while onstage in

front of a big audience. With just a few sessions and the occasional brush-up session, people can get very good at this kind of autonomic self-regulation. Hypnosis, in other words, is about learning how to set your state of mind.

If you have trouble with focus, or any of the other issues mentioned above, you may consider hiring a licensed clinical hypnotist to work with in person or online. Alternatively, some years back, Dr. Spiegel developed an app called Reveri that provides this tool to all (I’m an advisor for Reveri). It has you listen to a brief recorded hypnosis script (in Dr. Spiegel’s voice) on your phone, a few times per week. Reveri has hypnosis scripts for improving focus, and also for improving sleep, reducing chronic pain, and much more. Each takes about eight minutes to complete. If you try Reveri, remember this: It’s not magic. It’s also not mind control and it’s most de�nitely not stage hypnosis. It is a tool for teaching your brain how to access di�erent states, including focus.

###### Behavioral Tool 3: 40 Hertz Binaural Beats, 20 Hertz Oscillatory Induction, and White, Brown, and Pink Noise

The use of sound as a tool for focus is all about entrainment, or the matching of our internal rhythms to an external sensory event—in these cases, the frequency of sound waves. You may remember the term entrainment from chapter 1 and chapter 5. There, I talked about entraining your circadian rhythm to light, for example, by viewing bright light in the �rst hour after waking up. There are also ways to entrain to events in the outside world. For example, when you exercise at roughly the same time of day, you experience an increase in catecholamines and certain hormones at that time. Then after about three days or so, you automatically start to feel an increase in energy just prior to when you usually exercise. Entrainment works based on your nervous system’s expectation of certain things happening.

Sound waves can entrain our brain, too, and they do so very quickly. When we hear certain frequencies or rhythms, our brain starts to entrain to the predictable features in the sound by our neurons �ring in regular fashion. Scientists have �gured out how to leverage that and have created speci�c sound patterns that increase brain activity in areas that underlie focused states.

One example is binaural beats. Two distinct frequencies of sounds are played in each ear. When that happens, a cluster of neurons in your brainstem called the medial superior olivary nucleus performs a subtraction of the two frequencies. So if a 400 hertz (Hz) sound arrives at one ear and 440 Hz at the other ear, it leads you to perceive a 40 Hz beat. That sound frequency, in particular, has been shown to improve levels of focus, and even certain forms of memory ~~.~~ 64 The precise mechanisms for this are still being parsed but there is evidence that 40 Hz sound can do this in part by causing release of acetylcholine from the medial superior olivary nucleus and the release of dopamine in the striatum, a brain area involved in movement and motivated attention ~~.~~ 65

Some evidence even shows that 40 Hz sounds can trigger the brain circuits involved in focus and memory to enter what are called gamma oscillation states, a pattern of neural activity that is favorable for learning.66 (Interestingly, there is parallel evidence that activating these circuits using clinical devices may also help o�set some of the early symptoms of age-related cognitive decline in Alzheimer’s disease.67)

Not everyone appears to bene�t from this tool however. It seems if people already have elevated levels of these neuromodulators prior to the sound exposure, the bene�ts of binaural beats are less apparent or even absent ~~.~~ 68 Alas, without doing an fMRI and blood draws, there is no way to know your baseline dopamine and acetylcholine levels. Considering 40 Hz binaural beats are safe and cost nothing (there are dozens of free apps, videos, and audio recordings of these on Apple music, Spotify, and YouTube), why not try them and see? You have nothing to lose and perhaps something signi�cant to gain in your e�orts to focus better.

Here’s how: Try listening to 40 Hz binaural beats for �ve minutes prior to a learning bout or work session. Once you determine if that works for you, try listening to the beats continuously throughout. (Of course, if you are trying to learn something that requires you to listen to instructions, you’ll only be able to use the 40 Hz tones prior to the learning bout.) Also, note that it’s recommended you use headphones for binaural beats as it’s the best way to

entrain your olivary nucleus and other brain circuits to 40 Hz gamma frequencies.69

There are exciting new data suggesting that sounds of about 12 to 20 Hz— which cause the brain to entrain to beta, not gamma, waves—may also improve concentration and reduce mental fatigue ~~.~~ 70 Music with 20 Hz as the dominant frequency may be especially e�ective here.

I personally have tried 40 Hz binaural beats, using one of the many free binaural beat apps out there (I like BrainWave). I’ve also used white and pink noise, both of which have been shown to improve focus, albeit in a small number of studies ~~.~~ 71 I’ve heard anecdotal evidence that brown noise can also be helpful. (In case you’re wondering, white noise is noise with all sound frequencies present at equal energy, pink noise sounds less “hissy” than white noise, and brown noise is lower pitched than either white or pink noise.) Brown and pink noise work a bit to increase my focus but I was not terribly impressed by the magnitude of the e�ect. I have also tried Brain.fm and, for me, it works well (I have no a�liation with Brain.fm, I just like their product). I listen to it while reading, and during learning bouts and even writing sessions lasting anywhere from one to three hours. (I do take a break every �fty to ninety minutes, and avoid looking at my phone in those breaks… more on phone use to come.)

###### Behavioral Tool 4: Music
