The data on listening to music to enhance focus is very clear: Silence is best. (That is unless the music is 12–20 Hz binaural beats, per the above.)

If you like to listen to music when reading or learning, music with no lyrics is better ~~.~~ 72 All that said, some people like to work in cafés, in airports, or in busy o�ces. The backdrop of auditory noise helps them focus. I suspect there is a lot of individual variation when it comes to this. You’ll have to experiment and see what works for you, and when.

As I write this I am in a completely silent room and it’s early evening—the only audible noise is the air conditioner and the keys of my computer, but this morning I listened to Brain.fm for two full hours while I worked on an earlier

part of this chapter. I felt extremely focused during both sessions, so go �gure. Be a scientist of yourself, and customize your own protocols for focus. One thing is certain: Sound can be a powerful tool for entraining brain states required for learning.

A note before we continue: Throughout this chapter I’ve been highlighting the important role that adrenaline and norepinephrine play in focus, and the formation of memories and learning. Soon we will cover ways to boost these and some other closely related neuromodulators, like dopamine, using pharmacology. But �rst, there are established behavioral tools to signi�cantly and safely increase adrenaline and norepinephrine without taking anything. These won’t surprise you because I covered them earlier, in di�erent contexts.

###### Behavioral Tool 5: Physical Exercise

Physical exercise causes meaningful increases in adrenaline through now- _well_ - understood neural circuits, stemming from your motor cortex in your brain all the way down to your adrenal glands near your lower back ~~.~~ 73 Any vigorous physical activity that involves the large musculature of your legs and core (abdominals, lower back, etc.), will trigger the release of adrenaline, in a manner that scales with the intensity of the activity. Think: compound lower body exercises like squats or deadlifts, running, martial arts, tennis, and on and on. Adrenaline does not cross the blood-brain barrier, but it binds to receptors on your vagus nerve—the two-way neural superhighway that bridges your body and brain.74 That, in turn, stimulates the release of norepinephrine from your locus coeruleus (remember that, from chapter 1?) and other brain areas involved in generating a state of focus.75 That’s one mechanism, but there are others at play, including increased blood �ow and brain oxygenation, and lactate-induced elevations in brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) (which you’ll recall from chapter 2… see how all of this comes together?). The e�ects of all this on your focus and cognition are signi�cant, and can last several hours afterward.

One of the best ways to use exercise as a tool for focus is brief high-intensity interval training (HIIT)—for example, after a �ve- to ten-minute warm-up, I like to do a thirty-second near-all-out sprint, followed by thirty seconds of rest, and again, for a total of eight sprint-rest cycles.

Other HIIT options work too. You can �nd dozens of ideas for these online with a simple web search. It’s crucial to warm up for a few minutes before the �rst round and important too that you select a form of exercise that you can perform without getting injured. I like to run outside on a track or use a stationary assault bike, but you may prefer to swim, use a rower, a stair climber, et cetera.

There are also studies showing improved focus and cognition after sustained twenty to forty-�ve minute cardio training sessions at lower intensity (60–75 percent of maximum heart rate), although the e�ects of this on focus appear more transient compared to more intense exercise ~~.~~ 76 That makes sense, given HIIT elevates adrenaline and norepinephrine more than lower intensity steady state cardio.77

Fewer studies have explored how focus might be increased after resistance training. But assuming the sessions are not overly long or intense, I would expect them to impart a similar focus-enhancing e�ect as cardio training sessions (see chapter 2 for more on the ideal duration and intensity for those sessions).

Experiment to �nd the form of exercise you like best to enhance focus. Make sure to time the duration and adjust the intensity of e�ort so it doesn’t exhaust you.

###### Behavioral Tool 6: Proper Breathing

Sleep apnea is a condition where people under-breathe during sleep. Nasal obstructions, excessive weight, and certain medications cause it. If you snore, there’s a good chance you have sleep apnea.

The result? Your brain is deprived of oxygen at night.

Sleep apnea is a dangerous condition, because the health impacts creep up over time—causing fatigue, cognitive impairments, heart issues, and more.78 Some of these can be reversed with tools to correct breathing while you sleep, but long-lasting impairments can occur.

Why am I discussing sleep apnea in a protocol on focus? Because many people have daytime apnea that impairs their focus too ~~.~~ 79 Daytime apnea is when you hold your breath while working. Chronic mouth breathers experience

the same. When your brain doesn’t get enough oxygen, you get tired and you can’t focus. To feel alert and focus intensely, you need to �x sleep and any daytime apnea.

Luckily, it’s easy to do. First, make sure you’re breathing through your nose anytime you don’t have to speak, eat, or exercise hard. Second, learn to breathe with your diaphragm, also known as _belly breathing_ , in which your belly expands as you inhale. This approach increases the amount of oxygen in the blood and promotes a more relaxed state. You’ll be amazed what a di�erence that will make for your energy levels and focus.

Check right now. If you’re mouth breathing, switch to nasal breathing. Does your belly move out as you inhale and move in as you exhale through your nose? If so, great, you’re nasal diaphragmatic breathing. If you’re having trouble, imagine inhaling through your nose as if trying to direct the air backward—in other words, think about drawing the air “in and back” through your nose at an angle parallel to the roof of your mouth, as opposed to inhaling “up” your nostrils toward the top of your head. I know that sounds weird, but try it. You’ll notice that you immediately shift. And no, you don’t have to think about your breathing all day. After two to three breaths done consciously that way, it will carry on re�exively. Nasal diaphragmatic breathing in the daytime also helps you default to the right breathing pattern when you sleep, which can help o�set sleep apnea, so it’s a twofer.

A few other issues with breathing to address here. If you have a badly deviated septum or challenged nasal breathing brought about by cartilage growth in your nasal passages, you need to �x that. The simplest way to open your nasal passages is to, again, practice nasal diaphragmatic breathing. Your sinuses are not �xed, but over time this e�ort will help open them up. Extreme cases of nasal passage collapse or other blockage may require surgery. People can often achieve some results from wearing a magnetic nose bridge for a few hours a day and/or at night. They gently pull your nasal passages open and lead to instant improvement in airway �ow. Yes, they look silly. No, you don’t have to wear them in public. And it won’t make your nostrils or nose bigger. Intake Breathing makes a product that is easy to use. It certainly helped me breathe better at night and when I wore it for a few hours each day, the improvement in

breathing, alertness, and focus was immediate, and signi�cant. (Note: I have no a�liation with Intake Breathing.)

Keep in mind that it’s 100 percent normal to be able to breathe more easily through one nostril than the other at any one time, and which nostril switches every ninety minutes or so due to a neural circuit mechanism governed by your autonomic nervous system ~~.~~ 80 That’s right: The whole right versus left nostril breathing thing practitioners often talk about in yoga classes is supported by modern science, although the reasons for it remain unclear.

Nasal breathing has been shown to improve learning and memory. The reason is simple. It allows for better blood �ow and oxygenation of the brain, and thus elevated activity of neural circuits involved in learning and memory.81

So �nd out if you snore. Again, it’s an indicator that you may have sleep apnea. There are lots of free apps that record you while you sleep and track your snoring patterns. If you snore, address it. Try di�erent devices and exercises. You may need to get �tted with a CPAP machine. Talk to your doctor to explore your options. Eliminating sleep apnea is a big deal for your health, and it will powerfully impact your ability to feel alert and focused.

###### Behavioral Tool 7: Cyclic Hyperventilation

Cyclic hyperventilation might sound familiar, but there’s new context for this powerful tool.

It’s quite simple. You hyperventilate. Intentionally. Not a bunch of quick shallow breaths—that’s panting! Instead do ten to twenty cycles of a big deep inhale through your nose, using diaphragmatic breathing as described in the section above, and exhale, letting the air passively “fall out” from your mouth. You don’t have to heave into the inhale to get the e�ect you’re seeking. Work up to it gradually, and focus on long, diaphragmatic inhales through the nose. Increase the vigor after a few repetitions. After ten to twenty breaths this way, you will reliably feel much more alert.

As covered in chapter 3, you can spike your levels of adrenaline and norepinephrine and dopamine—the so-called catecholamines—and thereby increase your alertness and focus, by breathing in this speci�c way. It works by causing increased discard of carbon dioxide, which is called hypocapnia, and

increased alkalinity of your blood pH, which is called alkalosis. That in turn triggers fast and signi�cant increases in adrenaline and norepinephrine release in your body and brain.

If you think breathing to shift catecholamine levels is not very potent, think again. This tool works fast and extremely well to increase alertness, so you can focus on whatever task lies before you. It’s a causal relationship. In experiments where people hyperventilated through an air mask with arti�cially elevated CO2, their epinephrine and norepinephrine levels did not increase, nor did they achieve alkalosis.82 This tells us it’s not just the mechanics of deep breathing, it’s about increased discard of CO2. By the way, that is why people having a panic attack are told to breathe into a paper bag; it’s to encourage them to re-breathe the CO2 they expelled, and bring their epinephrine and norepinephrine back to baseline.

When you do cyclic hyperventilation, you won’t have a panic attack as long as you pay attention to your autonomic state as you do. If you feel alert after ten breaths, stop. If not, do ten more breaths. If you want, complete twenty breaths, then take a long exhale and hold your breath for ten to sixty seconds until you feel the gasp re�ex, and then start another round of cyclic hyperventilation. When you’re as alert as you want to be, resume normal nasal diaphragmatic breathing.

Sure, cyclic hyperventilation looks a little wacky but so what? It costs nothing, and it works. It may also have bene�ts for your immune system.83 Just don’t ever do it in or near water, or while driving, because when your CO2 is low, the impulse to breathe is delayed. People have drowned practicing this breathing pattern as a way to extend how long they can hold their breath underwater.

###### Behavioral Tool 8: Deliberate Cold Exposure

Deliberate cold exposure works very well to increase alertness and focus for hours afterward. That’s not surprising: As you now know, it can more than double or triple your circulating levels of epinephrine and norepinephrine and dopamine—our now-familiar friends, the catecholamines—and it does it within seconds. The data on deliberate cold exposure and learning and memory are

mixed because most studies have explored if people can learn during deliberate cold exposure, while they are in the cold ~~.~~ 84 You can already guess what happens there: Deliberate cold exposure generally puts people at the far end of the inverted U-shape curve of autonomic arousal, where focusing ability sharply drops o�. That is not the idea here.

This is: Try thirty seconds to three minutes of deliberate cold exposure, then shower and start your learning bout or work session. It’s about using deliberate cold exposure to create a long-lasting window of moderate catecholamine increase. Depending on the duration of the cold exposure, the increase in alertness and focus can last for many hours afterward.

The challenge is there is no one-size-�ts-all protocol for this one because people’s cold tolerance varies.

My suggestion is that if you decide to use deliberate cold exposure as a tool to increase focus, select your method, then choose an uncomfortably cold (for you) but safe temperature. Refer to Stress Control Protocol 2 for more information. If you’re using a shower, get all the way under the water. If you’re submerging yourself in a plunge or pool, submerge your feet, legs, and torso completely, up to your neck. And yes, put your hands in the water, too, unless you need to grip the sides for safety. The water should be cold, but shouldn’t cause pain. Remember that the �rst ten to thirty seconds are going to feel like mild panic. Your breath will quicken, but then try long, slow, and controlled inhales and exhales. You can opt to distract yourself, or not. It makes no di�erence. Deliberate cold exposure bypasses most all attempts to reframe the experience as enjoyable. Pretty much the only thing that helps is to remember that it never feels good to be in the cold, but you’ll feel great when you get out.

When you do get out, towel o� and take a warm or hot shower (or if you’re a real masochist, cold), get dressed, and go about your day. Again, to derive the focus-increasing bene�ts of deliberate cold exposure you don’t have to do it immediately before a learning bout or work session because the e�ects last hours. Enjoy! (Getting out of the cold, that is.)

###### PHARMACOLOGICAL TOOLS FOR INCREASING FOCUS

“What can I take to focus?” is one of the most common questions I get. So here goes.

###### Pharmacological Tool 1: Caffeine

With 90 percent of the world’s adult population drinking ca�eine every day, it’s hard to run a study on how ca�eine a�ects alertness and focus… because most participants would be ca�eine adapted, meaning they drink ca�eine just to achieve normal, or what I call baseline, levels of alertness. This is an important concept to understand.

So many people rely on ca�eine for basic alertness that pretty much any experiment comparing one group that takes ca�eine to another that doesn’t ends up telling us more about the e�ects of ca�eine withdrawal in the control group than anything else. Alas, most people just won’t quit ca�eine for two to three weeks—which is the duration needed to get through the withdrawal—to participate in research. So we are left with very limited studies, all of which point to ca�eine as a good way to enhance alertness, but not focus per se.

Let me explain. As we discussed in chapter 1, ca�eine staves o� fatigue by thwarting the action of adenosine, a molecule that builds up in our brain while we are awake and that causes us to feel sleepy as a result. If you drink ca�eine regularly, you’re getting some modest focus-enhancing e�ects, as alertness is a prerequisite for focus.

Ca�eine also increases adrenaline and norepinephrine in a dose-dependent manner ~~.~~ 85 A single cup of strong co�ee—about 250 milligrams of ca�eine—can increase circulating adrenaline by more than 200 percent over baseline levels, and norepinephrine 75 percent over baseline levels.86 Ingesting ca�eine daily also may increase the density of brain dopamine receptors, allowing the same amount of dopamine to impart a greater e�ect ~~.~~ 87 The largest alertness and focusenhancing e�ects of ca�eine are likely to be felt if you don’t regularly drink ca�eine, or if you were to ingest more ca�eine than is typical for you.

A note of caution: Remember the inverted U-shape curve that relates arousal and focus? If you are not a regular ca�eine user and you suddenly consume 100

to 250 milligrams more ca�eine than is typical for you, it will excessively elevate your sympathetic tone, and you may �nd it challenging to focus.

I drink ca�eine every day, usually in the form of cold brewed or hot yerba maté. I have done that for more than three decades, and by now my ca�eine tolerance is very high. Like most people, I swear that it helps me focus though it probably just does that by bringing my levels of alertness up to baseline. If I were to stop drinking ca�eine, and push through the withdrawal, I could �nd my non-ca�einated baseline level of alertness… but I’m uninterested in doing that experiment. I love yerba maté and I love co�ee. I sip ca�eine from about an hour after I wake up until about 2:00 p.m. daily, and most days I do at least one, and often two or three, long learning bouts or work sessions in that time frame. You’ll need to experiment to see what is best for you. I know people who avoid ca�eine entirely, those that only use it as a tool for alertness and focus, and I know many like me who use it every day. (Return to Sleep Protocol 11 for more about how ca�eine a�ects your sleep as you experiment with this tool.)

###### Pharmacological Tool 2: Theanine

I suggest at some point you try taking 100 milligrams of theanine alongside your ca�eine. The ca�eine-theanine combination can heighten focus, even for those who consume ca�eine regularly.88 What’s more, the combination of theanine and ca�eine has been shown to improve task-switching capacity and reduce susceptibility to distractions ~~,~~ 89 in part because it’s thought to increase alpha wave brain activity, which allows for selective attention.90 It also increases levels of the inhibitory transmitter GABA, serotonin, and dopamine, which can help make the alert state created by ca�eine feel a little more relaxed. For non-regular ca�eine users, it reduces any jitteriness ca�eine might cause, as it prevents some of ca�eine’s vasoconstrictive and blood pressure elevating e�ects ~~.~~ 91 In fact, even though at doses of 100 to 400 milligrams (depending on someone’s body weight and tolerance) ca�eine is considered safe for adults without anxiety, taking 100 to 200 milligrams theanine with it may further improve ca�eine’s safety pro�le for non-regular and regular users alike.

Theanine may even allow you to get more of a focus-enhancing e�ect from less ca�eine. In one study, people who ingested as little as 40 milligrams of ca�eine combined with 100 milligrams theanine experienced improved focus.92 Keep in mind that most commercially sold 12 ounce co�ees deliver about 200 to 300 milligrams of ca�eine depending on the roast, and 16 ounce co�ees can contain as much as 400 to 500 milligrams.

Together, the ca�eine-theanine combination tends to induce the “alert but calm” state of mind favorable for learning bouts. With its focus-enhancing e�ect, and various health bene�ts—such as reduced blood pressure and anxiety—I consider theanine a good tool for ca�eine users, which means for nearly everyone.

###### Pharmacological Tool 2: Alpha-GPC

I consider alpha-GPC a valuable tool for increasing focus and energy levels, if it’s used correctly and very occasionally.

Even small increases in acetylcholine—a neuromodulator—can improve focus ~~.~~ 93 Alpha-GPC does that by increasing the amount of choline that reaches the brain, which in turn indirectly raises acetylcholine levels.94 Research has found an enhancement of concentration and cognitive �exibility in subjects who take alpha-GPC about thirty minutes prior to a learning bout,95 and at least one study showed modest improvement in cognition in people with dementia.96 Other studies, however, show a minimal e�ect ~~.~~ 97 The variation in outcomes may re�ect people’s baseline levels of acetylcholine before they take alpha-GPC, similar to what we discussed earlier with people’s baseline levels of dopamine before they listen to 40 Hz binaural beats. If a person’s natural levels of a given neuromodulator are already high, adding more may not help. If natural levels of acetylcholine are low to moderate, however, boosting it seems to have a positive e�ect ~~.~~ 98

Alpha-GPC is often added to energy drinks, and most nootropic formulas (that is, substances marketed for improving cognition). If you’re looking to experiment with ways to increase focus for late afternoon or nighttime work or workouts, and you don’t want to disrupt your sleep, you can try 300 to 600

milligrams of alpha-GPC taken thirty minutes or so before you begin. Limit your intake to two to four times per week, because your system will quickly adjust to it.

If you take alpha-GPC, make sure to take 600 milligrams of garlic extract (in capsule form, to avoid the taste and smell of raw garlic) at some point in the same twenty-four hours, to help o�set the increase in TMAO that alpha-GPC can cause. 99 TMAO is a metabolite formed by gut bacteria in response to high levels of choline and it can pose a cardiovascular risk if elevated too frequently. Garlic contains an antimicrobial chemical called allicin, which may help o�set the buildup of TMAO, and garlic extract is very inexpensive ~~.~~ 100

Some of you may be wondering if you can combine ca�eine and alpha-GPC, or even combine ca�eine, theanine, _and_ alpha-GPC. Yes, that combination works very well to increase focus and energy levels… but it might be too stimulating for some people, raise blood pressure too high, and increase anxiety, too, so don’t go from none to all three. I can take 200 to 300 milligrams ca�eine, 600 milligrams alpha-GPC, and 100 milligrams theanine together before a particularly demanding exercise session or learning bout. I probably take that combination once or twice a month. And I still practice the foundational tools described in this chapter: getting great sleep, practicing NSDR, exercising, et cetera. Stimulants and things that increase neuromodulators tend to work best on that solid foundation. I can’t emphasize that enough: Great sleep is still the most important tool for focus. Pharmacologic stimulants taken when you are very sleep-deprived sets you up for cardiac issues. Supplements should be used to augment a stable foundation. Not just for safety, but because that is how they work best.

###### Pharmacological Tool 3: L-tyrosine

This amino acid is used in the body to synthesize dopamine, as well as adrenaline, norepinephrine, and certain thyroid hormones.101 It comes from foods we eat but, as a nonessential amino acid, our body can also make it from other compounds if needed. That said, consuming more L-tyrosine from foods or supplements leads to a net increase in catecholamine levels.

L-tyrosine is abundant in nuts and seeds, meats, and some cheeses. Parmesan Reggiano has so much tyrosine that you can often see the L-tyrosine crystals on the surface of the cheese block. Yes, it’s safe to eat those L-tyrosine crystals, and yes, that is one of the reasons some people like certain cheeses so much—the taste combined with the dopamine increase it causes is highly reinforcing.

L-tyrosine gets converted into L-dopa by the rate-limiting enzyme tyrosine hydroxylase, which means �ooding your system with L-tyrosine is not su�cient to increase dopamine—the amount of tyrosine hydroxylase is the bottleneck on dopamine production.102 Nonetheless, there is some evidence that supplementing with L-tyrosine can improve alertness, focus, and learning under certain conditions.103 The problem is that most studies used ridiculously high dosages of L-tyrosine to observe these e�ects—as much as 8 grams or more delivered in capsule or pure powder form. I do not suggest taking that much all at once!

Anecdotally, many people �nd that supplementing L-tyrosine at doses of just 500 to 2,000 milligrams can help improve alertness and focus, but the published studies indicate L-tyrosine supplements really only help when people are stressed or fatigued.104

I have tried 500 to 1,000 milligrams L-tyrosine and I’ve tried _Mucuna pruriens_ , an over-the-counter naturally occurring form of L-dopa. Both increased my alertness, focus, and energy levels for a few hours but, at least for me, they both led to a signi�cant dip in energy afterward. Some people love L- tyrosine at 500 to 1,000 milligrams before work or exercise sessions, and swear by the focus-enhancing e�ects. That is why L-tyrosine is found in a lot of energy drinks and pre-workout formulas. I take it from time to time because it happens to be in one of the energy drinks I sometimes consume. So now to energy drinks.

###### Pharmacological Tool 4: Energy Drinks

More than a third of the world’s adult population consumes at least one energy drink per month, and about 9 percent consumes them every day.105 Studies of adolescents aged thirteen to nineteen have reported that a quarter of those who regularly consume energy drinks have at least one a day, and another quarter

have at least two per day ~~.~~ 106 In 2024, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention noted that 30 to 50 percent of adolescents report some amount of energy drink consumption.107 These rates are enormous.

To be clear, if you swallow a capsule of 300 to 600 milligrams of alpha-GPC, another capsule of 100 to 200 milligrams theanine, and down both with 100 to 300 milligrams of ca�eine from co�ee, tea, or diet soda, you’re basically making your own energy drink. But there is an important di�erence. Many commercially sold energy drinks contain anywhere from 200 to 400 milligrams ca�eine, 400 to 900 milligrams alpha-GPC, and 100 to 200 milligrams theanine _per serving_ , and contain one to two servings per can. Many also include L- tyrosine, and more are starting to include huperzine A, an alkaloid that blocks the enzyme that breaks down acetylcholine, leading to overall increases in acetylcholine levels in the brain.108 Many energy drinks are also now starting to include racetams, a family of synthetic compounds that lead to increased activity of acetylcholine and other neuromodulators in the brain ~~.~~ 109 Now you know why energy drinks are so habit forming: They are carefully engineered neuromodulator-increasing cocktails that taste like candy. They can even cause withdrawal e�ects if you regularly drink one or more per day, and then try to suddenly stop.

I rarely drink commercially sold energy drinks, preferring instead to get my ca�eine from yerba maté or black co�ee, and sometimes also taking theanine and/or alpha-GPC in capsule form. If I do have an energy drink, it’s usually before a particularly hard workout, as opposed to a learning bout.

I suggest that kids under the age of eighteen avoid energy drinks or preworkout formulas, which are similar. We have no idea how all that neuromodulator augmentation impacts brain wiring. I hear from people young and old saying they “can’t focus,” only to learn that they drink one to three energy drinks per day, or a 20 ounce co�ee every morning. That’s likely 600 milligrams of ca�eine just to feel baseline levels of alertness.

Homeostasis is a nonnegotiable rule of biology. If you want to boost focus and energy levels from ca�eine or other substances, a daily high dose is not recommended. Put di�erently: Whatever stimulant you take every day will soon

be needed to merely reach your baseline levels of alertness. Better in my opinion to use stimulants as an augmentation, not a requirement.

That said, I am not going to give up my daily ca�eine. I enjoy the taste and the feeling far too much. I drink just enough of it to bring about a mild increase in my level of alertness. Co�ee has also been shown to bene�t longevity by a variety of mechanisms, and yerba maté and green tea both have additional health bene�ts from the antioxidants and polyphenols they contain ~~.~~ 110

Most days I rely on the foundational tools described here: good sleep, nutrition, and hydration. I practice the brief daily meditation I described, and I add ca�eine. These generate the alertness and focus I need for learning bouts, work, and exercise.

I include over-the-counter pharmacologic tools like alpha-GPC and theanine here because they _do work_ , and I and many others have derived bene�t from them. I also consider them a far safer and less expensive alternative to nicotine and prescription drugs for focus. Which brings me to nicotine.

###### Pharmacological Tool 5: Nicotine

Ah, nicotine. Humans love the e�ects of nicotine so much they keep coming up with new delivery methods and every time there is a health hazard associated with one way, they develop another.

This plant alkaloid has been used for centuries to increase focus. It was put into soldiers’ kits in the early 1900s because of its known stimulant and stressreducing e�ects ~~.~~ 111 By the 1960s, more than half of adults in the United States and Europe smoked tobacco daily, with many starting upon waking and only stopping at bedtime.112

Nicotine, the primary psychoactive ingredient in tobacco, increases alertness and focus, and also heart rate and blood pressure,113 but it has the unique property among stimulants of inducing relaxation ~~.~~ 114 It makes you feel “alert yet calm”—that state where the autonomic seesaw is tilted ever so slightly toward increased sympathetic tone. It’s the perfect state for focus. It also didn’t hurt tobacco sales that smoking alongside a stranger or asking for a light was an icebreaker, and that nicotine reduces appetite. Pair all that with advertising that

romanticized the act of smoking, and the cost, foul odor, stained teeth, and stagnant breath that smoking causes all went largely overlooked.

Of course, until people �nally realized that smoking, dipping, chewing, or snu�ng tobacco is dangerous. It signi�cantly increases cancer and stroke risk.115 And yet, that went largely overlooked for a long time too. Public health announcements started to make these risks clear in the mid-1960s, but it was a rather slow and reluctant campaign until the 2000s, when the tobacco industry started to be heavily taxed and regulated.116 By 2010, the tobacco industry— formerly one of the most powerful in the world—saw its sales plummet. I was born in 1975 and I can still remember people smoking in airports and on planes, and how every dining table had an ashtray on it. Even the squat racks in the �rst commercial gym I joined back in 1993 had ashtrays molded into them so you could set your cigarette down while you performed your set! How times have changed.

Or have they? From 2005 to 2015, as smoking was progressively banned from most every indoor and even some outdoor public spaces, the use of electronic cigarettes, aka vaping, exploded. Vaping is somewhat safer than smoking, but carries its own risks.117 Nicotine itself doesn’t cause cancer, though the contaminants in vape solutions cause lung damage. Also, since nicotine is highly addictive, people struggle to quit vaping just as much as they struggle to quit cigarettes. Health warnings about vaping have curbed the market signi�cantly in recent years, but because no other substance creates that alert-but-calm state like nicotine does, as they always have, people make sure to �nd a way to get their �x.

Which is why since 2020 the use of oral nicotine products like pouches, gums, and mints has exploded in popularity ~~.~~ 118 Notice the pattern? I get asked about oral nicotine almost daily. “Is it safe? Is it addictive? Is using four 6 milligram pouches worse than vaping?” Some people even use it when exercising; millions more use it to work. An increasing number of women and teens are using oral nicotine products now too.

So, here is what you need to know about oral nicotine: It absolutely works to sharply increase focus… if you take it occasionally. Meaning no more than two to three times a week, at a dose of 1 to 6 milligrams each time. If you take nicotine

daily, you’ll soon need that same dose just to reach your former baseline levels of alertness, and without it you’ll be in a mild state of withdrawal. You’ll feel foggy and more tired than usual. And it is very habit forming. That is why so few people can limit their oral nicotine use to 3 to 6 milligrams once per day. I hear from countless people who started with that amount, loved the e�ect, then increased to 3 milligrams twice per day, and now use 4 to 6 milligrams or even 8 milligram pouches pretty much all day long.

There’s more to discuss as you consider this tool. Nicotine may also protect against Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s. You read that right. Nicotine may prevent the neuronal degeneration underlying Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s disease.119 Clinical trials show, however, that once these diseases start, nicotine is unlikely to be of bene�t.120 Whether any neuroprotection that nicotine provides is great enough to o�set the other health problems nicotine is known to cause is also still unclear. Remember, nicotine itself doesn’t cause cancer—it’s not mutagenic. But it may accelerate tumor progression ~~.~~ 121 It also raises blood pressure and causes vasoconstriction, which increases heart attack and stroke risk, and because of its vasoconstrictive e�ects, it has the potential to cause sexual side e�ects too, especially in men ~~.~~ 122 Experts on oral health are noticing that patients who use nicotine have more gum disease. Experts on skin health observe that it may cause premature aging of skin ~~.~~ 123 Both are likely as a result of its vasoconstriction e�ect (i.e., reduced blood �ow to the gums and skin). That all makes sense, as reducing the blood supply means less oxygen and nutrients get delivered to an organ or tissue, and fewer waste products of cellular metabolism are removed from it.

Curious about the oral nicotine hype, I tried 4 milligrams nicotine gum and it worked to make me feel alert but calm. And it worked quickly, like �ipping a switch. The next day, however, I felt a bit less mentally sharp. I also felt I needed to clear my throat a lot. I spoke to an MD friend who works on neural pathways for speech, and he told me that nicotine binds to both nicotinic and muscarinic acetylcholine receptors—the latter of which are abundant in the smooth muscles of the throat, larynx, and pharynx. He explained that after nicotine wears o�, those muscles go into a slight spasm. Sure enough, taking 4 milligrams nicotine

again �xed all that right away… until the next day. That experience was enough for me to end the experiment. Fortunately, the throat issue resolved after about three days.

I share this story because it made me understand the appeal—the focusenhancing e�ect of nicotine is remarkable—and yet, people should know all the e�ects, which I’ll recap one more time here to underscore them. There’s addiction potential, increase in blood pressure and vasoconstriction, and of course how quickly the cravings begin and many of the positive e�ects evaporate. I have friends who are otherwise very health conscious, and they need nicotine to do any sort of focused work or exercise. It’s become part of the way they just get to baseline. Are they addicted? The classic de�nition of addiction is continued use despite harm to self or others. One way that I de�ne addiction is something that causes a progressive narrowing of the things that bring you pleasure. According to both de�nitions, they are not addicted to nicotine (unless you consider the long-term health harms). But I do think they are dependent on it.

As with all things, my motto is this: Do what you want, but know what you’re doing. If you want to use nicotine, use the lowest possible dose that is e�ective for you. Stick to pouches, mints, or gums because the cancer risk appears to be lower than with cigarettes, but be aware that we do not yet have enough data to know this risk conclusively ~~.~~ 124 Limit your use to two to four times per week, and at most 6 milligrams per use (2–4 milligrams would be even better). That is, if you want the potent focus-enhancing e�ect of nicotine to last.

###### Pharmacological Tool 6: Prescription Drugs: Adderall, Ritalin, Modafinil and Armodafinil, Sunosi, Wellbutrin

These are the heavy guns for pharmacologically increasing alertness and focus. Collectively, these drugs are referred to as sympathomimetics: They increase levels of sympathetic tone by directly increasing levels of dopamine and norepinephrine in the brain, albeit each through di�erent mechanisms.125 Some block reuptake of dopamine and norepinephrine at synapses, leading to more availability of these two neuromodulators in the brain; others stimulate more

release _and_ block reuptake. Some also weakly increase other neuromodulators like serotonin. But they all potently increase alertness and focus.

I hesitated to include these drugs in this book, because they were developed to treat speci�c clinical conditions like ADHD (Adderall, Vyvanse, and Ritalin), or excessive daytime sleepiness (moda�nil and Sunosi), or depression and smoking cessation (Wellbutrin), and they were not developed or marketed for merely increasing alertness and focus. The reality, however, is many millions of people get them prescribed or obtain them illicitly for that purpose. Knowing how they work and their margins of safety therefore feels warranted. Also, I hear often from parents wondering if they should medicate their child for ADHD. Or I hear from someone who thinks they themselves may have mild to severe ADHD, and they want to know what to do about it. They know I am not an MD, but they tell me it is hard to �nd a US doctor who doesn’t almost immediately default to prescribing these medications. They are confused and con�icted about what to do.

Here is what everyone should know: All prescription drugs for focus have side e�ects. These vary by drug, dosage, and by person in ways that can only be determined empirically, meaning by trial and error. Also—and this is very important—the dosage at which some of these drugs are e�ective is enormously variable. Adderall works to treat ADHD in some people at 5 milligrams, whereas others need 40 milligrams or even more.126 It’s simply impossible to know how someone will respond, and it requires time to �nd the minimum e�ective dose. Of course, all the drugs in this section require a prescription to acquire legally. Illegal and questionably legal sources carry signi�cant risk. Fentanyl—a deadly opioid—has frequently been found in counterfeit Adderall ~~.~~ 127

The reason I call these “the heavy guns” is they work so well that people quickly become dependent on them, and some, such as the amphetamine-based stimulants like Adderall, carry abuse potential because they can create euphoria ~~.~~ 128 It’s also important to note, however, that failure to treat kids or adults who have ADHD puts them at a much higher risk for addiction than not, due to the impulsivity associated with ADHD ~~.~~ 129 That said, amphetamines may stunt growth,130 cause sleep disturbances ~~,~~ 131 and even lead to psychosis if abused

or taken by people with bipolar depression or a predisposition to psychosis.132 And all these drugs are hard to quit.133 When someone does try, they often su�er from excessive daytime sleepiness and mood and focus issues, aka withdrawal. It’s much worse than ca�eine or nicotine withdrawal, which is why most people don’t quit—they use these drugs inde�nitely. Thus, the decision to medicate a child or adult with Adderall or Vyvanse (both amphetamines) or Ritalin (a non-amphetamine stimulant) needs to be carefully considered.

There are also a lot of nondrug therapies for ADHD that can be e�ective and/or can help reduce dosage needs. They are the foundational and behavioral tools mentioned above. What about supplements? Can alpha-GPC replace a genuine need for Adderall to treat ADHD? Unlikely, but a lifestyle that follows the foundational behaviors described in the protocols here (sleep, hydration, nutrition that favors stable blood sugar levels and satiety, etc.) along with regular meditation or hypnosis for increased focus, and timed use of ca�eine and theanine, may allow people to use a lower dose of a prescription drug for ADHD. There are also many cases where these lifestyle changes have allowed people with ADHD to stop taking their medications and still thrive, or thrive even more. It’s all highly individual.

That’s ADHD. What about the person who doesn’t have ADHD, but wants to use a prescription medication to induce states of intense focus one to three times per week? They may be doing everything else correctly, adhering to the foundational tools I’ve described in this chapter, but they want an “edge.” And what about the many millions of people who, due to smartphones, have what clinicians are now calling _mild ADHD_ , which is not a diagnosis but a catch-all for no longer being able to focus? Should they take a sympathomimetic? We can no longer pretend that smartphone-induced mild ADHD doesn’t exist. My stance is that we should be aware of all the tools available for focus that are legal, and consider their relative potency and risks.

RITALIN

This non-amphetamine stimulant has largely fallen out of favor for the treatment of ADHD and for focus purposes because it’s short acting, and people prefer the stronger, longer lasting e�ects they get with Adderall and

Vyvanse.134 A recent brain imaging study found that methylphenidate—the active ingredient in Ritalin—did not actually increase activation of attentional networks in the brain.135 It merely reduced the feeling of fatigue and the e�ects of sleep deprivation on attention. It also made boring work feel more tolerable, and even rewarding—thus allowing for more sustained e�ort at tasks. The study didn’t look at other stimulants, but this may be a general theme of the drugs covered in this section because few if any stimulants directly increase focus. Raising dopamine levels can reduce background “noise” in the brain, and therefore the tendency to get distracted, and raising norepinephrine increases alertness ~~.~~ 136 Together, that can make trivial things feel more engaging. It’s important to know that people with ADHD can focus quite well—they just have a much harder time focusing on things they don’t enjoy than do people without ADHD. Alas, much of life requires focusing on things we may prefer not doing. Apparently, stimulants like Ritalin trick the brain into ignoring our preferences.

###### ADDERALL AND VYVANSE

Make no mistake. These are amphetamines, aka speed, but they are not meth. There is a prescription drug for ADHD called Desoxyn, which is pharmaceutical grade methamphetamine, but it’s rarely prescribed due to the addiction and abuse potential ~~.~~ 137 (Only a few hundred prescriptions exist in the US currently.)

Adderall and Vyvanse are similar to each other but the former works faster, within minutes, and lasts four to six hours; whereas Vyvanse’s e�ects come on more slowly and last ten or more hours. An estimated 16.5 million people (adults and kids combined) take these amphetamines every day in the United States ~~.~~ 138 Some for ADHD, and some just to help with focus. They get them with valid prescriptions from board-certi�ed MDs. If that is surprising, consider that despite being 5 percent of the world’s population, the US accounts for more than 80 percent of the prescribed Adderall and Vyvanse taken worldwide.139 You can be sure that it is not all being prescribed for clinical levels of ADHD.

Here is my suggestion: If you are considering using these drugs for focus and don’t have diagnosed ADHD (and even if you do), �rst do an inventory of the foundational and behavioral tools for focus that are listed in this chapter. Are

you getting enough sleep and exercise? Are you drinking enough water? Have you tried brief meditation or hypnosis for focus, and perhaps the ca�eine, theanine, and/or alpha-GPC combination I described? If not, I suggest you do before resorting to use of prescription-level amphetamines. (Also, see the section “A Note on Phone Management” at the end of this protocol, as the phone is a severe impediment to focusing for many people.)

To be clear, I am not against prescription drugs per se, and if you do take one, don’t stop suddenly. Talk to your doctor. Many prescription drugs have their place in treatment, but unless there is a genuine clinical need, using stimulants as powerful as Adderall or Vyvanse on a regular basis will soon cause dependence, and other tools you try will pale in comparison.

###### MODAFINIL AND ARMODAFINIL

These drugs were designed to treat “excessive daytime sleepiness” caused by narcolepsy or sleep apnea or jet lag. Today, they are commonly prescribed to people simply wishing to improve their focus for work or school. They are not amphetamines, but they can similarly disrupt sleep and appetite, and they still pose some cardiac risk—a feature of all sympathomimetics because they elevate blood pressure and heart rate ~~.~~ 140 These drugs are interesting because while they raise alertness and focus, they also have the rare feature of also improving cognition, in particular executive functions that allow for orchestrated task switching and working memory—the ability to hold relevant information in mind for only as long as is necessary ~~.~~ 141 At the same time, they may impair creative divergent thinking ~~.~~ 142

In speaking with psychiatrists who prescribe these drugs, I’ve learned that people’s sensitivity to moda�nil and armoda�nil varies tremendously. Some �nd 50 milligrams much too stimulating and their sleep is disrupted; others need 200 milligrams to achieve the bene�ts and sleep just �ne. I have tried both armoda�nil and moda�nil and found they can erase my jet lag but they impair my recall memory. Armoda�nil is essentially longer lasting moda�nil, but even at the lowest dose of moda�nil (I broke a 100 mg tablet in half), I struggled to fall asleep later that night. That said, I have a colleague who takes 100 to 200 milligrams of moda�nil four to �ve times a week, which was prescribed to him

for “mild ADHD,” and he has no issues sleeping afterward. These drugs used to be expensive—but the release of generic versions made it less than one dollar per 100 milligram pill. That, combined with their mild cognitive-enhancing e�ects, makes me think that moda�nil and armoda�nil use will increase in years to come.

###### SUNOSI

This is a relatively new drug that also acts to increase dopamine and norepinephrine in the brain.143 It is FDA approved for o�setting excessive daytime sleepiness due to sleep apnea, and recently it performed well in clinical trials for ADHD ~~,~~ 144 making it likely to soon be approved for that purpose as well. This dopamine and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor is much more noradrenergic than dopaminergic as compared to the other compounds in this section ~~.~~ 146 This means it raises norepinephrine more than it raises dopamine. ###### A Note on Phone Management

It’s clear we messed up. Smartphones are a great technology for many things: texting, apps, and more. And I do think social media can be used to inform, learn, and teach, and of course for entertainment and social connection (of sorts) too. A study that looked at the e�ect of having your phone on your desk versus in a bag in the same room versus in an entirely separate room found that having your phone on your desk or even zipped up in a backpack reduces your working memory and �uid intelligence—the ability to �gure things out on the �y—compared to when your phone is placed in a di�erent room ~~.~~ 149 The authors of the study were able to disentangle focus—people’s ability to direct their attention to a task—from how much mental energy they could devote to what they were focusing on. ###### **LEARNING PROTOCOL**

2

Use Mental Contrasting to Achieve a “State of Urgency” and Reach Your Goals

###### WHAT TO DO:

- Think of being in “a state of urgency,” rather than a state of motivation. Urgency is an experience we are all familiar with. We tend to know what it feels like in our mind and body. Motivation can be vague and ephemeral.

- The most reliable method to create this state is a psychological tool called mental contrasting. It asks you to imagine your goals, and the obstacles to achieving them, in a structured way. Even if you’re already on your way toward your goals, this strategy can further assist you.

###### HOW IT WORKS:

“Motivation is everything.” We hear this all the time and know it’s true, yet people vary in their abilities to get and stay motivated. Especially to do things that require sustained focus and energy.

The tools I mentioned in the previous protocol were based on physiology as the primary lever. The idea is if we increase sympathetic tone and deploy catecholamines, we can create the neurochemical milieu required for plasticity. I made no mention of psychological tools.

Mental contrasting is a psychological tool, and a powerful one.

Imagine being able to instantly switch on a state of urgency whenever you want. Someday we’ll have that. I’m certain because my colleague at Stanford,

neurologist Joe Parvizi, MD, PhD, conducted incredible experiments showing that if activity in a brain area called the anterior midcingulate cortex (aMCC) is increased, people feel an immediate surge in mental energy and readiness to lean into challenges ~~.~~ 150 Alas, currently the only way to instantly and selectively switch on your aMCC is to drill a hole in your skull, lower an electrode into this region, and pass an electrical current into it. It will be a while—probably �ve to seven years—before selective aMCC stimulation can be achieved noninvasively. In the meantime, if we want to activate a state of urgency we’re going to have to rely on something else. There is a pill to make you feel more alert and focused, but there is no pill that can make you feel motivated to do a speci�c task.

Fortunately, a solution does exist. It’s this psychological tool that can reliably shift your mindset, allowing you to become more mentally and physically able to exert e�ort. But �rst we should get clear on what a mindset is.

People use the word mindset all the time nowadays but in the context of motivation psychology, it has a very speci�c meaning and purpose. Alia Crum, a professor of psychology and researcher who directs her own lab at Stanford, explained it best: “A mindset is a setting for your brain.”151 Meaning, a mindset is a psychological stance that makes certain thoughts and actions easier to access, and other thoughts and actions harder to access. Alia’s de�nition also speaks to the power of mindsets to simultaneously in�uence di�erent aspects of your physiology—your brain directs many systems, including your nervous system, your hormones, even your immune system, in speci�c ways ~~.~~ 152 That, in turn, guides our behavior. When we switch to a mindset that embraces a challenge, it activates neural circuitries and chemical reactions that make us feel more capable of running that extra mile, putting in extra study hours, or going for one more hour of piano practice. Physiology is also a lever here, but a secondary one.

You may have heard the term “growth mindset,” coined by Stanford psychologist Carol Dweck. The term refers to the belief that ability is not �xed but rather can improve with e�ort ~~.~~ 153 With a growth mindset, a teenager who is failing calculus understands that studying hard will lead to better comprehension. That state unlocks the possibility for even more: You believe in the e�ort that learning requires, and take the action that it requires too.

Upholding a growth mindset means you actively avoid identity-based and valuation labels of being good or bad at something. You aren’t “good” or “bad”; you simply haven’t put in the e�ort and taken the action yet. A growth mindset never says, “I’m not a math person”; it says, “I can get better at math if I work at it.” Experiments from Carol and others show that adopting a growth mindset can drive signi�cant improvements in learning, especially when paired with a stress-can-enhance-performance mindset ~~.~~ 154 That last bit—that stress can help with growth—implies that challenge can improve your outcome, rather than limit you.

Maybe you are wondering: If stress is so great for learning, then why aren’t we all great learners? We all certainly feel stress. I think it’s because for most of us, the feeling we have when we fail at doing something di�cult overrides the desire to keep striving. That is one reason I continually share ways for real-time autonomic self-regulation, like the physiological sigh described in chapter 3. These protocols are designed to lower stress not only to help people feel calm, but also to expand people’s sense of what’s possible to learn. If we have the tools to control stress, we can seek out more challenge.

No matter how well we control our stress, however, we are still left with the challenge of how to activate a growth mindset and stress-can-enhanceperformance mindset. In other words: How do we actually get motivated? Should we use self-talk? Watch an inspirational clip on YouTube? Fantasize about achieving our goal? Scare ourselves with the fear of not achieving it? How many milligrams of fear should we take? Just kidding. Sort of.

The answer starts, I believe, with swapping the word _motivation_ with _a state of urgency_ . Here is why:

A state of urgency is less prone to parsing than motivation, which immediately raises questions about context. Friedrich Nietzsche o�ered powerful wisdom when he wrote, “ _Hat man sein warum? des Lebens, so verträgt man sich fast mit jedem wie?_ ”155 Some readers may be more familiar with the English translation made famous by Austrian neurologist, psychiatrist, and Holocaust survivor Viktor Frankl: “He who has a why to live for can bear with almost any how.”156

- Sometimes the why is clear. But what about when it isn’t? What about the many aspects of learning and life that require persistent e�ort and for which the why, the deeper meaning and larger purpose, is unclear? Often the why only becomes clear during, or even after, the how. Maybe a person is forced to take a course they hate in order to get a degree. Once they complete the course, however, they may realize the new opportunities have been made accessible to them only because of the material they learned in the course; it wasn’t just a means to an end after all. A state of urgency doesn’t require you to have all the answers yet.

- A state of urgency stimulates catecholamine release, which further increases sympathetic tone, which therefore increases focus.157 This helps dim distractions, both internal and external, which improves performance… and increases your state of urgency.158 It’s a positive feedback loop.

- It’s obvious why a sense of urgency would help you maximize the number of repetitions that you can do in a given time frame. That’s huge because genuine attempts are the fundamental unit of all forms of learning. It’s speci�c enough that we know what to aim for, experientially, but broad in the sense that it applies to all activities and pursuits. Motivation drives you to try something, a state of urgency keeps you practicing.

So now the question is not, “How do we get motivated?” It’s “How do we create a state of urgency?”

The answer is mental contrasting, which is a tool based on the research of Gabriele Oettingen, PhD, a professor at New York University and the University of Hamburg.159 The term is the result of her deep dive into understanding two psychological tools long thought to be helpful to this topic: positive thinking and visualization. The terms are likely familiar to you. Positive thinking refers to the practice of deliberately holding an optimistic view about an outcome as a way to help that hoped-for result come true. Visualization refers to the practice of imagining a desired future outcome, again as a way to help that result come true. Research had shown that a positive mindset can have bene�cial e�ects on health and well-being.160

But as Oettingen and others have discovered, although positive thinking and visualization are great, they often undermine motivation just as easily as they can increase it. And get this: Too much positive thinking about goal outcomes undermines performance ~~.~~ 161 Apparently, visualization causes people’s brain reward mechanisms to get su�ciently activated, so they feel less energy to continue to strive for the goal ~~.~~ 162 And positive thinking provides a big but transient boost in motivation.

All that is consistent with what we know about dopamine in the context of goal seeking and rewards. As Anna Lembke, an expert on dopamine, put it, dopamine is about wanting, not about having ~~.~~ 163 That’s another downside of positive thinking: It activates the “want” circuitries but not the “have” ones. Anna further pointed out that the neural circuits underlying motivation evolved in times of scarcity, where e�ort almost always preceded reward—think hunting, gathering, seeking shelter, �nding a mate, and so on. Because of the abundance of stimulation in modern life, which was designed to satisfy and even exploit our dopamine circuitry, most of us have recalibrated our motivation and reward circuits to expect more reward from less e�ort ~~.~~ 164 And while Anna’s work has mainly focused on addictive and compulsive behaviors, we’ve all seen this play out for goals too ~~.~~ 165 Too much reward prior to e�ort, or too much reward without e�ort, undermines future e�ort.

A friend of mine, an MD turned successful startup investor, warned me to be careful about telling too many people about a big goal. Most will respond, he explained, by saying “You would be great at that, go for it!” Unless you have a lot at stake, the reward of all that positive feedback can undermine your drive to actually pursue the goal. I asked him if he thought it would be better if we responded instead by saying, “Don’t try, you’ll never succeed!” “I don’t think that helps either,” he replied.

He was right. Oettingen found that if people focus too much on the challenge they’ll likely face, that too prevents them from pursuing goals, at least in the long run.

So much for just “Focus on the journey not the destination.”

We can thus all be grateful to Oettingen for carrying out experiments that tested various common motivational tools, alone and in combination. She also explored their e�cacy for helping people achieve di�erent types of goals: learning cognitive skills, learning physical skills, making better food choices, exercising more, and on and on.166 She eventually discovered that it is the contrast between visualizing the goal and thinking about the obstacles to achieve it that creates a state of heightened physical and mental energy, and that state is what leads us to be more likely to start—and to persist.167

In other words, Oettingen figured out how people can activate a state of urgency. She calls the approach mental contrasting, and she calls the way to implement it WOOP, an acronym that stands for _Wish, Outcome, Obstacles, Plan_ ~~.~~ <u>168</u> The four steps of WOOP can be done in your head, but it works best if you record your answers. Try writing them down, or hitting the record button on your phone. It works for both short- and long-term goals.

WISH: Name the big, overall goal. What do you want to happen?

For example:

- “I want to learn guitar well enough to play with a band live in front of a thousand people.”

- “I want to get a PhD in neuroscience from a top program.”

- “I want to learn to speak �uent German.”

- “I want to paint well enough to make a living selling my art.”

It takes only a few seconds to complete the _W_ step in WOOP. You don’t need to include a lot of detail, but some helps. For instance, “I want to be happy and successful” is too general. Instead of focusing on what you want to feel, name skills, credentials, and proficiencies that you’re hoping to achieve.

OUTCOME: Here is where you think about what you want to feel from having achieved the goal.

For example:

- “I will experience the thrill of performing live with other great musicians and knowing that I’m giving people the live music experience I know and love so much too.”

- “I will feel the freedom and excitement of being able to work for any number of di�erent companies exploring for cures to neurodegenerative diseases.”

- “I will enjoy going to Germany to visit my spouse’s family, be able to relate to them better, and maybe even work and start a life there someday. And I can help our kids become bilingual.”

- “I will �nally get to indulge my desire to be creative. And I can sleep in late and stay up late painting while listening to music, which is what I always wanted!”

You’ll notice this outcome step is aspirational—you’re encouraged to daydream about how you want to feel. I gave short examples here but feel free to expand on the many things you look forward to feeling. The reality check is next.

OBSTACLES: Get clear on the obstacles you anticipate en route to your goal.

Be hyperrealistic. Record the roadblocks you might face. Include how you might feel as you do. People’s temperaments vary, but you know yourself—so be honest about how you’ll react when things don’t go to plan.

For example:

- “I tend to be really tired from work at the end of the day. I’m going to feel frustrated when I am too tired to practice guitar or when tra�c makes me late to guitar lessons.”

- “I will miss the chance to attend weddings and go on fun vacations with my friends because I’ll be in the lab doing experiments or studying. I won’t have much money because PhD students don’t get paid much.”

- “It will be a long time before I am truly �uent in German because I learn really slowly. And writing in German is even more di�cult than speaking it, so I will get discouraged a lot.”

- “The art I make is not likely to appeal to a lot of people because I like melancholy themes and darker tones, and most people seem to buy art that is happy and playful.”

Again, feel free to expand as much as you want to for this step.

PLAN: Come up with if-then statements to address the obstacles you anticipated. These are _action_ steps.

For example:

- “On days when I’m too tired to practice guitar after work, I will go to sleep early and get up thirty minutes earlier than usual the next day. That way I can get �fteen to twenty minutes of practice done in the morning. My mind is much sharper then anyway. Playing in the morning also makes me feel good for hours, so maybe work might not feel so exhausting. If I’m late to guitar practice because of tra�c, then I will do my best to stay calm and practice in my head on the way there. I will add a few minutes of practice in my car after the lesson to really drill in what I learned.”

- “When I can’t attend fun events because of time or money restrictions, I will remember that having a PhD in neuroscience puts me at a unique advantage for job choices and long-term �nancial security because there is so much still to discover about nervous system diseases… and we still don’t have cures to most all of them. Also, a lot of my friends who make more money than me now are bored with their jobs or have already maximized their earning potential. I will be able to consult and/or invest in biotech companies because I really understand where the �eld is and where it might grow. Also, I will remember that I love doing experiments.”

- “If I feel frustrated at my slow progress learning German, I will remind myself that the frustration is a signal my brain is getting the message to change, and that a lot of learning happens in bursts; it’s rarely linear. I will ask my spouse (who is �uent) if we can do an only-in-German dinner once per week as a family, so I and the kids can practice. I will use AI to generate some free German language quizzes for me that I can listen to when I’m alone in the car.”

- “I will remind myself that the best art has always come from people who really care about the work they are doing, and that I really feel and believe in the messages that motivate the art I create. I’ll set up a website and social media platform so I can connect with other artists with similar tastes, and learn from them about marketing my work.”

You may have noticed what happened there. Mental contrasting quickly moves you from idealizing and making aspirational statements about goals and feelings to concrete action steps… and, more importantly, clarity about how you will deal with setbacks. It customizes the process of getting motivated. If you’re optimistic and un�appable and start new projects all the time or if you’re pessimistic and tend to talk yourself out of things or if it depends on the circumstances or the time of day or the goal, mental contrasting still works. It also serves as a strategy setting session. It’s not a pep talk. It’s a preparation exercise that has been proven to help people get started and persist in pursuit of their goals. It’s also zero cost, and takes around ten minutes at the outset. It’s a real gift to us all, and we have Oettingen, along with the students and postdocs that ran the experiments, to thank for it.

###### In My Experience

I used mental contrasting for a goal that I had been procrastinating on forever. I followed the WOOP process. I typed out the WOOP answers into a word processing document and hit Save. That took about ten minutes.

And it worked spectacularly well for me. It somehow cleared away the laziness and analysis paralysis and all the other stu� that had been holding me back, and I enjoyed two solid work sessions that very day, and then two months of steady e�ort toward the goal thereafter, even though I was in my busiest season of work and I had many other commitments.

When I started feeling a bit unmotivated again, I reread the document. I made some edits and additions based on new changes in life. That only took about �ve minutes. I now do mental contrasting for learning goals, for work goals, for �tness goals, and for personal goals too. I reread and update the WOOP documents whenever I am feeling a bit unmotivated. It’s become

re�exive. I don’t share my WOOP answers with anyone, they are for me and for me only, but you can decide if you want to keep yours private or not.

###### The Mechanisms Behind Mental Contrasting

I was struck that mental contrasting seemed to increase my motivation across the board, not just for my speci�c goal. I procrastinate far less on everything now. I’m not aware of any data showing that doing mental contrasting rewires speci�c brain areas, but given what we know about the aMCC, I wonder if it might. Recall how Joe Parvizi conducted incredible experiments showing that if activity in the aMCC is increased, people feel an immediate surge in mental energy and readiness to lean into challenges. Especially since every instance of learning— whether that’s a new behavior or a new piece of information—is the consequence of plasticity and our aMCC is the brain structure most closely associated with tenacity ~~.~~ 169 It has been shown to increase in volume in successful dieters, people who push themselves to stick to a new exercise program, and other situations where thinking about and overcoming a challenge is called for. Parvizi discovered the role of the aMCC in 2013, and only recently has it been discussed in the larger �eld of neuroscience and media, so I doubt that Oettingen was aware of its potential role in WOOP. I look forward to a day soon when someone explores whether the aMCC is activated by going through the steps of the WOOP Protocol. In the meantime, I plan to keep using mental contrasting any time I need to generate a state of urgency for something, and I hope you’ll consider it too.

###### Why Some People Will Avoid Mental Contrasting

This may surprise the dreamers and go-getters, but a lot of people are afraid to strategize around—let alone think about—their big goals. Some of that is cultura ~~l~~ 170 but in my observation a lot of people are afraid to change, even if they are unhappy with their current circumstances. It’s just not re�exive (and in many cases it feels aversive) for them to do so. Before you conclude that a resistance to change is just the way you’re wired, consider the experiment where people preferred to get strong electrical shocks they knew were coming at speci�c times… versus weaker electrical shocks that arrived without warning.171

The same general conclusion comes from studies of pain. People like what’s predictable, even if it isn’t good. That de�es logic until we remember that our nervous systems are prediction machines that seek to minimize energy expenditure ~~.~~ 172 So, while mental contrasting is merely a mental exploration of a goal, I anticipate some people will shy away from it… because change is hard. I hope you don’t and instead, go with the data. Put it to work for you. WOOP is a really cool tool to explore new things, and I’m grateful Gabriele Oettingen and colleagues came up with it. And learning to switch on a state of urgency to increase focus and achieve your goals and get things done in life is a valuable superpower, for SDAP and beyond.
