###### **LEARNING PROTOCOL**

3

### Embrace Errors to Improve Your Performance

###### WHAT TO DO:

- Embrace the fact that errors are an essential trigger for learning. Errors that come from genuine attempts to learn something are the signal for plasticity to occur. This is true for all forms of skill development: cognitive, motor, musical, mathematical, et cetera, and why it’s an essential step in SDAP.

- Strive to perform at a level of difficulty just slightly beyond your current ability. Studies show that the right level is such that it produces an error rate of 15 to 30 percent. The 30 percent level tends to work best for learning motor skills, whereas 15 percent is the approximate level to shoot for with cognitive skills. Don’t make errors deliberately. That won’t have the same result. Work on pushing yourself past what you think you can do and using your mistakes as learning tools.

###### HOW IT WORKS:

If you can do something with pro�ciency, your nervous system won’t change. The gap between your current level of ability (even if it’s zero!) and the level you are striving for is what triggers learning and plasticity. No gap, no change.

Before I dive into this protocol, I need to make something clear. There are many forms of learning and plasticity that don’t require making errors. Just look at what happens with children. As every parent knows, a toddler learns that ice

cream is delicious in a matter of seconds, and never forgets it. They also learn that tablets and phones can display cartoons after seeing them only once. No errors needed. (By contrast, learning to walk, to speak, or to eat with utensils are all examples of learning and plasticity that require errors to eventually master.) Traumatic events, at any age, are also examples of error-independent learning and plasticity. So is the learning that comes from experiencing a welcome surprise. Let’s say you drop by a friend’s party expecting to say hello and then go home early, but you end up meeting someone you really like there. You can be sure you will remember their name, their job, et cetera. Should a great long-term relationship emerge from it, you’ll no doubt maintain fond memories of the party, the friend who hosted it, and the events of the entire weekend when the party occurred.

You can thank dopamine for that. Dopamine helps us learn by linking our memories of prior actions, and the contexts in which they took place, with our sense of whether things went better or worse than we expected—a phenomenon known as _reward prediction error_ .173 It makes perfect sense why this evolved: to help us �nd and remember the paths we took to life-sustaining resources—food, water, shelter, potential mates, et cetera. Unwelcome surprises, even if they are not traumatic, shape our memories, help us learn, and guide our future actions too. Whereas positive events simultaneously increase dopamine and lower serotonin, negative events do the opposite. Say that instead of meeting a new friend at a party, you unexpectedly run into an old boss you hoped to never see again. That would shape your expectations and motivations around future gatherings at that house. It may even change your feelings about the friend—a phenomenon known to neuroscientists as _context-dependent plasticity_ .174

###### Why We Need To Make Mistakes

You’ll notice that none of the examples of learning I just described require that we make errors. Stu� happened, for better or worse, and learning occurred. It speaks to the many types of plasticity.

SDAP is di�erent. We _need_ to make errors. With errors often comes some amount of agitation, of limbic friction, which by now you know is a good thing because it increases the release of catecholamines that facilitate focus and

plasticity. But also, perhaps more importantly, mistakes provide the signal that sets the size and type of neural circuit changes (and thus skill improvement) that follow learning attempts.

I’ll use motor skills as an example but the same holds true for all types of skills. Let’s say you want to learn tennis. You need to learn to serve the ball. At �rst, it’s likely that you’ll hit the ball into the net often. Each time you do, it’s an error that you register as objective performance feedback. You adjust your serve accordingly. You may decide “that last serve was too hard, I’ll use less force this time” or “perhaps I am gripping the racket too high on the handle, I’ll hold it lower” or “I’m throwing the ball too high before I swing,” and so on. Even if you have a tennis coach who gives you instructions, you are the only one who has access to the proprioceptive information associated with each serve attempt—by that I mean the awareness of your body’s movements. Your nervous system tracks each and every one of those, and compares it to the performance outcome. Some of that is conscious, and some is unconscious, working below your level of awareness.

Remember back in chapter 3, when we discussed what your nervous system does? As you may recall, whether you are asleep or awake, your nervous system is handling the basic stu� of survival, making sure that your heart keeps beating, your lungs keep expanding, your digestion keeps �owing, and so on. It is also letting you perceive the world around you. And, as we also discussed, your nervous system is also a _prediction machine_ . It’s constantly trying to make causal inferences: “If I do A, then B seems to happen immediately afterward… If I don’t do X, then Y happens a few hours later…” When you are awake, your nervous system is running a ceaseless if-then analysis of you and your actions and feelings, thoughts and memories; of others and their actions and feelings, thoughts and memories; of the world around you, and on and on.

Here is the key thing to remember: Any time your nervous system �gures out that one of your actions leads to a successful outcome, it starts to shift the pattern of neural �ring that occurred from your conscious awareness into your _implicit motor memory_ . It works to make the action automatic. The rationale for that is obvious: Thinking and doing and making associations is metabolically demanding. As is rewiring brain circuitry.175 The more your brain can make

things automatic, the more energy it can devote to other things. This is especially true in the case of skill learning. With maintaining focus, moving into a state of urgency, making errors, and calibrating adjustments, we can all learn to execute new skills. Once we do, we don’t need to think about each step. We simply activate performance of the skill. We serve the ball, play the chord, �nish the math problem. Voila!

I acknowledge that your reaction to this point might be: “Duh!” But I said there was a key thing to remember. It will forever change the way you approach learning.

First, your brain doesn’t work alone here. It needs your second brain. No, not your gut. I’m referring to the mini brain tucked right under your occipital lobe. If you touch the top of your neck where it meets the back of your skull, you’re touching the area just above your cerebellum, aka your mini brain. Many people have heard of the cerebellum for its role in balance, but your cerebellum is also crucial for eye movements related to attention, for proprioceptive awareness, for speaking, for estimating time, for your sense of rhythm, and much more. Your cerebellum is also a key site of action for comparing what you are trying to do with what you’re currently doing, and sending the rest of your nervous system the signals it needs to close the gap in performance.

I would love to devote a thousand pages to the function of the cerebellum in learning because it is that cool, but I’ll keep it (relatively) brief. When you make errors in the context of trying to learn a new skill, you activate neurons in your cerebellum. The bigger the error, the larger the response from your cerebellum. Your cerebellum is kind of like that tennis coach in this regard, except unlike a coach that observes you and makes educated guesses as to what you need to do in order to improve, your cerebellum has full access to both your inner and outer workings: the angles of your limbs and joints, the speed and stretch of your muscles; it knows when you blinked relative to your maximum e�ort, your level of autonomic arousal, et cetera. Thus, your cerebellum is also uniquely suited to be your coach because of both the _specificity_ and the _interconnectedness_ of its wiring. Di�erent cerebellar neurons respond to the movement of di�erent parts of the body, even your eyes and lips and tongue. It also encodes how movement of one body area changes the movement of all the others. If you consciously

adjust the angle of your elbow and it improves your serve, your cerebellum registers the many other changes that accompanied the elbow adjustment and then makes sure they become part of your serve “motor program” going forward. If your elbow angle adjustment makes things worse, your cerebellum registers that too. With repeated e�ort, your brain eventually stamps down the exact motor program needed to serve the ball properly.

I wish we all learned about the role of the cerebellum in learning when we were kids. Instead, we watched _Star Wars, Harry Potter, X-Men_ , and Marvel movies, et cetera, which are all wonderful stories, but sadly also embed the false idea in us that skills are things that just need to be activated, as if by magic. Of course, that’s �ction. The real-life superpower all of us possess from birth is our ability to focus and learn. We can progress from unskilled to skilled, and from skilled to mastery. Your cerebellum, and the larger neural circuit it participates in, is the coach that guides the entire progression. If that were the message, I believe the frustration that comes from errors would take on a whole new meaning. We would (and should) view errors and the agitation that come from genuine attempts to learn as something to seek out, not to avoid. _Errorful learning_ , as some researchers call it, appears to be the most e�cient approach to acquiring new skills.176

###### The Goldilocks Zone for Errors

You may be asking, “How many errors are needed? And what kind?” In a study published in 2019, researchers set out to determine the optimal level of di�culty —the Goldilocks zone for learning new skills ~~.~~ 177 They calculated the ideal rate of error using several learning algorithms and found that training progressed much faster when the level of di�culty set was associated with an accuracy rate of about 85 percent (an error rate of 15 percent). A few additional insights emerged from this study. First, when something is too hard such that 50 percent of attempts were unsuccessful, the brain can’t seem to capture the right strategy for neural circuit modi�cation. It was much better, the researchers found, to continually adjust the training level to maintain the approximately 15 percent error rate. This was a quantitative modeling study, meaning the �ndings are

based on a simulation, but it was aligned with studies of visual-perception-based decision-making and motor learning.

It works for cognitive tasks too. For example, students who are allowed to �gure out how to solve complex math problems on their own—and therefore can make mistakes—tend to do better than students who are told the right way to do it from the start.178 And we seem to know this intuitively. In one study, researchers at Columbia University asked �fty-two people to play a series of computer games.179 They were free to choose from a range of games, some of which were easy, some harder, and some impossible to learn. As the task progressed, participants chose increasingly di�cult games and preferred to repeat the challenging games rather than repeat the easy ones.

Remember the 15 percent “rule” is an approximate measure. There’s no need to become obsessed with maintaining this exact error rate. To put it in simple terms, you want to work at a level at which you’re getting things right much of the time, but also wrong some of the time.

This insight can be used in education as well. Given the relationship between errors and plasticity, and the pivotal role of the cerebellum in that process, teachers should consider reserving verbal feedback to students in cases where the students thought they got something right but actually didn’t. Otherwise, it’s better to give students the opportunity to register their own errors.

The moment immediately following making a mistake is critical for learning. Negative reactions typically occur within 100 milliseconds ~~,~~ 180 but the sympathetic arousal lasts longer and provides the milieu for enhanced focus and plasticity as we have discussed many times now. Which means our systems are primed for learning in those immediate post-error moments. This internal state improves the e�ectiveness of the whole learning bout. Studies of motor learning show that within-trial errors and across-trial errors both provide valuable signals for plasticity and learning.181 If you leave a language class or tennis lesson or other learning bout thinking, “Darn, I couldn’t seem to get that right on that one part,” well, congratulations! The learning process set in motion by withinand across-trial errors was triggered. You’ll no doubt come back better next time… but only if you do what’s in the next protocol.

### Prioritize Sleep the Night After a Learning Bout

###### WHAT TO DO:

- Get adequate sleep the night after a learning bout. That’s when plasticity actually occurs, and why it’s an essential step in the SDAP process.

- Enhance plasticity by practicing ten to thirty minutes of NSDR at any point after a learning bout. Done prior, as described in Protocol 1 of this chapter, it will increase your mental and physical vigor.

###### HOW IT WORKS:

During sleep, our brains rapidly replay what we tried to learn during the day, including what errors to avoid in the future. Brain imaging and electrophysiological recordings show that the very same neural �ring sequences that occurred during learning bouts occur again at that time ~~.~~ 182 If the patterns of brain activity in sleep are disrupted, we don’t learn as well. Sleep isn’t just a time for consolidation, it’s also when we build schemas—which are extractions of common themes of movement or ideas that let our brain store information in a more e�cient way. They serve as patterns that become part of our foundational understanding of how the world works.

Evidence points to REM sleep in the �rst night after a learning bout as being the most crucial for the learning consolidation process, a phenomenon known as the _night after learning effect_ , but depending on the skill you’re trying to master,

deep slow wave sleep may matter more ~~.~~ 183 I wouldn’t parse things that �nely. Rather, do your best to get adequate (for you) sleep every night, but especially in times of striving to master new information and skills. I de�ne adequate sleep in chapter 1, and give you lots of tools to use to achieve it. If you su�er a poor night’s sleep, however, don’t make things worse by fretting about the learning lost from it. Do NSDR the next morning, and get your sleep schedule back on track that night.

### Incorporate Micro Rests into Your Learning Bouts

###### WHAT TO DO:

- Pause now and then between repetitions as you practice a new motor or cognitive skill. These _waking micro rests_ have been shown to accelerate learning by increasing repetition density at the level of neural circuit activation.
  - Short breaks of five to thirty seconds during a learning bout in which you do nothing at all (meaning, no checking your phone!) can signi�cantly accelerate motor learning.

  - Short breaks of five to ten minutes during a learning bout focused on cognitive learning can do the same. These micro rests induce ten to twenty times accelerated replay of the neural circuit �ring pattern related to what you are trying to learn.

###### HOW IT WORKS:

We try to perform a new skill and we fail, and fail again, and get close, but fail again. We get a few nights’ adequate sleep, and when we come back for our next attempt, somehow we’ve improved.

The previous protocol explained how sleep reinforces neural circuit �ring patterns that allow our brains to integrate new skills. But recent studies show that a waking micro rest can increase consolidation on fast timescales too— meaning in just seconds to minutes, and even during the learning bout.

The observation that people learn faster if they pause from time to time between repetitions goes back to the late 1800s, when the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus measured his ability to learn new material.184 He saw that spaced repetitions led to faster and more stable learning than continuous repetition. That was self-experimentation, but many years later, in a study led by National Institutes of Health physiologist Marlene Bönstrup, twenty-seven participants were asked to practice several keyboard-based motor skills, tasks that were well established in the research of memory and learning ~~.~~ 185 Participants had to tap out a sequence of �ve items using their nondominant hand. They were given thirty-six tries to learn the sequence, with each attempt lasting ten seconds followed by ten seconds of rest. Performance was measured according to both speed and accuracy.

At �rst, Bönstrup and her colleagues examined the learning curve across all thirty-six attempts of a given sequence. They could see the performance improved rapidly, and then petered out at around the eleventh cycle. That’s a familiar pattern. We often get better at a new skill fast and then reach a ceiling when further improvements become harder.

But the researchers noticed something interesting. All along, they had been monitoring the participants’ brain waves. During very brief periods of rest between repetitions—lasting about ten seconds—the patterns of brain activity showed a unique signature. They tended to occur in regions connected to our ability to plan our movements. The researchers hypothesized that some form of additional rehearsal was occurring in their brains during the micro-rest periods, and it might be important for plasticity. That mapped well onto Ebbinghaus’s observation. A second study, carried out in 2020 by Ethan Buch and others, found that micro rests induce rapid plasticity and learning, most likely because the same neural circuits active during the attempt to perform the motor skill get replayed during the micro rest in between repetitions, but at about twenty-fold the speed and forward and backward ~~.~~ 186 In other words, waking micro rests increase repetition density. This _wakeful consolidation_ seems to allow you to integrate the new motor sequence with prior learned sequences. Of course, it’s during sleep when our brains really engrave the circuits carrying newly learned

information. Nonetheless micro rests of ten to thirty seconds during motor learning bouts, and �ve to ten minutes during cognitive learning bouts, have been shown to improve many di�erent types of skills ~~.~~ 187

You may be wondering what to do during the micro rests, and how often to take them. For a learning bout focused on motor learning, the key is to simply pause and not do another rep for �ve to ten seconds. A bit longer, say �fteen or seventeen or twenty seconds is not a problem, so don’t obsess about the exact duration. Just pause for a short time, and then continue. You can draw a bit or just sit there—which sounds boring and might make you feel lazy, but the data say you are learning faster. Yes, you can get up and walk around, use the bathroom, et cetera. Just stay o� your phone, web browser, or email…!

Introduce micro rests somewhat at random. How often you do them depends on the complexity and the duration of a repetition. Practicing serving a tennis ball is very di�erent, for instance, from practicing an entire song on the piano. I suggest you start the learning bout by doing continuous repetitions one after the other, and when you start to make errors, introduce a pause every third or �fth trial, then go back to continuous repetitions, and then pause after every error or every other or every third error. If you want, you could set a chime to go o� at random intervals. A website that o�ers that feature for free is www.random.org/clock-times and there is another great, no-cost website at www.microbreaks.co/timer.html that lets you set the parameters, including (1) learning bout duration, (2) duration of micro-break, and (3) the tone you want to hear, et cetera. It’s terri�c for both cognitive and motor skill learning. (Note: I have no a�liation to it but I use it.)

Waking micro rests are a great tool for accelerating learning and plasticity that are based in behavioral and neuroscience-backed data. I suggest trying them.

### Increase Retention of New Skills and Information with Mental Rehearsal

###### WHAT TO DO:

- Take one to five minutes to reflect on what you read or did during a learning bout at some point after the learning bout concludes. The key is to test yourself for what you do and do not remember, do or do not comprehend. That’s why it’s the �nal step of SDAP.
  - For cognitive skills and new information, this can be informal, done simply as a mental exercise, or more formal, such as by having a friend or ChatGPT test you for comprehension on the exact same material.

  - For motor skills, think about where you were challenged and made errors.

###### HOW IT WORKS:

All of learning is anti-forgetting.

On the one hand, that statement is another giant “DUH!” But through the lens of what we know about how humans learn and remember new information and skills, it’s a very important concept to integrate.

The human brain can’t remember all it senses and perceives. Even though neuromodulators can serve as a sort of highlighter pen for certain experiences, most information is forgotten. Neuroimaging studies have shown that for people who learn to juggle as adults, their brain circuits rewire to re�ect the speci�c skills of juggling but those changes are quickly lost if they don’t

practice ~~.~~ 188 Both memories and new skills extinguish quickly, in days to weeks, unless they are locked in by rehearsal. The exception to this is, of course, the information related to very emotionally charged events, for reasons partially discussed earlier in this chapter. When adrenaline is very high, a second memory pathway involving our amygdala and other limbic-associated structures opens up and we remember more “snapshots” of whatever took place while in the high arousal state ~~.~~ 189

Rehearsal in the form of self-testing turns out to be the best way to protect newly acquired skills and information against forgetting. A classic 2006 study from psychologists Henry Roediger and Je�rey Karpicke compared repeated reading of a passage of text with one-time reading of the text combined with later mental re�ection, and found that mental re�ection was far superior when it came to both retention and comprehension of the material ~~.~~ 190 That’s pretty wild if you think about it. People who spend less time with the actual material but attempt to review what they do and don’t remember, and what they do and don’t comprehend, can work with it more �exibly. That tells us that what we remember is not simply a matter of how much time we spend with information or in an experience, but that re�ection somehow reinforces and enhances the circuits carrying that information or experience.

This research has vast implications for educational settings, particularly for how best to study. We know that underlining and highlighting information only helps us remember it if we also later write down what was highlighted and underlined. It also means that testing—whether by our teacher or ourselves—is not just a form of evaluation to gauge our level of knowledge, it also represents a valuable “anti-forgetting” tool that helps us remember the information for months or years to come ~~.~~ 191

The takeaway is clear: Tests work. If you’re a teacher or coach, yes, this justi�es pop and scheduled quizzes. It may help to test on recently learned material in exercises that count toward a grade. And, yes, don’t tell the students that until after the quiz.

For those without a teacher or coach navigating SDAP, re�ect on what you learned, and most of all: self test! You can do so informally or formally. AI is a

great tool for this. Ask ChatGPT to quiz you on a given set of material as a teacher would. Or simply take a few minutes and test your level of recall or physical skill on your own. Try to �nd where your ability drops o�. It takes only a few minutes and is immensely valuable. You’ll learn faster and retain more of what you learn.

Thus far I’ve focused on protocols, and the science they’re based on, for bolstering key pillars of your health and performance: sleep, exercise, nutrition, stress management, light exposure, as well as focus, motivation, and learning. You’ll notice I did so mostly through the lens of biology, not psychology. Even when talking about mindsets or ways to generate a sense of urgency, the emphasis unabashedly has been on the biological underpinnings of what makes these protocols work. That re�ects my training and interests, but as I mentioned in the introduction it’s also an essential part of how these protocols work. They are customizable to your needs. When you know how a machine works—how the parts �t together—you come away knowing which aspects you can modify.

We, however, are _not_ machines. We think and feel, and hope and fear, and more. That needs attention too. The quality of our lives is strongly driven by our emotional lives, our relationships to others and to ourselves. After all, what good is it feeling vital and rested, focused and resilient, �t and capable, if we don’t also enjoy our time with others, and with ourselves? We just can’t overlook these aspects of life.

Scores of data now tell us the obvious: that social connection is vital to our health and longevity.1 Like all the other Old World primates, we have an immense need to care for and be cared for by others.2 Our nervous system evolved to crave and require these types of interactions we consciously or unconsciously register as safety ~~.~~ 3 Not just safety from harm, but also the sort of safety that makes us feel capable of seeking out challenges: healthy risk-taking in our work, new goals in our hobbies, going on adventures; all things that give us a sense that life, our life, matters.

Equally important but far less discussed is our relationship to ourselves. That’s an admittedly squishy term. What I mean is how we talk to ourselves, and how we think about ourselves—the decisions we make, the paths we choose. In fact, this chapter could have been called “Protocols for Thinking.” My goal here is not to get you to second-guess yourself. Quite the opposite. It’s about clearing

the clutter from your mind so you can think better. It’s about moving forward on the right path and not mindlessly slaving away on the wrong one.

What are thoughts anyway?

Marcus Aurelius famously said, “Our life is what our thoughts make it”4 and nearly identical statements were made by René Descartes,5 the Buddha ~~,~~ 6 Ralph Waldo Emerson ~~,~~ 7 William Shakespeare,8 and in the Bible ~~.~~ 9 Most people would agree their thoughts are a crucial feature of their experience of life but few ever stop to ask, “What are thoughts?” Most neuroscience textbooks don’t even attempt to answer that question. They include chapters on sensation, perception, emotions, behaviors, even memories and dreams, but not a single textbook that I am aware of provides a good explanation of what thoughts are. Fortunately, researchers are starting to �gure it out.

Jennifer Groh, PhD, neuroscientist at Duke University, researches how our brain maps, or _represents_ , to use the neuroscience term, the world around us.10 That makes her particularly well suited to answer the question “What are thoughts?” because thoughts are representations too. They are estimates, approximations, best guesses. She explained to me, “When we are thinking, we are running simulations with the sensory and motor infrastructure of our brain.” She gave me the following example, posed as a brief series of questions. If you want, you can answer them now as well.

Think of a cat.

What comes to mind �rst?

Chances are the partial or complete mental image of a cat, or maybe the sound of a cat. Something cattish.

Now ask yourself: What color is the cat?

What next comes to mind?

For me, it was a gray cat and very soon afterward, the smell of kitty litter, which I intensely dislike. Then a memory of the laundry room in the house where I grew up, which is where my sister’s cat Samantha often slept.

The point is that anything that we focus on—an image seen or imagined, a song, a memory, and so on—causes the sensory areas of our brain to become active. That means our visual areas, auditory areas, the areas involved in

processing touch, et cetera, all ramp up their levels of electrical activity. And while each of these areas has a di�erent name and a di�erent job in representing the world around us, they are all extensively interconnected too. They don’t work in isolation. They work as parts of what are called distributed networks. Which sensory area is activated �rst and which ones follow depends on what “seeds” the thought. In the above example it was the word _cat_ but think about the extremely soft fur of a chinchilla. That may set o� a thought that activates the touch area of your brain, and you might experience a simulation of touch, what neuroscientists call somatosensation. From there, the patterns of brain activity expand.

Regardless of where it starts, focusing on something—anything—causes your brain to call up memories, as well as any potential motor actions you might take in relation to it. In some, it also conjures up emotions related to that thing. This “simulation” aspect of human brain function is vitally important. Not just as a way to navigate our lives, but for how we eventually come to make sense of our di�erent life experiences. It is among our most valuable mental resources and a key feature of what sets us apart from the other species on earth.

As Groh explained, “Humans don’t hear or see any better than a macaque monkey. What we do have is more brain areas devoted to each of the same senses, which makes our brain capable of building up very elaborate simulations of what we perceive.” In other words, the more we focus on something the richer the simulation of that thing becomes. That valuable mental resource is adaptive. It’s what allows us to make predictions of “If A then B, and if B then maybe C” and so on. It’s what allows us to imagine solutions to certain problems, and to build tools and technologies to overcome them. It’s what gave us electricity, planes, the internet, smartphones, and so much more.

Our brains can only run a certain number of simulations at once. Groh described an experiment she does that illustrates this, and why. She stops one of her class lectures midway through and asks her students to try to think of a word totally unrelated to what they have been discussing. Sounds easy, right? Wrong. Eventually the students come up with a word, but it takes signi�cantly more time and e�ort than if she asked them to think of a word related to what they have been discussing. It’s as if thoughts are roads: The more time you spend

thinking about something, the farther you travel down that road. Sounds obvious, but is it true? Yes. Neuroimaging and direct recordings of brain electrical activity con�rm that as thought-triggered simulations get more elaborate, they outcompete other simulations.11 Neuroscientists call these _attractor states_ , which is when brain activity increases in a certain set of circuits and as it does, activity in other circuits diminishes.12

Incidentally, this phenomenon may be what led to the idea that humans only use a small percentage of our brain at any one time—which unfortunately made it seem like we were dumber than we could be if only we used more of our brains. Now that you understand a bit about how thoughts work, it should be obvious why that’s a silly idea. Who would want too many thoughts happening at once?!

Thought competition and attractor states are vital, in fact. Groh used a great example to explain why. Think about when you’re driving and you say to someone, “Hold that thought for a second, I need to change lanes.” You are re�exively limiting the amount of information coming in so you can switch simulations—from talking and listening, to driving and navigating. You are allocating resources to di�erent brain circuits.

So maybe you’re now asking, “What in the world does that mean for improving our relationship to ourselves?” Turns out: everything. Improving our relationship to ourselves is about being intentional with what thoughts we sow.

Gone unchecked, our thoughts grow, and grow, and grow. This can be a good or a bad thing for our mental and physical health and how we show up in the world.

It’s important you know that your thoughts occur downstream of your perceptions. It’s hard to overstate how strong this link really is. The way we see our lives, the way we narrate our lives and the events of the world at large to ourselves, shapes the thoughts we have. If you tell yourself that every time you try to do something new, you fail—well, your thoughts will re�ect that perception. This realization is the �rst step in having control over them. So yes, I’m saying you _can_ control your thoughts. Below I explain how. I promise none of what follows is about the power of positive thinking. I will not be guiding you

through a series of manifestations. The �rst protocol in this section is, of course, a science-supported tool.

The other protocols that follow are about resolving a tension that exists for many people, regardless of age or stage of life, which is the push-pull between “needing to perform outward roles in life” and “being true to oneself.” That is one of the most common challenges I hear from people and it can produce varying degrees of confusion, con�ict, and in some cases, crippling paralysis. I’ve often been asked by people forty and younger who are not already wholeheartedly committed to a career path, “What should I study, do, or be?” By contrast, people older than forty usually ask me about making meaning of their life.

With all the books and news articles and podcasts out there about �nding a sense of purpose, I started to wonder: How can science help us answer these questions? It turns out there is a way. In my opinion, it’s been best addressed by James Hollis, an eighty-six-year-old Jungian psychologist with more than �ve decades of clinical experience treating patients of all ages and backgrounds. He has helped them build their best life by taking speci�c steps daily. He’s not a life coach, mind you. He’s a credentialed therapist who has also authored twentytwo books on this subject. He was a guest on the _Huberman Lab_ podcast in 2024, and I personally have used the tools he described then every day since our conversation to great bene�t.13 They resolve the tension between “needing to perform outward roles in life” and “being true to oneself.” Hollis’s “Daily Protocols for Creating Your Best Life,” as I refer to them in this chapter, are something I wish I had heard long before that conversation. They help us make decisions aligned with our interests, and reduce a lot of second-guessing that can arise when we consider such actions. No matter your age or level of contentment with your life, I am certain these protocols will be of great bene�t for you too.

Finally, I include a protocol related to resolving inner con�icts that stem from unresolved pain. Formal trauma therapies are beyond the scope of this book and usually require working with a licensed practitioner, whether that’s done in talk therapy, eye movement desensitization and reprocessing (often just called EMDR), hypnosis, psychedelics, or other modality. But there is a heavily researched approach to self-healing that has been shown time and time again to

It also costs nothing. It only requires that you are willing to confront the thing that is weighing on you. I provide the speci�c and most e�ective protocol for that here.

In short, what follows will set you up for more success in all the protocols listed up until now—and for whatever else you decide to focus on and achieve in your life. It will improve your self-understanding in ways that unburden your mind.

###### **PERSONAL GROWTH PROTOCOL**

1

### Replace Mind Wandering with PresentTethered Awareness

###### WHAT TO DO:

- Throughout your day, periodically ask yourself if your thoughts are focused on the present. For example: “Are my thoughts focused on what I am doing and where I am, or are they related to the past or future?” Be honest in your response.

- If your thoughts are elsewhere, re-tether them to the present. Ask questions anchored in your current surroundings, such as these: “How cold or warm is it in this room? What does it smell like? How many people in line in front of me are on their phone?” That seemingly trivial line of inquiry returns your perceptions to the present because they can only be answered right here, and now.

###### HOW IT WORKS:

Most people would like to be happier. Among the many bene�ts, a better mood allows us to access more focus and creativity, enhances our rational assessment of information, and improves countless objective health metrics.14 On the �ip side, psychologist Jamil Zaki’s lab at Stanford has shown that a cynical mindset signi�cantly limits people’s problem-solving abilities, creativity, and physical health.15 Similar reductions in problem-solving abilities and creativity have been shown among people with low mood.16 Fortunately, there is now good,

actionable science on how to be happier _and_ how to avoid unhappiness. Both involve—you guessed it—controlling your thoughts. But not by suppressing bad thoughts, or replacing them with positive ones. Quite the opposite in fact. Let me explain.

The 2010s marked an interesting shift in the Western perspective on happiness, and life goals generally. The change was catalyzed in part by a prominent study by Nobel Prize–winning psychologist Daniel Kahneman showing that beyond a certain threshold income level, having more money does not increase happiness.17 (If you want to know, in 2010 that threshold amount was $75,000 annually—equal to about $110,000 today.) I confess, those results always gave me pause because let’s face it: Money may not buy happiness, but it sure can help bu�er against many common forms of stress, some obvious ones being housing, food, and healthcare. Turns out, there is a rarely mentioned aspect of the Kahneman study that found that more income did not increase daily happiness but it did improve people’s overall sense of life satisfaction. Nevertheless, the notion that money can’t buy happiness stuck around. I would argue one of the reasons for that is because it came at the same time as a rising interest in “mindfulness.” That interest was accompanied by the idea that being “present” to our daily experiences, a mindset long embraced in Eastern traditions, is vital to our well-being. Just as important as material wealth, if not 18 more so ~~.~~

The 2010s also brought a growing interest in the neural and psychological changes associated with mindfulness and also meditation, both of which are intended to help with being present. These practices are by no means new; they had existed in Eastern cultures for thousands of years, experienced �eeting popularity in the US in the 1970s, and then became trendy again. Now some �fteen to twenty years later, mindfulness is a familiar term, and meditation is a common practice. We also have a lot of data from lab studies and clinical trials showing that our level of “presence” is not just the outcome but a _cause_ of happiness, both in the short and long term.19 Okay, so we should “be present.” Got it. But the whole “be present” thing is another pretty squishy term. Even for scientists wishing to study our level of presence, de�ning it is no easy task.

To shift away from catchy phrases like “Be Here Now” (I love that phrase by the way) and run actual experiments, capture data, and suggest actionable tools on the basis of those data, scientists needed to create an operational de�nition of presence. They also needed to study it in the real world, which is not easy. Such studies were done by a few pioneering scientists to whom we owe a debt of gratitude, such as Richard Davidson, PhD, from the University of Wisconsin– Madison, and Matthew Killingsworth, PhD, and Dan Gilbert, PhD, from Harvard.

In 2010, Killingsworth and Gilbert published what is now considered a landmark study in _Science_ ~~.~~ 20 First, they created an app to collect real-time information on participants’ thoughts and feelings as they went about their day. The app sent question prompts to people at random moments during waking hours, such as, “How are you feeling right now?” and “What are you doing right now?” Every prompt also included the question “Are you thinking about something other than what you’re currently doing?” The researchers amassed a database of nearly 250,000 responses from around 5,000 people ages eighteen to eighty-eight from eighty-three di�erent countries.

Then they dove in. Killingsworth and Gilbert analyzed the responses from 2,250 adults, most from the US, to look for any connections between the speci�c activity they were doing, their level of presence with that activity, and their mood. Their results showed that for nearly 50 percent of our waking lives, our minds are elsewhere, thinking about times and places and things that have nothing to do with the present. But the researchers also showed the �rm connection between presence and happiness. When study participants were focused on speci�c activities and on their immediate physical surroundings, they were happier. Even when those speci�c activities were boring or unpleasant, that focus was still a bu�er against unhappiness. “A wandering mind is an unhappy mind,” the researchers wrote in a summary of their study.21

But perhaps the most interesting �nding from the study was the causative link between mind wandering and unhappiness. When it came to feeling happy, mind wandering was a much bigger deterrent than whatever they were doing. It didn’t even matter what they were thinking about. Being present during a less enjoyable activity seemed to make people happier than daydreaming about

pleasant things unrelated to the present activity. When we are focused on the present moment, we are happier. This is the power of present-tethered awareness.

While that study has some obvious limitations—for a start, it’s based on subjective self-reports—it is notable for a few reasons. First, it has a real-world context. It drew from large sample sizes. And it has readily implementable �ndings. It tells us that one of the most powerful determinants of our current and future levels of “happiness” is giving what we are doing as much of our undivided attention as we can. Notice I didn’t say all our attention. Fully focusing 100 percent of our mental attention can happen, and that can be great —we discussed ways to do just that in the previous chapter. But it appears that the mere act of periodically devoting a bit more of your attention to the present can be of meaningful bene�t to your level of happiness. The data tell us that striving to anchor your thoughts to the present forms the sca�olding of your well-being. So if you’d like to be happy, and you want your children to be happy, �nd ways to practice present-tethered awareness alone or together. The questions included in the protocol above are a good way to start.

Of course, feeling sad, disappointed, angry, et cetera, is sometimes warranted. It’s also healthy.22 Suppressing negative feelings has consistently been shown to lead to poorer mental and physical health outcomes ~~.~~ 23 The problem is when we get stuck in those low-mood states too long.

Studies that followed supported general �ndings from this landmark study but brought some important revisions too. There are bene�ts to letting your mind wander too. It also helps explain why people report getting some of their best insights while in the shower, while doing routine tasks such as washing dishes or mowing the lawn, while on walks or commuting, and so on. The takeaway is clear: Whenever you can, bring your thoughts back to what you are doing. Don’t chastise yourself for letting your mind wander but understand its negative impact on your mood. Use the simple recommendation above to re-tether your mind to the present.

If you tend to daydream, try to do so during activities that don’t require much focus. In today’s world, where the �rst seconds of waiting in line at the store, airport, or a doctor’s o�ce has us immediately reaching for our smartphone to text or scroll, a bit of good old-fashioned daydreaming is probably a better idea.

###### Getting Off Your Phone

Is browsing social media and the internet violating present-tethered awareness?

As that 2010 study discussed above indicates, people’s minds were already wandering about 50 percent of their waking hours before social media became such a prominent—arguably even _dominant_ —feature of modern life that it is now. Tech companies just �gured out how to get people to devote a signi�cant percentage of that time to scrolling on their social media platforms.

My view is that, in moderation, meaning about an hour or so per day, engaging on social media platforms can be great for learning, social interaction, and entertainment. The key is to not use social media to blunt your presenttethered awareness. We are starting to see the damage to mental and physical health that this can cause ~~.~~ 25 Put simply, scrolling can become just another form of mood-lowering mind wandering. The algorithms are strong. Their superpower is to get you to use them for as long as possible. Your superpower is your ability to consciously redirect your thoughts to speci�c activities and your immediate physical surroundings. That’s a skill worth developing. If the bene�ts of doing so for your mood and well-being are not incentive enough, perhaps the longevity bene�ts I’ll describe next will be.

One of the causes of aging is the shortening of our telomeres, small molecular structures that form protective caps on the ends of our chromosomes in each of our cells. In cell types that duplicate, such as our immune cells, as telomeres get

shorter, they stop dividing. At that point they become what are called _zombie cells_ , and they secrete in�ammatory molecules that damage nearby cells. Preclinical studies suggest that this zombie cell–induced damage may be a factor in aging and age-related illnesses such as cancer, dementia, and heart disease.26 Conversely, having cells with longer telomeres is a biomarker of youthful, healthy, and (for cell types that replicate) division-competent cells ~~.~~ 27

With that knowledge in hand, UCSF psychologist Elissa Epel and colleagues conducted a study where they measured the average telomere length of immune cells from women who scored either high, moderate, or low on measures of mind wandering ~~.~~ 28 She discovered that the women engaged in the greatest amount of task-irrelevant thought throughout the day had telomeres that were on average two hundred base pairs (a base pair is a functional unit of DNA) shorter than the telomeres of women with low amounts of mind wandering. We all lose about 50 telomere base pairs for each year of life, so the di�erence between being someone who is present and someone whose mind wanders was equivalent to about four years of additional aging. This was an especially remarkable �nding because the bene�ts appeared independent of variables known to impact longevity, such as body mass index and stress level. The takeaway: Make the e�ort to be present in your daily activities, tasks, and relationships. This doesn’t mean you have to be a Luddite. Texting a friend, sending a work email, or updating a family schedule on your phone can de�nitely be about the “here and now.” So is scrolling for education or entertainment. _The thing to be wary of is texting and scrolling or doing anything out of boredom or avoidance._ Ask yourself: “Am I numbing out or getting drawn in by things that I can’t actually have an impact on?” If you answer yes, that’s a good indicator that you are engaged in deleterious mind wandering. Retired Navy SEAL and two-time world-record-holding athlete Andy Stumpf talks about this in his book _Drownproof_ ~~.~~ 29 And he shared a tool that I have found immensely useful, even life-changing. Here it is: Take a sheet of paper and draw a line down the middle from top to bottom. On the left side, list all the things that concern you at that

moment. On the right side, list all the things you can actually control, and what you can do to directly impact your life that day, right then and there. Try it. You’ll be amazed at what you learn about your mental preoccupations and re�exes, and what it opens up in terms of your ability to better direct your mind and actions. Doing this exercise makes you keenly aware of what really matters to you. And it gives you a heightened sense of agency around those things. It places you in a great mental stance to lean into the important stu� in your life. It also makes time spent relaxing on the couch or doing nothing feel restorative again. It’s a simple tool, but a super valuable one. Yes, it’s a good idea to do it every few weeks or once a month, but it’s quick: �ve minutes at most. Do it.

###### Getting Out of Your Head

I am a fan of certain forms of structured introspection. I’m referring to journaling, therapy with a well-trained expert who o�ers useful points of action, or other deliberate, timed self-re�ection done within a speci�c framework. There are very good data to support those practices as tools for mental health.30 What none of us want, however, is to be stuck in our own heads and feeling anxious. Turns out, we don’t have to. We just need to understand a bit more neuroscience. And then apply that knowledge.

Your brain has cells that are grouped into circuits, which in turn are grouped into networks. Think of a network sort of like a setting for your brain: You have sleep networks, feeding networks, language networks, math networks, and on and on. And you have a network that turns on when you do nothing, aptly named the default mode network, or DMN. It was discovered to be active when people were getting their brains scanned, in between moments where they were asked to focus on certain tasks.31 That alone wasn’t terribly surprising. What was surprising was that the DMN is hyperactive in ruminators, people with cognitive impairments like Alzheimer’s disease, and in depressed patients ~~.~~ 32 More than a decade of studies now show that many antidepressants work in part by dampening activity in the DMN ~~.~~ 33 Guess what? So does dancing, exercising, socializing with friends, drawing… essentially anything that requires your attention. 34 That’s the key takeaway about the DMN. You can’t just “turn it

o�” or even reduce its activity unless you do something to activate a competing brain network, such as the salience network—a di�erent collection of circuits that, you guessed it, become active when you focus your attention on something external to you ~~.~~ 35

So while your DMN has important healthy functions, like simulating what other people are thinking or feeling, which is useful for some kinds of social interactions, to stop ruminating and to alleviate depressive states, you want to actively inhibit your DMN. Practicing present-tethered awareness is the way to do that too. If you are too much in your own head, feeling anxious or depressed, you would do well to focus outside yourself, literally on your surroundings. Better yet, engage in an activity that forces you to do that, such as exercising, reading a book, or listening to a podcast or music. If you feel your mind is still looping even while doing those things and that you can’t seem to turn o� that dominant inner narrative, try the exercise Andy Stumpf wrote about. Of course, clinical major depression deserves professional support. But for anyone seeking to be happier, more ful�lled, and more on track in life, learning to recognize what thoughts are, understanding how we can direct them, and then directing them to the present, especially toward the things in the present we can have a positive impact on… that’s the ticket to a great life.

A great outward life requires that we show up and perform well in roles at school and work, and in our relationships. That requires we handle our responsibilities, even when we don’t feel like it. It’s applicable in both good and hard times. It’s good, actionable science on how to be happier and how to avoid wasting valuable years of your life.

The key, as Hollis says, is to never expect your best self to emerge by default. Hollis has a simple motto he recites to himself every morning, and throughout the day. He recommends his patients write it down and carry it with them, and recite it to themselves every morning, and throughout the day too.

This protocol is named after his motto: “Shut Up. Suit Up. Show Up.” While that might sound harsh, it’s not what it seems. The motto is the inspiration for a collection of science-based tools that can help you build your best life. Let me explain.

###### Shut Up

It’s especially important to avoid whining and practice gratitude when you are feeling overwhelmed or down. I know many people are probably thinking, “So I’m supposed to suppress my feelings?” Hollis is a psychologist not a coach. He’s all about acknowledging feelings. But he also is aware of what it takes to build a life that brings a person lasting joy. So stay with me.

###### Suit Up

This means be prepared. Take the steps you can each day to arrive at your outward roles as best you are able. This sometimes looks like self-care: Get adequate sleep and don’t overbook yourself. It can also look like work: Finish your assignments, be on time, keep your belongings in order, schedule your kids’ activities, and so on. Homework doesn’t end when we �nish school.

Now before you tell me all that just sounds like Boomer diligence, consider this: Our inner narratives about our self-worth, and our self-esteem, are strongly impacted from ful�lling these outward roles.36 Now is that the whole picture? Of course not. There are many factors at play when it comes to how we talk and think and feel about ourselves. But this is a signi�cant fraction of it. Holding ourselves accountable to our chosen roles also leads us into a state of thankfulness for the opportunity to perform well in them. Hollis explained to me that this state is the most important aspect of the practice. We choose a role, we commit to it, we do well, and then we are lifted into gratitude. Giving our roles our best each day becomes an act of gratitude—the act of living our life becomes a devotional practice of being thankful. Sound corny? Perfect! Because it’s not about saying it. It’s about the actions associated with each of the sentences. Let’s get to it.

At �rst glance, you might think that “shut up” means stop complaining. But what Hollis is after here is replacing complaining with something more bene�cial. ###### Suit Up, Redefined

“Suit up” may sound somewhat, well, obvious: We all know to shower, get dressed for school or work, pack our lunch and perhaps the kids’ too, and get on with the day. But this isn’t about any of that. It’s about what neuroscientists call task switching.

Moving our attention from one chore or job or activity to another is fundamental to being e�ective in whatever outward roles we perform. Your own short task-switching ritual will make you more e�ective at moving from one task to the next, which has outsized positive bene�ts in all your outward roles.

###### Show Up, Redefined

This task-switching protocol can add bene�t to our cognitive, emotional, and physical capabilities.58 And yes, many of the things that you may already do— taking a few long exhale breaths as you return home at the end of the day, or

before getting into work mode when you arrive at the o�ce or into workout mode when you step inside the gym—are about this whole notion.

I’m guessing that when you �rst read Shut Up. Suit Up. Show Up., you probably weren’t thinking about gratitude practices, or about your basal ganglia, but what makes Hollis’s approach uniquely powerful is that it balances introspection with action. It’s neither coddling nor harsh. And it’s realistic to the demands of life we all have to meet, as well as the internal challenges most all of us feel at some point or another. We’re an oddly fortunate species. On the one hand we are born with unmatched cognitive capacity, as well as the ability, through neuroplasticity, to continually learn. No other creature alive has that and yet, because of those very gifts, we can get stuck in our own heads on big decisions before we make them or sometimes wake up one day to realize we took the wrong path after we did. Building your best life requires making Shut Up. Suit Up. Show Up. a daily practice, just as Hollis suggests. And to know, with con�dence, what those values and desires are, and that they are worthy of our time and attention. There’s a clear way to do that. Here’s how that is done:

###### Take time every day to update your internal maps.

The other piece of the puzzle is to make sure you know yourself well. Your fears, hopes, aspirations. This kind of self-knowledge is hard to come by. The combination of life’s demands and the ever-present noise of modern life can make it hard to simply know ourselves.

That’s where the second part of this protocol comes in. Is this necessary? Yes. People who excessively focus on excelling in outward roles often feel unful�lled

or they end up neglecting other important areas of life. Yet those who are excessively focused on self-knowledge and self-care—another admittedly squishy term—often put o� taking action that would allow their careers and relationships to thrive. There needs to be a balance.

The solution, Hollis explains, is to incorporate a second daily practice of exiting the stimulus-response mode that our outward roles—employee, parent, spouse, et cetera—require of us, giving us a chance to direct our attention inward instead. There are two sure�re ways to go about exiting the stimulus-response mode. First, engage in an activity unrelated to any ambitions or outward roles. Swiss psychiatrist Carl Jung believed that this process is a core aspect of human existence.59 Hollis’s writings and lectures, too, often focus on the importance of this process as a foundation for any other relationship we may have.

These insights might sound wishy-washy or even self-indulgent, but they are neither. Pausing from the constant need to respond to this or that stimulus gives us the chance to hear, then question, what we have internalized from others, and to hear, then acknowledge, what we know to be true for us, irrespective of what

others say. To not explore and continually seek to know our true selves in this way, Hollis explains, is to not live life fully. In his clinical experience, not periodically exiting the stimulus-response mode is what causes people to make choices that can seriously harm themselves or others in the long run.

A di�erent perspective on the bene�t of this protocol comes from psychologist Alfred Adler, who believed the need to spend time alone is crucial for us to avoid an _inferiority complex_ , a term he coined ~~.~~ 60 As Adler saw it, the feeling that we aren’t as good as other people is something that gets internalized as we grow up. Maybe someone made fun of us for a particular piece of clothing we wore, maybe a parent compared us to an older brother or sister… we all encounter things like this. They are part of life. The problem is that we tend to take them on board. When someone teases us for how we look, we may end up thinking we look bad. When someone expresses disappointment in a grade, we may end up thinking we’re not smart. You get the idea. The result is a whole lot of negative opinions about ourselves that we did not create but that we treat as our own thoughts. Adler saw self-encouragement as a powerful way out of this dynamic ~~.~~ 61

But how? What would impactful self-encouragement even look like if—as we discussed several times already in chapters 3 and 6—positive self-talk isn’t e�ective?

The answer is: Get yourself out of stimulus-response mode. Not forever. We have to ful�ll our roles after all. Just for brief periods of time, but daily. Take a few minutes alone without inputs from others or even your phone.

Spending time alone can help quiet negative voices we’ve internalized so that we can better hear our own inner voice. It’s a skill to learn to hear your own inner voice, and understand it. But it is one well worth cultivating.

This isn’t to suggest that we already have the answers to every challenge. Sometimes we need to ask for help, and encouragement, from others. Psychotherapy, for instance, can be extremely bene�cial. Data show that it can improve symptoms of psychological di�culties, that these improvements remain stable for years, and that these patients use less healthcare than the population at large after completing therapy.62

Still, for all these reasons, alone time tends to cause peaceful feelings, even for extroverts. Researchers from the Netherlands and the UK asked 178 people to keep a daily diary for twenty-one days in which they noted how much time they spent in solitude each day, regardless of the activity they were doing, among other re�ections.63 On average, days with more hours in solitude were lonelier for the participants. However, the researchers found that choice made the di�erence. People were happier being alone when that was what _they chose_ . And across the entire study group, days with more alone time were less stressful. People tended to feel more themselves and more free from external pressure on days when they had comparably more solitude.

Combining alone time with activities that aren’t part of the daily demands of life (work, errands, and such) adds to the bene�t, because these “extra” activities also tend to be good for our mental health. In September 2023, _Nature Medicine_ published a remarkable study by an international group of researchers in which they looked at data from �ve long-term studies conducted in sixteen countries enrolling more than 93,000 people ~~.~~ 64 This analysis found that having a hobby was tied to fewer depressive symptoms, greater happiness, and a greater sense of life satisfaction. The more time spent with these pursuits, the greater these bene�ts. This study focused on older adults, so one might wonder whether the bene�ts of a hobby are because they give people who’ve left the workforce something to do. But the percentage of retirees ranged from 56 percent to 99 percent among the studies included in the analysis, which means that some of the participants still held a job; the bene�ts cannot be explained by the notion that the hobby is simply replacing a career. Carving out time to pursue our personal interests is good for our health, whether we are still in the workforce or not.

We need time to get to know ourselves. Constantly reacting to external demands leaves no space for thoughts and feelings to surface into our full awareness. It can be tempting to think that who we are is what we do, who we know, where we live—that these are the ingredients of our identity. But when we exit the stimulus-response mode, we can tune in to questions, or even answers, that have been quietly brewing but not fully acknowledged. Hollis speaks about

these pauses as moments to “recollect,” as in re-collect ourselves. I would encourage you to try it.

If you �nd it hard to just… sit there in silence, then try a di�erent entry point. I often turn to drawing. There is no outside demand about what I draw or how I draw it. For you, it may be playing an instrument or gardening. “But those activities have to be done correctly, and I can’t introspect while doing them,” you might say. I get it. There is a format to many such activities, and there are often metrics by which to gauge your success at them. But that doesn’t matter. The key thing is that what you’re doing is not about occupying an outward role that others place on you; it’s about just being you.

It is easy to fall into the trap of thinking we don’t have time for these things. We do. There is always time, if not every day then at least a few times each week. I have an immensely demanding schedule and have for the last thirty or so years. I try to step away from my devices and stand or sit quietly for at least �ve minutes per day. Time with hobbies can be admittedly more sporadic, based on my work schedule, but I aim to spend at least an hour a week doing something completely unrelated to work or the routine demands of life.

By stepping away, you’ll develop a closer relationship with your own inner voice. Insights and ideas inevitably surface. Not always right away, but everyone I know who does this protocol has described a moment when something related to a thought they had during solo time days prior suddenly shot to the surface of their awareness. The idea was a clear “go,” a call to action. Or a clear “no go,” a call to halt certain patterns in their life going forward—either small or large. Somehow what was previously suppressed or hidden from their awareness became clear. And it changed their life for the better.

Stories like that are not uncommon, and become the norm when we take the time to regularly exit the stimulus-response mode. They speak to the incredible power of our unconscious mind, but also to our brain as a whole. Most of us have barely tapped into our capacity to link our outward roles and inner narratives, to balance comfort and striving, and to build a life that is uniquely ours. Hollis has said, “Ask large questions, you’ll live a large and interesting journey.”65 To be clear, I don’t think we are all meant to be artists, just as I don’t think we are all meant to be engineers. I know for certain, however, that we all

have an inner and an outward life, and that learning to understand and bridge the two is key to our sense of ful�llment. That, as I understand it, is what Hollis means when he talks about creating our best possible life.

###### COMMON QUESTIONS:

There is no time of day that is best for a gratitude practice. But it may work best if you decide on a speci�c time and place to do so, as a way to boost that conscious awareness and to help yourself stay committed.

Absolutely, as long as you are not turning the walk into a physically demanding exercise (see Exercise Protocol 1 for more about walking, and Exercise Protocol 3 for more about how to know when movement tips over into cardio work). And leave the phone at home. The point here is to give yourself some aimless time where the only variable worth measuring is your connection to yourself.

###### **PERSONAL GROWTH PROTOCOL**

3

### Resolve Inner Pain Points Through Expressive Writing

###### WHAT TO DO:

- Write for fifteen to twenty minutes about a challenging experience that affected your life. Do this exercise four times, once per day for four consecutive days. Keep in mind:
  - Do not write for longer than twenty minutes. Set a timer and stop even if you feel you could keep going.

  - Do not worry about the quality of your writing. No one will read this but you.

  - Write about what happened, what you felt at the time, what you feel now, and any lasting repercussions, however large or small, from this experience. Be honest about everything you felt, and everything you still feel.

###### HOW IT WORKS:

Not everyone has experienced trauma, but if you have, I encourage you to seek out the resources to address it. Whether it happened in childhood or adulthood, trauma and the shadow it leaves can be utterly destructive to our relationship to ourselves, and ultimately to those around us. It can lead to self- or outwardly destructive patterns.66

How do we know if we have trauma? Trauma has a speci�c de�nition. As Paul Conti, MD, an expert on trauma, explains, it’s a negative event, or set of events, that happens to you or that you observe that causes changes in your brain that signi�cantly reduce your functionality in other areas of life ~~.~~ 67 Symptoms of this can show up in our behavior as hypervigilance, dissociation, or both. It can manifest as sleep disruptions, irritability, or even OCD-like or ADHD-like symptoms ~~.~~ 68 It can also lead to substance abuse. The challenge is that all the symptoms of trauma can arise from other causes as well. There is no blood test or even brain image to rule in or rule out psychological trauma. Not yet anyway.

For now, the only way to know if you have trauma is to seek out a formal assessment from a quali�ed psychologist or psychiatrist, and as Dr. Conti pointed out, “Always engage the best possible self-care, in or out of treatment.” I pressed him a bit more on this.

“As people seek out help, is there anything they can do on their own?” I asked.

Turns out there is. And at �rst Dr. Conti’s answer surprised me. Until I looked at the peer-reviewed data on it. The protocol? Expressive writing. But not a journal entry, or a poem, or a novel. Rather, a very speci�c form of repetitive recall of a troubling event or events. This is the protocol I mentioned in chapter 6, as a way to undo the kind of rewiring that happens in their wake.

Social psychologist James Pennebaker developed the research for this protocol, beginning with a study in the 1980s ~~.~~ 69 He and a colleague asked fortysix participants, all university students, to write about traumatic life events once a day for four days consecutively. For comparison, another group followed the same writing schedule but focused only on trivial occurrences. The researchers collected health records and recorded moods and physical symptoms selfreported by the participants. People writing about traumatic events experienced a decline in mood and an increase in blood pressure immediately following the exercise. But over the following six months, they had fewer visits to the university health center.

Two years later, Pennebaker followed up with another study in which �fty students did the same exercise: Write about a traumatic experience or trivial

topic four days in a row ~~.~~ 70 This time, though, the researchers did not use selfreported data. Instead, alongside measuring blood pressure and heart rates before and after the writing exercise, the researchers also collected blood samples and tested blood for two markers of immune system function. Here, again, the exercise proved bene�cial to health and mood. Writing about trauma, the researchers concluded, boosted immune function, led to less physical illness, and reduced stress.

A deluge of work on journaling about di�cult experiences followed. More than 1,400 papers on expressive writing are now part of the scienti�c literature, with interest increasing in the forty years since Pennebaker’s �rst studies ~~.~~ 71 A 2004 meta-analysis of nine papers con�rmed the improvements in health tied to this type of expressive writing ~~.~~ 72 Among the groups for which this approach has shown a bene�t are adolescents, people undergoing cancer treatment, caregivers, people su�ering from post-traumatic stress disorder, people experiencing depression, along with many others. Expressive writing isn’t a cure. But decades of data provide undeniable evidence that it helps with mental health—and physical health.

Why? What is going on under the surface that makes this simple act work? The mechanisms behind this are multiple, but studies suggest that the most powerful lies in how this type of writing a�ects the prefrontal cortex. Creating cohesive narratives that are honest—that is, truthful, even when the experience is painful to recount—appears to stimulate this region of the brain in a way that bene�ts us both psychologically and physically.

Let’s zero in on the “honest” part of the equation. A study from 2017 shows the hardwiring of this trait to the prefrontal cortex. Researchers from the University of Zurich, the University of Chicago, and Harvard University gave the 145 study participants a cash reward every time they won a die-rolling game ~~.~~ 73 Only the person who threw the die knew their own results. The test was rigged in a way that put the chances of winning any round at 50 percent.

Here’s where the experiment gets interesting: During the challenge, the researchers applied transcranial stimulation (a noninvasive application of a weak electric current to the scalp) to the prefrontal cortex of half the participants.

Speci�cally, this electric current reached the dorsolateral region of the prefrontal cortex, an area activated when we are choosing whether or not to be honest. The group with this stimulation reported winning 58 percent of their rolls, which meant they had lied approximately 15 percent of the time. The group without this stimulation reported winning 68 percent of the time, which meant they had lied about their rolls about 37 percent of the time. The full study included more tests to gain insight into what exactly was going on here. The researchers concluded that this brain region regulates honesty speci�cally when lying would bene�t us.

The amygdala, by contrast, is connected to stress, fear, and anxiety. People under duress tend to have heightened activity in this part of the brain.74 Activation of the amygdala triggers the release of adrenaline and cortisol,75 which are crucial for responding to challenges and processing the memory of them. That helps when we’re faced with similar challenges in the future. But the overabundance of these chemicals appears to a�ect the immune system, decreasing our ability to mount an immune response over time ~~.~~ 76

The speci�c journaling exercise pioneered by Pennebaker likely works because it avoids activating the amygdala and instead connects to the prefrontal cortex. An added bene�t is that any time spent with tasks that deliberately engage the prefrontal cortex may improve brain plasticity, which has a long-term bene�t on cognitive function (for more on this link, turn back to chapter 6).77

This type of journaling is not necessarily comfortable. It asks us to revisit the most di�cult experiences in our lives—four times. But the point of this exercise is not to feel good in the short term. The point is to create a better relationship with our past, with our emotions about the past, and with ourselves. And remember, this isn’t about moving through current con�icts or other di�culties but rather about moving past old wounds that hold us back.

As for doing the writing exercise four times, for four days in a row, the reason is simple. That time frame allows us greater depth of re�ection. It takes time to process old wounds, partly because they are just that—wounds. Sticking with this exercise for four days gives you the chance to see how you felt about it then and how you feel about it now, but without that internal dialogue becoming an

open-ended rumination, which ends up occupying even more mental real estate. The idea here is to deal with those past pains in a way that lets you make peace with them, and then move forward. Four days is a low commitment. And Pennebaker himself has given this advice: If it doesn’t work for you, then stop doing it.78

###### COMMON QUESTIONS:

No. There is nothing about the mechanisms behind expressive writing that draws on physiological changes associated with day and night. Do this protocol at whatever time of day you’re able to set aside the time, about �fteen to twenty minutes, plus perhaps a few minutes to recover before moving to the next part of your day.

This exercise is not designed to resolve emotional pain entirely. It has physical and psychological health bene�ts, but it is not a cure. Therapy or other interventions are often needed in order to work through emotional pain so that it no longer a�ects us negatively. Meditation, EMDR, hypnosis, exercise, and other techniques are all widely available. I cannot say what approach will work for you but if you are su�ering from emotional pain, then do not hesitate to seek professional help.
