###### **PERSONAL GROWTH PROTOCOL**

4

### Reframe Loss to Effectively Move Through Grief

###### WHAT TO DO:

- Understand grief as a lack of reward. Over time, your brain has learned to predict certain events, like our expectation of someone’s voice or smell. It is a process that draws on our expectation of a “reward” that is no longer there.

- Spend ten to thirty minutes a day to deeply feel your attachment to the person, animal, or thing you are grieving. Do not try to reduce the intensity of your reaction to this attachment. Experience it fully.

- Avoid what-if thoughts. Try not to dwell on how else a situation might have gone.

###### HOW IT WORKS:

Losing people, animals, and things is part of life. It’s healthy and normal to experience grief in the wake of those events, provided it eventually wanes. What’s “eventually”? That depends. The loss of a parent or sibling is devastating. The loss of a keepsake can be, too, but in a very di�erent way. These are obviously not the same. But no matter who or what we lose, grief has some hallmark features because in every case it is a fracture in our reward-prediction brain circuitry. What’s more, it requires our brain to remap; these circuits, which once had us expecting someone we love to walk in the room, are still there, even if that someone is no longer there. We must reorganize our awareness

of what’s now in our proximity and come to learn what actions related to the person or thing lost are no longer, well, actionable.

The purpose of this protocol is not to intellectualize, avoid, nor exacerbate grief. It’s to ensure you don’t get stuck in what is called maladaptive grief, also called complicated or prolonged grief disorder, in which grief interferes with life long after the loss initially occurred, which can be extremely detrimental to your physical and mental health.79

I want to note too that this protocol should not replace tools and insights derived from extensive studies of bereavement, like cognitive behavioral therapy for prolonged grief ~~,~~ 80 which call for being wary about heavy drinking in the year or two immediately following a death,81 and for doing things that keep you in the �ow of life like still holding dinner plans and getting exercise ~~.~~ 82 Rather, it o�ers an understanding about grief, based in neuroscience, that may help you cope with these strong and di�cult feelings that come in after loss.

The �rst component of this framework requires a shift in thinking: Consider grief not as a state of sadness but rather as a state of longing. Brain-imaging studies have found that grief activates regions and circuitries that are involved with motivation and craving. A study led by neuroscientist and grief researcher Mary-Frances O’Connor, at UCLA, proved just that. O’Connor and her team imaged the brains of twenty-three women who were actively experiencing grief, eleven of whom were experiencing a state referred to as prolonged or complicated grief,83 generally de�ned as intense, debilitating, and unrelieved grief lasting more than a year. The women viewed photographs of the deceased and words related to their death as brain images were taken using functional magnetic resonance imaging.

Brain images of the women with complicated grief showed activity in pathways connected to motivation and reward during moments when the women reported feelings of yearning. These neural circuitries lead to the release of chemicals that make us feel good, like dopamine, serotonin, and oxytocin, keeping us motivated to obtain things that are good for us, like food and social connections. Speci�cally, the images showed activation of the nucleus accumbens, which releases dopamine during social interactions.84 This (at the

time) surprising observation led the researchers to hypothesize that grief is akin to searching for a reward that never arrives. We stay motivated to keep �nding it, but we don’t—and can’t. That makes sense to anyone who has experienced grief but until O’Connor’s work, neuroscientists were unaware that grief was tied to reward anticipation circuits in the brain.

We all experience loss. This is a lesser example than the one described above, but simply for example: Anyone who’s lost a large bill knows what it’s like to look in their wallet and not �nd it. You can tell yourself it’s just money, and you will get over it, but the loss of it brings the sudden understanding that whatever it made possible is now gone. Translate that to more emotional losses, such as a loved one or a friend or a pet. Suddenly our neural circuitry around that attachment is no longer actionable. The pathways that used to �re are still there, but they aren’t useful anymore. What is possible has changed. The circuit of anticipation and action resolution remains open. And that’s painful.

But motivation circuitries aren’t the only ones at play in this state of longing. Our brains contain cells dedicated to mapping the world we move through— think of it like a sort of mental map of where things are.85 Likewise, we also map our relationships, keeping track of the ties that connect us, albeit with di�erent brain cells.

Studies have found some overlap among neurons we use to orient ourselves in space and time and those we use to understand our relationships to other people.86 Researchers at Dartmouth College found that physical distance, proximity in time, and social closeness activate the same region of the brain, namely the inferior parietal lobe.87 The circuitries that store information about the distance from your bed to the bathroom, from your house to the supermarket, and from your town to Paris overlap with circuitries that store information about how close another person is to you socially.

Rewiring the neural circuitries that orient us with regard to the people in our lives takes time. We experience this physically often: If you’ve ever rearranged the furniture in your living room, for example, you know that it can take time to remember that the couch isn’t where it used to be. Grieving includes a similar reorientation but, of course, with heightened emotionality. We have to get used

to our loved one not being where we always found them—arriving home from work at 6:00 p.m., at the other end of the phone, across from us at the dinner table. We no longer experience the rush of chemicals we once did when that happened, what our brain registered as a reward. Grief exists where these circuitries contradict with reality, what O’Connor refers to as the “Gone-ButAlso-Everlasting” theory of grief ~~.~~ 88 It takes time for our brains to update. Thus grief is not only a disruption to our circuitries connected to motivation and reward, but also a di�cult learning process.

Avoidance makes this learning process even harder because it prevents us from incorporating new information into the map ~~.~~ 89 If we are refusing to face reality, then our brains can’t integrate it. As O’Connor has written, “Learning requires experience, and avoidance of things that remind the bereaved of the loved one’s death or absence will prevent accommodation of the information.”90

Instead, allowing ourselves to really feel our attachment to a person we’ve lost, a pet who’s died, or even a missing object that held sentimental value, without denying what happened, gives our brains a chance to decouple the object of our love from our current environment and our brain’s expectation of being able to interact with the person (or pet) that was lost. This decoupling— accepting a death while also savoring the memories and the essence (meaning our internal representation of the person themselves)—allows us to hold on to these important feelings without triggering a prediction that, say, the person will be waiting for us in the kitchen when we arrive home from work. Taking time to feel this attachment allows our brains to consolidate new memories and create maps, or expectations, about our lives.

Some researchers suggest what they call grief rituals as a way to “be” with a deceased loved one ~~.~~ 91 A person might light a candle, spend time with a photograph, or write a letter to the person, for example. Visiting a grave can be understood as a grief ritual. These ceremonial acts allow us to experience feelings of loss in a way that helps us begin to separate the person (or other object of our grief) from our new reality.

Finally, a word about counterfactual thinking that sometimes arises during the grief process, those “what-if” thoughts that have us imagining a di�erent

outcome if only we’d come home earlier, taken a di�erent route, said a kind word, or spent more time with them. A psychologist friend of mine once told me “if only” are the two most destructive words we can think, say, or write. Had I known that long ago, I would have saved myself a lot of pain, and had I known the modern neuroscience of grief, I would have understood that pain I felt (and sometimes still feel) is one of yearning, a natural re�ex to act—call, write, see that person—that is impossible to carry out.

It’s a mistake to wonder why we still aren’t over that pain, to suppress it. But the biggest mistake is to ruminate in “if only.” That type of thinking inhibits the grief process. It’s a lie about an alternate reality that truly blocks recovery. In one study, researchers examined links between counterfactual thoughts and symptoms stemming from prolonged grief and depression among �fty-nine people su�ering a recent loss.92 They found a strong correlation. People who engaged in what-if thinking experienced a longer period of grieving and symptoms of depression.

Besides, grief is hard enough without the guilt. Psychology, philosophy, religion—all these disciplines have considered grief, tried to help us understand why we experience it and how to live with it. The protocol above is one of neuroscience’s o�erings. Understand that grief is like a craving for a reward that is no longer coming. Make space to feel the deep attachment, whether through small rituals or just �nding moments in your day to pause and fully experience your feelings. This time will allow your brain circuitries to rewire, creating memories along with new mental maps. Finally, resist engaging in counterfactual thinking, which can prolong su�ering, trigger feelings of guilt, and exacerbate any depressive symptoms arising during this period.

###### COMMON QUESTIONS

Psychologists tend to consider prolonged grief to be grief that is debilitating and lasts more than a year. With prolonged grief, people feel depressed and hopeless, often stop engaging socially, and may have little appetite.

Not all grief is like this, but it’s hard to put a time frame on when any grief should end, since the process is so personal. It’s more important to understand what healthy grieving is, rather than putting a time frame on the process. Allow yourself the time and space to be with your deep feelings of attachment and closeness and let the process unfold

What I can say, though, is that one day, you might be walking along and remember someone you lost, and you might experience that person—not just the memory of them, but _them_ —as a completely positive presence that somehow (and I don’t have any science to explain this) is fully integrated into who and where you are now, right at that moment. Meaning: You know they are gone, and yet they are still very present. The remapping has occurred. That’s happened in my life many times over. To me, that is the end stage of the grief process, one that fortunately never subsides. It just takes some time to get there.

## Before You Turn the Last Page

Although this is the end of the book, I hope you see it as a beginning—the start of a new direction for your health that is rooted in a deeper understanding of the incredible thing that is the human brain and body, and how each and every one of us can improve our mental and physical health and learn new things that rewire our nervous system. As I mentioned in the introduction, each of our lives is its own kind of laboratory. There is no question that there are hardwired aspects of the human brain and body, common to us all, and thank goodness for those aspects. They are much of what the protocols in this book are based on, and why they work.

But we should all also acknowledge our individuality. So whether you are working on improving your sleep or stress control, changing your exercise regimen or nutrition to get leaner, stronger, more mobile, or all the above, it’s important that you honor the universal aspects of human biology but also feel free to make adjustments to suit your needs. The right way to do that—the scienti�c approach that is—is to become a systematic observer of you. Record your results. Then raise hypotheses, ask questions, and make changes one at a time to customize the protocols to, again, suit your needs. For reasons stated at the outset, I included a lot of science in this book. Even if you don’t remember each and every mechanism, what you do recall, even vaguely, will a�ord you a greater sense of control over your health. My not-so-hidden wish is that you have also come to appreciate, perhaps even marvel in (as I do), the beauty and utility of biology. Together your body and brain are a miracle of astonishing precision and possibilities. They are to be honored and explored for your well-being and so you can better serve others with more vigor, joy, and meaning along the way.

Thank you for embarking on this learning journey with me and for taking your health and well-being seriously.

And, as always, thank you for your interest in science.

## About the Author

Andrew D. Huberman, PhD, is a neuroscientist and tenured professor in the departments of neurobiology and ophthalmology and, by courtesy, psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Stanford School of Medicine. He has made numerous signi�cant contributions to the �elds of brain development, brain function, and neural plasticity. His laboratory at Stanford School of Medicine has published work in top journals such as _Nature, Science_ , and _Cell_ and in top media outlets like the BBC, _Time, Scientific American_ , and Discover.
